L21: ## I. Executive Summary
L22: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L23: Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) proposed for the prevention of heterotopic ossification in adults and children aged 8 years and older for females and 10 years and older for males with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. This new drug application (NDA) received a Complete Response action letter on December 23, 2022. The Applicant's response to the action letter was reviewed by the multidisciplinary review team and an Advisory Committee meeting was held on June 28, 2023. All disciplines recommend approval with a revised indication of treatment to reduce the volume of new heterotopic ossification in adults and children aged 8 years and older for females and 10 years and older for males with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. Palovarotene is the first pharmacologic therapy that is being approved for the treatment of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva.
L24: The Applicant submitted one adequate and well-controlled trial and confirmatory evidence providing substantial evidence of effectiveness for the approved indication. The available safety data show that the risks of palovarotene are consistent with the known effects of the drug class and can be mitigated through product labeling which includes a boxed warning for teratogenicity and premature epiphyseal closure. A postmarketing observational registry study will be conducted to obtain further information on the incidence of flare-ups, premature epiphyseal closure, and fractures. The overall benefit-risk is favorable as described in the Benefit-Risk Framework below. For detailed information supporting the basis for this approval, please refer to the detailed reviews included in this Integrated Assessment document and the Product Quality Review.
L25: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L26: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L27: Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework
L28: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare, severely disabling disease caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the activin A type I receptor ACVR1 (ALK2) which renders ALK2 constitutively active to bone morphogenetic protein ligands, drives ectopic chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, and leads to heterotrophic ossification (HO) in connective tissue, joints, and muscle.
Approximately 800 confirmed cases of FOP have been reported globally. Patients with FOP develop extraskeletal bone formation in muscles, tendons and ligaments, known as HO, beginning in early childhood. HO is episodic, with some events starting with soft tissue inflammation (flare-up). The accumulation of extraskeletal bone is cumulative and irreversible, causing restriction of movement, deformities, and severe disability. Complications include chest wall deformity (thoracic insufficiency syndrome), ankyloses of the temporomandibular joints resulting in severe tooth decay and malnutrition, and localized skin breakdown. Most patients require mobility assistance by their 20's due to HO around the hips. Survival is shortened (median 56 years), most often by cardio-respiratory failure and pneumonia. There are currently no approved therapies for the treatment of FOP, thus patients face a high unmet medical need to control their disease.
Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation indirectly via dampening bone morphogenetic protein signaling. This is thought to lead to blockade of chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation.
FOP is a rare and serious debilitating condition caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the ALK2 receptor that manifests starting in early childhood. Patients with FOP face a high unmet medical need, as no therapies have been shown to treat or slow progression of FOP, specifically the formation of HO and the resulting morbidity associated with chronic HO accumulation.
Palovarotene is a retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation and is thus being developed for the treatment of FOP.
L29: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current treatment options	
There are currently no approved treatments for patients with FOP. Current conventional therapy is used to provide symptom relief by decreasing inflammation and chronic pain. Attempts at surgical excision of lesions usually leads to reactivation of disease and new HO. Symptomatic treatment with high dose steroids is often used to treat symptom “flares,” however, short term burst steroid therapy has not shown benefit in reducing overall HO burden or slowing disease progression. There are currently no approved therapies for the treatment of FOP.
FOP is a rare disease with no approved therapies, thus only supportive care can be used to decrease pain and inflammation.

Benefit	
Two studies were conducted in support of palovarotene in the treatment of FOP: Study 201 which was extended as Study 202 which had multiple parts; and Study 301 which utilized the natural history study as an external control.
The proposed dosing regimen includes chronic daily treatment (5 mg), with higher dose treatment (20 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks, with extension if needed, referred to as “20/10 mg”) during symptomatic “flare-up” episodes of FOP (all proposed doses are adjusted based on body weight in skeletally immature patients under 18 years of age). This dosing regimen was used in Study 301 and in Part C of Study 202 (202C).
The primary endpoint for all studies is new heterotopic ossification as determined by radiologic methods. Earlier studies (Study 201/202A/202B) evaluated the incidence of new HO at the flare-up sites only. However, data from the natural history study revealed that HO frequently occurred outside of flare-ups and the primary endpoint for studies 202C and 301 was changed to annualized change in new HO volume as assessed by whole body CT. This endpoint is clinically meaningful because patients with FOP are known to have progressive accumulation of heterotopic ossification. Based on data from the natural history study, there is a correlation between total body HO volume with increasing Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale for FOP (CAJIS) score which indicates increasing restrictions on movement and joint range of motion.
Overall, the Agency has concluded that the Applicant demonstrated substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene to reduce new volume HO in pediatric and adult patients with FOP, but has not provided substantial evidence to support an indication for the prevention of HO in patients with FOP. Further, efficacy of palovarotene treatment in patients with FOP appears to be present only when chronic daily dosing is combined with flare-based dosing, when needed, for flare-up episodes.
Substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene in the treatment of FOP was provided by data from the phase 3 Study 301, using the NHS as an external control, and by supportive efficacy data, primarily from Study 202C, which used the same dosing regimen and protocol design as Study 301, and showed similar trends in reduction in HO volume in palovarotene-treated patients compared to untreated patients in the NHS. Additional confirmatory evidence of effectiveness was provided by comparisons of HO volumes during ‘pre-pause’ (i.e., active treatment) periods, dose interruption periods, and ‘post-pause’ periods (i.e., after dosing was resumed), which showed similar trends of reductions in HO volume during treatment with palovarotene compared to periods when dosing was stopped. Finally, mechanistic evidence from nonclinical studies in a FOP mouse model provide strong support for the mechanism of action of
L30: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Demonstration of the effectiveness of palovarotene comes from Study 301 using the linear mixed effects model where the mean annualized new HO volume was 9.4 cm3/year in subjects receiving palovarotene (study 301) compared with 20.3 cm3/year in untreated subjects from the NHS with a treatment difference of 10.9 cm3/year (95% CI: -21.2, -0.6). Confirmatory evidence of effectiveness comes from post hoc analyses of palovarotene-treated subjects in study 202C compared to untreated subjects from the NHS. Using the matched propensity score analysis, the mean annualized new HO volume was 16.1 cm3/year in subjects receiving palovarotene (study 202C) compared with 28.4 cm3/year in untreated subjects from the NHS with a treatment difference of 12.3 cm3/year.
The most concerning weakness of the submitted data include the reliance post hoc analyses and use of an external control group.
Post hoc analyses are generally considered hypotheses generating only and not appropriate for providing substantial evidence of effectiveness. However, in this case, the Agency acknowledged that the prespecified primary analysis for Study 301 was inherently biased against palovarotene. Therefore, the review team considered that it was reasonable to look at alternative, more appropriate analyses. The analysis chosen was the primary analysis for the protocol prior to the applicant's amendments. Various post hoc analyses performed by the review team demonstrated a consistency of results across the analyses performed that supported a conclusion of effectiveness.
Data from Study 301 and the NHS support the conclusion that chronic daily dosing (i.e., palovarotene 5 mg daily), in addition to flare-based dosing, is needed to achieve benefit. Specifically, these data demonstrate that subjects who reported no flare-ups developed relatively small quantities of new whole body HO, either with or without chronic daily treatment. By comparison, subjects who experienced flare-ups generally developed large quantities of new whole-body HO without chronic daily therapy and derived greater benefit from palovarotene (i.e., reduced volume of new HO, both at and away from flare-up sites). Therefore, both chronic daily and flare-up dosing
palovarotene to inhibit overactivation of the ALK2 receptor and thereby reduce HO volumes.
Despite the limitations of these data overall (as discussed above and in additional detail below), the Agency has ultimately concluded that the potential benefits of palovarotene for reducing HO volume in patients with FOP outweigh the known and potential risks associated with this drug, particularly given the progressive and debilitating nature of FOP and the unmet medical need in the FOP patient population.

However, these findings rely on an unverifiable assumption that no other unmeasured confounding factors mainly related to the use of an external control group could have substantially impacted the study results. When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. Compared to Study 301, NHS subjects were older and had more severe disease severity at baseline. The review team performed various analyses to assess the impact of baseline imbalances in selected covariates. These analyses suggested that the observed difference in the primary outcome in treated and untreated subjects was unlikely due to any systematic difference in the measured baseline factors that are deemed clinically important. Some NHS subjects were enrolled into Study 301 or other intervention studies after some period of observation in the NHS. The possibility of subject selection bias could not be ruled out. However, sensitivity analyses conducted by the applicant and the review team suggested that it is unlikely that the potential selection bias drove the conclusion of a treatment effect.
Treatment with palovarotene showed an effect in decreasing the volume of new heterotopic ossification in patients with FOP. The reduction in HO volume provides a clinically meaningful benefit to patients because of the irreversible, progressive nature of the disease. It is recognized that progressive accumulation of HO over time is associated with worsening mobility. Therefore treatment with palovarotene which leads to small changes in HO volume in short term trials, is expected to slow the progression of the disease with the potential to preserve joint range of motion and movement for longer periods of time.
L32: Risk and risk management	
Safety risks associated with palovarotene include those directly associated with the retinoid drug class of medications, as well as risks seen specifically in patients with FOP. Boxed Warnings and Warnings and Precautions contained in the retinoid class product labels include teratogenicity, psychiatric disorders, pseudotumor cerebri, serious skin reactions, pancreatitis, lipid abnormalities (hypertriglyceridemia), hearing impairment, hepatotoxicity, inflammatory bowel disease, skeletal abnormalities (including decreased bone mineral density, hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure), and vision impairment.
Regarding the risk of premature epiphyseal closure (PPC) seen with the retinoid class, treatment with palovarotene caused PPC in subjects with open growth plates despite lower, weight-based dosing in younger patients. Potentially, this could result in significant adverse effects on growth, especially in younger age groups. The Applicant proposed an indication that would allow most patients with at least 80% skeletal maturity (bone age 8 years in girls and 10 years in boys) to receive palovarotene for the prevention of HO despite the risk of PPC, given the severity of the disease.
Palovarotene is a known teratogen as a member of the retinoid class; however, there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP, and consensus guidelines urge serious consideration before women with FOP attempt pregnancy given that pregnancy is extremely high risk. As a precaution, clinical studies of palovarotene have included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements, and to date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. The Applicant proposed a Boxed Warning in labeling to mitigate this risk.
Regarding effects on bone mineral content, bone density and fractures, results of a biomechanical CT and vertebral fracture analysis suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD, and a higher risk of new onset morphometric vertebral fractures. These effects are consistent with some data involving other retinoids and are consistent with the BMD findings by DXA in osteochondroma subjects. However, the data do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post
Palovarotene is associated with multiple significant risks related to its mechanism of action as a retinoid derivative (e.g., teratogenicity, premature epiphyseal closure, etc.), as well as specific risks associated with its use in patients with FOP (e.g., potential increase in incidence of “flares”).
The Applicant proposed enhanced labeling to communicate the risks of teratogenicity and PPC in a Boxed Warning, Warning and Precaution, and contraindication of pregnancy, along with educational materials for prescribers, pharmacists, patients and their caregivers.
To mitigate the risk of PPC associated with palovarotene use in growing children, the Applicant proposed a lower, weight-based dosing regimen for pediatric subjects and to limit treatment to pediatric patients who have achieved at least 80% of their final adult height, which is approximately >8 years of age in girls and >10 years in boys.
The potential risk of increase in disease “flares” with flare-based treatment needs to be further investigated in the postmarket setting to better clarify this potential risk.
A PMR to assess long term safety of palovarotene in pediatric and adult patients enrolled into an observational safety study will be implemented to further assess the risk of HO flares and other risks associated with palovarotene, including PPC, bone fractures, and any pregnancy data available. This will be a long-term post marketing observational safety study in at least 100 patients with FOP, 50% of whom are pediatric patients and 2/3 of whom are treated with palovarotene, will be required in the form of a PMR.

hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures and differing amounts of follow-up data between the nonrandomized populations of Study 301 and the NHS.
There is an unresolved concern that palovarotene could increase the incidence of HO flare-up episodes in patients with FOP. Flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in Study 301 compared to untreated subjects in the NHS and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month), and within Study 301, new flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Most of the new flare-ups occurred at sites distant from the initial site. Similarly, data from Studies 201/202 showed higher rates of new flare-ups during flare-up dosing with palovarotene 10/5 mg or 20/10 mg (0.18 to 0.29/month) in comparison to placebo or NHS untreated subjects (0.11 to 0.12/month), or chronic 5 mg dosing (0.10/month). However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS, so the validity of these findings remains unclear. Additional postmarketing data will be necessary to better determine the potential for palovarotene treatment to worsen HO formation and thereby worsen disease severity.
L34: Abbreviations: ACVR1, activin A type I receptor; ALK2, activin receptor-like kinase 2; BMC, bone marrow concentrate; BMD, bone mineral density; CAJIS, cumulative analogue joint involvement scale; CT, computed tomography; DXA, dual x-ray absorptiometry; FDA, Food and Drug Administration; FOP, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressive; FOP-PFQ, FOP physical function questionnaire; HO, heterotrophic ossification; NDA, new drug application; NHS, natural history study; PPC, premature epiphyseal closure; PMR, post marketing requirements; PROMIS, patient reported outcomes measurement information system; R206H, arginine 206 to histidine; RAR, retinoic acid receptor; RAR\gamma, retinoic acid receptor gamma; ROM, range of motion
L35: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L36: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is a rare and severely disabling disease caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the activin A type I receptor ACVR1 (ALK2), which renders ALK2 constitutively active to bone morphogenetic protein ligands, drives ectopic chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, and leads to HO in connective tissue, joints, and muscle.
L37: Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable RAR\gamma selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation indirectly by dampening bone morphogenetic protein signaling, leading to blockade of chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation in animal models.
L38: Approximately 800 confirmed cases of FOP have been reported globally. Patients with FOP develop extraskeletal bone formation in muscles, tendons, and ligaments known as HO beginning in early childhood. HO formation is episodic, with some events starting with soft tissue inflammation (flare-up). The accumulation of extraskeletal bone is cumulative and irreversible, causing restriction of movement, deformities, and severe disability. Chronic complications may include chest wall deformity (thoracic insufficiency syndrome), ankyloses of the temporomandibular joints resulting in severe tooth decay and malnutrition, and localized skin breakdown. Most patients require mobility assistance by their 20's due to HO around the hips, and survival is shortened (median 56 years), usually by cardio-respiratory failure and pneumonia.
L39: Patients with FOP face a high unmet medical need, as there are no approved therapies and no therapies have been shown to treat or slow progression of HO formation and reduce overall disease burden. Current conventional therapy for FOP is aimed at symptom relief by decreasing inflammation and chronic pain. Symptomatic treatment with high dose steroids is often used to treat HO symptom “flares,” however, short term burst steroid therapy has no benefit in reducing the overall burden of HO or slowing disease progression. Attempts at surgical excision of lesions usually leads to reactivation of disease and new HO.
L40: ## Assessment of Effectiveness of Palovarotene in the Treatment of FOP
L41: In support of this application, the Applicant conducted a phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study in patients with FOP (Study 201), with a phase 2 open-label single arm extension study (Study 202), and a single arm, open-label, externally controlled phase 3 study (Study 301). Studies 201 and 202 Parts A and B evaluated short term treatment of acute flare-ups with assessments of new HO at the flare-up site, while Study 202 Parts B and C evaluated chronic plus flare-up treatment with assessments of new whole-body HO. The external control group for Study 301 was a 36-month NHS, also conducted by the Applicant, in pediatric and adult patients with FOP. The proposed dosing regimen includes chronic daily treatment (5 mg), with higher dose treatment (20 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks, with extension if needed, referred to as “20/10 mg” or “flare dosing”) during symptomatic “flare-up” episodes (all proposed doses are adjusted based on body weight in skeletally immature patients under 18 years of age). This dosing regimen was used in Study 301 and in Part C of Study 202 (202C).
L42: The primary endpoint for Studies 201/202A/202B was the incidence of new HO at the flare-up site 12 weeks after flare-up initiation. The primary endpoint for Study 202C and Study 301 was annualized change in new whole-body HO volume, and the key secondary endpoint was proportion of subjects with any new HO. Volume of HO is a clinically meaningful endpoint because patients with FOP are known to have progressive, irreversible accumulation of heterotopic ossification as the hallmark of the disease. HO volume was assessed by whole-body CT scans based on prespecified body regions using appropriate adjudication. CT scans from Study 202 B/C were read by the same imaging contractor as in Study 301 and the NHS; however, there were differences in the precise methodology for assessing changes in HO by whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) between the phase 2 and phase 3 studies.
L43: Additional secondary endpoints in Study 301 included the number of body regions with new HO, the proportion of subjects reporting flare-ups, and the rate of flare-ups per subject-month. Exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in ROM assessed by CAJIS for FOP, change from baseline in physical function using age-appropriate forms of the FOP-PFQ (FOP Physical Function Questionnaire), and change from baseline in physical and mental function using age-appropriate forms of the PROMIS Global Health Scale.
L44: Both Studies 201/202 and Study 301 failed to meet the prespecified primary efficacy endpoints. In addition, none of the secondary or exploratory endpoints in Study 301 showed statistically significant differences between palovarotene-treated and untreated/control subjects and thus did not provide supportive evidence of efficacy of this product in the treatment of FOP. Due to failure to achieve the prespecified primary endpoints, the Applicant relied on post hoc analyses from Study 301 to support the effectiveness of palovarotene. The following key efficacy issues were identified during the review.
L45: ## Appropriateness of Reliance on Post Hoc Analyses To Support Efficacy
L46: Post hoc analyses are generally considered hypothesis generating and are usually not appropriate for providing substantial evidence of effectiveness. However, in this specific setting, the Agency acknowledged that the prespecified primary analysis for Study 301 had an inherent bias against palovarotene. Therefore, the FDA statistical team considered that it was reasonable to look at alternative, more appropriate analyses. Various post hoc analyses performed by the review team suggested that there may be a nominally significant difference between the primary outcomes of Study 301 and NHS subjects when more appropriate analyses are used. The consistency of results from the analyses performed by the FDA review team supports the robustness of this conclusion. However, this finding relies on an unverifiable assumption that no other unmeasured confounding factors could have substantially impacted the study results.
L47: Because Study 201 did not meet its primary endpoint, the Applicant also used post hoc analyses to evaluate the efficacy of palovarotene “flare-up only” dosing (i.e., treatment of flares without chronic daily therapy) with respect to development of new HO at flare-up sites. Pooled data from Studies 201, 202A/B and the NHS showed trends of reduced volume of new HO at flare-up sites in treated compared to untreated FOP patients. However, the data were inconclusive due to differences in study design and patient populations across studies, lack of control and randomization involved in most of the data, and lack of positive dose response across various flare-up treatment regimens. Thus, the evidence to support the efficacy of a “flare-up only” dosing regimen was not considered sufficient to justify approval of flare-based dosing without background chronic daily therapy.
L48: Data from Study 301 and the NHS support the conclusion that chronic daily dosing (i.e., palovarotene 5 mg daily), in addition to flare-based dosing, is needed to achieve benefit. Specifically, these data demonstrate that subjects who reported no flare-ups developed relatively small quantities of new whole-body HO, either with or without chronic daily treatment. By comparison, subjects who experienced flare-ups generally developed large quantities of new whole-body HO without chronic daily therapy and derived greater benefit from palovarotene (i.e., reduced volume of new HO, both at and away from flare-up sites). Therefore, both chronic daily and flare-up dosing appear to be important components of the overall palovarotene dosing regimen to support efficacy.
L49: ## Use of an External Control Group (NHS) for Evaluation of Efficacy of the Chronic/Flare-Up Regimen
L50: When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. Compared to Study 301, NHS subjects were older and had more severe disease severity at baseline. The FDA statistical team performed various analyses to assess the impact of baseline imbalances in selected covariates.
L51: FDA's analyses suggested that the observed difference in the primary outcome in treated and untreated subjects was unlikely due to any systematic difference in the measured baseline factors that are deemed clinically important. However, these analyses could not address the impact of unmeasured and unknown confounding.
L52: Nevertheless, findings from within-subject comparisons for subjects who restarted treatment after dose interruption, along with findings from subjects who transferred from the NHS to Study 301, may complement the between-subject comparisons and seem supportive of a drug effect. How much the within-subject comparisons could mitigate the concern for unmeasured and unknown confounding depends on the extent to which the natural progression of the disease would be expected to be relatively stable within the two-year study period. However, it should be acknowledged that the impact of disease progression on the within-subject comparisons could not be fully characterized without a randomized concurrent untreated control.
L53: Furthermore, some NHS subjects were enrolled into Study 301 or other intervention studies after some period of observation in the NHS. The possibility of subject selection bias could not be ruled out. Regardless, sensitivity analyses conducted by the Applicant and FDA suggested that it is unlikely that potential selection bias drove the conclusion of a positive treatment effect.
L54: ## Uncertain Clinical Implications of Negative New HO Volume Data
L55: Based on the natural history of disease progression in FOP, in which HO accumulates gradually over time, the clinical significance of negative HO volumes (as assessed by whole body CT) remains unclear. Whether negative HO volume represents "noise" on CT imaging due to inflammation occurring at an initial flare-up site, or a natural process of bone consolidation as the transition from cartilaginous tissue to bone occurs, or some other physiologic mechanism, remains unknown. The clinical implication of occurrence of negative HO, if any, may continue to be monitored in the postmarketing setting.
L56: ## Consistency of Phase 2 and Phase 3 Whole-Body HO Data
L57: As treatment regimens and study endpoints evolved, chronic daily dosing was introduced in Study 202 Part B, but flare-up dosing was not used extensively in this part based on relatively strict protocol criteria to define flare-up events. In contrast, all flare-up symptoms were treated with flare-up dosing in Study 202 Part C and Study 301. Despite use of the same treatment protocol, mean new whole-body HO volume was greater in Study 202C compared to Study 301, and not substantially different from untreated NHS subjects. Although Study 202 was not powered to demonstrate efficacy via comparisons to the NHS, consistency of these data with Study 301 data has been a review issue. With additional information and analyses, FDA reviewers have now concluded that the different outcomes of Studies 301 and 202C do not present a major concern due to differences in the respective study populations, new analyses of 202C versus NHS data and favorable data in 202C subjects who restarted treatment following the extended treatment pause.
L58: ## Conclusions on Effectiveness
L59: Overall, the Agency has concluded that the Applicant demonstrated substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene to reduce new HO volume in pediatric and adult patients with FOP but has not provided substantial evidence to support an indication for the prevention of HO in patients with FOP. Reductions in volume of HO is a clinically meaningful endpoint because patients with FOP are known to have progressive accumulation of heterotopic ossification. Based on data from the natural history study, there is a correlation between total body HO volume with increasing CAJIS score which indicates increasing restrictions on movement and joint range of motion.
L60: Substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene in the treatment of FOP was provided by data from the phase 3 Study 301, using the NHS as an external control. Using the linear mixed effects model, the mean annualized new HO was 9.4 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in subjects receiving palovarotene (study 301) and 20.3 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in the NHS with a treatment difference of 10.9 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} (95% CI: -21.2, -0.6). Confirmatory evidence of the efficacy of palovarotene to reduce new HO volume was provided from similar data seen in the phase 2 study, Study 202C, which used the same dosing regimen and protocol design as Study 301. Using the matched propensity score analysis, the mean annualized new HO volume was 16.1 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in subjects receiving palovarotene (study 202C) compared with 28.4 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in untreated subjects from the NHS with a treatment difference of 12.3 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}. Additional, but not as robust, supportive evidence was provided by data from Studies 201 and 202A/B, as well as by nonclinical data in a FOP mouse model that supports the mechanism of action of palovarotene to inhibit overactivation of the ALK2 receptor and thereby reduce HO formation. The efficacy of palovarotene treatment in patients with FOP appears to be present only when chronic daily dosing is combined with flare-based dosing, when needed, for flare-up episodes.
L61: ## **Risk Assessment of Palovarotene in the Treatment of FOP**
L62: Safety risks associated with palovarotene include those directly associated with the retinoid drug class of medications, as well as risks seen specifically in patients with FOP. Boxed Warnings and Warnings and Precautions contained in the retinoid class product labels include teratogenicity, psychiatric disorders, pseudotumor cerebri, serious skin reactions, pancreatitis, lipid abnormalities (hypertriglyceridemia), hearing impairment, hepatotoxicity, inflammatory bowel
L63: disease, skeletal abnormalities (including decreased bone mineral density, hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure), and vision impairment.
L64: Regarding the risk of PPC seen with the retinoid class, treatment with palovarotene caused PPC in subjects with open growth plates despite lower, weight-based dosing in younger patients. Potentially, this could result in significant adverse effects on growth, especially in younger age groups. The Applicant proposed an indication that would allow most patients with at least 80% skeletal maturity (bone age 8 years in girls and 10 years in boys) to receive palovarotene for the prevention of HO despite the risk of PPC, given the severity of the disease.
L65: Palovarotene is a known teratogen as a member of the retinoid class; however, there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP, and consensus guidelines urge serious consideration before women with FOP attempt pregnancy given that pregnancy is extremely high risk. As a precaution, clinical studies of palovarotene have included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements, and to date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. The Applicant proposed a Boxed Warning in labeling to mitigate this risk.
L66: Regarding effects on bone mineral content, bone density and fractures, results of a biomechanical CT and vertebral fracture analysis suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD, and a higher risk of new onset morphometric vertebral fractures. These effects are consistent with some data involving other retinoids and are consistent with the BMD findings by DXA in osteochondroma subjects. However, the data do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures and differing amounts of follow-up data between the nonrandomized populations of Study 301 and the NHS.
L67: There is an unresolved concern that palovarotene could increase the incidence of HO flare-up episodes in patients with FOP. Flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in Study 301 compared to untreated subjects in the NHS and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month), and within Study 301, new flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Most of the new flare-ups occurred at sites distant from the initial site. Similarly, data from Studies 201/202 showed higher rates of new flare-ups during flare-up dosing with palovarotene 10/5 mg or 20/10 mg (0.18 to 0.29/month) in comparison to placebo or NHS untreated subjects (0.11 to 0.12/month), or chronic 5 mg dosing (0.10/month).
L68: However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS, so the validity of these findings remains unclear. Additional postmarketing data will be necessary to better determine the potential for palovarotene treatment to worsen HO formation and thereby worsen disease severity.
L69: A PMR to assess long term safety of palovarotene in pediatric and adult patients enrolled into an observational safety study will be implemented to further assess the risk of HO flares and other risks associated with palovarotene, including PPC, bone fractures, and any pregnancy data available.
L70: ## Conclusions on Risk
L71: The risks associated with palovarotene use include risks associated with drugs in the retinoid class (e.g., teratogenicity, PPC with the potential for disproportionate growth, fractures, among others) and potential risks specific to patients with FOP (e.g., increase in HO flares with use of
L72: the medication). These risks will be clearly identified in product labeling and further addressed through a PMR for a long-term observational study in children and adults with FOP that will collect data on PPC, fractures, rates of flare episodes, and pregnancy outcomes data. To promote adequate capture of pregnancy outcome data should pregnancy occur during palovarotene use, enhanced pharmacovigilance will also be requested.
L73: ## Conclusions on Benefit-Risk Assessment
L74: Overall, the Agency has concluded that the Applicant demonstrated substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene to reduce the volume of new HO in pediatric and adult patients with FOP when chronic daily dosing is combined with flare-based dosing, when needed, for flare-up episodes. The Applicant has not provided substantial evidence for palovarotene's efficacy to prevent HO formation in FOP, the originally proposed indication.
L75: Palovarotene represents the first pharmacologic agent for the treatment of any manifestation of FOP. Treatment with palovarotene showed an effect in decreasing the volume of new HO in patients with FOP. The reduction in HO volume provides a clinically meaningful benefit to patients because of the irreversible, progressive nature of the disease. It is recognized that progressive accumulation of HO is associated with worsening of a patient's movement and mobility. Therefore, treatment with palovarotene which leads to small changes in HO volume in short term trials, is expected to slow the progression of the disease with the potential to preserve joint range of motion and movement for a longer period of time. While there are risks associated with use of palovarotene, these can be managed through product labeling along with further assessment in a postmarketing safety study.
L76: In conclusion, despite the limitations of the efficacy data presented by the Applicant (e.g., efficacy based on post hoc analyses, use of an external control, differences in design across studies, etc.), the Agency has ultimately concluded that the benefits of palovarotene in pediatric and adult patients with FOP outweigh the risks associated with this drug, particularly given the progressive and debilitating nature of FOP and the unmet medical need in the FOP patient population.

L98: ## 4. Patient Experience Data
L99: The fibrodysplasia ossificans progressive (FOP) natural history study (NHS, Study PVO-1A-001) and the palovarotene intervention studies included patient-reported outcome measures related to physical function and a clinician-reported index of range of motion. Changes in these measures were found to correlate with more advanced age of FOP patients and with more severe disease but were insufficiently sensitive to show changes over the time scale of the clinical studies, with or without treatment. For this review, these data provided general supportive information but were not central to the regulatory decision.

L102: ## 5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical Pharmacology
L103: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L104: The original NDA included a series of in vitro and in vivo pharmacodynamic data generated by the Applicant and from published research studies. These nonclinical studies were reviewed in detail and included in the first cycle Integrated Review (December 23, 2022). In this review cycle, no new nonclinical data were submitted. Rather, the NDA resubmission contained a 'white paper' that discussed the available nonclinical pharmacology data in the context of supportive mechanistic evidence of benefit.
L105: ## In Vitro Studies Supporting the Mechanism of Action
L106: In patients with FOP, abnormal bone formation, including ectopic chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, and heterotrophic ossification, are driven by a gain-of-function mutation in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) type I receptor activin receptor-like kinase 2 (ALK2) (ACVR1) and overactivation of downstream SMAD signaling proteins. The rationale for evaluating palovarotene for FOP is based on the knowledge that retinoid acid receptor (RAR) activity is an inhibitor of chondrogenesis (Pacifici et al. 1980; Hoffman et al. 2006; Shore and Kaplan 2010; Kaplan et al. 2012). In in vitro studies, palovarotene demonstrated binding and functional selectivity towards retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR\gamma), which is expressed in chondrogenic cells and chondrocytes. Pretreatment with palovarotene inhibited BMP-induced chondrogenic differentiation and led to the loss of skeletogenic potential of the chondrogenic progenitor cells (ADTC5) and skeletal stem cells (bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells), respectively. Similar findings were recapitulated in a BMP-treated human fibroblast cell line carrying the human relevant gain-of-function R206H mutation of the ALK2 receptor. In these cell lines, palovarotene dampened the BMP/ALK2 downstream signaling pathway by reducing the levels of phosphorylated Smad effector proteins (Smad1, Smad5 and Smad8). The effect of palovarotene on Smad proteins was abrogated in the presence of proteasome inhibitors, suggesting that palovarotene might promote proteasome-mediated degradation of Smad proteins.
L107: ## In Vivo Nonclinical Data Showing Proof of Concept
L108: Proof of concept in vivo studies with palovarotene were conducted in various injury-induced heterotopic ossification (HO) and FOP mice models, including BMP-2 implant, transgenic mice expressing constitutively active ALK2Q207D mutant and the human relevant ALK2R206H mutation (Shimono et al. 2011; Chakkalakal et al. 2012; Chakkalakal et al. 2016). Across these animal models, treatment with palovarotene led to dose-dependent reductions in the volume of new HO at the site of injury (muscle) compared to vehicle treated animals. These results from the injury-based ALK2Q207D mouse were used to develop a dose-response model that suggested a maximally effective mouse dose of 6 mg/kg (20 mg human equivalent dose by body surface area comparison) may provide greater efficacy in inhibiting HO than the chronic maintenance dose, and these data served as a basis for the selection of the human flare-up initiation dose. Further analysis of the effectiveness of palovarotene at various time points following the induction of
L109: HO showed that the HO inhibitory effect of palovarotene only covered a narrow window of treatment, primarily during pre-treatment prior to Day 1 up to Day 3 postinjury, but effectiveness was lower if treatment initiation was delayed until 7 days postinjury. This observation suggests that palovarotene might block HO by preventing chondrogenic cell differentiation and cartilage formation (pre- and chondrogenic proliferative phase) but not the ossification phase when bone is already present. Palovarotene also improved joint mobility, and reduced mast cell infiltration and fibroproliferative responses at the site of injury. In addition to the injury-based models described above, palovarotene blocked noninjury (spontaneously) induced HO formation in the fore- and hind-limbs of pups when palovarotene was administered orally to nursing transgenic Prrx1^{R206H} mice, which carry the R206H mutation in Prrx1^{+} skeletal progenitor cells (Chakkalakal et al. 2016).
L110: Overall, the information available from published studies and Applicant-provided nonclinical data support the purported mechanism of action: by selective binding to RAR\gamma, palovarotene inhibits chondrogenic differentiation by decreasing the overactivated ALK2 signaling pathway through the reduction in phosphorylation of downstream effectors (Smad1/5/8). As such, palovarotene may reduce the volume of new HO in humans, consistent with the robust and consistent nonclinical observations in animal models of FOP.
L111: Nevertheless, the utility of the nonclinical data to provide confirmatory evidence of clinical effectiveness on its own is limited by several factors, including species-specific differences and study design issues (Table 5). Human FOP is a complex, heterogeneous disease without a well understood pathology, and flare-ups are located in various tissues (muscles, tendons, or ligaments). On the other hand, the injury-based animal models used in this program lack heterogeneity in disease expression, as the animals only had a single injury site at a specified location that was standardized across the treatment groups. Moreover, the disease mechanism between animal and human FOP is different as the BMP-implantation model is created with supraphysiological rhBMP-2 levels. The genetic model bearing the ALK2^{Q207D} mutation is not found naturally in FOP patients. The ALK2^{R206H} and Prrx1^{R206H} mice do carry the most common mutation found in human FOP and do display many of the phenotypic features of FOP patients (hind limb digit malformation, joint fusions, and extensive HO development), but these conditional knock-in models only allow the study of one gene. Furthermore, treatment with palovarotene was initiated at an early age in all transgenic mouse studies (birth to 2-month), corresponding to the period of maximal skeletal growth and maturation, and generally translating to pre-pubertal human childhood but not to sexually and skeletally mature adults. It is also worth noting that the timing for initiation of treatment varies between the nonclinical and clinical studies. In animal models, dosing with palovarotene was initiated prior to or immediately following injury (aligned with the catabolic and chondrogenic phases), whereas flare-up dosing in the clinical trials was targeted after the initiation of the catabolic and chondrogenesis process. Comparisons of nonclinical pharmacology models and study data are shown in Table 5 below.

Primary excretion pathways (% dose)	97.1% and 3.2% radioactivity were recovered in feces and urine, respectively.
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	Based on population PK analysis, AUC and Cmax were 8% and 12% higher for a 51 kg subject and 18% and 26% lower for a 98 kg compared to a 70 kg subject, respectively.
Age	According to population PK analysis of PK data from subjects aged 2-85 years, there was no evidence that age has a clinically relevant influence on the PK of palovarotene.
Renal impairment	A PK study was not conducted in subjects with renal impairment because only 3% of radioactivity was recovered in urine and there were no case reports of renal impairment in FOP patients enrolled in clinical studies. Population PK analysis suggests that serum creatinine or renal impairment status are not significant covariates on palovarotene PK.
Hepatic impairment	A postmarketing requirement (PMR) will be issued to conduct a hepatic impairment study and evaluate the effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) and severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) on the PK of palovarotene to inform the dosing recommendations in subjects with hepatic impairment. Per the Applicant, hepatic impairment was not reported in the FOP patients enrolled in the natural history study submitted with this application (N ~100). Population PK analyses suggest that there was no significant difference in the PK of palovarotene in subjects with mild (Child-Pugh A, N=66) hepatic impairment compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene is not conclusive based on the population PK analyses as only a limited number of subjects (N=5) with moderate hepatic impairment. The effect of severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene has not been evaluated. Given that 97.1% of radioactivity was recovered in feces in the mass balance study and that palovarotene is extensively metabolized by CYP enzymes, palovarotene exposure may be increased in subjects with moderate or severe hepatic impairment.

L126: ## 6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential Effectiveness
L127: Regarding details regarding the dose selection for the phase 3 study and exposure-response (E-R) relationship for efficacy, please refer to the Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022. The following key review question regarding dosing of palovarotene has been evaluated under this review:
L128: **Is body weight-based dosing necessary for all patients or only for pediatric patients &lt;14 years of age?**
L129: In the NDA submission, the Applicant proposed to apply body weight-based dosing for pediatric patients who are less than 14 years old, and to use the fixed dosing for patients who are \ge 14 years of age (i.e., chronic daily dosing of 5 mg once daily (QD) and flare-up dosing of 20/10 mg). In the advisory committee meeting briefing document, the Applicant updated their position to apply body weight-based dosing for all patients, including adults, adolescents, and children (Table 7). According to this new proposal, patients who weigh less than 60 kg and are 14 years and older would receive lower doses than the doses investigated in Study 301 (Table 7). Both proposals allow for a reduction in dosage to lower levels if palovarotene is not well tolerated.

L133: ## Applicant's Justification
L134: The Applicant's justification for body weight-based dosing for all patients is that the population PK analysis revealed a significant impact of body weight on the PK of palovarotene. Specifically, it was observed that there is an association between body weight and the exposure of palovarotene, with exposure increasing as weight decreases at the same administered dose. This finding highlights the importance of considering body weight as a significant covariate when determining the appropriate dosing regimen for palovarotene.

L145: The proposed weight-based dosing only for pediatric subjects who are younger than 14 years is the same dosing regimen used in Study 301 for patients younger than 14 years of age. In this study, patients ≥18 years of age received orally administered 5 mg palovarotene once daily and 20 mg/10 mg dosing at the time of flare-up, whereas a weight-adjusted dose was used for skeletally immature patients under 18 years of age. The study results show that 20 out of 23 pediatric subjects aged 14 to 18 years had bone closure and received the flat adult doses. Three (3) out of 23 pediatric subjects aged 14 to 18 years had partial closure at some checking
L146: point of the treatments but received adult doses during most of the treatment period. Nonetheless, no premature epiphyseal closure (PPC) incidence was observed in these patients. Overall, there were no events of PPC in 38 subjects aged 14 to 18 years in Studies 301 and 202B/C. Overall, although more than 40% of patients had a dose reduction due to tolerability during the high dose flare-up treatment, the impact of dose reduction on efficacy has been reflected in the phase 3 study results.

L152: ## Note 3
L153: Large variability was observed in the E-R analyses with the efficacy endpoint of HO volume; thus, the review team considered no obvious E-R relationship for palovarotene and new HO volume up to 12 months. L154: ## 6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended To Demonstrate Efficacy
L155: ## 6.2.1. Phase 3: Study PVO-1A-301
L156: ## 6.2.1.1. Design, Study 301
L157: Study PVO-1A-301 (Study 301) was a phase 3 study with the primary objective of evaluating the efficacy of the chronic/flare-up dosing regimen of palovarotene to decrease new HO development in adult and pediatric patients with FOP. The Applicant chose to use untreated patients from the NHS as an external control arm. The single-arm design of Study 301, with use
L158: of the NHS as an external control group, raises issues of the comparability of these studies/groups, which are discussed in detail in Section 6.3.2.
L159: ## 6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria, Study 301
L160: Adult and pediatric patients \ge 4 years of age with a clinical diagnosis of FOP and no flare-up symptoms within the previous 4 weeks were eligible to enroll in Study 301. To facilitate comparisons with the NHS, most of the subjects (i.e., the Principal Analysis population) were required to have the classic R206H mutation and no prior exposure to palovarotene. There were exclusion criteria based on known retinoid safety issues, including pregnancy and increased suicide risk.
L161: ## 6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Study 301
L162: The primary endpoint was the annualized change in new HO volume as measured by whole body computed tomography (WBCT). The prespecified primary analysis for the primary endpoint was based on a Bayesian compound Poisson model. The Bayesian compound model was estimated based on the number of regions with positive new HO and the average growth per region where positive new HO occurred since the previous WBCT scan. Negative new HO values were set to 0 in the analyses. The prespecified analysis included a square root transformation of each change in HO since the previous scan by region. The Applicant chose this statistical model “to more appropriately accommodate the high degree of variability in the volume of new HO assessed by WBCT.” The square root transformation was included in the Bayesian compound Poisson analysis because simulations suggested that if palovarotene reduced the probability of new HO as much or more than it reduced the new HO volume given new HO, introducing a square root transformation could marginally increase power. Additionally, square root transformation would likely decrease the variance of the endpoint by shrinking any extremely large values of new HO volume.
L163: The trial crossed the futility boundary at the second interim analysis and the study was paused for dosing. However, additional post hoc analyses, including the same Bayesian compound model but without square root transformation and a frequentist weighted linear mixed effects (wLME) model, appeared to show evidence of potentially clinically meaningful benefit of palovarotene. Upon review of the additional post hoc analyses, the data monitoring committee (DMC) noted that the impact of the prespecified square root transformation was unexpectedly large and appeared to have moved the statistical conclusion from significant therapeutic benefit to showing futility of the treatment. The DMC concluded that “the dilemma created by these highly disparate results precludes a confident conclusion about futility.” Dosing in Study 301 was thus allowed to resume, and the DMC recommended that “palovarotene be continued in skeletally mature children \ge 14 years” (due to the risk of PPC in skeletally immature individuals).
L164: In the previous NDA review cycle, the post hoc analyses performed by the Applicant and the additional analyses requested by the FDA review team have been summarized in detail (refer to Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022).
L165: ## 6.2.1.4. Results of Analyses, Study 301
L166: Results from the Applicant's prespecified analyses and post hoc analyses were extensively discussed in the previous NDA review (December 23, 2022). Some main results were included in this review to facilitate discussion. The appropriateness of these post hoc analyses to support efficacy will be further discussed in the review issue section below. For purposes of this discussion, the “pre-pause” period refers to the period from study start to dosing interruptions (due to partial clinical hold and/or crossing the futility boundary), the “post-pause treatment” period refers to the time after subjects restarted palovarotene treatment, the “interruption” period spans the time between the last scan prior to dosing interruption and the first scan after restart, and the “post off-treatment” period refers to the period from first WBCT scan off treatment secondary to dosing interruption to last subjects last visit for subjects who remained off treatment.

L194: ## Applicant's Post Hoc Weighted Linear Mixed Effect Model Analysis
L195: The Applicant's post hoc wLME analysis with baseline annualized HO (calculated as baseline total HO volume divided by baseline age) as the only covariate achieved nominal significance (Table 13). In this analysis, the annualized new HO for each subject was calculated using the change in total HO volume from baseline associated with the longest follow-up divided by the length of follow-up. The length of follow-up varied substantially among subjects and between studies. For example, annualized new HO was based on the Month 18 observation for 66% of subjects in Study 301 and the Month 36 observation for 32% of subjects in the NHS. The wLME model accounted for the various follow-up lengths using a weighted approach. We note that the estimated treatment effect based on various lengths of follow-up could be difficult to interpret without the assumption of a constant rate of change in HO.

L202: ## **Subgroup Summary by Sex, Age, Race and Ethnicity**
L203: Subgroup summaries indicate a smaller effect size among females and among subjects older than 18 years (Table 14). This finding may be explained by the smaller annualized growth of new HO in the control group (NHS) subjects in these subgroups. However, it is not possible to rule out that the drug's effect is less in older subjects for whom the disease stage is often more advanced. An explanation for the smaller effect in females is uncertain. Findings from these subgroup analyses should be interpreted with caution because with a smaller number of subjects in each subgroup, the influence of a few large values and imbalances in confounders in the absence of randomization could be greater on the mean difference, compared with analyses based on the overall population.

L208: ## **Secondary Efficacy Endpoint Results**
L209: The key secondary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of subjects with any new HO at month 12. There was no difference in the proportion of subjects with any new HO (64% in treated subjects, 62% in untreated subjects) at month 12. There was also no difference in the mean (SD) number of body regions with new HO at month 12 [1.3 (1.4) in treated subjects, 1.5 (1.6) in untreated subjects].
L210: Exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in range of motion assessed by the Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale (CAJIS) at month 24, change from baseline in physical function assessed by FOP-FPQ at month 24, and change from baseline in physical and mental function in subjects 15 years and older as assessed by the Patient Reported Outcomes
L211: Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health Scale at month 24. The results do not reveal any significant difference between treated and untreated subjects.

L228: ## 6.2.2. Phase 2: Studies PVO-1A-201 and PVO-1A-202A/B/C
L229: ## 6.2.2.1. Design, Studies 201/202
L230: Study 201 was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 40 FOP patients who were experiencing an acute flare-up episode. Subjects were assigned to receive one of two palovarotene regimens, or placebo, for 6 weeks followed by 6 weeks of observation; development of HO at the flare-up site was assessed through week 12. In the open-label extension Study 202, Parts A and B evaluated the treatment of additional flare-up episodes, including the use of new dosing regimens, with similar assessments of HO at the flare-up site at week 12. HO data obtained from a subset of flare-up events reported by untreated patients with FOP in the NHS were used for some comparisons. Please refer to the Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022, for details of dosing regimens and assessments. Similar data, obtained from a subset of flare-up events reported by untreated patients with FOP in the NHS, were used for some comparisons.
L231: Study 202 Parts B and C introduced the palovarotene chronic/flare-up regimen, administered to skeletally mature patients in Part B and then to all patients in Part C, with primary efficacy assessments of whole-body HO by WBCT imaging. The criteria for initiating flare-up dosing changed when subjects transitioned from Study 202 Part B to Part C. Because Study 202C and the separate phase 3 Study 301 began around the same time (2017) and followed an essentially identical protocol for palovarotene treatment, Study 202C is considered relevant confirmatory evidence to the assessment of palovarotene efficacy and is discussed in this subsection. In comparison, flare-up dosing was used more sparingly in Study 202B due to protocol differences with respect to defining flare episodes; the Applicant submitted data to support the view that some subjects were undertreated in Study 202B due to the stricter flare-defining criteria, purportedly impacting efficacy. Upon review by FDA, the validity of this rationale is unclear.
L232: Overall, data from Study 202B are difficult to interpret and are not presented here. Additional details regarding Study 202B were included in the prior NDA review (see Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022).
L233: ## Study 202C
L234: All subjects in Study 202 Part C transitioned from 202 Part B. Most of the subjects in 202B had initially enrolled in Study 201 at the onset of an acute flare-up and then participated in Study 202 Part A, while an additional group of patients with FOP was newly enrolled and began palovarotene treatment in 202B.
L235: In Study 202C, all subjects (pediatric and adult) received the same regimen as subjects in Study 301:
L236: - Chronic palovarotene 5 mg daily dose
- Flare-up dosing: 20 mg for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg for 8 weeks, extended if needed for persistent symptoms
- Any number of symptoms (\ge 1) was sufficient to begin flare-up dosing
- Intercurrent flare-ups at a different site, or marked worsening at an original site could restart the flare-up dosing cycle
- Reduced doses for skeletally immature subjects
- Protocol amendments (for both Studies 202C and 301) in 2019 added a provision that flare-up dosing could also be triggered by a traumatic event considered likely to result in a flare-up
L237: As in Study 301, all treatment in Study 202C was paused from December 2019 until January 2020, and later restarted in some subjects aged \ge 14 years.
L238: HO was assessed solely by whole body CT in Study 202C; flare-up site-specific imaging was not conducted. For skeletally mature subjects, who began chronic treatment in 202B, Parts B and C were continuous, with WBCT performed annually starting at Part B baseline. For skeletally immature subjects, WBCT scans were obtained at the initiation of chronic dosing in Part C and then annually. During and after the treatment pause, additional scans were conducted on subjects who restarted palovarotene, through the study conclusion in September 2022.
L239: ## **6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria, Studies 201/202**
L240: The majority of phase 2 subjects enrolled initially in Study 201 for treatment of an acute flare-up and then continued into Study 202. The initial Study 201 cohort consisted of subjects with clinically diagnosed classic FOP, at least 15 years of age and \ge 90\% skeletal maturity, with symptomatic onset within 7 days of a distinct flare-up and at least two out of 6 specified symptoms (pain, swelling, decreased range of motion (ROM), stiffness, redness, warmth), consistent with their previous flare-ups. Following the initial cohort, enrollment in Study 201 was expanded to children age \ge 6 years.
L241: An additional group of subjects, whose initial enrollment was in Study 202 Part B, was restricted to subjects who were \ge 90\% skeletally mature, with at least two flare-ups within the past 2 years, but no flare-up symptoms within the past 4 weeks; a confirmed R206H mutation; and a CAJIS
L242: score of 6 to 16. Most of the subjects in this group transferred from the NHS to 202B; any NHS subject meeting these enrollment criteria was eligible for the transfer.
L243: ## 6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan, Studies 201/202
L244: ## Flare-Up Site Outcomes (Studies 201, 202 A/B, NHS)
L245: Please see prior Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022, for a discussion of assessments and endpoints related to the treatment of acute flare-ups through Week 12.
L246: ## Chronic/Flare-Up Dosing Outcomes (Study 202C)
L247: WBCT readings for 202B/C were conducted at the same central imaging facility used for Studies 301 and the NHS, using the same process involving HO measurement in each of nine body regions as described above.
L248: The primary efficacy endpoint for Study 202 at the initiation of Part C (protocol amendment 4) was annualized new HO volume as assessed by low-dose WBCT scan. WBCT readings for 202B/C were conducted at the same central imaging facility used for Studies 301 and the NHS, using the same process involving HO measurement in each of nine body regions as described above. Although Studies 202 and 301 used the same the primary endpoint and imaging methods, Study 202 was an extension study that was not powered to demonstrate efficacy via comparisons to the NHS.
L249: Analyses specific to 202 Part C were conducted on subjects who underwent at least two WBCT scans during Part C, when the first scan was not obtained within 1 month of a flare-up. This provision was intended to align with the enrollment criteria for Study 301 and the NHS and minimize any residual HO accrual that might have resulted from a pre-baseline flare-up.
L250: In the February 16, 2023 NDA resubmission, analyses of data from the “Pre-Pause” treatment period were conducted by the Applicant on the subset of 202C subjects with at least two WBCT scans that were obtained prior to the treatment pause (which occurred from December 2019 to January 2020). Other analysis subgroups included subjects with data from the “Interruption” phase (mostly, but not entirely off-treatment for an interval of variable duration in 2020 to 2022); and subjects who subsequently restarted palovarotene in 2020 to 2021 (referred to as the “Post-Pause” treatment population).
L251: ## 6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses, Studies 201/202
L252: ## Flare-Up Site Outcomes (Studies 201, 202A/B, NHS)
L253: As described in the previous Integrated Review (dated December 23, 2022), these studies were unable to demonstrate that palovarotene treatment of acute flare-up episodes reduced the incidence of new HO at the flare-up sites, which was the primary endpoint in Study 201. There were trends of reduced volume of new HO at these sites (a secondary endpoint) associated with treatment, but this finding was not definitive due to differences in study designs and treatment regimens, and there was no clear benefit with respect to clinical endpoints such as pain and swelling.
L254: ## **Chronic/Flare-Up Dosing Outcomes (Study 202C)**
L255: A total of 46 subjects enrolled in 202C and received treatment for a mean of 20 months in the Pre-pause period, including 36 subjects who required flare-up dosing in this phase. Among 202C subjects, there were 30 who underwent at least two WBCT scans in Part C, wherein the baseline scan was not within 1 month of a flare-up. Among these 30 subjects, there were 23 subjects with \ge 2 scans prior to dose interruption (Pre-pause population); 19 subjects with \ge 2 scans during the Interruption period; and 15 subjects with \ge 2 scans following restart (Post-Pause Treatment population). As in Study 301, no information is available regarding the criteria used for selection of subjects to restart treatment.
L256: Study 202C subjects were 50% female, similar to Study 301 and the NHS. The mean age of the subjects in 202C was 21.1 years, which is older than the mean age of subjects in the NHS (17.5 years) or Study 301 (15.1 years). Whole body HO volume at baseline was also greater in 202C compared to the other studies, likely due to the age differential.
L257: There were no interim analyses planned for Study 202, and the original NDA included only limited descriptive summaries of the Pre-pause 202B/C whole body HO data, which appeared to be inconsistent with findings from Study 301. This raised concerns about consistency of the efficacy data, which were communicated to the Applicant in the Complete Response letter, with requests from FDA for additional analyses of 202 versus NHS data.
L258: The FDA review team requested that the Applicant conduct analyses comparing outcomes of Study 202C subjects with NHS subjects with similar baseline characteristics using propensity score based matching methods. The difference between the annualized new HO of treated subjects in Study 202C and those matched untreated NHS subjects was about 12.3 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} favoring palovarotene, which was consistent with the treatment effect estimated by comparing Study 301 and NHS subjects. The difference did not achieve nominal statistical significance, likely due to the small sample size of matched subjects.
L259: The Applicant also conducted weighted analyses to estimate the average treatment effect among all subjects. It should be noted that the targeted treatment effect based on the Applicant's weighted analysis is different from that of the matched analysis, which estimated the average treatment effect among the treated 21 subjects, a more relevant estimand in this context given the much smaller number of treated subjects. Nevertheless, the two analyses produced estimates of treatment effects in the same direction.

L278: ## 6.3. Key Efficacy Review Issues
L279: ## 6.3.1. Phase 3: Appropriateness of Reliance on Post Hoc Analyses to Support Efficacy
L280: ## Issue
L281: Appropriateness of reliance on post hoc analyses comparing Study 301 with the NHS to support efficacy.
L282: ## Background
L283: The prespecified primary analysis for the primary endpoint failed to demonstrate efficacy of palovarotene. The Applicant purported that the failure of the prespecified Bayesian analysis was due to the use of a square root transformation and the difference in WBCT assessment schedules between Study 301 and the NHS. Additional post hoc analyses, including the same Bayesian compound model but without square root transformation and a frequentist weighted linear mixed model, appeared to show evidence of clinical benefit of palovarotene.
L284: Therefore, the submission relies on post hoc analyses to support the efficacy of palovarotene.
L285: ## Assessment
L286: Post hoc analyses are generally considered hypotheses generating, as they could inflate the chance of a false positive finding and raise concerns of potential bias caused by selection of analyses toward the intended favorable outcome. However, in this specific context, FDA acknowledges that the prespecified primary analysis may not have been the appropriate method for analyzing the primary endpoint for the reasons outlined in detail in the previous NDA review (refer to Integrated Review dated December 23, 2022 in DARRTS). In fact, the prespecified primary analysis had an inherent bias against palovarotene. Acknowledging the limitations of the prespecified analysis, FDA finds it reasonable to consider alternative, more appropriate analyses to assess the evidence of efficacy. Our assessments focus on the robustness and consistency of the conclusions from various post hoc analyses that we considered valid for the primary endpoint under reasonable assumptions.
L287: ## **FDA's Assessment of Post Hoc Bayesian Analysis Without Square Root Transformation**
L288: The Applicant's post hoc Bayesian analysis without square root transformation resulted in a high posterior probability in support of efficacy. Adjusting for additional covariates yielded similar results. The Applicant also conducted a post hoc Bayesian analysis with the square root transformation but adjusted for the visit schedule (that is, Study 301 visit schedule collapsed into a single Month 12 WBCT to match the timing of the first NHS postbaseline WBCT). The results were also in favor of palovarotene, with a posterior probability of reduction of HO greater than 0.9. These post hoc analyses indicate that the use of square root transformation in conjunction with the differential assessment schedule contributed to the failure of the prespecified primary analysis.
L289: We note that inference from the Bayesian model could be affected by different specification of prior distributions of the multiple parameters in the model and the results could differ if
L290: influential priors are specified. Additionally, the model targeted only positive changes in HO and set negative changes to zero.
L291: FDA's analyses focused on frequentist methods that directly analyze the annualized new HO for each subject with minimal assumptions.
L292: ## FDA's Assessment of the Applicant's Post Hoc wLME Analyses
L293: As noted previously, the Applicant's post hoc wLME analysis (Table 13), based on the CT scan associated with the longest follow-up and without square root transformation, achieved nominal statistical significance. However, results from the Applicant's wLME could be difficult to interpret as the annualized new HO for each subject was based on various length of follow-up.
L294: To assess whether the conclusion is sensitive to the assumption of a constant rate of change, we compared the changes in HO volume between Study 301 and NHS subjects during a 12-month observation period as a landmark analysis given that the majority of the subjects provided 12-month data, which does not rely on assumptions of a constant rate of change. We performed the landmark analyses using different methods for subjects who did not have 12-month data to investigate the consistency of findings. For all these analyses, a robust sandwich variance estimator was used to account for heteroscedasticity in variance.
L295: Results from these landmark analyses with different ways of handling subjects without 12-month data and including different covariates were consistently in favor of palovarotene (Table 16). Our analyses did not transform negative new HO values to zero.
