L303: The FDA review team also conducted analyses based on a random slope model, with change in HO volume from baseline as the response and time from baseline as a continuous variable, adjusting for relevant baseline covariates. Results from these analyses are similar to results of the landmark analyses with generally smaller nominal p-values. We note that the random slope model also assumes a constant rate of change, similar to the Applicant's wLME method, but it is more efficient as it utilizes all available observations rather than just the last observation.
L304: To evaluate whether inference of the treatment effect was affected by the skewness of the distribution or a few extreme large values, the FDA review team performed ordinal logistic regression analyses on annualized new HO. The ordinal logistic regression models the odds of having an annualized new HO larger than an observed value, adjusting for selected covariates and only considering the rank of the outcome, but not the magnitude. This logistic regression model can be viewed as an extension of a nonparametric Wilcoxon rank sum test with covariates adjustment. The results were in favor of palovarotene with high nominal significance, indicating that the conclusion from the Applicant's wLME and FDA's landmark analyses were not likely driven by outliers or skewness of the distribution of the outcome.
L305: ## **Conclusion**
L306: The prespecified Bayesian compound Poisson model incorporating square root transformation is not valid and appears to have a bias against palovarotene due to the more frequent assessment in Study 301. FDA finds it reasonable to use valid and more appropriate post hoc analyses to assess evidence of efficacy in this specific setting. Post hoc analyses without the square root transformation conducted by either the Applicant or FDA support that the annualized new HO of Study 301 subjects was lower than that of NHS subjects. These analyses used regression adjustments to account for baseline differences between subjects in the two studies. Analyses methods based on matching and weighting to account for the use of an external control will be described below.
L307: ## **6.3.2. Phase 3: Use of an External Control Group (NHS) for Evaluation of Efficacy of the Chronic/Flare-Up Regimen**
L308: ## **Issue**
L309: The use of an external control group (NHS subjects) as a comparator.
L310: ## **Background**
L311: The Applicant initiated the NHS study in 2014 and enrolled 117 subjects, a relatively large proportion of the known global population of approximately 800 FOP patients. During the subsequent planning of Study 301, despite the FDA recommendation for a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, the Applicant considered that the NHS study population and assessments were suitable to serve as an external control group to compare to Study 301, as the two studies would be conducted at the same centers, with generally consistent standards of care and associated background treatment. In addition, the relative objectivity and blinded assessment of the primary outcome measure—change in HO volume—would minimize the potential for bias. Based on
L312: these considerations and the small number of FOP patients available for recruitment, Study 301 was designed as an open-label, single arm study with the NHS as an external control.
L313: ## Assessment
L314: Despite the limitations associated with using an external control rather than a randomized concurrent control, FDA recognizes that support for effectiveness can emerge using an externally controlled trial when the following are met (December 2019):
L315: - the natural history of the disease is well defined,
- the external control population is very similar to that of the treatment group,
- concomitant treatments that affect the primary endpoint are not substantially different between the external control and the trial population, and
- the results provide compelling evidence of a change in the established progression of disease.
L316: The concomitant treatments in this population are not expected to affect the outcome of interest. The NHS study was performed to characterize the disease process and outcomes. The focus of our assessment was to determine whether the differences between the study populations in the NHS and Study 301 impacted the conclusion regarding efficacy, whether the results are compelling enough to overcome the general concerns of potential confounding factors when using an external control, and if there were impacts on the primary outcome measure from potential selection bias due to differential loss to follow-up between the NHS and Study 301.
L317: ## **FDA's Assessment of Comparability of Study Populations and Potential Selection Bias**
L318: The enrollment criteria for the NHS and Study 301 were generally similar. Because the NHS was restricted to subjects with the classic R206H mutation, which represents approximately 97 percent of FOP patients, the P-FAS population of Study 301 excluded a small number of participants with other mutations.
L319: Recruitment of subjects into the NHS and Study 301 was sequential, as NHS enrollment was complete before Study 301 was initiated. All NHS study sites also participated in Study 301, and any NHS subject who met enrollment criteria (e.g., without retinoid-safety-related exclusions) was eligible for this transition. A total of 39 subjects transferred from the NHS into Study 301 and contributed efficacy data to both studies. In addition, eight subjects discontinued the NHS to enroll in Study 201 at the onset of a flare-up, 13 subjects discontinued the NHS to enroll in Study 202B, and 6 subjects discontinued the NHS to enroll in other interventional studies, including for other investigational products for FOP. Given that transfers out of the NHS were voluntary and driven in part by clinical factors that are largely unknown, unmeasured confounding is likely to have occurred. Further, selection bias due to differential loss to follow-up may be of concern if transferring from the NHS to interventional studies was related to disease progression or other outcome-related factors, whereas loss from Study 301 may not be similarly related to such factors, resulting in potential differential capture of outcome between the two studies.
L320: Table 21 presents baseline data for three cohorts within the P-FAS: the 39 transition subjects who contributed efficacy data to both the NHS and Study 301; 62 NHS subjects who did not enroll in Study 301; and 58 subjects in Study 301 who had not participated in the NHS. Transition subjects' data at both NHS baseline and Study 301 baseline (at an average of 2.3 years later) are presented.
L321: As shown, NHS subjects who remained in the NHS were older (mean age of 20.5 years) than subjects who transitioned to Study 301 (mean age of 13.5 years) and other Study 301 subjects (mean age of 14.6 years). Consistent with older age, the NHS-only subjects tended to have more advanced disease, with generally higher whole-body HO volumes, greater number of body regions with HO, and higher scores on CAJIS, indicating more severely impaired range of motion and physical function. Transition subjects reported a higher number of flare-ups prior to NHS enrollment (mean 5.8 within 12 months) than the other groups; however, this observation was primarily driven by two subjects with high numbers of reported flare episodes.

L363: These within-subject comparisons complemented a between-subject comparison by using each subject's own observations in the NHS as the control, which may potentially have reduced unmeasured confounding.
L364: Interpretation of results from this analysis should consider to what extent the disease would be expected to progress on average, over time, without treatment (similarly to what was observed in the NHS) after these subjects transitioned to Study 301. However, the impact of disease progression when enrolled into Study 301 could not be fully assessed without a concurrent control.
L365: Nevertheless, the observed average within-subject increase in the rate of HO after the dosing interruption and the subsequent decrease in rate of HO after restarting palovarotene treatment as observed in Study 202C and Study 301 subjects is also supportive of the conclusions from the wLME analysis.
L366: ## **Sensitivity Analysis to Address Potential Selection Bias**
L367: Propensity score weighting or matching considering baseline characteristics does not address the concern that loss to follow-up when transferring from the NHS to interventional studies may have been related to disease progression (or other outcome-related factors), whereas loss from Study 301 was minimal or was not similarly related to such factors. The implicit characteristics of NHS subjects who drove self-selection into interventional studies may have been unknown or uncaptured at study baseline. Even if captured, the confounding control methods are inadequate to address potential differential loss to follow-up (i.e., selection bias).
L368: In response to FDA's inquiry, the Applicant conducted analyses comparing new HO during the NHS between subjects who transitioned into interventional studies (Studies 201, 202, or 301) and subjects who remained in NHS. The results indicated slower disease progression in NHS subjects who transferred to interventional studies, compared with subjects who remained in the NHS. Although the difference was not statistically significant, the magnitude of intrinsic difference between transition and nontransition NHS subjects might explain the observed drug effect to some extent, supporting the theoretical concern of presence of selection bias and the potential impact on efficacy assessment. To address this specific concern, the Applicant conducted sensitivity analyses considering palovarotene treatment a time-varying exposure and HO volume by WBCT scan a time-dependent confounder. The sensitivity analysis results were consistent with the wLME analysis in terms of the direction of association between palovarotene treatment and annualized new HO. Of note, specification of such a causal inference model required several strong and untestable statistical assumptions.
L369: To further address the concern for potential selection bias due to the transfer of some NHS subjects to Study 301, the FDA review team additionally conducted analyses excluding subjects who transferred from the NHS to Study 301. The transfer subjects were excluded from the Study 301 analysis population but included in the NHS analysis population. The analyses results based on regression adjustments or propensity score weighting were similar to those for the overall population; however, the same concern of informative censoring in the NHS cohort remains in this subset of the analysis population.
L370: ## **Conclusion**
L371: When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. There were some differences in baseline characteristics between subjects in the NHS and Study 301, such as subjects in the NHS were relatively older and had worse disease severity. To address the potential impact of measured confounding factors, various analyses using methods that are commonly used for
L372: causal inference were performed and these analyses provided consistent results. It appears that the difference in annualized new HO between treated and untreated subjects was not driven by any systemic differences in baseline covariates that are expected to be clinically important, although the impact of unknown confounding factors remains uncertain.
L373: To assess the impact of potential selection bias due to subjects' self-selection to interventional studies, the Applicant and the FDA review team conducted several sensitivity analyses. Although these analyses have limitations, and no single analysis categorically addresses the concern of selection bias, the results were consistent in the direction of association, suggesting an effect of palovarotene in reducing the volume of new HO.
L374: In addition, results from within-subject comparisons, including findings from subjects who restarted treatment after dose interruption, may complement the between-subject comparisons and seem supportive of a drug effect. However, the magnitude of treatment effect could not be accurately quantified without a concurrent randomized control.
L375: ## 6.3.3. Uncertain Clinical Implications of Negative New HO Volume Data
L376: ## Issue
L377: Negative new HO volume data: clinical significance, and implications for primary phase 3 efficacy analysis.
L378: ## Background
L379: FOP is characterized by accumulation of HO, which is considered to be irreversible. It was anticipated that the extent of negative HO data would be limited. However, results of these intervention studies showed substantial declines in HO volume in some instances, raising questions about the clinical significance of such changes.
L380: ## Assessment
L381: In Studies 301 and the NHS, postbaseline WBCT scans were compared to the previous scan. If any new HO was qualitatively present in a certain body region, all HO in that region was remeasured. In many cases, the net change in HO volume was negative (&lt;0 cm3/year) for a specific body region. There were more palovarotene-treated versus untreated subjects (47% and 24% in Study 301 and the NHS, respectively) with negative changes in new HO volume in at least one body region at the last measured timepoint. Net negative changes for total body HO also occurred more frequently in Study 301 compared to the NHS (29% in Study 301 versus 5% in the NHS).
L382: Literature reports indicate that shrinkage of HO lesions may occur in untreated FOP patients, as well as in nongenetic forms of HO. While the mechanism is unknown, it is plausible that this may be related to resolution of edema in newer lesions with progressive calcification and consolidation to mature cortical bone, analogous to the remodeling of callus around a fracture (according to the Applicant's response to IR submission to the NDA on August 5, 2021).
L383: Because negative HO volume changes were reported more frequently in Study 301 than in the NHS, the Applicant contends that palovarotene treatment may cause HO regression. However, it
L384: is important to note that all HO volume measurements in these studies were by body region, therefore, shrinkage in individual lesion(s) could be offset or masked by increasing size of other lesions within the same region. NHS subjects generally had more HO lesions that were growing in size, thus negative changes would tend to be underestimated in these untreated patients to a greater extent than in palovarotene recipients. Because of the lack of data on individual HO lesions in these studies, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the negative HO volume data resulted from palovarotene-related regression of existing lesions as seen radiographically (e.g., due to consolidation of the lesion or decreased inflammation), in addition to inhibition of new HO formation.
L385: The HO volume calculations were in part dependent on subjective assessments and varying orientation of axial slices on different CT scans; however, given the processes of double read and adjudication, measurement error is unlikely to explain some of the larger HO volume declines observed. Moreover, measurement error would apply equally to scans from treated and untreated subjects, therefore this mechanism alone cannot explain the disproportionate number of treated subjects with net negative HO.
L386: It is possible that in at least some instances, negative new HO volume changes are likely to reflect actual shrinkage of lesions, possibly as a natural process of lesion maturation or due to a decrease in inflammation, rather than a decrease in HO itself. However, the data are insufficient to conclude that palovarotene promotes this process. Regardless of the exact mechanism, there does not appear to be a plausible rationale for excluding negative HO changes from analyses. On the other hand, if the reduction in volume was due to consolidation or a decrease in the underlying inflammatory process rather than inhibition of the growth of new HO, it is unclear whether the occurrence of negative new HO should be viewed as a treatment benefit, given that neither lesion consolidation nor decrease in inflammation has been associated with improvement in functional status in patients with FOP.
L387: ## Conclusion
L388: The clinical implication of the occurrence of negative new HO volumes in Studies 301, 202B/C and the NHS remains unclear. However, there is no convincing evidence that these data could have created a bias in favor of palovarotene, or that exclusion (i.e., zeroing out) of negative HO data from analyses, as in the prespecified primary analysis of Study 301, was justified from a clinical perspective.
L389: ## 6.3.4. Consistency of Phase 2 and Phase 3 Whole-Body HO Data
L390: ## Issue
L391: Phase 2 efficacy data pertaining to chronic/flare-up dosing was not consistent with phase 3 data.
L392: ## Background
L393: During the phase 2 extension Study 202, chronic daily dosing of palovarotene was introduced in 202 Parts B and C, with higher doses (20/10 mg) for flare-ups, and efficacy was assessed using annual whole-body HO. In 202 Part C, the primary endpoint was the annualized change from
L394: baseline in whole-body HO volume, similar to Study 301. However, 202C was a smaller study which was not powered to demonstrate efficacy via comparisons to the NHS.
L395: ## Assessment
L396: No interim analyses were planned for Study 202, and the original NDA included only descriptive summaries of the 202B/C data, which showed large apparent discrepancies between overall new HO volume (raw data) for Study 202B (mean 28.0 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) and Study 202C (mean 24.3 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}), compared to Study 301 (mean 9.4 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) and the NHS (23.7 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}). Because the chronic/flare-up treatment protocol was similar for Studies 202 and 301, and essentially identical for Studies 202C and 301, concerns were raised about consistency of these efficacy data.
L397: The original NDA highlighted differences between the Study 202B protocol versus the 202C/301 protocol as a reason for the discordant results. Specifically, the 202B protocol required documentation of at least two flare-up symptoms within the previous 7 days to initiate flare-up dosing and did not allow resetting of the flare-up treatment cycle for intercurrent flare-ups at a new site, marked worsening of the initial symptoms, or trauma considered likely to lead to a flare-up. As a result, flare-up dosing was used more sparingly in Study 202B compared to 202C and 301. The Applicant conducted a review of potential flare-up symptoms and treatments in 202B, purportedly showing that multiple subjects had, in retrospect, remained untreated or undertreated for certain flare-up symptoms (and thus remained at the 5 mg chronic daily dose without flare-up dosing), and in some cases accrued large volumes of new HO at the site of the symptoms. FDA reviewers requested additional information regarding undertreatment of flares in 202B, but ultimately, did not find these data or rationale convincing and determined that the 202B efficacy data cannot be reliably interpreted.
L398: The study populations of Studies 202 and 301 differed in certain aspects: most of the subjects in Study 202 began treatment in Study 201 because of an acute flare-up, so they may have had a more active disease state compared to subjects in Study 301, in which enrollment required the absence of a recent flare-up. In addition, subjects began chronic treatment in 202B or 202C without regard to the timing of their last flare-up. Therefore, subjects with flare-up symptoms within 1 month of chronic treatment baseline (thus, experiencing possible residual HO formation at the flare-up site) were excluded from analyses to align with Studies 301 and NHS. With these exclusions, the mean new HO volume for 202C subjects (unadjusted data) declined somewhat, to 19.0 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}.
L399: Study 202C subjects were also older than Study 301 and NHS subjects, with more advanced disease, and had already undergone treatment with palovarotene under various regimens prior to 202C, whereas the Study 301 subjects were treatment-naïve at enrollment. In order to increase comparability between the Study 202C and NHS populations, FDA requested matched and propensity score weighted analyses, which suggested similar efficacy to that observed in Study 301 (See Section 6.2.2.4).
L400: In addition, data from 202C subjects following the extended treatment pause were requested by FDA. The new HO volume data showed a pattern similar to Study 301 subjects, with an initial increase from the pre-pause treatment to the treatment interruption phase, followed by a decline after treatment re-start.
L401: ## Conclusion
L402: Based on additional data and analyses, FDA reviewers have concluded that the differing outcomes of Studies 301 and 202C do not present a major concern. When differences in study populations were partially accounted for in matched pair and propensity score weighting analyses, Study 202C versus NHS comparisons were favorable to palovarotene treatment, and consistent with the Study 301 versus NHS data. In addition, data on 202C subjects who restarted treatment following the 2019 to 2020 treatment pause show substantially smaller volumes of new HO compared to the pre-pause period, which were similar to an analogous group in Study 301.
L403: ## 7. Safety (Risk and Risk Management)
L404: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L405: The preclinical safety of palovarotene was adequately assessed in a comprehensive nonclinical development program that was submitted and reviewed with the original NDA and included general, reproductive, and genetic toxicity studies. Dedicated rodent carcinogenicity studies to assess the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene have not been conducted; instead, the Applicant assessed the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene using a weight of evidence (WoE) approach outlined in an amendment to International Council for Harmonization S1B(R1). The nonclinical review team in consultation with the CDER Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee (ECAC) concluded that the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene in humans is uncertain and assessment in a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study, in addition to a mouse in vivo carcinogenicity study, would add value to the assessment of human carcinogenic risk. Carcinogenicity bioassays were not considered necessary prior to submission and review of a marketing application because of the unmet medical need for the severely debilitating nature of heterotopic ossification in patients with FOP. However, while a determination of potential clinical benefit could be compared to known risks identified in the development program and unknown long term carcinogenic risk, characterization of carcinogenic potential will still be important given that FOP patients are anticipated to use palovarotene chronically.
L406: The uncertainty of palovarotene carcinogenic potential is mainly related to 1) complex target pharmacology (e.g., activation of the target transcription factor promotes cellular proliferation and RAR\gamma acts as tumor promoter in some animal models, and RAR\gamma is abundant in many human cancers); 2) positive carcinogenic outcomes associated with the retinoid class from activating the same drug target; and 3) histopathological changes of concern (epithelial hyperplasia and chronic inflammatory changes in the skin and stomach), which occurred at clinically relevant exposures with inadequate alternative mechanistic explanation in the 6-month rat study and which were supported by similar findings (skin) in cynomolgus monkeys (see Section 13). Therefore, rodent carcinogenicity studies in two species to assess the carcinogenic potential from long-term oral exposure to palovarotene are being recommended as post marketing requirements.
L407: ## 7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L408: Retinoids are associated with numerous class-related adverse effects. For this application, the two most serious safety concerns are PPC and embryo-fetal toxicity, which have been reported with other retinoids and are discussed in Sections 7.7.2 and 7.7.3, respectively. Reduced bone mineral density appears to be associated with palovarotene and other retinoids and is discussed in Section 7.7.4. Other potential retinoid class effects include neuropsychiatric effects, including depression, suicidality, seizures and pseudotumor cerebri; mucocutaneous adverse effects; serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome; musculoskeletal effects including arthralgia and back pain; hypersensitivity reactions; acute pancreatitis; hepatotoxicity; elevated triglycerides; inflammatory bowel disease; hearing impairment; and eye abnormalities including decreased night vision.
L409: ## 7.3. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L410: Palovarotene was approved to treat patients with FOP in Canada in January 2022, but no patients have yet been treated with commercially supplied drug, therefore, no postmarketing data are available. Palovarotene has not been approved in any other country to date.
L411: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L412: The bulk of the FOP/palovarotene safety data comes from patients exposed to the 5 mg chronic (nonflare) dose or the 20/10 mg flare-up regimen (all doses weight adjusted when appropriate) in Studies 202B, 202C and 301. This review focuses primarily on pooled safety data from these studies for each of these two regimens in the Applicant's intended target population of females \ge 8 years of age and males \ge 10 years of age (referred to as \ge 8/10), which represents 139 of the total 164 FOP subjects who received palovarotene in any study (the FOP-FAS). Safety data for younger children (ages &lt; 8/10) are generally consistent with the intended target population, with the possible exception of PPC, as discussed below. Palovarotene exposure related to lower-dose flare-up regimens (10/5 mg and 5/2.5 mg) was relatively limited and is not discussed in this review, except for data related to new flare-ups.
L413: The \ge 8/10 safety data presented here were compiled by Clinical Data Scientist staff from Studies 202B/202C/301 from the integrated summary of safety (ISS) datasets in the first NDA resubmission (April 29, 2022), using the cutoff date of July 31, 2021. Subsequent safety updates were submitted on August 10, 2022, and on February 16, 2023 (with this second NDA resubmission) and are of interest primarily for updated bone safety information related to PPC and growth.
L414: The NDA includes extensive safety data related to non-FOP indications: pediatric patients with multiple osteochondromas; six phase 1 and 2 studies in adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); and 12 single- and multiple-dose studies in healthy volunteers.
L415: In addition to routine safety assessments (adverse events [AEs], concomitant medications, vital signs, electrocardiogram, physical exam, safety labs), the FOP palovarotene studies included
L416: frequent pregnancy testing, the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), and assessments related to bone safety and growth; the latter are discussed in Section 7.7.1. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were protocol-defined as AEs that developed or worsened after administration of the first dose to 7 days after the last dose of study drug and were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 22.0. AEs were not collected systematically in the NHS because there was no treatment. As discussed in the previous Integrated Review of this NDA, no major data quality or integrity issues were identified that would preclude performing the safety review.
L417: ## 7.5. Adequacy of the Clinical Safety Database
L418: The NDA 215559 safety database for palovarotene is adequate to evaluate the proposed FOP indication and dosage regimens. The FOP phase 2 and 3 studies enrolled a relatively large proportion of the known patients with this disease globally. Although comparison safety data in untreated FOP patients is very limited, there is substantial placebo-controlled data available for palovarotene in prior COPD studies (adults) and a multiple osteochondromas study (pediatric), and the safety profile of retinoids as a drug class is well known from extensive experience with other retinoids.
L419: A total of 164 patients with FOP received at least one dose of palovarotene, including 139 patients in the Applicant's intended target population (age \ge8/10 years). Serious AEs were reported in 24% of subjects while receiving the chronic 5 mg regimen, and in 23% of subjects while receiving the 20/10 mg flare-up regimen. These two regimens were also similar with regard to overall AEs (97% versus 94%) and AEs leading to drug interruption or discontinuation. L446: ## 7.6.1.2. Deaths
L447: No deaths were reported during palovarotene treatment or for 30 days post-treatment in the FOP-FAS, including the post-pause period per the most recent safety update. As discussed in the previous Integrated Review for this NDA, one FOP subject from Study 301 died 2.5 months after discontinuing palovarotene, attributed to restrictive lung disease from complications of FOP. In addition, there was one death of a FOP NHS subject who never received palovarotene.
L448: There have been no deaths reported in the multiple osteochondroma or healthy volunteer study populations from other programs. Deaths reported in the COPD program were generally related to age and underlying disease; none were assessed as related to study treatment by the Investigator.
L449: ## 7.6.1.3. Serious Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
L450: Serious adverse events (SAEs) were frequently reported in all FOP palovarotene studies, including 24% of subjects during chronic dosing and 23% of subjects during flare-up dosing within the \ge8/10 target population. The most frequently reported system organ class of SAEs was musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders, which in addition to PPC included events that could be associated with retinoids or with the underlying disease FOP, such as arthralgia, back pain and pain in extremity. The next most frequently reported system organ class of SAEs was infections, especially pneumonia, cellulitis and COVID; FOP patients are known to be at increased risk for pneumonia, right-sided heart failure and thoracic insufficiency, and 16% of NHS subjects experienced pneumonia. There were SAEs of tonic chronic seizure, epilepsy, syncope and myoclonus reported in one phase 2/3 subject each. While other retinoids may be associated with seizure, numerous NHS and Study 301 subjects reported a prior history of
L451: seizures. Overall, many of the reported SAEs (with the exception of PPC) appear to be more likely related to the disease rather than treatment, but this is difficult to determine in the absence of a suitable control group in these studies.
L452: For further details, see the previous NDA Integrated Review (December 23, 2022, in DARRTS), which included a list of all SAEs reported in the \ge 8/10 subset of the FOP-FAS through the July 31, 2021, cutoff date. Because numerous subjects in Studies 202C and 301 restarted palovarotene after the treatment pause at various dates in 2020 to 2021, additional SAEs are included in safety updates through the most recent cutoff (April 27, 2022). The new events are most notable for a substantial increase in the number of SAEs of COVID-19 infection, and do not change the safety profile of palovarotene in the FOP population.
L453: The labeled prescribing information for other retinoids (e.g., isotretinoin, soriatane, bexarotene) includes warnings regarding certain AEs that appear to be class-related: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperlipidemia, serious skin reactions (e.g., Stevens Johnsons syndrome) and intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) (Teva 1982; Stiefel 1996; Ligand 1999). In FOP clinical studies of palovarotene, there were no reported instances of serious or severe AEs in these categories. Therefore, the clinical judgment of reviewers is that current evidence does not support labeled warnings/precautions for these conditions, but rather these will be included in section 6: Adverse Reactions based on assumed class effects.
L454: ## 7.6.1.4. Adverse Events Leading to Treatment Discontinuation
L455: Among FOP subjects age \ge 8/10 years, treatment was discontinued due to an AE in 6/131 subjects (4.6%) during treatment with chronic 5 mg dosing, and in 5/105 subjects (4.8%) during treatment with 20/10 mg flare-up dosing. The only AE resulting in &gt;1 treatment discontinuation was dry skin (1 subject with each regimen). The other AEs causing discontinuation during chronic dosing were furuncle, amylase increased, lipase increased, epiphyses premature fusion, myoclonus, intentional self-injury, and erythema. The other AEs causing discontinuation during flare-up dosing were cellulitis, hemophilus infection, localized infection, malnutrition and mobility decreased.
L456: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
L457: Mucocutaneous adverse effects such as dry skin, rash, pruritus, alopecia and dry mouth were the most frequently reported adverse effects, similar to previous experience with other retinoids and hypervitaminosis A. The previous NDA Integrated Review included summaries of TEAEs in the \ge 8/10 population according to the most frequent preferred terms and by System Organ Class/Narrow FDA Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities query (FMQ).

Most of the adverse reactions included in the table represent narrow FMQ groupings of &gt;1 preferred term, which are listed in the table footnotes. Many of these reactions are characteristic of retinoids, and in most cases the incidence in chronic versus flare-up dosing was similar.

L475: Severe mucocutaneous AEs were reported in 51% of FOP subjects and included skin exfoliation (31%), drug eruption (i.e., retinoid dermatitis, 18%) and blisters (7%). Mucocutaneous events were the most common reason for dose reductions, especially at the higher 20/10 mg flare-up doses; in almost all cases, subjects were able to continue treatment with lower doses and/or supportive measures such as skin lotions, lip balm, artificial tears, etc.
L476: Because of the association of retinoids with depression and potential suicidality, the C-SSRS was administered to all study participants age ≥8 years in Study 301 as well as the NHS. There was no evidence of an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior. The FMQ for depression identified 11% of subjects, and one subject discontinued treatment after 1 month due to “non-suicidal/intentional self-injury.”
L477: Hearing impairment is a common feature of FOP and was reported by 43% of NHS subjects. Audiometry in Study 301 confirmed high rates of hearing loss at baseline; the incidence and type of abnormal clinically significant findings at 12 months was similar to baseline. Hearing impairment TEAEs were reported in 12% of palovarotene-treated subjects in the FOP-FAS, with similar incidence during chronic and flare-up treatment (7% versus 8%, respectively); none of these events were considered severe or led to discontinuation of treatment. AEs of hearing
L478: impairment were much less frequent in subjects with multiple osteochondroma or COPD, with no imbalances between palovarotene and placebo.
L479: ## 7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings
L480: As discussed in the previous Integrated Review, several FOP subjects developed minor triglyceride elevations, and one healthy subject in a phase 1 drug-drug interaction study was hospitalized with acute pancreatitis with elevated lipase, probably due to interaction with the CYP3A inhibitor ketoconazole. There were no other clinically meaningful changes in hematology or serum chemistry evaluations.
L481: ## 7.6.1.7. Assessment of Drug-Induced Liver Injury
L482: Moderate transaminase elevations were observed in several palovarotene-treated FOP subjects, particularly with the higher 20/10-mg doses, consistent with a retinoid effect. No subjects met Hy's Law criteria.
L483: ## 7.6.1.8. Vital Signs
L484: As previously reviewed, there were no consistent or clinically meaningful changes from baseline in blood pressure or heart rate associated with palovarotene treatment.
L485: ## 7.7. Key Safety Review Issues
L486: ## 7.7.1. Increased Rate of Reported Flare-Ups During Palovarotene Treatment; Potential for Retinoid-Induced Myositis
L487: ## Issue
L488: Increased rate of reported flare-ups during palovarotene treatment; potential for retinoid-induced myositis.
L489: ## Background
L490: The rate of new FOP flare-up episodes was assessed in the NHS and palovarotene studies and is relevant to both efficacy and safety. Flare-up incidence and rate were designated in phase 3 as secondary efficacy endpoints to assess whether chronic palovarotene treatment may suppress the initiation of new flare-ups, in addition to potentially suppressing formation of new HO. However, retinoids, and vitamin A in toxic doses, have been associated with hyperostosis and calcification of ligaments and tendons; musculoskeletal adverse effects including back pain, arthralgia, myalgia; and rare reports of severe myositis, sometimes associated with strenuous physical activity. Because FOP flare-ups are frequently triggered by local inflammation or trauma and are characterized by ossification of muscle and other soft tissues, there is a theoretical concern for induction or exacerbation of flare-ups by palovarotene.
L491: ## **Assessment**
L492: In all FOP studies, subjects were instructed to call the study site immediately for potential flare-up symptoms, but the process by which flare-ups were treated and reported varied.
L493: In the NHS, subjects reporting potential flare-ups were evaluated in clinic or monitored with weekly phone contacts. Subjects were also contacted by phone every 6 months between the yearly clinic visits but were not systematically asked about new flare-ups at visits and did not record symptoms in diaries.
L494: In the early phase 2 Studies 201/202A/B, flare-ups were treated if they met the following criteria: the subject had at least two out of six pre-defined symptoms (pain, soft tissue swelling, decreased ROM, stiffness, redness and warmth), it was within 7 days of symptom onset, symptoms were consistent with the subject's previous flare-up symptoms, and flares were confirmed by the investigator. Flare-ups that were not treated (i.e., not meeting these criteria, or intercurrent flare-ups at a different location during flare-up treatment) were recorded not as flare-ups per se, but as AEs under the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities preferred term of "condition aggravated."
L495: In the later phase 2 Study 202C and phase 3 Study 301, the criteria for initiating flare-up treatment were expanded such that only one symptom or a traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up was required, if consistent with previous flare-ups and confirmed by the investigator, with no requirement to start treatment within 7 days of onset. Additionally, intercurrent (or markedly worsened) flare-ups were recorded and treated as new flare-ups.
L496: ## **Flare-Up Incidence and Rate in Phase 2 Studies**
L497: During the 12-week period of treatment/follow-up of the index flare-up in Study 201, new symptoms consistent with a flare-up (i.e., condition aggravated AEs) were reported by more subjects randomized to the palovarotene 10/5 mg regimen (13/21, 62%) in comparison to the 5/2.5 mg regimen (2/9, 22%) or placebo (3/10, 30%). In addition, some of the subjects treated with the 10/5 mg regimen experienced more than one new flare-up event within the 12-week observation period, therefore the rate of new events was highest in this treatment group. However, it should be noted that subjects in this 10/5 mg arm reported a greater number of flare-ups in the year prior to enrollment (4.6) compared to the placebo and 5/2.5 mg arms (2.3, 2.0). The majority of new events occurred at a new location rather than at the original flare-up location. Two of the events in the 10/5 group were categorized as SAEs of condition aggravated.

L520: As noted by the Applicant, these differences in flare-up rate may be explained, at least in part, by differences in reporting related to study design and conduct. Although Studies 301 and the NHS were conducted mostly at the same institutions, with similar adjunctive care (e.g., corticosteroids for certain flare-ups), NHS subjects generally had less frequent contact with study staff. Phone contacts were primarily every 6 months in the NHS; in Study 301, subjects were contacted every three months during chronic dosing and every 4 weeks during flare-up dosing. Study 301 subjects were asked to maintain daily symptom diaries, which were reviewed at clinic visits; NHS subjects did not use diaries and may have been less motivated to report symptoms that were not intended for any treatment. In addition, worsening of flare-ups was not systematically recorded in the NHS, unlike Study 301. A published survey of untreated FOP patients has reported an average rate of 0.16 flare-ups per month, (Pignolo et al. 2016), potentially supporting that these events may have been under-reported in the NHS.
L521: In addition, among the 39 subjects who crossed over from the NHS to Study 301, the mean number of flare-ups recorded prospectively in the last 12 months of the NHS was 0.6; at the time of enrollment in Study 301, the same 39 subjects reported (retrospectively) a mean of 1.1 flare-ups during the previous 12 months (the same time period) (Table 20.1.35.1 in the integrated summary of effectiveness resubmission).
L522: In Study 301, many subjects experienced multiple flare-ups, often in succession, whereby a new event within 12 weeks of the onset of the last event would restart the 20/10 dosing regimen before chronic dosing (5 mg) could resume. Thus, a flare-up “cycle” could include one or multiple flare-ups; the mean number of flare-ups per cycle in Study 301 was 2.2 and the maximum was 23. The table below compares the rates of new flare-ups occurring during chronic dosing (i.e., the first or index flare-up of a new cycle) and during flare-up dosing (any subsequent flare-ups within a cycle). The rate of reported new flare-ups was greater during the higher dosing periods (0.33 versus 0.12 events/month). Among these follow-on events within a flare-up cycle, 82 (42%) were categorized as worsening of the initial flare-up, and 114 (58%) were categorized as intercurrent flare-ups at a new location (Table 35).

L529: The clinical significance of the number of flare-ups in these studies with regard to disease progression is unclear. Subjects reporting at least one flare-up, compared to subjects reporting no flare-ups, developed larger quantities of new whole-body HO, both in the NHS (mean 38.1 versus 6.2 cm3) and in Study 301 (mean 11.7 versus 3.2 cm3). Otherwise, the number of flare-ups did not appear to be closely related to the quantity of new whole-body HO in these studies, but the high degree of variability of HO volume data makes assessment of these relationships challenging. Among the five subjects in either the NHS or Study 301 with annualized new HO &gt;100 cm3/year, 3 of the 4 NHS subjects had reported only 1 or 2 flare-ups. The only Study 301 subject with &gt;100 cm3/year of new HO (236.8 cm3/year) was an exception, having reported 13 flare-ups; however, other subjects reporting greater numbers of flares developed much less, or even negative, new HO.
L530: Among the 39 subjects who transferred from the NHS to Study 301, the change in number of flare-ups for a given subject did not appear to predict the change in new HO. The two subjects with the largest increases in number of flare-ups between the NHS and Study 301 (one event to 18 events, and one event to 14 events, respectively) nevertheless had large declines in rates of new HO from the NHS to Study 301.
L531: In response to FDA request, the Applicant analyzed the relationship between the rate of flare-ups and the volume of new HO. In each study (301, 202B/C, NHS), there was a positive relationship between flare rate and new HO volume, as would be expected based on the documentation of new HO at some flare-up sites (Figure 3). However, the correlations were modest even in Study 301. This is consistent with the primary analysis demonstrating significantly smaller quantities of new HO in treated subjects, despite the greater number of flare-ups. The correlation was weakest in the NHS, which may seem surprising given that flare-ups in this study were not treated; this may be related to the apparent under-reporting of flare-ups in the NHS.
L532: **Figure 3. Studies 301, 202B/C and 001 (NHS): Flare-Up Rate vs. Annualized New HO Volume**
L533: Source: NDA resubmission February 16, 2023, M1.11.4 Response to FDA CR Letter
L534: Flare-ups defined as including AEs of condition aggravated
L535: Abbreviations: AE, adverse event; CR, complete response; FDA, Food and Drug Administration; HO, heterotopic ossification; NDA, new drug application; NHS, natural history study; PVO, palovarotene; STUDYID, study identification; vs, versus
L536: The Applicant also conducted an analysis of the association between the extent of palovarotene flare-up dosing (total number of weeks exposure) with annualized new HO, and again found a weak correlation, thus no clear evidence that flare-up dosing may be a risk factor for new HO.
L537: ## Conclusion
L538: Uncertainty remains as to why flare-ups were reported more frequently during palovarotene treatment, particularly during higher-dose treatment of an initial flare-up. Anecdotally, some patients with FOP are reported to experience clusters of flare-ups at different sites in a short time. In some cases, this might be related to a rebound in symptoms following the withdrawal of glucocorticoids often used to treat the acute symptoms. Potentially, retinoids could cause myositis resulting in a flare-up, or adverse effects such as myalgia or arthralgia that could be misinterpreted as symptoms of a new flare-up.
L539: Also uncertain is whether the increase in reported flare-ups has any clinical significance with regard to disease progression. In both Study 301 and the NHS, subjects who reported at least one flare-up developed, on average, much larger quantities of new HO compared to subjects who reported no flare-ups. However, the data were highly variable. Overall, the rate of flare-ups, and the extent of palovarotene dosing, were not strong predictors of new HO in these studies. Given these uncertainties, this issue should be evaluated further in the postmarketing setting.
L540: ## 7.7.2. Premature Epiphyseal Closure in Growing Children With Potential for Adverse Effects on Growth
L541: ## Issue
L542: PPC was reported in many pediatric subjects treated with palovarotene, with potential for adverse effects on growth.
L543: ## Background
L544: Systemic retinoids, as well as vitamin A toxicity, have long been associated with a variety of adverse musculoskeletal effects. Among these are published case reports of PPC occurrence and impaired growth in children with prolonged exposure to various retinoids prescribed for the treatment of dermatologic conditions or cancer. Growth plate abnormalities and premature closure were also observed in juvenile rats exposed to palovarotene and were consistent with retinoid class effects (see Section 7.1). Prior to palovarotene studies, PPC had not been reported in patients with FOP.
L545: Because of this potential risk, palovarotene studies for the FOP indication included a Bone Safety Management Plan in pediatric subjects (&lt;18 years of age). Based on hand/wrist x-rays at screening to assess growth plates, subjects with &lt;90% skeletal maturity, defined as bone age &lt;12 years (girls) or &lt;14 years (boys), received weight-adjusted dosing. In those with open growth plates, continued monitoring included scheduled PA hand/wrist and AP knee radiographs to monitor growth plates and bone age; measurements of standing height (stadiometry) and knee height (knee caliper); and use of whole-body CT scans to measure femur and tibia length. These assessments were conducted every 6 months in Study 301 and every 6 to 12 months in Study 202B/C. Growth assessments were conducted every 12 months in the NHS.
L546: Study 301 began enrollment in November 2017. In 2019, multiple instances of PPC among pediatric subjects in this study were reported based on scheduled radiographs. In December 2019, a partial clinical hold was imposed for the dosing of any children under 14 years of age; dosing was never resumed except for children who subsequently reached age 14. Protocol Amendment 5 added an extended 2-year safety follow-up for pediatric subjects, including annual assessment of growth, hand/wrist radiograph and WBCT.
L547: ## Assessment
L548: Regarding bone safety, three pediatric age categories were evaluated in the ISS:
L549: - &lt;8 years (girls)/&lt;10 years (boys), representing a prepubertal population;
- ≥8/10 to &lt;14 years of age, representing an early adolescent population (generally early- to mid pubertal) which has, on average, attained approximately 80 to 90% of adult height; and
- ≥14 to &lt;18 years, representing a late adolescent population.
L550: In Study 301 at baseline, pediatric patients with FOP exhibited generally normal skeletal maturation: mean chronologic age and bone age by x-ray were closely matched (11.4 and 11.5 years, respectively), and all adolescents age ≥14 years had achieved ≥90% skeletal maturity, i.e., bone age ≥12 (girls) or ≥14 (boys). During palovarotene treatment, mean increase from baseline
L551: in bone age was slightly greater than mean increase in chronologic age: mean ratios of \Delta bone age/\Delta chronologic age were 1.2 to 1.4 at months 6, 12, 18 and 24. Individual changes were highly variable.
L552: Standing height was also in the normal range at baseline in most children with FOP. Table 36 presents mean height Z-scores, which ranged from -0.50 to +0.44 at baseline across the three pediatric age categories in Studies 301 and the NHS. Although there was great variability among individual subjects, these data showed a trend toward lower height Z-scores in adolescents compared to younger children at baseline; this may reflect the development of spinal deformities in some adolescents with FOP. At Month 12, mean height Z-scores declined moderately from baseline among palovarotene-treated subjects &lt;14 years of age; there were slightly smaller mean declines among untreated NHS subjects. Differences in growth between treated and untreated subjects were most apparent in subjects who developed PPC, as discussed below.

Subjects who developed PPC had received weight-based dose reductions at enrollment based on bone age indicating &lt;90% skeletal maturity.
L557: With one exception, all cases of PPC first became apparent on x-rays of the knee (partial or complete closure of distal femur and/or proximal tibia growth plates), typically on the scheduled x-rays at month 12 of treatment. PPC appeared to be bilaterally symmetric and synchronous at other joints, based on a very limited number of subjects with bilateral or additional x-rays; this issue (i.e., proportionality of PPC) was not systematically evaluated. Advances in bone age at the hand/wrist were generally similar in subjects with and without PPC. In the ISS, the Applicant evaluated palovarotene exposure (cumulative dose, duration of chronic or flare-up dosing, area under the concentration [AUC] for concentration versus time curve) for pediatric subjects with and without PPC; no consistent trends were apparent.
L558: Table 37 shows that while palovarotene treatment was associated with trends of slower growth overall in comparison to NHS subjects, the subset that developed PPC accounted for most of the difference, especially among early adolescent subjects (age \ge8/10 to &lt;14 years). In Study 301, mean standing height increase was 1.2 cm/year in this age group with PPC, compared to 3.5 cm/year in treated subjects without PPC and 4.2 cm/year in untreated subjects, and the proportion with growth velocity &lt;4 cm/year was greater (86%, 54% and 41% in these respective
L559: groups). It should be noted that this is a small subgroup (seven subjects age \ge 8/10 to &lt;14 years with PPC).

L564: Knee height and femur/tibia lengths (by CT) are presumed to be less susceptible than standing height to measurement difficulty in the presence of FOP-related deformities such as scoliosis. There were generally only small differences in these parameters between untreated NHS subjects and treated subjects without PPC. However, as with standing height, PPC was associated with trends of smaller gains in these growth parameters among subjects age \ge 8/10 to &lt;14 years.
L565: In addition to the risk of reduced stature based on growth slowing or arrest, PPC at the distal femur and/or proximal tibia has the potential to create leg length discrepancy due to asymmetric effects on the right and left leg, or abnormal knee angulation due to differential growth of medial and lateral aspects of the growth plate. These issues were systematically addressed in all pediatric subjects: the difference between right and left leg length was derived from the sum of femur and tibia lengths, as measured by whole-body CT scans, on each side; and knee angulation was measured on AP knee radiographs. These evaluations found no evidence of any differences between subjects in Studies 202B/C or 301 and the NHS overall or for subjects with or without PPC. For further details of these evaluations, refer to prior NDA Integrated Review (dated December 23, 2022, in DARRTS).
L566: ER analyses were conducted to assess the impact of palovarotene exposure on PPC risks. The results show that the risk of PPC is increased at higher palovarotene AUCs (Figure 4). However, this result is likely to be driven by patients &lt;8 years old. When only considering patients 8/10 to 13 years, there is absence of a clear relationship between the proportion of subjects with PPC and AUCs (Figure 4).

L573: In general, there is no ER relationship for palovarotene exposure and proportion of patients with PPC events for subjects greater than 8 years of age. Lowering the dose of palovarotene for patients younger than 12 years of age is not predicted to reduce risks of PPC. The review team acknowledges that this conclusion is limited by the small number of reported PPC events in the clinical studies.
L574: ## **Conclusion**
L575: The review team agrees with the Applicant that palovarotene treatment of pediatric patients with FOP is associated with a serious risk of PPC. Premature epiphyseal closure development was most apparent at the active growth plates of the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia), which is consistent with literature reports involving other retinoids. Premature epiphyseal closure was not generally associated with rapid advances in bone age as assessed by x-rays of the hand/wrist.
L576: All patients with open growth plates are likely to be at risk of PPC. Younger children (&lt;8/10 years) may be at greatest risk, but 33% of older pediatric patients (age \ge8/10 to &lt;14 years) also showed evidence of PPC in the clinical studies. The Applicant could not identify specific risk factors or a safe level of palovarotene exposure to predict the occurrence of PPC. Because PPC involved the knee and appeared to be irreversible, reduced height is expected to result.
L577: In addition to reduced stature, and potentially disproportionate growth (e.g., short legs relative to trunk), PPC of growth plates at the knee poses a potential risk of leg length discrepancy or abnormal knee angulation. Radiographs have shown no evidence of such effects in study subjects to date, but the duration of treatment and/or follow-up has been limited in most cases; longer-term data are needed.
L578: PPC and impaired growth represent a major safety risk of palovarotene treatment in children with FOP and open growth plates, which will be further investigated in the planned postmarketing safety study. To mitigate this risk to the extent possible, the indicated population should be limited to girls over the age of 8 and boys over the age of 10. Although skeletal abnormalities are a known risk for the retinoid class of products and the finding is labeled as a Warning and Precaution, palovarotene is intended to be a chronically administered product unlike other retinoid agents. Additionally, the PPC risk for palovarotene occurred earlier and more frequently. Therefore, product labeling should include a Boxed Warning for PPC because this is a serious risk in the population of patients with open growth plates and careful monitoring can mitigate that risk. Therefore, the Boxed Warning will include recommendations for patient monitoring, including height measurements and imaging of growth plates.
L579: ## **7.7.3. Embryo-Fetal Toxicity (Retinoid Class Effect)**
L580: ## **Issue**
L581: Embryo-fetal toxicity (retinoid class effect).
L582: ## **Background**
L583: Embryo-fetal toxicity has been reported with multiple retinoids and may result in irreversible fetal malformations, adverse pregnancy outcomes and stillbirths. The labeling of all approved retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin, tretinoin, bexarotene) includes Boxed Warnings for pregnancy and teratogenicity.
L584: ## **Assessment**
L585: Embryo-fetal toxicity consistent with retinoid effects was observed in fetal rat studies of palovarotene (Section 7.1).
L586: The disease burden of FOP results in low reproductive fitness, and there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP (almost all known cases of FOP result from new spontaneous mutations). Maternal FOP poses life-threatening risks for both the mother and fetus, including cardio-respiratory complications, thromboembolism, delivery complications, fetal distress, and premature birth. Consensus guidelines for FOP advise of these life-threatening risks and urge serious consideration and family planning before attempting a pregnancy. As a result of the high-risk nature of pregnancy in women with FOP, reports of miscarriage are common amongst the small number of FOP pregnancies documented in case reports. The risk of embryo-fetal toxicity from palovarotene would potentially add to the incidence of these events in the population likely to use the drug.
L587: Clinical studies of palovarotene included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements as a precaution. To date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. Based on a phase 1 study showing very low palovarotene levels in semen, administration to a male is considered to be of low risk to female partners who become pregnant.
L588: ## Conclusion
L589: The risk of teratogenicity, and other pregnancy-related risks is a class warning for retinoid products. Therefore, the palovarotene label will contain a Boxed Warning for teratogenicity. The Applicant has proposed a risk management plan that does not include a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy with the goal of educating prescribers, pharmacists, and patients about the teratogenic potential of palovarotene. This is a reasonable approach based on the following: the FOP patient population is very small and is largely managed by experts in the disease; the pregnancy risks of FOP and importance of family planning discussions are already included in consensus guidelines; pregnancy is very infrequent in FOP patients due to low reproductive fitness; and off label use of palovarotene for other indications such as acne is not expected to occur.
L590: ## 7.7.4. Apparent Adverse Effects of Palovarotene on Vertebral Bone Mineral Density, Bone Mineral Content, and Fractures
L591: ## Issue
L592: Apparent adverse effects of palovarotene on vertebral bone mineral density (BMD), bone mineral content (BMC), and fractures.
L593: ## Background
L594: Literature reports indicate that retinoids and vitamin A toxicity may cause bone demineralization, osteoporosis, or “slender long bones” in children. Labeling for isotretinoin in the treatment of acne includes a Warning for negative effects on BMD seen in clinical trials. There is no definitive evidence of an increase in fractures related to retinoid use.
L595: ## Assessment
L596: Assessments of BMD and BMC by dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) were not included in the palovarotene FOP studies because of the likely confounding effects of extensive HO in overlying
L597: soft tissues. However, DXA was conducted on subjects ages 2 to 14 years with multiple osteochondromas in study PVO-2A-201 under another program. Although treatment duration was limited in most subjects due to early termination of the trial, there were discernable trends of reduced BMC accrual in the palovarotene 5 mg treatment group compared to the 2.5 mg and placebo groups. Figure 6 shows that lower BMC in the 5 mg group appeared to persist at the follow-up visit 6 months after discontinuation of the drug.
L598: **Figure 6. Lumbar Spine BMC, Percent Change From Baseline, in Subjects With MO Who Completed 12 Months of Treatment (Study PVO-2A-201)**
L599: Source: Study PVO-2A-201 CSR Figure S27B.1C
L600: Abbreviations: BMC, bone mineral content; CSR, clinical study report; MO, multiple osteochondromas; n, number of subjects; PVO, palovarotene; SD, standard deviation
L601: Because of this adverse BMC trend in the multiple osteochondroma trial, the FOP DMC requested retrospective re-evaluation of the WBCT scans from FOP patients in Studies 301 (palovarotene treated) and the NHS (untreated) for the assessments related to vertebral structural integrity listed below. It should be noted that these measures have not been validated by FDA for assessment of fractures or estimation of fracture risk in clinical trials; standard radiographs are considered the gold standard for assessment of vertebral fractures. In addition, the populations of Studies 301 and the NHS differed in age and possibly other factors due to the lack of randomization.
L602: Biomechanical CT (BCT) analysis was conducted at L1, L2 or adjacent vertebrae (i.e., T12 if either L1 or L2 was not evaluable) to derive the following parameters:
L603: - Estimated bone compressive strength (Newtons) by finite element analysis
- Trabecular volumetric BMD (\text{mg}/\text{cm}^3) of the central vertebral body
- BMC (g) of the entire vertebral body
L604: The Applicant analyzed the data for changes from baseline, with adjustments for covariates, and reported nominally significant associations of palovarotene treatment with lower values for each of these parameters.
L605: Vertebral fracture analysis of T4 through L4 vertebrae was conducted using automated placement of six points to outline vertebral morphometric shape, which were used to calculate deformity ratios for grading using established criteria of Genant:
L606: - Normal (Grade 0; deformity &lt;20%)
- Mild (Grade 1; deformity \ge 20\% to &lt;25%)
- Moderate (Grade 2; deformity \ge 25\% to &lt;40%)
- Severe (Grade 3; deformity \ge 40\%)
L607: The prevalence of these fractures on baseline imaging was 21.5% in palovarotene-treated subjects (Study 301) and 23.6% of untreated subjects (NHS). At 12 months, 28.4% of palovarotene-treated subjects (Study 301) and 11.6% of untreated subjects (NHS) were found to have at least one new-onset vertebral fracture that was not present at baseline. For the target \ge 8/10-year-old population, these proportions were 24.2% and 11.8%, respectively. The 12-month incidences of at least one new-onset moderate/severe fracture (Grade 2 or 3) were 8.6% (palovarotene) and 4.7% (untreated) overall, or 9.1% and 4.4% for the \ge 8/10 population. The report indicates that all of these apparent fractures were asymptomatic.
L608: The Applicant also analyzed clinical fracture AEs in the FOP-FAS: normotopic bone fractures were reported in 13/164 subjects (7.9%), including 2/23 subjects (8.7%) in the placebo arm.
L609: ## Conclusion
L610: The results of the BCT analysis suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD. Prior vertebral fractures appeared to be highly prevalent at baseline in FOP studies given the young age of the population, which may be disease related, and new abnormalities occurred at a higher rate in palovarotene-treated versus untreated patients over 12 months. These effects are consistent with some data involving other retinoids, but do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures, and differences between the populations of the two nonrandomized studies. This issue will be further explored in the planned postmarketing study.
L611: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L612: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L613: ## Age, Sex, Race, and Health Status
L614: Based on a population PK analysis of palovarotene plasma concentration data from 577 subjects, age (2 to 85 years), sex, race (Asian, black, white, and other), and health status (healthy volunteers, FOP, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and multiple osteochondromas) were not significant covariates on the PK of palovarotene. According to the population PK analysis, body weight (13 to 130 kg) has a significant impact on palovarotene PK, resulting in increasing exposure with decreasing weight at the same dose.
L615: ## **Renal Impairment**
L616: Renal excretion is a minor elimination route of palovarotene based on the mass balance study. No dedicated PK study was conducted in subjects with renal impairment. According to the Applicant's population PK analyses, there was no evidence that serum creatinine affected palovarotene PK. However, since severe renal impairment may potentially affect the drug's hepatic metabolism, there is a concern of increased exposure in severely renally impaired patients. While no dose adjustment is needed for patients with mild-to-moderate renal impairment, the use of palovarotene in patients with severe renal impairment is not recommended.
L617: ## **Hepatic Impairment**
L618: No dedicated PK study was conducted in subjects with hepatic impairment. Population PK analyses suggest that there was no significant difference in the PK of palovarotene in subjects with mild (Child-Pugh A, N=66) hepatic impairment compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene is not conclusive based on the population PK analyses as only a limited number of subjects (N=5) with moderate hepatic impairment were included. The effect of severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene has not been evaluated. Given that 97.1% of radioactivity was recovered in feces in the mass balance study and that palovarotene is extensively metabolized by CYP enzymes, palovarotene exposure may likely be increased in subjects with moderate or severe hepatic impairment.
L619: Therefore, the use of palovarotene is not recommended for subjects with moderate and severe hepatic impairment. A postmarketing requirement will be issued to conduct a hepatic impairment study and evaluate the effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) and severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene to inform the dosing recommendations in subjects with hepatic impairment.
L620: More details on intrinsic factors of palovarotene can be found in the Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022.
L621: ## **8.2. Extrinsic Factors**
L622: ## **8.2.1. Food Effect**
L623: The Applicant proposed taking palovarotene capsules with food, preferably at the same time each day. The capsules may be swallowed whole or opened and the contents emptied onto a teaspoon of soft food. This proposal is supported by the food effect data and the administration instructions from Study 301.
L624: Following oral administration of two 10 mg palovarotene capsules after a high-fat breakfast, palovarotene maximum plasma concentration (C_{max}) and AUC_{0-inf} were 15% and 39% higher, respectively, when compared to exposures under fasting conditions. Following administration of the palovarotene capsules by sprinkling the contents onto one teaspoon of apple sauce after a high-fat breakfast, both AUC and C_{max} were comparable to when the capsules were swallowed whole after a high-fat breakfast.
L625: The review team adds several examples of soft food such as apple sauce, low-fat yogurt, or warm oatmeal under the administration instruction section of the label, if patients choose to take palovarotene with soft food. The stability of palovarotene when mixed with low-fat yogurt and warm oatmeal was found to be acceptable from a chemistry, manufacturing, and controls perspective. In addition, the Study 301 protocol did not specify any soft food, which allows multiple soft food options with palovarotene. The review team also recommends adding “do not administer with grapefruit, pomelo, or juices containing these fruits” under administration instructions, as palovarotene should not be taken concomitantly with strong/moderate CYP3A inhibitors. This is also consistent with the dosing instruction in the study protocol of Study 301.
L626: ## 8.2.2. Drug Interactions
L627: ## Effect of CYP3A Inhibition and Induction on Palovarotene PK
L628: Study 17041B showed that co-administration of ketoconazole 400 mg QD (a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor) and palovarotene 1 mg QD caused an increase of palovarotene AUC by 3.1-fold. Study NP17040 showed co-administration of rifampin 600 mg QD (a strong inducer of CYP3A4, 2C8, 2C19 and several transporters) and palovarotene 1 mg QD caused a decrease of palovarotene AUC by 89%. The review team agrees that the Applicant's PBPK analyses are adequate to evaluate the effects of the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin on the PK of palovarotene. The simulated geometric mean ratios of AUC_{0inf} and C_{max} for palovarotene in the absence and presence of erythromycin (500 mg QID) are 2.54 (90%CI of 2.39, 2.69) and 1.64 (90% CI of 1.59, 1.69), respectively.
L629: The review team therefore recommends that 1) palovarotene should not be taken with a strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor; and 2) if concomitant use with moderate CYP3A inhibitor is unavoidable, the dose of palovarotene should be reduced by half. In addition, the review team concludes that the PBPK analyses are inadequate to evaluate the effect of the moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz on the PK of palovarotene and agreed with the Applicant's proposal to avoid concomitant use with strong to moderate CYP3A inducers.
L630: In Study NP21025, a single oral dose of 40 mg prednisone decreased the AUC of co-administered palovarotene by 14%. However, maximum induction of CYP3A4 was not achieved with a single dose of prednisone. The results from Study NP21025 cannot be used to justify that co-administration of multiple-dose prednisone does not affect the PK of palovarotene. Population PK analyses of the PK data of 59 subjects concomitantly taking prednisone did not detect the use of prednisone as a significant covariate on the PK of palovarotene. Therefore, the review team agrees that no dose adjustment is needed for palovarotene in patients who concomitantly use prednisone.
L631: ## Effect of Palovarotene on Other Drugs
L632: Palovarotene is not expected to impact the PK of prednisone (5 mg QD of palovarotene) and midazolam (20 mg QD of palovarotene).
L633: ## **In Vitro Drug Interaction Characterizations of Palovarotene**
L634: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) Enzymes: Palovarotene is an inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, but not CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19. Palovarotene is not an inhibitor of CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4.
L635: Uridine diphosphate (UDP)-glucuronosyl transferase (UGT) Enzymes: Palovarotene is not an inhibitor or a substrate of UGT1A1, UGT1A3, UGT1A4, UGT1A6, UGT1A9 or UGT2B7.
L636: Transporter Systems: Palovarotene is not an inhibitor of P-gp, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, MATE2 K, BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and BSEP. Palovarotene is not a substrate of P-gp, BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1.
L637: More details on extrinsic factors of palovarotene can be found in the Integrated Review in DARRTS dated December 23, 2022.
L638: ## **8.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development**
L639: Palovarotene is indicated for the treatment of adults and children (females 8 years and older, and males 10 years and older) with FOP. A six-week toxicity study was conducted in juvenile rats with oral palovarotene administered daily at 0.1, 0.5 or 1.2 mg/kg/day from postnatal Weeks 3 through 9 (prior to the closure of epiphyses, which normally occurs between Weeks 15 to 16).
L640: Palovarotene adversely affected skeletal growth and development resulting in abnormal bone size, shape, mass and/or geometry in juvenile rats treated at \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day (below the clinical exposure, based on AUC). Palovarotene caused dose-related thinning/closure of the physis, physeal hypertrophy and chondrodysplasia in multiple bones, decreased endochondral ossification and hypertrophic hyaline cartilage, and hypertrophy and chondrodysplasia in articular cartilage. Additionally, decreased bone density, avascular necrosis in the femoral head and neck region, and microfractures were notable at 1.2 mg/kg/day. These changes occurred with correlating decreases in bone formation markers, radiological changes (abnormal shape, diffuse bone loss, increased/decreased physis thickness, and increased space between bones). No recovery for effects on thinning/closure of the physis or chondrodysplasia were observed at \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day; partial to complete recovery of decreased bone growth were seen in animals at 0.5 mg/kg/day.
L641: ## **8.4. Pregnancy, Lactation, and Females/Males of Reproductive Potential**
L642: ## **8.4.1. Animal Data**
L643: The Applicant conducted fertility and early embryonic development studies in male and female rats and an embryo-fetal development study in a single species (rat). The Agency agreed that there was no benefit in conducting an embryo-fetal development study in pregnant animals of a second species, as palovarotene adversely affected fetal development in pregnant rats, which was consistent with the retinoid class known to carry fetal development risks. Refer to the Integrated Review dated December 23, 2022 in DARRTS for additional details regarding the outcomes and conclusions of these studies.
