L653: ## 11. Advisory Committee Summary
L654: An Advisory Committee meeting was held on June 28, 2023, to discuss the substantial evidence of effectiveness for palovarotene in the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with FOP. The committee was asked to consider if the available evidence provided by the Applicant demonstrates that palovarotene has effectiveness in treating FOP, and whether or not any potential benefit of this product outweigh its risks, both known and potential.
L655: ## **With Respect to Voting Question 1:**
L656: Does the evidence from Study 301 of palovarotene's treatment effect show the drug is effective in patients with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP)? Provide the rationale for your vote.
L657: ## **The Committee Vote Was:**
L658: Yes: 10 No: 4
L659: The majority of the Committee members (10 of 14) voted "Yes," that the evidence from Study 301 demonstrates that palovarotene is effective in patients with FOP. The members that voted yes stated that, although palovarotene failed to meet its primary endpoint, the post hoc analyses and external control NHS were consistent and supported evidence of disease management in the treated population. The four members who voted "No" cited insufficient evidence to demonstrate effectiveness, no symptomatic improvement in treated subjects, statistical design flaws, and inappropriate post hoc analyses as factors that contributed to the data being unreliable and inconclusive regarding efficacy. These members recommended that additional studies be conducted to measure endpoints related to patient function and quality of life.
L660: ## **With Respect to Voting Question 2:**
L661: Do the benefits of palovarotene outweigh its risks for the treatment of patients with FOP?
L662: - If you voted yes, provide the rationale for your vote.
- If you voted no, provide the rationale for your vote, and provide recommendations for additional data that may support a conclusion that the benefits outweigh the risks.
L663: ## **The Committee Vote Was:**
L664: Yes: 11 No: 3
L665: The majority of the Committee members (11 of 14) voted "Yes," that the benefits of palovarotene outweigh its risks for the treatment of patients diagnosed with FOP. The members that voted yes highlighted the rarity and severity of FOP, as well as the lack of current treatment alternatives, as important factors in their vote. They added that the risk of delaying access to an approved treatment in favor of gathering more conclusive evidence is outweighed by the unmet medical need in patients with FOP. The members who voted "Yes" acknowledged that the magnitude of effectiveness shown by palovarotene could be small based on the confidence intervals but emphasized that these benefits can positively impact the quality of life of those affected by this debilitating disorder. They recommended that patient selection criteria be carefully specified to mitigate palovarotene's safety risks as well as patient/family-provider discussion to ensure risks are communicated. They also recommended monitoring bone mineral density in patients, screening for premature epiphyseal closure in pediatric patients, and creation of a patient registry to better understand the FOP patient population and HO volume changes over time. The three members who voted "No" stated that Study 301 did not provide enough evidence of effectiveness in patients with FOP, thus the risk: benefit ratio could not be considered favorable. They recommended that the Applicant conduct additional studies to better characterize if palovarotene provide clinically meaningful benefit in patients with FOP, and if so, what specific patient population (e.g., severity of disease and ages) might benefit most from palovarotene.
L666: ## III. Additional Analyses and Information
L667: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L668: Refer to Integrated Review in DARRTS, dated December 23, 2022, for a summary of the product development leading up to the original NDA submission on March 31, 2021, and withdrawal of the NDA on August 12, 2021.
L669: Palovarotene is a new molecular entity. On April 29, 2022, Ipsen resubmitted their NDA for palovarotene for the 'prevention of heterotopic ossification in adults and children (aged 8 years and above for females and 10 years and above for males) with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). On December 23, 2022, FDA issued a Complete Response (CR) letter, which conveyed that Ipsen had not demonstrated efficacy of palovarotene, thus the anticipated clinical benefit in the treatment of pediatric and adult patients with FOP, specifically a benefit of palovarotene to prevent the formation of new heterotopic ossification (HO) (the proposed indication), had not been established.
L670: The CR letter further conveyed a number of major review issues that remained unresolved including: 1) the appropriateness of reliance on post hoc analyses to support efficacy; 2) the acceptability of the external control group (natural history study [NHS]) for evaluation of efficacy of the chronic/flare-up dosing regimen; 3) the uncertain implications of the observed negative new HO volume data; 4) the lack of demonstration of efficacy of flare-up-only dosing in the phase 2 studies, and inconsistency in the efficacy data pertaining to chronic/flare-up dosing between phase 2 and 3 data; 5) the potential for increased incidence of flare-ups with palovarotene treatment, particularly with higher doses, which is a concern pertaining to both the efficacy and safety of the drug in patients with FOP; and 6) the unclear plan for demonstration of substantial evidence of effectiveness to support approval.
L671: To address the review issues, FDA recommended that additional data and data analyses, as well as any other available data that may support the efficacy of palovarotene, be submitted. Refer to the CR letter in DARRTS, dated December 23, 2022, for the specific additional data and data analyses requested.
L672: On February 16, 2023, Ipsen submitted a complete response to the deficiencies outlined in the CR letter.
L673: ## 13. Pharmacology Toxicology
L674: ## 13.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application
L675: A comprehensive nonclinical development program consisting of in vitro and in vivo pharmacology and toxicology studies was conducted and reviewed under the original NDA review cycle (see Integrated Review, December 23, 2022).
L676: ## 13.2. Individual Reviews of Studies Submitted With the New Drug Application
L677: ## Carcinogenicity
L678: No rodent carcinogenicity studies were conducted with palovarotene. The Applicant conducted and submitted a weight-of evidence (WoE)-based risk assessment of palovarotene carcinogenic potential using the available nonclinical data and published information in the public domain. Based on this, the Applicant argued that palovarotene is unlikely to pose a carcinogenic hazard to patients and concluded rodent carcinogenicity studies (neither rat nor mouse) would not contribute any significant value to the human risk assessment. The following WoE factors were used to support the Applicant's conclusion:
L679: - Maximum duration of patient treatment and patient population (FOP).
- The absence of preneoplastic or neoplastic lesions in palovarotene's nonclinical chronic toxicology program or in human data.
- The lack of association between carcinogenicity risk and activation of retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR\gamma) in the publicly available literature.
- Low carcinogenicity potential identified for other marketed retinoids.
- The absence of hormonal or immunosuppression effects.
- No signal of genotoxicity.
- Reduction of unnecessary use of animals in testing.
- To remain consistent with worldwide regulatory assessments of applications, based on EMA and Health Canada acceptance of the Applicant's proposal to not conduct all routine rodent carcinogenicity studies.
L680: The nonclinical review team disagreed with the Applicant's WoE carcinogenicity conclusions. A brief discussion of WoE factors supporting the nonclinical review team's conclusions are given below:
L681: - Palovarotene pharmacology and RAR\gamma target biology
L682: Palovarotene is a retinoic acid receptor (RAR) agonist with selectivity towards the retinoic acid receptor gamma subtype (RAR\gamma), without clinically relevant off-target activity. RAR belongs to the nuclear receptor superfamily, which act as ligand-activated transcription factors, and plays a critical role in cellular proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis. Published studies describe RAR\gamma as a transcription factor for both tumor oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, depending on the type of cancer studied (Soprano and Soprano 2002; Brown and Petrie 2021). RAR\gamma overexpression has been reported in several human tumors including liver, colon, stomach, renal, ovarian, and some cases of acute myeloid leukemia (Yan et al. 2010; Huang et al. 2013; Zhu and Luo 2016; Huang et al. 2017; Conserva et al. 2019; Petrie et al. 2020; Xiu et al. 2022).
L683: Upregulation of RAR\gamma was correlated with cancer cell proliferation, metastasis, chemoresistance and poor survival of cancer patients. On the other hand, retinoids inhibit the development of different types of tumors (e.g., epithelial tumors associated with the skin, respiratory tract, stomach lung and mammary gland) (Jiang et al. 1999; Altucci and Gronemeyer 2001; Pettersson et al. 2002; Bogos et al. 2008; Bettoli et al. 2013). In fact, there are U.S. listed retinoids approved for the treatment of blood and skin related malignancies. The exact molecular mechanism of the retinoid-mediated anticancer effect is not known but is thought to be mediated primarily through induction of apoptosis and promotion of cell differentiation (Chen et al. 2014; Jin et al. 2022).
L684: Overall, the WoE suggested complex biology of the target RAR\gamma in tumor development and progression, thus there is significant potential for a target-based malignancy risk of RAR\gamma cooperating with an oncogene pathway. The palovarotene data available to date has not addressed this.
L685: ## Carcinogenicity Information With the Retinoid Class
L686: Positive tumor outcomes were reported with most of the tested retinoids in rodent carcinogenicity studies at clinically relevant exposures. In rats, pheochromocytoma in the adrenal gland was observed with oral isotretinoin (1- and 5-fold clinical dose based on body surface area comparisons) and adapalene (\ge2-fold maximum recommended human dose, body surface area). In mouse, topical tretinoin gel caused cutaneous squamous carcinoma/papilloma in females and liver tumors in males. Blood vessel tumors (hemangiomas and hemangiosarcomas at several sites) were noted with etretinate (a metabolite of acitretin) in male but not female mice at 0.5-fold maximum recommended human dose (body surface area). Moreover, photocarcinogenesis and tumor promotion were reported with approved retinoids. The human relevance of observed nonclinical tumor profiles within the retinoid drug class is unknown.
L687: ## Potential Evidence of Carcinogenicity From Nonclinical Studies With Palovarotene
L688: Palovarotene was evaluated in chronic, repeat dose toxicity studies in rats and dogs for up to 26- and 39/52-weeks, respectively. In the chronic rat study, there were preneoplastic and inflammatory findings noted in the skin (hypergranulosis, epithelial hyperplasia (acanthosis), chronic inflammation and ulceration) and forestomach (epithelial degeneration/dyskeratosis and acute keratin layer inflammation) at clinically relevant doses. The rat skin changes were consistent with similar skin findings in monkeys. The epithelial hyperplasia findings, which were not species-specific, suggest carcinogenic potential in long-term rodent carcinogenicity studies.
L689: ## Conclusion
L690: The nonclinical review team, with concurrence from the Executive CDER Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee, concluded that the cancer risk to humans is uncertain and therefore carcinogenicity studies in rats and mice would add value to human carcinogenesis risk assessment. Therefore, the nonclinical review team recommends the conduct of rodent carcinogenicity studies in two species as a postmarketing requirement to adequately assess the clinical carcinogenicity risk from long-term oral exposure to palovarotene.

- Hips – flexion (standing, sitting, or supine) [0–2 for each hip]
- Knees – flexion/extension [0–2 for each knee]
- Ankles – dorsiflexion/plantarflexion [0–2 for each ankle]
L733: Scores for each assessed area:
L734: - 0=normal to &lt;10% deficit
- 1=10% - 90% deficit
- 2≥90% deficit
L735: Possible scores:
L736: - Axial=0–6
- Upper limbs=0–12
- Lower limbs=0–12
- Total=0–30
L737: The examiner MUST also note and record if the patient:
L738: - Can walk [yes/no]
- Uses a wheelchair [yes/no]
- Needs SOME help with activities of daily living [yes/no]
- Needs COMPLETE help with activities of daily living [yes/no]
L739: Source: Bone 101 (2017): 123-128.
L740: Forearm rotation (pronation/supination), subtalar motion, and finger/toe motion are not assessed. The CAJIS for each region is based on the greatest limitation in ANY aspect of assessed function. For example, if forward flexion of the thoracic and lumbar spine is not possible but chest expansion is only minimally affected (or vice versa) then the score for the thoracic and lumbar spine would be a 2 (maximal).

L753: Details of additional statistical analyses performed for the purposes of contributing to the demonstration of the efficacy of palovarotene in the treatment of FOP are shown in the tables below.
L754: To investigate robustness of the weighted linear mixed effects (wLME) results to the impact of extreme large values of annualized new HO, the Applicant performed a threshold analysis with a threshold of 100 cm3/year. In this analysis, the values of annualized new HO greater than 100 cm3/year were replaced with the threshold 100 cm3/year (Table 41).
L755: Similar analyses with different thresholds from 90 cm3/year (new HO &gt;90 cm3/year set to 90 cm3/year) to 30 were performed (Table 42). These analyses indicate that the difference in the original wLME analysis was not likely driven by extreme large values of subjects in NHS.

L781: ## 24. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L782: - Conduct a clinical trial to evaluate the impact of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of palovarotene in subjects with moderate (Child-Pugh B) and severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment relative to healthy adult subjects with normal hepatic function, in accordance with the study design described in guidance for industry Pharmacokinetics in Patients with Impaired Hepatic Function: Study Design, Data Analysis, and Impact on Dosing and Labeling. (May 2003) Submit the subject-level datasets with the final report.
- Conduct a carcinogenicity study in rats to assess the carcinogenic potential from long-term oral exposure to palovarotene.
- Conduct a carcinogenicity study in mice to assess the carcinogenic potential from long-term oral exposure to palovarotene.
- Conduct a prospective observational registry study with safety objectives of comparing palovarotene exposed and unexposed patients with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). Evaluate risks of increased flare-up episodes, alterations in growth, and bone fractures. The registry should also collect information on women exposed to palovarotene during pregnancy to assess for adverse events related to pregnancy through the first year postpartum, and birth and developmental outcomes through the infant's first year of life. Begin safety data collection within 90 days of protocol agreement. After protocol finalization, the PMR progress report should be submitted annually as part of the NDA annual report that also includes an evaluation of the effectiveness of meeting the registry study's safety objectives. Collect 10-year safety data from a minimum of 100 subjects, approximately half of whom will be pediatric patients (8 years to less than 18 years of age for girls and 10 years to less than 18 years of age for boys), and approximately two-thirds of whom will be exposed to palovarotene.

L915: ## I. Executive Summary
L916: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L917: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare and severely disabling disease caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the activin A type I receptor ACVR1 (ALK2), which renders ALK2 constitutively active to bone morphogenetic protein ligands, drives ectopic chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, and leads to heterotrophic ossification (HO) in connective tissue, joints, and muscle.
L918: Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation indirectly by dampening bone morphogenetic protein signaling, leading to blockade of chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation in animal models.
L919: Approximately 800 confirmed cases of FOP have been reported globally. Patients with FOP develop extraskeletal bone formation in muscles, tendons and ligaments known as beginning in early childhood. HO is episodic, with some events starting with soft tissue inflammation (flare-up). The accumulation of extraskeletal bone is cumulative and irreversible, causing restriction of movement, deformities, and severe disability. Chronic complications may include chest wall deformity (thoracic insufficiency syndrome), ankyloses of the temporomandibular joints resulting in severe tooth decay and malnutrition, and localized skin breakdown. Most patients use mobility assistance by their 20's due to HO around the hips, and survival is shortened (median 56 years), usually by cardio-respiratory failure and pneumonia.
L920: Patients with FOP face a high unmet medical need, as there are no approved therapies and no therapies have been shown to treat or slow progression of HO formation and reduce overall disease burden. Current conventional therapy for FOP is aimed at symptom relief by decreasing inflammation and treating chronic pain. Symptomatic treatment with high dose steroids is often used to treat symptom “flares,” however, short term burst steroid therapy has no benefit in reducing the overall burden of HO or slowing disease progression. Attempts at surgical excision of lesions usually leads to reactivation of disease and new HO.
L921: In support of this application, the Applicant conducted a phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with FOP (Study 201), with a phase 2 open-label single arm extension study (Study 202), as well as a single arm, open-label, externally controlled phase 3 study (Study 301). The external control group for Study 301 was a 36-month natural history study (NHS), also conducted by the Applicant, in pediatric and adult patients with FOP.
L922: The proposed dosing regimen includes chronic daily treatment (5 mg), with higher-dose treatment (20 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks), with extension if needed, during symptomatic “flare-up” episodes (referred to herein as “20/10 mg” flare-up dosing). All proposed doses are adjusted based on body weight in skeletally immature patients under 18 years of age. This dosing regimen was used in Study 301. A “flare-up only” dosing
L923: regimen is proposed as an alternative treatment option for patients who are unable to tolerate chronic daily treatment, even at reduced doses. This option would consist of the same treatment for flare-ups (20/10 mg), with no chronic treatment during clinically quiescent periods (i.e., between flare-ups). The 20/10 mg “flare-up only” regimen, and 5/2.5 mg and 10/5 mg flare-up-only regimens, were used in Studies 201 and 202.
L924: The primary endpoint for Studies 201/202 was the incidence of new HO at the flare-up site 12 weeks after flare-up initiation. The primary endpoint for Study 301 was annualized change in new whole-body HO volume, and the key secondary endpoint was proportion of subjects with any new HO. Additional secondary endpoints in Study 301 included the number of body regions with new HO, the proportion of subjects reporting flare-ups, and the rate of flare-ups per subject-month. Exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in range of motion (ROM) assessed by CAJIS (Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale) for FOP, change from baseline in physical function using age-appropriate forms of the FOP-PFQ (FOP Physical Function Questionnaire), and change from baseline in physical and mental function for subjects \ge15 years old and mental function for subjects &lt;15 years old using age-appropriate forms of the PROMIS (Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) Global Health Scale.
L925: HO volume was assessed by whole-body CT scans based on prespecified body regions in Study 301 and NHS subjects using appropriate adjudication. Whole-body CT scans from Study 202 Parts B and C were read by the same imaging contractor as in Study 301 and the NHS; however, there were differences in methodology between the phase 2 and phase 3 studies. Specific inconsistencies in CT read methodology included the following: in Study 202B/C, CT scans were read by a single radiologist without concurrent comparison to any control group; CT assessments of HO volume were performed using 15 body regions in 202B/C compared to 9 body regions in 301; and 202B/C did not include systematic evaluation of intrareader agreement, similar to the random rereads conducted in Study 301/NHS.
L926: Both Studies 201/202 and Study 301 failed their respective prespecified primary efficacy analyses. In addition, none of the secondary or exploratory endpoints in Study 301 showed statistically significant differences between palovarotene-treated and untreated/control subjects and thus did not provide supportive evidence of the efficacy of palovarotene in the treatment of FOP.
L927: ## Key Efficacy Issues
L928: The Applicant relied on post hoc analyses from Study 301 to support effectiveness. The following key efficacy issues were identified during the review.
L929: ## Appropriateness of Reliance on Post Hoc Analyses To Support Efficacy
L930: Post hoc analyses are generally considered hypotheses generating and usually not appropriate for providing substantial evidence of effectiveness. However, in this specific setting, the Agency acknowledged that the prespecified primary analysis had a bias against palovarotene. Therefore, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) statistical team considered it was reasonable to look at alternative, more appropriate analyses. Various post hoc analyses performed by the review team suggested that there could have been a nominally significant difference between the primary outcomes of Study 301 and NHS subjects if appropriate analyses had been used.
L931: However, this finding relied on an unverifiable assumption that no other unmeasured confounding factors could have substantially impacted the study results.
L932: In additional post hoc analyses, the Applicant pooled treated subjects from Study 201/202 and Study 301 and compared HO volumes to all untreated control patients from Study 201 and the NHS. These analyses pose multiple statistical challenges for the following reasons: multiple different dosing regimens were used in phase 2 and phase 3; different criteria for treating flares were used in phase 2 versus phase 3 (such that flares were generally undertreated in Study 201/202); a large variability in “placebo” response was observed in the NHS, in which change in HO volume ranged from ~-91000 to +39000; the methods used to determine changes in HO volume by whole-body CT scan differed between the phase 2 and phase 3 trials; and some patients carried over from the NHS to one of the intervention trials, which may have introduced selection bias.
L933: ## **Use of an External Control Group (NHS) for Evaluation of Efficacy of the Chronic/Flare-up Regimen**
L934: When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. Compared to Study 301, NHS subjects were older and had more severe disease severity at baseline. The FDA statistical team performed various analyses to assess the impact of baseline imbalances in selected covariates. However, these analyses could not address the impact of unmeasured and unknown confounding. Furthermore, some NHS subjects were enrolled into Study 301 or other intervention studies after some period of observation in the NHS. The possibility of subject selection bias could not be ruled out. The submission did not address these concerns adequately.
L935: ## **Uncertain Clinical Implications of Negative New HO Volume Data**
L936: Based on the natural history of disease progression in FOP, in which HO accumulates gradually over time, the clinical significance of negative HO volumes remains unclear. Whether negative HO volume as assessed by CT scan represents “noise” due to inflammation occurring at an initial flare-up site, or a natural process of bone consolidation as the transition from cartilaginous tissue to bone occurs, or some other physiologic mechanism, remains unknown. Therefore, how to account for negative HO volume change in a study assessing effects of a drug on total HO volume, in which negative HO volumes were seen in both treated and untreated subjects, was not made evident or justified by the Applicant.
L937: ## **Phase 2 Studies: Efficacy of Flare-up-Only Dosing Was Not Established; Efficacy Data Pertaining to Chronic/Flare-up Dosing Were Generally Not Consistent With Phase 3 Data**
L938: The primary efficacy endpoint in phase 2 was the proportion of flare-ups resulting in significant new HO (Studies 201, 202A, 202B), and this endpoint was not met with palovarotene treatment compared to placebo. Thus initially, only flare-up dosing (without chronic dosing) was given in phase 2, in contrast to phase 3 (Study 301), in which patients were treated with both chronic and flare-based dosing. Complicating the phase 2 analyses, Studies 202B and 202C subsequently added chronic daily 5 mg dosing to the flare-based regimen, and the primary endpoint was changed to reduction in annualized new whole-body HO volume compared to untreated NHS patients (similar to the primary endpoint for Study 301). Although the data comparing chronic + flare dosing in Studies 202B/202C and Study 301 to the NHS could be informative, particularly
L939: in the subsets of patients who received consistent dosing regimens, Study 202C was ongoing at the time of this NDA submission and these comparisons were not presented.
L940: Additional factors that further complicate such analyses include the following: 1) the rate of annualized new HO in Study 202B (\sim 29 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) was much higher than in Study 301 (\sim 9 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) and the NHS (\sim 24 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}), suggesting that these patient populations may have had different baseline disease severities; 2) a subset of patients were enrolled de novo into Study 202B, whereas others were initially enrolled in Study 201 after an acute flare-up and then transferred to Study 202B/C; 3) patients in Study 202B/C were 3 to 5 years older compared to patients in Study 301 and the NHS; and 4) Study 202B and Study 301 had different criteria defining a “flare,” such that some flares in Study 202B were untreated compared to Study 301.
L941: In addition, subgroup analyses suggested that patients in Study 202B, who were undertreated for flare-up symptoms that did not meet the stricter flare-defining criteria, had a higher mean volume of new HO (33.5 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) compared to patients in Study 202B whose flare symptoms were treated (-3.0 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) because they met the stricter flare-defining criteria. This finding is inconsistent with the data specific to 202 Part C, in which all flare-up symptoms were treated but rates of new HO remained high. Further, the data from Study 202B/C for patients who received chronic 5 mg dosing and experienced no flare symptoms or flare-based dosing suggest that chronic dosing had no effect to prevent new HO, as these patients had high levels of new HO (\sim 29 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) despite continuous 5 mg dosing; this is inconsistent with the Study 301 and NHS data, in which patients who did not require flare-based dosing had low volumes of new HO (\sim 3 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year} in Study 301 and \sim 7 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year} in the NHS, respectively).
L942: Because of these inconsistencies of the Study 202B/C versus Study 301 data and the complicating factors of interim protocol changes and differences in study populations, a more complete assessment of palovarotene efficacy in FOP will require further analyses of the 202B/C data, including (but not limited to) comparisons to untreated NHS subjects; control of covariates; comparisons including additional data collected after the original cut-off date submitted in the NDA; and analyses comparing whole-body CT data from Study 202C and Study 301 to the NHS.
L943: ## Risk Assessment
L944: Safety risks associated with palovarotene include those directly associated with the retinoid drug class of medications, as well as risks seen specifically in patients with FOP. Boxed Warnings and Warnings and Precautions contained in the retinoid class product labels include teratogenicity, psychiatric disorders, pseudotumor cerebri, serious skin reactions, pancreatitis, lipid abnormalities (hypertriglyceridemia), hearing impairment, hepatotoxicity, inflammatory bowel disease, skeletal abnormalities including decreased bone mineral density, hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure, and vision impairment.
L945: Regarding the risk of premature physeal closure (PPC) seen with the retinoid class, treatment with palovarotene caused PPC in subjects with open growth plates despite lower, weight-based dosing in younger patients. Potentially, this could result in significant adverse effects on growth, especially in younger age groups. The Applicant proposed an indication that would allow most patients with at least 80% skeletal maturity (bone age 8 years in girls and 10 years in boys) to receive palovarotene for the prevention of HO despite the risk of PPC, given the severity of the disease.
L946: Palovarotene is a known teratogen as a member of the retinoid class; however, there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP, and consensus guidelines urge serious consideration before women with FOP attempt pregnancy given that pregnancy is extremely high risk. As a precaution, clinical studies of palovarotene have included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements, and to date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. The Applicant proposed a Boxed Warning in labeling to mitigate this risk.
L947: Regarding effects on bone mineral content, bone density and fractures, results of a biomechanical CT and vertebral fracture analysis suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD, and a higher risk of new onset morphometric vertebral fractures. These effects are consistent with some data involving other retinoids and are consistent with the BMD findings by DXA in osteochondroma subjects. However, the data do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of non-validated measures and differing amounts of follow-up data between the nonrandomized populations of Study 301 and the NHS.
L948: There is an unresolved concern that palovarotene for patients with FOP could increase the incidence of HO flare-ups. FOP flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in Study 301 compared to untreated subjects in the NHS and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month), and within Study 301, new flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Most of the new flare-ups occurred at sites distant from the initial site. Similarly, data from Studies 201/202 showed higher rates of new flare-ups during flare-up dosing with palovarotene 10/5 mg or 20/10 mg (0.18 to 0.29/month) in comparison to placebo or NHS untreated subjects (0.11 to 0.12/month), or chronic 5 mg dosing (0.10/month). However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS, so the validity of these findings remains unclear. The potential risk of an increase in HO flares during treatment with palovarotene was not identified by the Applicant nor was this risk included in proposed product labeling. Additional analyses will be necessary to better determine the potential for palovarotene treatment to worsen disease severity and posing a safety risk by increasing HO formation.
L949: ## Conclusions
L950: Overall, the Applicant has not demonstrated substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene in the treatment of pediatric or adult patients with FOP. As the benefit has not been established, a meaningful benefit-risk assessment cannot be performed. Thus, the data submitted in NDA 215559 do not support approval of palovarotene for prevention of HO in pediatric or adult patients with FOP, and the application will receive a Complete Response. A potential path forward for the Applicant to attempt to demonstrate substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene for the treatment of FOP would include additional data analyses comparing similarly treated subjects from the phase 2 and phase 3 trials and the NHS in order to resolve the numerous review issues pertaining to efficacy discussed above, particularly the inconsistencies and discrepancies in the results between the phase 2 and phase 3 trials. It is recommended that such analyses include all patients and trial data until study close-out for the intervention trials and the NHS so that the Agency can make the most informed decision about a benefit-risk assessment for palovarotene in patients with FOP in a future resubmission.

Analysis of Condition	
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare, severely disabling disease caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the activin A type I receptor ACVR1 (ALK2). The most common mutation (>90%) is arginine 206 to histidine (R206H), which renders ALK2 constitutively active to bone morphogenetic protein ligands, drives ectopic chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, and leads to heterotrophic ossification (HO) in connective tissue, joints, and muscle.
Approximately 800 confirmed cases of FOP have been reported globally. Patients with FOP develop extraskeletal bone formation in muscles, tendons and ligaments, known as HO, beginning in early childhood. HO is episodic, with some events starting with soft tissue inflammation (flare-up). The accumulation of extraskeletal bone is cumulative and irreversible, causing restriction of movement, deformities, and severe disability. Complications include chest wall deformity (thoracic insufficiency syndrome), ankyloses of the temporo-mandibular joints resulting in severe tooth decay and malnutrition, and localized skin breakdown. Most patients use mobility assistance by their 20's due to HO around the hips. Survival is shortened (median 56 years), most often by cardio-respiratory failure and pneumonia. There are currently no approved therapies for the treatment of FOP, thus patients face a high unmet medical need to control their disease.
Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RARγ) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation indirectly via dampening bone morphogenetic protein signaling. This is thought to lead to blockade of chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation.
FOP is a rare and serious debilitating condition caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the ALK2 receptor that manifests starting in early childhood. Patients with FOP face a high unmet medical need as no therapies have been shown to treat or slow progression of FOP, specifically the formation of HO and the resulting morbidity associated with chronic HO accumulation.
Palovarotene is a retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RARγ) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation and is thus being developed for the treatment of FOP.

The Applicant submitted post hoc analyses from Study 301 to support the effectiveness of palovarotene in treating FOP. However, the validity and acceptability of these post hoc analyses using an external control group (with multiple differences compared to the treated group with respect to demographics and disease status) are questionable. Furthermore, the post hoc analyses included negative new HO volume data, which was seen in both treated and untreated patients. The clinical significance of a decrease in HO volume over time in patients with FOP is unclear, as HO volume is known to accumulate over time as the disease progresses. Additionally, none of the secondary or exploratory endpoints in Study 301 supported a benefit of treatment with palovarotene over nontreated subjects.

Whether negative HO volume as assessed by CT scan represents "noise" due to inflammation occurring at an initial flare-up site, or a natural process of bone consolidation as the transition from cartilaginous tissue to bone occurs, or some other physiologic mechanism, remains unknown. Therefore, how to account for negative HO volume change in a study assessing effects of a drug on total HO volume, in which negative HO volumes were seen in both treated and untreated subjects, was not made evident or justified by the Applicant.
Phase 2 studies: Efficacy of flare-up-only dosing was not established; efficacy data pertaining to chronic/flare-up dosing were generally not consistent with phase 3 data.
The primary efficacy endpoint in phase 2 was the proportion of flare-ups resulting in significant new HO (Studies 201, 202A, 202B), and this endpoint was not met with palovarotene treatment compared to placebo. Thus initially, only flare-up dosing (without chronic dosing) was given in phase 2, in contrast to Study 301, in which patients were treated with both chronic and flare-up dosing. Complicating the phase 2 analyses, Studies 202B and 202C subsequently added chronic daily dosing to the flare-based regimen, and the primary endpoint was changed to reduction in annualized new whole-body HO volume compared to untreated NHS patients (similar to the primary endpoint for Study 301). Although the data comparing chronic + flare dosing in Studies 202B/202C to the NHS could be informative, especially given that the dosing was consistent across these studies,
L958: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Study 202C was ongoing at the time of this NDA submission and none of these data were presented. Further complicating these analyses, the rate of annualized new HO in Study 202B (~29 cm3/year) was much higher than in Study 301 (~9 cm3/year) and the NHS (~24 cm3/year), suggesting that these patient populations may have had different baseline disease severities; a subset of patients were enrolled de novo into Study 202B, whereas others were initially enrolled in Study 201 after an acute flare-up and then transferred to Study 202B/C; patients in Study 202B/C were 3-5 years older compared to Study 301 and the NHS; and Study 202B and 301 had different criteria defining a “flare,” such that some flares in 202B were untreated compared to 301.
Subgroup analyses suggested that patients in Study 202B who were undertreated for flare-up symptoms had a significantly higher mean volume of new HO (33.5 cm3/year) compared to patients in Study 202B whose flare symptoms were treated because they met the stricter flare-defining criteria (-3.0 cm3/year). This finding is inconsistent with the limited data specific to Part C, in which all flare symptoms were treated but rates of new HO were high. The data from Study 202B/C from patients who received chronic 5 mg dosing but no flare symptoms or flare-based dosing suggest that chronic dosing had no effect to prevent new HO, as these patients had high levels of new HO (~29 cm3/year) despite continuous 5 mg dosing; this is inconsistent with Study 301 and NHS data, in which patients who did not require flare-based dosing had low volumes of new HO (~3 cm3/year in Study 301 and ~7 cm3/year in the NHS, respectively).
Because of these inconsistencies of the Study 202B/C versus Study 301 data and the complicating factors of protocol changes and differences in study populations, a more complete assessment of palovarotene efficacy in FOP will require additional analyses of the 202B/C data, including (but not limited to) comparisons to untreated NHS subjects; control of covariates; comparisons that include additional data collected after the original cut-off date submitted in the NDA; and analyses comparing whole-body CT data from Study 202C and Study 301 to the NHS, given that the 202C and 301 treatment regimens were the same.
L959: Risk and Risk Management	
Palovarotene is a member of the retinoid class of medications and carries the risks associated with the class. Boxed Warnings and Warnings and Precautions contained in the retinoid class product labels include teratogenicity; psychiatric disorders; pseudotumor cerebri; serious skin reactions; pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity; hypertriglyceridemia; hearing impairment; inflammatory bowel disease; skeletal abnormalities, including decreased bone mineral density, hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure; and vision impairment, including corneal opacities and decreased night vision.
Palovarotene may also be associated with risks that are specific to patients with FOP. Of major concern is the potential for increased incidence of flare-ups with palovarotene treatment. FOP flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in Study 301 compared to untreated subjects in the NHS, and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month). However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS based on the study design. In addition, within Study 301, flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month, versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Similarly, data from Studies 201/202 showed higher rates of new flare-ups during flare-up dosing with 10/5 mg (0.26/month), 20/10 mg (0.18-0.20/month) and 20/10 mg (0.29/month), in comparison to flare-up dosing with 5/2.5 mg (0.08/month), placebo/NHS (0.11-0.12/month), or chronic 5 mg dosing (0.10/month).
Premature Epiphyseal closure: Systemic retinoids have long been associated with a variety of adverse skeletal effects, including premature physeal closure (PPC) and impaired growth in children. Growth plate abnormalities and premature closure were also observed in juvenile rats exposed to palovarotene and were consistent with retinoid class effects.
Treatment with palovarotene caused PPC in subjects with open growth plates. This occurred despite the weight-based dosing in younger patients. There were trends of slower growth (standing height and femur/tibia length) among some though not all subjects with PPC, and no evidence of reversibility although long term data were limited. The Applicant proposes an indication that would allow most patients with at least 80% skeletal maturity (bone age 8 years in girls and 10 years in boys) to receive palovarotene despite the risk of PPC given the severity of the disease.
Teratogenicity: Embryo-fetal toxicity has been reported with multiple retinoids and may result in irreversible fetal malformations, adverse pregnancy outcomes and stillbirths. The labeling of all approved retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin, tretinoin, bexarotene) includes a Boxed Warning for pregnancy and teratogenicity. Embryo-
Palovarotene is associated with multiple significant risks related to its mechanism of action as a retinoid derivative (e.g., teratogenicity, premature epiphyseal closure, etc.), as well as specific risks associated with its use in patients with FOP (e.g., potential increase in incidence of “flares”).
The Applicant proposed enhanced labeling to communicate the risks of teratogenicity and PPC in a Boxed Warning, Warning and Precaution, and contraindication of pregnancy, along with educational materials for prescribers, pharmacists, patients and their caregivers.
To mitigate the risk of PPC associated with palovarotene use in growing children, the Applicant proposed a lower, weight-based dosing regimen for pediatric subjects and to limit treatment to pediatric patients who have achieved at least 80% of their final adult height, which is approximately >8 years of age in girls and >10 years in boys.
The potential risk of increase in disease “flares” with flare-based treatment will need to be further investigated to determine the validity of this finding.

fetal toxicity consistent with retinoid effects was observed in fetal rat studies of palovarotene.
There are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP, and pregnancy in women with FOP poses life-threatening risks for both the mother and fetus. Reports of miscarriage are fairly common amongst the small number of FOP pregnancies documented in case reports. The risk of embryo-fetal toxicity from palovarotene would add to the incidence of these events in the population likely to use the drug. As a precaution, clinical studies of palovarotene included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements. To date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene.
Psychiatric disorders: Treatment with retinoids have been associated with depression, psychosis, and suicidal ideation. Psychiatric adverse events, including depressed mood, suicidal ideation, depression, mood changes, and memory/attention impairment were reported overall in 25 (18%) subjects in the phase 2 and 3 trials.
Effects on bone mineral content, bone density and fractures: The data submitted suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD, and a higher risk of new onset morphometric vertebral fractures. These effects are consistent with data involving other retinoids and are consistent with the BMD findings in osteochondroma subjects. However, the data do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures and differing amounts of follow-up data between the nonrandomized populations of Study 301 and the NHS. Vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) has not been validated for assessment of vertebral fractures in clinical trials, and the data collected on vertebral density and estimated strength are exploratory measures that have not been demonstrated to predict fracture risk.

L962: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L963: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is a rare and severely disabling disease caused by a gain-of-function mutation in the activin A type I receptor ACVR1 (ALK2), which renders ALK2 constitutively active to bone morphogenetic protein ligands, drives ectopic chondrogenesis and osteogenesis, and leads to HO in connective tissue, joints, and muscle.
L964: Palovarotene is an orally bioavailable retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) that appears to interfere with ALK2-mediated bone formation indirectly by dampening bone morphogenetic protein signaling, leading to blockade of chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation in animal models.
L965: Approximately 800 confirmed cases of FOP have been reported globally. Patients with FOP develop extraskeletal bone formation in muscles, tendons and ligaments known as heterotopic ossification beginning in early childhood. HO formation is episodic, with some events starting with soft tissue inflammation (flare-up). The accumulation of extraskeletal bone is cumulative and irreversible, causing restriction of movement, deformities, and severe disability. Chronic complications may include chest wall deformity (thoracic insufficiency syndrome), ankyloses of the temporomandibular joints resulting in severe tooth decay and malnutrition, and localized skin breakdown. Most patients use mobility assistance by their 20's due to HO around the hips, and survival is shortened (median 56 years), usually by cardio-respiratory failure and pneumonia.
L966: Patients with FOP face a high unmet medical need, as there are no approved therapies and no therapies have been shown to treat or slow progression of HO formation and reduce overall disease burden. Current conventional therapy for FOP is aimed at symptom relief by decreasing inflammation and chronic pain. Symptomatic treatment with high dose steroids is often used to treat symptom “flares,” however, short term burst steroid therapy has no benefit in reducing the overall burden of HO or slowing disease progression. Attempts at surgical excision of lesions usually leads to reactivation of disease and new HO.
L967: ## Potential Benefit of Palovarotene in the Treatment of FOP
L968: In support of this application, the Applicant conducted a phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study in patients with FOP (Study 201), with a phase 2 open-label single arm extension study (Study 202), and a single arm, open-label, externally controlled phase 3 study (Study 301). The external control group for Study 301 was a 36-month natural history NHS, also conducted by the Applicant, in pediatric and adult patients with FOP.
L969: The proposed dosing regimen includes chronic daily treatment (5 mg), with higher-dose treatment (20 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks, with extension if needed, referred to as “20/10 mg”) during symptomatic “flare-up” episodes (all proposed doses are adjusted based on body weight in skeletally immature patients under 18 years of age). This dosing regimen was used in Study 301. A “flare-up only” dosing regimen is proposed as an alternative treatment option for patients who are unable to tolerate chronic daily treatment, even at reduced doses. This option would consist of the same treatment of flare-ups (20/10 mg), with no chronic treatment during clinically quiescent periods (between flare-ups). The 20/10 “flare-up only” regimen, along with 5/2.5 and 10/5 regimens, were used in Studies 201 and 202.
L970: The primary endpoint for Studies 201/202A/202B was the incidence of new HO at the flare-up site 12 weeks after flare-up initiation. The primary endpoint for Study 301 was annualized change in new whole-body HO volume, and the key secondary endpoint was proportion of subjects with any new HO. HO volume was assessed by whole-body CT scans based on prespecified body regions using appropriate adjudication. CT scans from Study 202 B/C were read by the same imaging contractor as in Study 301 and the NHS; however, there were differences in the precise methodology for assessing changes in HO by whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) between the phase 2 and phase 3 studies.
L971: Additional secondary endpoints in Study 301 included the number of body regions with new HO, the proportion of subjects reporting flare-ups, and the rate of flare-ups per subject-month. Exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in ROM (range of motion) assessed by CAJIS (Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale for FOP), change from baseline in physical function using age-appropriate forms of the FOP-PFQ (FOP Physical Function Questionnaire), and change from baseline in physical and mental function using age-appropriate forms of the PROMIS (Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) Global Health Scale.
L972: Both Studies 201/202 and Study 301 failed to meet the prespecified primary efficacy endpoints. In addition, none of the secondary or exploratory endpoints in Study 301 showed statistically significant differences between palovarotene-treated and untreated/control subjects and thus did not provide supportive evidence of efficacy of this product in the treatment of FOP.
L973: Due to failure to achieve the prespecified primary endpoints, the Applicant relied on post hoc analyses from Study 301 to support the effectiveness of palovarotene. The following key efficacy issues were identified during the review.
L974: ## - Appropriateness of reliance on post hoc analyses to support efficacy
L975: Post hoc analyses are generally considered hypotheses generating and are usually not appropriate for providing substantial evidence of effectiveness. However, in this specific setting, the Agency acknowledged that the prespecified primary analysis had a bias against palovarotene. The FDA statistical team considered it is reasonable to look at alternative, more appropriate analyses. Various post hoc analyses performed by the review team suggested that there could have been a nominally significant difference between the primary outcomes of Study 301 and NHS subjects if appropriate analyses had been used; however, this finding relied on an unverifiable assumption that no other unmeasured confounding factors could have substantially impacted the study results.
L976: In additional post hoc analyses, the Applicant pooled treated subjects from Study 201/202 and Study 301 and compared HO volumes to all untreated control patients from Study 201 and the NHS. These analyses pose multiple statistical challenges for the following reasons: 1) multiple different dosing regimens were used in phase 2 and phase 3; 2) different criteria were used for treating flares in phase 2 versus phase 3 (such that flares were generally undertreated in Study 201/202); 3) a large variability in the “placebo” response was observed in the NHS, in which change in HO volume ranged from ~ -91000 to +39000; and 4) the methods used to determine changes in HO volume by whole-body CT scan differed between the phase 2 and phase 3 trials; and 5) a subset of patients carried over from the NHS to one of the intervention trials, which may have introduced selection bias.
L977: - Use of an external control group (NHS) for evaluation of efficacy of the chronic/flare-up regimen
L978: When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. Compared to Study 301, NHS subjects were older and had worse disease severity at baseline. The FDA statistical team performed various analyses to assess the impact of baseline imbalance in selected covariates. However, these analyses could not address the impact of unmeasured and unknown confounding. Furthermore, some NHS subjects were enrolled into Study 301 or other intervention studies after some period of observation in the NHS and the possibility of subject selection bias could not be ruled out. The submission did not address these concerns adequately.
L979: - Uncertain clinical implications of negative new HO volume data
L980: Based on the natural history of disease progression in FOP, in which HO accumulates gradually over time, the clinical significance of negative HO volumes remains unclear. Whether negative HO volume as assessed by CT scan represents “noise” due to inflammation occurring at an initial flare-up site, or a natural process of bone consolidation as the transition from cartilaginous tissue to bone occurs, or some other physiologic mechanism, remains unknown. Therefore, how to account for negative HO volume change in a study assessing effects of a drug on total HO volume, in which negative HO volumes were seen in both treated and untreated subjects, was not made evident or justified by the Applicant.
L981: - Phase 2 studies: efficacy of flare-up-only dosing was not established; efficacy data pertaining to chronic/flare-up dosing were generally not consistent with phase 3 data
L982: The primary efficacy endpoint in phase 2 was the proportion of flare-ups resulting in significant new HO (Studies 201, 202A, 202B), and this endpoint was not met with palovarotene treatment compared to placebo. Thus initially, only flare-up dosing (without chronic dosing) was given in phase 2, in contrast to phase 3 (Study 301), in which patients were treated with both chronic and flare-based dosing. Complicating the phase 2 analyses, Studies 202B and 202C subsequently added chronic daily dosing to the flare-based regimen, and the primary endpoint was changed to reduction in annualized new HO volume compared to untreated NHS patients (similar to the primary endpoint for Study 301). Although the data comparing chronic + flare dosing in Studies 202B/202C and Study 301 to the NHS could be informative, particularly in the subset of patients who received consistent dosing regimens, Study 202C was ongoing at the time of this NDA submission and thus these comparisons were not presented. Additional factors that further complicate such analyses include the following: 1) the rate of annualized new HO in Study 202B (\sim 29 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) was much higher than in Study 301 (\sim 9 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) and the NHS (\sim 24 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}), suggesting that these patient populations may have had different baseline disease severities; 2) a subset of patients were enrolled de novo into Study 202B, whereas others were initially enrolled in Study 201 after an acute flare-up and then transferred to Study 202B/C; 3) patients in Study 202B/C were 3 to 5 years older compared to patients in Study 301 and the NHS; and 4) Study 202B and Study 301 had different criteria defining a “flare,” such that some flares in Study 202B were untreated compared to Study 301.
L983: In addition, subgroup analyses suggested that patients in Study 202B, who were undertreated for flare-up symptoms based on stricter flare-defining criteria, had a higher mean volume of new HO (33.5 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) compared to patients in Study 202B whose flare symptoms were treated (-3.0 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) because they met the stricter flare-defining criteria. This finding is inconsistent with the data specific to 202 Part C, in which all flare-up symptoms were treated but rates of new HO remained high. Further, the data from Study 202B/C for patients who received chronic 5 mg dosing but no flare-up symptoms or flare-based dosing suggest that chronic dosing had no effect to prevent new HO, as these patients had high levels of new HO (\sim 29 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) despite continuous 5 mg dosing; this is inconsistent with the Study 301 and NHS data, in which patients who did not require flare-based dosing had low volumes of new HO (\sim 3 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year} in Study 301 and \sim 7 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year} in the NHS, respectively).
L984: Because of these inconsistencies of the Study 202B/C versus Study 301 data and the complicating factors of interim protocol changes and differences in study populations, a more complete assessment of palovarotene efficacy in FOP will require further analyses of the 202B/C data, including (but not limited to) comparisons to untreated NHS subjects; control of covariates; comparisons including additional data collected after the original cut-off date submitted in the NDA; and analyses comparing whole-body CT data from Study 202C and Study 301 to the NHS.
L985: *Conclusions on Benefit:* Overall, the data submitted fail to adequately demonstrate substantial evidence of the effectiveness of palovarotene for the treatment of adult or pediatric patients with FOP.
L986: ## Risks Associated with Treatment of Patients with FOP with Palovarotene
L987: Safety risks associated with palovarotene include those associated with the retinoid drug class of medications, as well as risks specific to the FOP patient population. Boxed Warnings and Warnings and Precautions contained in the retinoid class product labels include teratogenicity; psychiatric disorders; pseudotumor cerebri; serious skin reactions; pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity; hypertriglyceridemia; hearing impairment; inflammatory bowel disease; skeletal abnormalities, including decreased bone mineral density, hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure; and vision impairment.
L988: Regarding the risk of PPC seen with the retinoid class, treatment with palovarotene caused premature growth plate closure in subjects with open growth plates. This occurred despite the weight-based palovarotene dosing in younger patients. The Applicant proposed an indication that would allow most patients with at least 80% skeletal maturity (bone age 8 years in girls and 10 years in boys) to receive palovarotene for the prevention of HO despite the risk of premature epiphyseal closure, given the severity of the disease.
L989: Palovarotene is a known teratogen as a member of the retinoid class, however, there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP, and pregnancy is considered very high risk when it does occur. As a precaution, clinical studies of palovarotene included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements, and to date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. The Applicant proposed a Boxed Warning and contraindications to pregnancy in product labeling to mitigate the risk of teratogenicity.
L990: Regarding effects on bone mineral content, bone density and fractures, vertebral fracture analysis (VFA) suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD, and a higher risk of new onset morphometric vertebral fractures. These effects are consistent with data involving other retinoids and are consistent with the BMD findings by DXA in osteochondroma subjects. However, the data do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures (e.g., VFA) and differing amounts of follow-up data between the nonrandomized populations of Study 301 and the NHS.
L991: Specific risks of palovarotene to patients with FOP include a potential increased incidence of HO flare-ups. FOP flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in Study 301 compared to untreated subjects in the NHS, and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month). Within Study 301, flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month, versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Similarly, data from Studies 201/202 showed higher rates of new flare-ups during flare-up dosing with palovarotene 10/5 mg or 20/10 mg (0.18 to 0.29/month) in comparison to placebo or untreated NHS (0.11 to 0.12/month), or chronic 5 mg dosing (0.10/month). However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS based on the study design, so the validity of these findings remains unclear based on the Applicant's submitted data.
L992: The potential risk of an increase in HO flares during treatment with palovarotene was not identified by the Applicant nor was this risk included in proposed product labeling. Additional analyses will be necessary to better determine the potential for palovarotene treatment to worsen disease severity by increasing HO formation.
L993: *Conclusions on Risk:* Palovarotene is associated with significant risk due to the drug's mechanism of action as a member of the retinoid drug class, as well as specific risks associated with its use in patients with FOP.
L994: ## Overall Benefit-Risk Assessment
L995: Given the significant risks associated with palovarotene as a member of the retinoid drug class (e.g., teratogenicity, PPC, decrease in BMC, etc.) and the risks associated with use of palovarotene specifically in patients with FOP (namely, a potential for increased incidence of HO "flares" in treated versus untreated patients), and the lack of convincing evidence that either palovarotene chronic or flare-based dosing benefits patients with FOP by preventing HO formation or decreasing the progression of HO accumulation, the risk-benefit balance for use of this product to treat FOP is unfavorable.
L996: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L997: ## 3. Introduction
L998: Palovarotene is an orally administered retinoic acid receptor (RAR) gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist (retinoid) and is a new molecular entity. The Applicant proposes an indication for the prevention of cartilage and bone formation within soft tissues (heterotopic ossification (HO)) in adults and children (aged 8 years and above for females, and 10 years and above for males) with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). FOP is a serious disease with no approved therapies. Palovarotene has been designated as a breakthrough therapy for this indication.
L999: The proposed dosing regimen includes chronic daily treatment (5 mg), with higher-dose treatment (20 mg daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks, with extension if needed, referred to herein as “20/10 mg”) during symptomatic “flare-up” episodes of FOP (all proposed doses are adjusted based on body weight in patients under 18 years of age). This regimen was intended to be supported by a pivotal single-arm phase 3 study (PVO-1A-301) in which the primary endpoint was the volume (cm3) per year of new whole-body HO in palovarotene-treated adult and pediatric FOP subjects. The efficacy data were compared to data from an external control group from the FOP natural history study (PVO-1A-001, NHS) that was also conducted by the Applicant.
L1000: A “flare-up-only” regimen is proposed as an alternative treatment option for patients who are unable to tolerate chronic daily treatment, even at reduced doses. This option would consist of the same treatment of flare-ups (20/10 mg), with no chronic treatment during clinically quiescent periods (between flare-ups). This regimen is supported by phase 2 studies (Study PVO-1A-201, “Study 201,” and Study 202A/202B, “Study 202”) in which patients were treated only with the 20/10 mg and other flare-up regimens, with a primary endpoint of new HO at the flare-up site. Control data for the phase 2 trials were provided by evaluation of untreated flare-ups in placebo recipients and the NHS.
L1001: The review division agreed with the use of new HO at the one-year timepoint, as assessed by whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) scan, for the primary assessment of efficacy, given that the severe clinical manifestations of FOP generally result directly from HO accumulation. The submitted FOP studies (Phases 2 and 3, and the NHS) are considered fit-for-purpose for this assessing this endpoint.
L1002: An Advisory Committee was originally planned to consider a variety of clinical and statistical issues related to efficacy and the potential for increased incidence of HO flares with treatment that complicate benefit/risk considerations. However, after further review of that data, the Division determined that the Advisory Committee meeting was premature until additional data and data analyses could be completed by the Applicant; therefore, the Advisory Committee meeting was postponed.
L1003: The key review issues relevant to benefit and risk are identified in Section 3.1 below and discussed in detail in Sections 6.3 and 7.7, respectively.

L1022: ## 4. Patient Experience Data
L1023: The FOP natural history study (NHS, PVO-1A-001) and the palovarotene intervention studies included patient-reported outcome measures related to physical function and a clinician-reported index of range of motion. Changes in these measures were found to correlate with more advanced age of FOP patients and with more severe disease but were insufficiently sensitive to show changes over the time scale of the clinical studies, with or without treatment. For this review, these data provided general supportive information but were not central to the regulatory decision.

Established pharmacologic class (EPC)	Retinoid
Mechanism of action	Binding of palovarotene to RAR\gamma antagonizes bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) / activin receptor-like kinase 2 (ALK2) downstream signaling by reducing BMP-mothers against decapentaplegic homolog (SMAD) 1/5/8 phosphorylation, potentially by promoting proteasome-mediated SMAD degradation. QT prolongation	At a dose of 2.5 times the maximum recommended dose, palovarotene does not prolong the QT interval to any clinically relevant extent.

Bioanalysis	Two validated LC-MS/MS methods were used to determine plasma and seminal fluid concentrations of palovarotene. The established benchtop stability, storage stability and freeze-thaw stability cover the maximum storage periods for corresponding clinical studies.
Healthy subjects versus patients	The PK data of healthy volunteers (N=238), FOP patients (N=123), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients (N=198) and multiple osteochondromas (MO) patients (N=18) were included in population PK analyses. There was no evidence that disease status has a clinically relevant influence on the PK of palovarotene.

L1030: Characteristic	Drug Information
Elimination
Mass balance results	Palovarotene and its four known major metabolites accounted for 40% of the total systemic exposure in plasma [palovarotene (14%), M3 (10%), M4b (7%), M2 (5%), and M4a (4%) based on AUC]. The pharmacological activity of M3 and M4b is approximately 1.7% and 4.2% of the activity of the parent drug based on an in vitro RAR\gamma transactivation assay. Over 13 days post dose, 97.1% and 3.2% radioactivity were recovered in feces and urine, respectively. Palovarotene and its four known major metabolites accounted for 67.2% of the dose in feces [M4a and M4b (32.2%), M2 (20.2%), M3 (12.4%), palovarotene (2.4%)].
Clearance	The apparent total body clearance (CL/F) across dose levels and across studies estimated by population PK analysis is 19.9 L/h. In FOP patients, the CL/F values across dose levels are 17.8 L/h (chronic dose), 17.0 L/h (low flare-up dose), and 16.5 L/h (high flare-up dose).
Half-life	In healthy subjects receiving 20 mg QD for 14 days, the mean steady-state T_{1/2} was 8.7 hours. In FOP patients, the terminal T_{1/2} values across dose levels are 4.9 h (chronic dose 5 mg QD or equivalent weight-based), 4.4 h (high flare-up dose 20 mg or equivalent weight-based), and 4.3 h (low flare-up dose 10 mg or equivalent weight-based).
Metabolic pathway(s)	Palovarotene is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, 2C8 and 2C19, but primarily by CYP3A4. Five metabolites, M1 (6,7-dihydroxy), M2 (6-hydroxy), M3 (7-hydroxy), M4a (6-oxo), and M4b (7-oxo) were observed for palovarotene in clinical studies.
Primary excretion pathways (% dosage)	97.1% and 3.2% radioactivity were recovered in feces and urine, respectively.
Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	Based on population PK analysis, AUC and C_{max} were 8% and 12% higher for a 51 kg subject and 18% and 26% lower for a 98 kg compared to a 70 kg subject, respectively.
Age	According to population PK analysis of PK data from subjects aged 2-85 years, there was no evidence that age has a clinically relevant influence on the PK of palovarotene.
Renal impairment	A PK study was not conducted in subjects with renal impairment because only 3% of radioactivity was recovered in urine and there were no case reports of renal impairment in FOP patients enrolled in clinical studies. Population PK analysis suggests that serum creatinine or renal impairment status are not significant covariates on palovarotene PK.
Hepatic impairment	A PK study was not conducted in subjects with hepatic impairment. Per the Applicant, hepatic impairment was not reported in the FOP patients enrolled in the natural history study submitted with this application (N ~100). Population PK analyses suggest that there was no significant difference in the PK of palovarotene in subjects with mild (Child-Pugh A, N=66) hepatic impairment compared to subjects with normal hepatic function. The effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene is not conclusive based on the population PK analyses as only a limited number of subjects (N=5) with moderate hepatic impairment were included. The effect of severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene has not been evaluated. Given that 97.1% of radioactivity was recovered in feces in the mass balance study and that palovarotene is extensively metabolized by CYP enzymes, palovarotene exposure may likely be increased in subjects with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Therefore, Applicant should conduct a hepatic impairment study and evaluate the effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) and severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) on the PK of palovarotene to inform the dosing recommendations in subjects with hepatic impairment.
L1031: Characteristic	Drug Information
Drug Interaction Liability (drug as perpetrator)
Inhibition/induction of metabolism	At clinically relevant plasma concentration, palovarotene did not significantly inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 or CYP3A4. Palovarotene did not pose a clinically relevant risk with respect to the inhibition of UGT enzymes. Palovarotene at clinically relevant concentration (0.32\muM) did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 but induced CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 mRNA expression by 3.8-5.0 folds and 1.8-2.4 folds in vitro, respectively. In clinical study, palovarotene 20 mg QD did not induce CYP3A4-mediated metabolism of co-administered midazolam.

In vitro studies showed that palovarotene inhibited BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and bile salt export pump (BSEP) transporter with IC50 values of 9.69\muM, 1.83\muM, >3\muM, >3\muM, and 14.7\muM, respectively. At the maximum recommended dose (20 mg QD), palovarotene does not pose a clinically relevant risk with respect to the inhibition of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, or BSEP transporters.
