L1034: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L1035: ## Proposed Mechanism of Action
L1036: In patients with FOP, abnormal bone formation, including ectopic chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, and heterotrophic ossification, are driven by a gain-of-function mutation in the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) type I receptor ALK2 (ACVR1). Palovarotene is an oral retinoid with selectivity towards the gamma subtype of RAR (RAR\gamma). RAR\gamma receptor is expressed in chondrogenic cells and chondrocytes, where it operates as an unliganded transcriptional repressor in the absence of retinoid ligands. Binding of palovarotene to RAR\gamma antagonizes BMP/ALK2 downstream signaling by reducing SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation, potentially by promoting proteasome-mediated SMAD degradation. This leads to blockade of chondrogenesis and osteogenic differentiation, reprogramming of progenitor cells into nonskeletal lineage, and prevention of abnormal endochondral bone formation. The Applicant also speculates that RAR\gamma agonist-mediated stimulation of canonical Wnt-b-signaling may also play an inhibitory role in chondro-progenitor cell differentiation. The BMP/ALK2 pathway and the mechanism of action of palovarotene are summarized in Figure 1 below.
L1037: **Figure 1. Mechanism of Action of Palovarotene**
L1038: Source: Ipsen, from Type B meeting package June 27, 2017
L1039: Abbreviations: ALK2, activin receptor-I\kappa kinase-2; BMP, bone morphogenetic protein; FOP, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva; RAR\gamma, retinoic acid receptor gamma; RXR, retinoid X receptor; SMAD, suppressor of mothers against decapentaplegic
L1040: Nonclinical data from the series of in vitro and in vivo studies generated by the Applicant and from published research studies support the proposed mechanism of action of palovarotene and
L1041: its efficacy in preventing HO formation in FOP. Palovarotene demonstrated specific RAR\gamma binding and functional selectivity towards RAR\gamma over RAR\alpha and RAR\beta, with IC50 and half maximal effective concentration (EC50) values of 450nM and 8nM, respectively. In the initial proof of concept studies, pretreatment with a panel of RAR\gamma agonists, including palovarotene, inhibited BMP2-induced chondrogenic differentiation of cultured ADTC5 cells (chondrogenic cells) and led to the loss of skeletogenic potential of bone marrow derived mesenchymal stem cells. Similar findings were recapitulated in a BMP4 treated human FOP fibroblast cell line carrying human relevant gain of function R206H mutation of the ALK2 receptor. In these cell lines, palovarotene reduced (43 to 50%) the levels of phosphorylated Smad proteins (Smad1, Smad5 and Smad8). The effect of palovarotene on Smad proteins was absent in the presence of proteasome inhibitors, suggesting that palovarotene might promote proteasome mediated degradation of Smad proteins.
L1042: Key pharmacodynamic studies were conducted in BMP-implant and transgenic mouse FOP models (ALK2Q207D and ALK2R206H and Prx1-R206H mice) (Figure 2). In the BMP-implant mouse model, injury-mediated HO was induced via implantation with matrigel containing skeletogenic factor rBMP2 inside calf muscle. The Applicant established that activation of the retinoid receptor is effective in preventing the formation of ectopic mineralized tissue masses at the operated sites when oral daily treatment with retinoids or palovarotene at 0.12 to 4 mg/kg (HED =0.6 to 19 mg) commences immediately following rBMP2 implantation and continues for 12 days. The strongest effect was seen with RAR\gamma selective agonists (CD1530 and palovarotene) as compared to pan-RAR and RAR\alpha agonists. The inhibition of HO formation was abolished in RAR\gamma KO mice, suggesting that inhibition of chondrogenesis is mediated exclusively via RAR\gamma.
L1043: Activating mutations in ALK2 are embryo-lethal during embryonic development; therefore, chimeric or conditional gene expression models are routinely used. Palovarotene inhibition of HO was evaluated in ALK2Q207D and ALK2R206H transgenic mouse models, which display abnormal HO formation in an inflammatory milieu. The ALK2Q207D mice conditionally express the Q207D mutant encoding a constitutively active form of ALK2, whereas the ALK2R206H model contains a mildly activating gain-of-function mutation R206H in the ALK2 receptor. Only the R206H mutation occurs naturally in &gt;97% of FOP patients and ALK2R206H mice recapitulate many of the phenotypic features of FOP patients, including hind limb digit malformation, joint fusions, and extensive HO development. Both FOP mouse models require muscle injury/inflammation via cardiotoxin injection to elicit the HO response. Moreover, local, and global induction of transgene expression is achieved by injection with adenovirus expressing Cre in the ALK2Q207D model and doxycycline in the ALK2R206H model.
L1044: Administration of palovarotene to Ad-Cre/cardiotoxin-injected ALK2Q207D mice (19-day old) starting from the day of muscle injury and for 15 consecutive days resulted in dose-dependent reduction in injury-induced HO volume (reduced 75% to 100%) at the injury site, with ED50 of 2 mg/kg/day (HED =7 mg/day). Joint mobility was retained in 100% of treated animals while it was reduced in 70% of the control mice. Further investigation of the window of intervention indicated that treatment with palovarotene is most effective (up to 93.5% HO inhibition) when initiated early (prior to and up to 3-days post injury), but the effect was decreased to 71% inhibition with heterotopic bone volume by 7-day post injury. This suggests that palovarotene targets the chondrogenic phase of HO, preventing its progression to osteogenesis.
L1045: **Figure 2. Microcomputed Tomography Analysis 2-Weeks Post Muscle Injury in Three Animal Models of FOP**
L1046: Source: Adopted from ; Study report CLM001-PD-002; and .
L1047: Abbreviations: BMP, bone morphogenetic protein; FOP, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva; HO, heterotopic ossification; HED, human equivalent dose; WT, wild type
L1048: ALK2R206H mice (1 month old) were treated with doxycycline to induce global expression of the mutant allele ALK2R206H and were then subjected to hindlimb muscle injury with cardiotoxin to induce local inflammation and HO.3 Treatment started from Day 1 to Day 3 postinjury (alien with chondrogenic phase) with palovarotene at 4 mg/kg [HED =19 mg]), followed by 0.6 mg/kg (HED =3 mg) from Day 4 to Day 14, or with vehicle for 14 days. Analysis by microCT and 3D image reconstruction at Day 14 showed that large HO tissue masses formed in the targeted injured muscles of ALK2R206H mice receiving vehicle. Vehicle-treated R206H mice also showed impaired movement of the HO-affected leg. In palovarotene-treated mice, HO was greatly diminished by more than 86% (to 14% of vehicle control) based on bone volume/total volume quantification; joint mobility of the HO-affected leg was also maintained (Figure 3). Histochemical analysis confirmed that newly formed heterotopic cartilaginous tissue and endochondral bone were present in vehicle-treated but not in palovarotene-treated ALK2R206H mice. Palovarotene treatment also reduced muscle damage-induced mast cell infiltration and fibroproliferative response.
L1049: Figure 3. Palovarotene Effect on Heterotopic Ossification in ALK2R206H Mice
L1050: Source:
L1051: Abbreviations: ALK2, activin-like kinase 2; FOV, field of view; H&amp;E, hematoxylin and eosin stain; HO, heterotopic ossification
L1052: In addition to the injury-based model, palovarotene was effective in inhibiting spontaneous HO formation in Prx1-R206H mice (which contain tissue specific expression of R206H mutation in skeletal progenitor cells). These mutant mice recapitulate many of the defects (malformed great toes at birth, development of HO postnatally in hindlimbs and later also in forelimbs) noted in FOP patients. Palovarotene markedly blocked noninjury (spontaneously) induced HO formation in the fore and hind limbs of pups when nursing dams were dosed orally with palovarotene at 2 mg/kg (HED =10 mg) beginning from delivery and continuing for 15 days and treatment was continued by oral gavage (2 mg/kg-HED =7 mg) on alternate days until age 30 days. Furthermore, the severe movement impediment and difficulties noted in vehicle group was absent as drug-treated mutants were mobile and appeared to function well.
L1053: Treatment of control mice with palovarotene caused reduction in skeletal growth. This study suggests a potential for palovarotene to pass to the pups through breastfeeding, but it does not provide compelling evidence, as pups were also exposed to the drug via oral administration from postnatal Days 16 to 30. When palovarotene treatment was delayed until Day 14 and given only to the young mice, it was not as effective at inhibiting HO and maintaining mobility (not shown), suggesting importance of early treatment.
L1054: In conclusion, the Applicant's in vivo pharmacology studies provided a proof-of-principle that palovarotene is effective in blocking injury-induced HO formation in different mouse models of FOP (BMP-2 implant, ALK2Q207D, ALK2R206H and Prrx1-R206H). Window of intervention studies indicate that palovarotene prevents HO formation during the prechondrogenic and chondrogenic stages but has minimal effect during the ossification phase.
L1055: This purported MOA justifies the rationale for treating at the time of flare-up before new cartilage and bone formation have taken place. It is worth noting that the animal models have limitations, as they do not replicate the human disease (i.e., heterotrophic implantation models are artificial local systems created with unphysiologically high concentration of osteogenic factors, genetic models contain mutation (Q207D) that is not found naturally in FOP patients, conditional knock-in models only allow the study of one gene). Furthermore, the efficacy of palovarotene in reducing spontaneous HO was evaluated in one mouse model (Prrx1-R206H), and even though this model recapitulates many of the features of human FOP, the clinical translatability of the findings from this study is questionable because the animals were exposed to palovarotene via breast milk until weaning and treated orally until postnatal day 30. For these reasons, the completed nonclinical pharmacology studies may not provide substantial evidence of efficacy in the prevention of HO in humans.
L1056: The details of the nonclinical pharmacology studies are provided in Section 13.
L1057: ## Secondary (Off-Target) Pharmacology
L1058: Palovarotene does not possess clinically relevant pharmacodynamic activity on off-target receptors or enzymes when screened in vitro on a panel of 75 molecular receptors and 24 enzymes at 10\muM.
L1059: ## 6. Assessment of Effectiveness
L1060: ## 6.1. Dose and Dose Responsiveness
L1061: The development program for palovarotene for the treatment of FOP explored four different dosing regimens in the phase 2 Studies PVO-1A-201 ("Study 201") and PVO-1A-202A/B ("Study 202A/B"). The primary endpoint was the volume of new HO as assessed by low-dose CT scan at the flare-up site 12 weeks after flare-up initiation. The dosing regimens included the following:
L1062: - Palovarotene 5 mg once daily for 2 weeks followed by 2.5 mg once daily for 4 weeks (5/2.5 mg flare-up only regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation.
- Palovarotene 10 mg once daily for 2 weeks followed by 5 mg once daily for 4 weeks (10/5 mg flare-up only regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation.
- Palovarotene 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks (20/10 mg) within 7 days of flare-up initiation, with treatment extension in 4 week increments for persistent symptoms.
- Palovarotene 5 mg daily with increased dosing at the time of a flare-up to palovarotene 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks (chronic/flare-up
L1063: regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation, with treatment extension in 4-week increments for persistent symptoms.
L1064: Skeletally immature pediatric patients enrolled in Studies 201 and 202A/B received weight-based flare-up dosing only according to four weight categories (10 to &lt;20 kg, 20 to &lt;40 kg, 40 to &lt;60 kg, and \ge60 kg).
L1065: The Applicant explored the relationship between change in HO volume on Day 84 (the last timepoint with available HO data in this study) and mean daily palovarotene dose during flare-up treatment based on 165 flares in 82 FOP patients enrolled in Studies 201 and 202A/B (Figure 4). No dose-response relationship for change in HO volume was observed in the regression analysis. Similarly, the Applicant explored the relationship between change in HO volume on Day 84 and mean daily palovarotene area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) during flare-up treatment based on 162 flares in 81 FOP patients (Figure 5). No exposure-response relationship for change in HO volume was observed. In addition, the relationship between change in HO volume on Day 84 and cumulative palovarotene dose during flare-up treatment was explored but no trend was observed. This ER analysis was based on Phase 2 and NHS data, and additional ER analysis with Phase 3 data is presented in Figure 7.

L1070: Flare-up new HO data from the NHS, Study 201 and Study 202A/B were integrated and pooled according to the corresponding palovarotene dosing regimens. The pooled analysis was based on a total of 151 flare-ups with evaluable CT imaging data at Week 12, including 38 untreated flare-ups from the NHS, 9 flare-ups treated with placebo from Study 201, 9 flare-ups treated with the palovarotene 5/2.5 mg dose in Study 201, 47 flare-ups treated with the palovarotene 10/5 mg dose in Studies 201 and 202A, 15 flare-ups treated with the palovarotene 20/10 mg dose (no prior chronic dosing) in Study 202B, and 33 flare-ups treated with the palovarotene 20/10 mg dose (prior chronic dosing) from Study 202B. As shown in Figure 6, both 10/5 mg and 20/10 mg flare-up dosing inhibited new HO volume by approximate 72% relative to the placebo/untreated group. Although a dose-dependent suppression of new HO volume was not observed, given the cumulative and irreversible nature of HO, the Applicant believes that the highest dose tolerated should be selected to prevent as much new HO as possible. Also, nonclinical pharmacology data suggested that a dose of ~6 mg/kg or 20 mg human equivalent dose (HED) once daily may provide greater efficacy in inhibiting HO in a FOP mouse model. Therefore, the 20/10 mg dose was selected as the flare-up treatment dose.
L1071: **Figure 6. Flare-up New HO at Week 12 for the Placebo/Untreated and Palovarotene-Treated Flare-ups in Pooled Studies PVO-1A-001 (NHS), PVO-1A-201 and PVO-1A-202A/B**
L1072: Source: Applicant's Integrated Summary of Efficacy, Figure 44
Abbreviations: AUC, area under the concentration versus time curve; HO, heterotopic ossification; NHS, natural history study; PBO, placebo; PVO, palovarotene; SE, standard error
L1073: The 5-mg chronic dosing was selected based on the following nonclinical and clinical observations: (1) In the FOP mouse model, chronic daily treatment with palovarotene at an HED of approximately 5 mg reduced new HO volume and improved mobility; and (2) Substantial soft tissue edema, muscle necrosis, and immature HO were detected in FOP patients within 7 days of flare-up symptom onset, suggesting new HO formation starts before clinical symptoms of a flare-up. Therefore, the chronic/flare-up dosing regimen (chronic 5 mg QD, flare-up 20/10 mg QD) was selected for further investigation in pivotal Study PVO-1A-301 (“Study 301”).
L1074: ## **6.1.1. Phase 2/3: Studies PVO-1A-202B/C and PVO-1A-301**
L1075: The annualized change in new HO volume as assessed by WBCT was used as one of the secondary efficacy endpoints in Study 202B and the primary efficacy endpoint in Study 202C and Study 301. The annualized changes in new HO volume in patients with and without flare-ups enrolled in Studies 202B/C, 301 and the NHS are summarized in Table 6. The criteria for initiating flare-up treatment in Study 202B (e.g., requiring at least two flare-up symptoms) were stricter than those in Study 301, which might result in undertreatment of flare-ups in Study 202B. An exposure-response analysis for annualized change in new HO volume at Month 12 and palovarotene exposure metrics (average daily dose, cumulative dose of palovarotene, average AUC and cumulative AUC of palovarotene) was conducted. Plots and regression analyses show a trend to decrease change from baseline or relative change from baseline in HO volume versus the assessed exposure metrics. Furthermore, a statistically significant relationship (linear
L1076: regression analysis) was observed between change from baseline in HO volume at Month 12 and cumulative AUC (p=0.0497), suggesting higher dose/exposure level might have better efficacy as measured by annualized change in new HO volume (Figure 7).

L1079: The results for ER analyses are different between phase 2 and phase 3 studies, possibly due to the longer duration of new HO volume measurement in the phase 3 study (12 months) as compared to the phase 2 study (84 days). However, we should also consider that this ER analyses based on the phase 3 study has some limitations due to the study design, as only one dosing regimen or placebo was tested in Study 301: (1) Patients with annualized change in new HO volume data were either treated with one dosing regimen (chronic 5 mg, flare-up 20/10 mg) or not treated with palovarotene; (2) patients with flare-ups were treated with high doses (20/10 mg QD) and patients without flare-ups were treated with the low dose (5 mg QD). In addition, we note that placebo response (mainly obtained from the NHS) has a large variability, in which HO volume change from baseline could range from -91300 \text{mm}^3 to 391730 \text{mm}^3 by Month 12 for the placebo group. This large variability limited the precision for interpreting the placebo response, and therefore we have less confidence in the detected ER relationship as shown in Figure 7. In general, we still consider that there is no obvious exposure-response relationship for
L1080: palovarotene and new HO volume up to 12 months, thus further change in the dose of palovarotene above the doses of chronic 5 mg and flare-up 20/10 mg is unlikely to further improve response for HO volume. Flare-up dosing controlling for new HO formation seemed to be appropriate.

L1087: ## 6.2. Clinical Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L1088: ## 6.2.1. Phase 3: Study PVO-1A-301
L1089: ## 6.2.1.1. Design
L1090: ## Study Title: A Phase 3 Efficacy and Safety Study of Oral Palovarotene for the Treatment of Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva (FOP)
L1091: Study PVO-1A-301 (Study 301) was a phase 3 study with the primary objective of evaluating the efficacy of the chronic/flare-up dosing regimen of palovarotene to decrease new HO development in adult and pediatric patients with FOP, in comparison to untreated patients in the Applicant's prospective FOP natural history study (NHS; PVO-1A-001). The single-arm design of Study 301, with use of the NHS as an external control group, raises issues regarding the comparability of these studies/groups, which are discussed below (see Section 6.3.2). The protocol synopsis is included in Section 15 of this review.
L1092: Study 301 subjects received chronic treatment of 5 mg palovarotene once daily outside of acute FOP flare-up episodes. At the onset of any symptom of a flare-up (e.g., pain, swelling) in any location or after a high-risk trauma event, as confirmed by the investigator, subjects increased to flare-up dosing of 20 mg daily for 4 weeks, followed by 10 mg daily for 8 weeks. If flare-up symptoms persisted, treatment could be extended further with 10 mg daily in 4-week increments. If a subject experienced an intercurrent flare-up at a new location, or marked worsening of the initial flare-up, the treatment cycle was restarted at 20 mg. When acute symptoms had resolved and the flare-up treatment cycle was completed, chronic 5 mg daily treatment resumed.
L1093: Subjects &lt;18 years old with &lt;90% skeletal maturity received reduced equivalents of the above doses based on body weight. Skeletal maturity of ≥90% was based on a bone age of ≥12 years 0 months for girls, and ≥14 years 0 months for boys, as determined by hand/wrist x-rays using the atlas of Greulich and Pyle and standards of Bayley-Pinneau. Subjects with bone age below these marks received body weight-adjusted doses according to Table 7. If a subject (of any age) experienced intolerable side effects, the dose could be reduced to the next lower dose listed for their weight category.
L1094: **Table 7. Study 301: Weight-Adjusted Palovarotene Doses for Skeletally Immature (&lt;90%) Subjects and Dose De-escalation Dosing for All Subjects**

L1096: Source: Study 301 protocol Table 3

L1098: HO was assessed by whole-body CT scan every 6 months in Study 301, and every 12 months in the NHS (or at the time of transfer into Study 301). The image acquisition methods in these studies were similar. At a central imaging facility, scans from the two studies were interspersed for readings that were blinded to the study/treatment group and other clinical data pertinent to the subject. In baseline scans from either study, each of 9 body regions (excluding the head, see Figure 8) was evaluated for the presence of HO by two radiologists. In each CT slice, regions of interest (ROIs) were delineated by reviewers around each area of HO; data from adjacent slices were integrated by image analysis software to yield volume of the ROI. Total volume of HO (\text{cm}^3) was calculated by consensus for each region, and summed to yield baseline total body HO.
L1099: Figure 8. WBCT Body Regions for Assessment of HO
L1100: Source: Study 301/NHS Independent Review Charter
L1101: Key: 1, 2: Chest, Neck, Shoulder (Right and Left); 3: Mid Torso; 4, 5: Arm (Right and Left); 6, 7: Hip (Right and Left); 8, 9: Lower Leg (Right and Left)
L1102: Abbreviations: HO, heterotopic ossification; WBCT, whole-body computed tomography
L1103: For postbaseline scans, HO volume was recalculated for any body region that appeared to contain, upon initial qualitative review, new HO in comparison to the previous scan (either a new area of HO, or enlargement of an existing lesion), with adjudication of any disagreements between reviewers. Any reduction in HO volume of other lesions in that region would also be captured as an offset to the total gains, and the change in volume from baseline could be positive or negative for any region and/or for total-body. HO volume was not remeasured postbaseline in regions where there was no apparent new HO compared to the previous scan. Intra- and inter-reader variability were evaluated via secondary rereads of a random subset of WBCT scans and considered to be acceptable.
L1104: Because HO volume measurements were reported by body region, and data pertaining to individual HO lesions were not recorded in the datasets, these studies were not designed to evaluate the extent to which palovarotene may inhibit the development of new lesions. When new HO was seen in a region, readers were instructed to classify the new HO as “new lesion” or “enlarged lesion” or “both new and enlarged lesion.” for the region as a whole. This information was entered in the comments section of the imaging raw data and was not analyzed in the submitted NDA. Pursuant to a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) request, the Applicant plans to tabulate this information for a future submission (not within the current review cycle).
L1105: A subset of subjects participated in both studies, having completed at least one post baseline assessment in the NHS and subsequently enrolling in Study 301. For most of these subjects, the NHS end-of-study WBCT scans also served as the baseline WBCT scan in Study 301. These scans were read twice (as NHS postbaseline, and as Study 301 baseline) because of the differing procedures involved.
L1106: ## 6.2.1.2. Eligibility Criteria
L1107: Adult and pediatric patients age \ge 4 years with a clinical diagnosis of FOP and no flare-up symptoms within the previous 4 weeks were eligible to enroll in Study 301. To facilitate comparisons with the NHS, most of the subjects (i.e., the Principal Analysis population) were required to have the classic R206H mutation and no prior exposure to palovarotene. There were exclusion criteria based on known retinoid safety issues, including pregnancy and increased suicide risk.
L1108: ## 6.2.1.3. Statistical Analysis Plan
L1109: The primary endpoint was the annualized change in new HO volume. This endpoint was compared between treated subjects from Study 301 and untreated subjects from the NHS. Scheduled WBCT scans were performed at baseline, Month 12, Month 24 and Month 36 in the NHS, and at baseline, Month 6, Month 12, Month 18, and Month 24 in the Study 301. WBCT scans were also performed at the time of early study discontinuation. The key secondary endpoint was the proportion of subjects with any new HO. The other secondary endpoints were the number of body regions with new HO, the proportion of subjects reporting flare-ups, and the rate of flare-ups per subject-month.
L1110: Exploratory endpoints included change from baseline in range of motion (ROM) assessed by CAJIS (Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale for FOP), change from baseline in physical function using age-appropriate forms of the FOP-PFQ (FOP Physical Function Questionnaire), and change from baseline in physical and mental function for subjects \ge 15 years old and mental function for subjects &lt;15 years old using age-appropriate forms of the PROMIS (Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System) Global Health Scale.
L1111: ## Primary Analysis
L1112: The prespecified primary analysis for the primary endpoint was based on a Bayesian compound Poisson model. Under this model, the change in new HO since previous CT scan was modeled as a compound distribution of the number of body regions with new HO and the new HO volume per region where new HO occurred. The compound Bayesian model counted the occurrence of a positive new HO as an event. The treatment effect was expressed as the ratio of the annualized new HO between treated and untreated subjects, which was estimated by the ratio of annual
L1113: event rates multiplied by the ratio of the growth rates per event. This method is equivalent to estimating the mean annualized new HO by multiplication of the mean annual number of events and the mean growth per event. More details regarding the Bayesian analysis are included in the Part III.
L1114: The Bayesian compound model was estimated based on the number of regions with positive new HO and the average growth per region where positive new HO occurred since the previous WBCT scan. Negative new HO values were set to 0 in the analyses. The prespecified analysis included a square root transformation of each change in HO since the previous scan by region. The Applicant chose this statistical model “to more appropriately accommodate the high degree of variability in the volume of new HO assessed by WBCT.” The square root transformation was included in the Bayesian compound Poisson analysis because simulations suggested that if palovarotene reduced the probability of new HO as much or more than it reduced the new HO volume given new HO, introducing a square root transformation could marginally increase power. Additionally, square root transformation would likely decrease the variance of the endpoint by shrinking any extremely large values of new HO volume.
L1115: Three early interim analyses and one final analysis were prespecified in the 2017 protocol. The first interim analysis was planned to occur when 35 subjects had completed at least one year of follow-up, and the second when all subjects enrolled in the Principal Enrolled Population had completed 12 months of follow-up. A Pocock alpha-spending function was prespecified for the interim analyses, with an overall Type I error rate of 0.025, one-sided. To preserve the overall Type I error rate, the alpha threshold for each interim and final analysis was set at 0.0091.
L1116: The trial crossed the futility boundary at the second interim analysis and the study was paused for dosing. However, additional post hoc analyses, including the Bayesian compound model without square root transformation, found evidence of potentially clinically meaningful benefit of palovarotene. Upon review of the additional post hoc analyses, the data monitoring committee (DMC) noted that the impact of the prespecified square root transformation was unexpectedly large and appeared to have moved the statistical conclusion from significant therapeutic benefit to showing futility of the treatment. The DMC concluded that “the dilemma created by these highly disparate results precludes a confident conclusion about futility.” Dosing in study 301 was allowed to resume. The DMC recommended that “palovarotene be continued in skeletally mature children \ge 14 years.”

L1126: As shown in Table 8, the two study populations were similar in demographics except that NHS subjects were somewhat older than Study 301 subjects (mean age 17.5 versus 15.1 years, respectively, at baseline). NHS subjects also tended to have worse measures of FOP disease severity (whole-body HO volume, number of body regions with HO, CAJIS and FOP-PFQ scores measuring impaired range of motion and physical function, respectively). These differences are likely age-related, as cross-sectional analyses of baseline data showed that increasing age correlates with greater HO accumulation and with worsening FOP-related functional impairments.
L1127: The mean number of flare-ups reported by the subject (or parents) within the 12 months prior to study enrollment was higher for NHS compared to Study 301 subjects (2.5 versus 1.4), but the median number was the same (1). The mean for the NHS was skewed by two subjects (b) (6), age 9 and 8 years) who, at NHS enrollment, reported 40 and 37 flare-ups in the previous year, respectively. During their participation in the NHS, the number of flare-ups reported by these two subjects was much lower (1 in 18 months, 4 in 30 months, respectively).
L1128: Study 301 and NHS subjects were generally similar with respect to other FOP-related history, including mean age at FOP diagnosis (6.6, 7.5 years); history of great toe malformations (99%, 100%); cervical spine malformations (44%, 51%); hearing loss (46%, 35%); and family history of FOP (1%, 5%).
L1129: ## Disposition
L1130: In Study 301, seven patients with FOP failed screening based on various enrollment criteria. In the NHS, three patients were not included in the Principal Enrolled Population because they did not have FOP or the required R206H mutation. In Study 301, there were eight patients with FOP who did not have this mutation and were allowed to enroll as a “Supplemental” population. The Principal Safety Set (PSS) used for many analyses was limited to patients with the R206H mutation and consisted of 99 patients in Study 301 who received at least one dose of palovarotene and 111 patients in the NHS with available comparison data. Within the PSS, the Principal Full Analysis Set (P-FAS) comprised subjects with evaluable whole-body HO data.

Because of the prolonged interruption and/or discontinuation of treatment in nearly all participants, the efficacy analyses in the original NDA, based on a cut-off date of February 28, 2020, have not been updated. Recently, the Applicant reported that new efficacy data (WBCT scans) have been collected on many participants following treatment restart through the study end in September 2022; these data will be submitted at a later date (not within this review cycle) to aid in the overall assessment of efficacy.

L1159: ## Applicant's Post Hoc Weighted Linear Mixed Effect Model Analysis
L1160: The Applicant's post hoc wLME analysis with baseline annualized HO (calculated as baseline total HO volume divided by baseline age) as the only covariate achieved nominal significance (Table 13). In this analysis, the annualized new HO for each subject was calculated using the new HO volume from baseline associated with the longest follow-up divided by the length of follow-up. The length of follow-up varied substantially among subjects and between studies. For example, annualized new HO was based on the Month 18 observation for 66% of subjects in study 301 and the Month 36 observation for 32% of subjects in the NHS. The wLME model accounted for the various follow-up lengths using a weighted approach. We note that the estimated treatment effect based on various lengths of follow-up could be difficult to interpret without the strong assumption of a constant rate of change in HO.

L1166: As the distribution of annualized new HO is skewed, the Applicant performed sensitivity analyses to investigate the influence of large values on the analyses conclusion. These analyses indicate that the conclusions are not driven by the few extremely large values seen in subjects in the NHS (see Section 16).
L1167: ## Subgroup Summary by Sex and Age
L1168: Subgroup summaries indicate a smaller effect size among females and among subjects older than 18 years (Table 14). This finding may be explained by the smaller annualized growth of new HO in the control group (NHS) patients in these subgroups. However, it is not possible to rule out that the drug's effect is less in older patients for whom the disease stage is often more advanced. An explanation for the smaller effect in females is uncertain. Findings from these subgroup analyses should be interpreted with caution because with a smaller number of subjects in each subgroup, the influence of a few large values and imbalances in confounders in the absence of randomization could be greater on the mean difference, compared with analyses based on the overall population.

L1173: ## Secondary Efficacy Endpoint Results
L1174: ## Proportion of subjects with any new HO
L1175: This endpoint was evaluated using HO data from month 12, which is the timepoint with the most consistent follow-up data across both Study 301 and the NHS (there were few subjects with data for Month 24 in Study 301, and for Month 18 in the NHS). In the Principal FAS, the proportion of subjects with any new HO (new volume &gt;0 cm^3 in any body region) at month 12 compared to baseline was essentially the same in palovarotene-treated subjects (59/92, 64%) and untreated subjects (56/90, 62%).
L1176: ## Number of body regions with new HO
L1177: This endpoint was also analyzed at month 12 based on the availability of HO data in most subjects at this point. The mean (SD) number of body regions with new HO per subject since baseline at month 12 was 1.3 (1.4) in Study 301 subjects and 1.5 (1.6) in untreated NHS subjects. The difference was not statistically significant according to the Applicant's prespecified analysis.
L1178: ## Proportion of subjects reporting flare-ups/ Flare-up rate per subject-month of exposure
L1179: Based on the hypothesis that chronic palovarotene dosing has the potential to interrupt initiation of a flare-up, the incidence and rate of new flare-ups were designated as secondary efficacy endpoints in Study 301. This hypothesis was not supported by the data: compared to the NHS, the proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects with reported flare-ups through Month 12 was slightly higher (67% versus 56%), and the rate of flare-ups per month was also higher (0.15 versus 0.07). Although this finding may be related to issues of study design, it is considered to represent a potential safety issue based on the known musculoskeletal effects of retinoids and is discussed as such in Section 7.7.3 of this review.
L1180: ## Exploratory Efficacy Endpoint Results
L1181: ## *Range of motion assessed by CAJIS*
L1182: Changes from baseline in CAJIS score were small and similar between treatment groups at Month 12. There was a mean (SD) increase of 0.5 (2.0) in Study 301 subjects and 0.6 (2.4) in untreated NHS subjects (based on 0 to 30 scale, with higher scores indicating more impaired ROM).
L1183: ## *Physical function assessed by FOP-PFQ*
L1184: At baseline, mean FOP-PFQ scores in Study 301 and NHS subjects were 44.3 and 47.0, respectively (scale of 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating worse physical function by patient report). Mean changes from baseline were 2.8 and 4.5, respectively, at month 12, a nonsignificant difference.
L1185: ## *PROMIS Global Health Scale*
L1186: Very small changes from baseline were seen in Study 301 subjects, similar to untreated NHS subjects.
L1187: ## 6.2.2. Phase 2: Studies PVO-1A-201 and PVO-1A-202A/B/C
L1188: ## 6.2.2.1. Design
L1189: The first study of palovarotene in patients with FOP was PVO-1A-201 (“Study 201”), a 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 40 FOP patients who were experiencing an acute flare-up episode, with at least 2 of 6 prespecified symptoms. The primary objective was to evaluate the ability of palovarotene to prevent new HO at flare-up sites, as assessed by radiograph. Starting within 7 days of symptom onset, patients received one of three treatment regimens:
L1190: - Palovarotene 10 mg daily x 2 weeks, followed by 5 mg daily x 4 weeks (10/5 regimen) (n=21)
- Palovarotene 5 mg daily x 2 weeks, followed by 2.5 mg daily x 4 weeks (5/2.5 regimen) (n=9)
- Placebo capsules x 6 weeks (n=10)
L1191: The study used an adaptive design. For the first 16 patients enrolling in this study (Cohort 1), the randomization ratio was 3:1 (palovarotene 10/5: placebo). Subsequently, the 5/2.5 regimen was added, and the randomization ratio was changed to 3:3:2 (10/5 mg: 5/2.5 mg: placebo) for the last 24 patients (Cohort 2). Treatments could not be extended beyond 6 weeks for any ongoing or new symptoms.
L1192: Enrollment began in July 2014 and was initially limited to FOP patients at least 15 years of age who were at least 90% skeletally mature (based on bone age, derived from hand/wrist x-ray). During enrollment of Cohort 2 (protocol amendment 6), the minimum age was lowered to 6 years with reduced doses for skeletally immature patients according to the following table (this schedule is nearly identical to the dose adjustments used subsequently in Study 301).
L1193: **Table 15. Study 201: Weight-Adjusted Palovarotene Doses for Skeletally Immature (&lt;90%) Subjects**
L1194: Weight Range Category	10 mg Equivalent	5 mg Equivalent	2.5 mg Equivalent*
20 to <40 kg	6 mg	3 mg	1.5 mg
40 to <60 kg	8 mg	4 mg	2 mg
≥60 kg	10 mg	5 mg	2.5 mg
L1195: Source: Study 201 CSR Table 1
*in the event of dose de-escalation
L1196: Prior to this study, plain radiographs were sometimes used in clinical practice to assess formation of new HO at FOP flare-up sites, but the sensitivity and optimal timing of this and other potential HO imaging modalities were largely unknown. In this study, imaging of the flare-up sites included assessments of HO by standard AP/lateral radiograph and CT scan, including measurements of HO area (mm2) and HO volume (mm3), respectively; and assessment of soft tissue edema at the site by MRI, or by ultrasound (US) if MRI was not feasible. This imaging was conducted at baseline, 6 weeks (end of treatment) and 12 weeks (end of post-treatment observation period).
L1197: All 40 subjects completed Study 201 and enrolled in the open-label extension study PVO-1A-202 (“Study 202”), which was conducted in 3 parts:
L1198: - Study 202 Part ASubjects who experienced up to 2 additional flare-ups following Study 201 received the palovarotene 10/5 regimen (weight-adjusted) used in Study 201 for 6 weeks, with assessments at Week 12. New HO at flare-up sites was evaluated mainly by CT, which was found to be more sensitive than standard radiograph. Subjects without flare-up symptoms were not treated. In addition, follow-up evaluations of the original flare-up site in Study 201 were conducted at 12 months.

- Study 202 Part B (Protocol amendment 3; known as study PVO-1A-204 in France; implemented March 2016)Based on new nonclinical data, the doses and duration of flare-up treatment were increased, and chronic dosing was introduced, with two new palovarotene regimens:

Chronic/flare-up regimen (“Adult Cohort”): skeletally mature subjects received 5 mg daily, with increased dosing during a flare-up to 20 mg for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg for 8 weeks, with treatment extension in 4-week increments allowed for flare-ups with ongoing symptoms.
- Flare-up-only regimen (“pediatric cohort”): skeletally immature patients received the same regimen for flare-ups, with weight-adjusted dose equivalents of 20 mg for 4 weeks and 10 mg for 8 weeks and treatment extension as necessary, but with no chronic dosing between flare-ups (as a safety measure). Dose adjustments for body weight 40 to &lt;60 kg, or 20 to &lt;40 kg, followed the same schedule as Study 301 (see table in Section 6.2.1.1 of this review).
L1199: Enrollment in Part B included most of the subjects from Study 201/202A, as well as new subjects not previously treated. As in Studies 201/202A, two or more symptoms were required to initiate flare-up treatment. Flare-ups treated with the new 20/10 regimen (with or without prior 5 mg chronic treatment) were assessed by CT of the flare-up site through Week 12, and end of treatment (EOT) for subjects with treatment extended. In addition, subjects receiving the chronic regimen underwent annual evaluations that included measurement of new whole-body HO by CT scan. Flare-ups with only one reported symptom, or intercurrent flare-ups at other sites during treatment of an initial flare-up, were not treated as flare-ups and were instead reported as AEs of “condition aggravated,” which is the MedDRA preferred term for a FOP flare-up.
L1200: - Study 202 Part C (Protocol amendment 4; PVO-1A-204 in France; implemented Sept 2017)
L1201: The chronic/flare-up regimen was continued and expanded to all subjects, including skeletally immature children who received weight-adjusted equivalents of the 5 mg, 20 mg and 10 mg doses. Flare-up dosing was expanded to include flare-ups with any number of symptoms (\ge 1), intercurrent flare-ups at a new location, or substantial trauma “likely to lead to a flare-up”; any such events restarted the 12-week 20/10 mg treatment cycle. Thus, the 202C treatment protocol was essentially identical to the phase 3 study, 301. Flare-up site imaging was not included in Part C, as efficacy was assessed by the annual whole-body CT scans. All 202C subjects were drawn from 202B; no new subjects
L1202: were enrolled in Part C. This study was ongoing at the February 28, 2020, cutoff date for the interim study report.
L1203: ## 6.2.2.2. Eligibility Criteria
L1204: In Study 201, the initial cohort consisted of subjects with clinically diagnosed classic FOP, at least 15 years of age and \ge 90\% skeletal maturity, with symptomatic onset within 7 days of a distinct flare-up; with at least two out of 6 specified symptoms (pain, swelling, decreased ROM, stiffness, redness, warmth); and consistent with their previous flare-ups. Flare-ups qualifying for enrollment and treatment were in an appendicular area (upper or lower extremity), abdomen or chest. Excluded were flare-ups in the head, because imaging would involve radiation to the brain, and flare-ups in the upper back, which were considered by consulting experts to be unpredictable and relatively difficult to assess. After the initial cohort and with availability of juvenile toxicity data, enrollment in Study 201 was expanded to children age \ge 6 years (Protocol amendment #6). In extension Study 202A and 202B, the criteria which qualified additional flare-up(s) for palovarotene treatment and evaluation/ imaging were the same as in Study 201, i.e., the presence of at least 2 symptoms, and onset within 7 days.
L1205: In the NHS, which began enrollment shortly after initiation of Study 201, any subject with a flare-up meeting the above criteria was eligible to transfer into Study 201 for treatment. Except for the requirement of \ge 2 symptoms, severity of the flare-up was not intended to be a determining factor. Most subjects remained in the NHS during flare-ups, and a subset of these events (maximum one per year per subject) were evaluated in-clinic over 12 weeks and provided untreated control data, including imaging, for comparisons to palovarotene-treated flare-ups.
L1206: The additional group of subjects who had not participated in Studies 201 and 202A, and who began palovarotene treatment in Study 202 Part B, was restricted to subjects who were \ge 90\% skeletally mature and who therefore joined the “Adult Cohort.” Additional enrollment criteria for these new subjects were a history of at least two flare-ups within the past 2 years, but no flare-up symptoms within the past 4 weeks; a confirmed R206H mutation; and a CAJIS score of 6 to 16. Most of these subjects whose initial Study 202 enrollment was in Part B transferred from the NHS. As in Study 301, the selection of specific NHS subjects for transfer into a treatment study among those eligible was apparently nonrandom, and any factors that may have been considered in these decisions are unknown.
L1207: ## 6.2.2.3. Statistical Analysis Plan
L1208: ## Flare-up Site Outcomes
L1209: In Studies 201, 202A/B and the NHS, flare-up site images were evaluated by radiologists at a central facility with blinding for study and treatment assignment. In Study 201, the primary endpoint specified in the protocol and SAP was the proportion of “responders” as defined by no or minimal new HO at the site (a grade of \le 3 on a 0 to 6 scale on both AP and lateral views) by standard radiograph at Week 6 compared to baseline. Although it was predicted that about 80% of untreated FOP flare-ups would result in new HO, the observed incidence in this and other studies was substantially lower, especially by standard radiograph (see below). Secondary imaging endpoints included the proportion of responders at Week 12; volume of new HO by CT; and soft tissue swelling and/or cartilage by MRI or US.
L1210: The Study 201 protocol and Independent Review Charter documents specified the interpretation of each imaging modality independently, with double-read review and consensus adjudication (the “primary read” process). Based on emerging data showing the limitations of plain radiograph, and general uncertainty about optimal imaging of HO, the SAP described an additional “global read” process in which radiologists and investigators (blinded to treatment group) determined the presence/absence of new HO based on a comprehensive evaluation of all images, including radiographs and CT, as well as MRI or US assessments of soft tissue edema at the flare-up site, at all timepoints.
L1211: Other secondary endpoints in Study 201 included flare-up related pain and swelling assessed by NRS (Numeric Rating Scale) or FPS-R (Faces Pain Scale-Revised), and range of motion at the joint closest to the flare-up site by goniometry.
L1212: The limited number of flare-ups evaluated in Study 201 was supplemented by flare-up data from the extension study 202A/B (palovarotene-treated events) and the NHS (untreated events). The Integrated Summary of Efficacy (ISE) presents pooled analyses by treatment regimen and by flare-up event rather than by subject (tabulated as “M” rather than “N”), because many subjects were evaluated in multiple events, including in some cases different studies/regimens. The F-FAS (Flare-up Full Analysis Set) consists of all reported flare-ups in these studies, and within the F-FAS, the IF-FAS (Imaged Flare-up Full Analysis Set) consists of all events with CT imaging across studies. Flare-ups in the head or upper back in the NHS were excluded from the IF-FAS, because flares in these locations were not eligible for evaluation in palovarotene-treated subjects. Also excluded from the IF-FAS were NHS flare-ups that were followed remotely by Telephone Contact (TC), without in-clinic evaluation and imaging.
L1213: Key endpoints for the pooled ISE flare-up analyses were the proportion of flare-ups with new HO (the primary endpoint in 201 and 202A/B), volume of new HO (\text{cm}^3), and new HO status/volume by baseline edema status. Other flare-up endpoints at Week 12 included range of motion at the flare-up site by goniometry; Global Assessment of Movement; local pain and swelling by NRS or FPS-R (&lt;8 y/o); physical function (FOP-PFQ); and general health (PROMIS Global Health Scale or PROMIS Pediatric Global Health Scale).
L1214: ## Chronic/Flare-up Dosing Outcomes
L1215: Whole-body (excluding head) CT scan was performed prior to the initiation of chronic dosing in Study 202 Part B (Adult Cohort) or Part C (Pediatric Cohort) to assess baseline whole-body HO, and then repeated annually during chronic/flare-up treatment. The ISE did not pool these data with Study 301 HO data based on the following rationale: most of the Study 202B/C subjects (36/54) were originally enrolled in Study 201 to treat an acute flare-up, and therefore may not be comparable to subjects in Study 301 and the NHS, who enrolled during relative disease quiescence (defined as no symptoms within 4 weeks). In addition, qualifying criteria for treatment of flare-ups in Study 202B were more restrictive than in Studies 202C and 301; therefore, many subjects continued only chronic (5 mg) dosing during symptomatic episodes that would have been treated with flare-up (20/10 mg) dosing in the later studies.
L1216: Whole-body CT scans from Study 202 B/C were read by the same imaging contractor as in Study 301 and the NHS, with some differences in methodology. Study 202 B/C scans were read by a single radiologist, without concurrent comparison to any control group. Baseline WBCT for each subject at the initiation of chronic dosing was evaluated for presence, severity
L1217: (mild/moderate/severe) and volume of HO in each body region (using 15 rather than 9 regions). Postbaseline scans were evaluated for change from prior scan(s), and HO volume was remeasured if a change was apparent. It does not appear that there was any systematic evaluation of intrareader agreement, such as the random rereads conducted in Study 301/NHS.
L1218: The primary endpoint of Study 202B (protocol amendment 3), similar to Studies 201 and 202A, was the absence of new HO at flare-up sites. Secondary endpoints of 202B with respect to nonflare-up based treatment were the change from Part B baseline in whole-body HO at months 12 and 24; change in CAJIS scores; and number of flare-ups per subject-month.
L1219: Since the implementation of Part C (protocol amendment 4), the primary efficacy endpoint of Study 202 has been the annualized change in new whole-body (less head) HO volume, with comparison of the annualized change in Parts B and C to data collected from the NHS. Secondary endpoints in Part C include percent of subjects with new HO at months 12, 24, 36 and overall; and changes in CAJIS, FOP-PFQ, and PROMIS Global Health Scale.
L1220: ## 6.2.2.4. Results of Analyses
L1221: ## Study 201: Flare-up Outcomes
L1222: In this randomized, placebo-controlled study, there were 40 patients with FOP with an acute flare-up who met eligibility criteria and were enrolled at one of four centers: UPenn (n=15), UCSF (n=14), one center in France (n=9) and one in UK (n=2). Among these were eight patients who enrolled initially in the NHS and subsequently transferred into Study 201 at the onset of a qualifying flare-up event. There were four other patients who failed Study 201 screening and were not enrolled or randomized; one of these patients enrolled in the NHS 17 months later.
L1223: All 40 enrolled subjects completed Study 201 and are included in the Full Analysis Set (FAS) population. One subject (# (b) (6)) in the 10/5 dosing arm was &lt;80% compliant with study medication; the other 39 subjects constitute the Per-Protocol (PP) population.

L1237: In the overall study, 15% of subjects attributed their flare-up to blunt muscle trauma and 8% cited muscle fatigue, while in most cases the cause was considered unknown. The mean time from onset of flare-up symptoms to first dose was 5.8 days; treatment was begun within 7 days in all cases except one subject in the 10/5 group who began treatment on day 8. L1238: ## Primary Endpoint: Incidence of New HO at Flare-up Sites
L1239: In Study 201, when compared to baseline, standard radiographs of the flare-up site at week 6 showed more than minimal new HO (grade &gt;3 on 0 to 6 scale) in only two subjects (one each in placebo and palovarotene 5/2.5 mg groups, none in 10/5 mg group) out of the total of 40 subjects. Therefore, 89%, 89% and 100% of subjects in these respective groups were classified as “responders,” yet because there was no difference between groups, the study did not demonstrate efficacy based on the prespecified primary endpoint. At Week 12, standard radiographs showed more than minimal new HO in 4/40 subjects compared to baseline (n=2, 1 and 1 subjects in the placebo, 5/2.5 and 10/5 groups, respectively). CT was more sensitive than radiographs, showing new HO in these four subjects and six additional subjects at Week 12.
L1240: The primary read data at Week 12 in Table 18 indicate a numerically higher incidence of new HO (by either radiograph or CT, or both) in placebo subjects (40%) compared to the two palovarotene groups (incidence 20 to 24%). However, one of the placebo subjects (# [b] (6)) with new HO exhibited only a small area of grade 3 (“minimal”) new HO by radiograph, and none by CT, and thereby met the protocol definition of “responder.” Therefore, only 3/10 (30%) of placebo recipients were “nonresponders” because the minimal HO by radiograph in subject # [b] (6) was considered to likely represent artifact.
L1241: The Global Read process also gave a numerically higher incidence of new HO at Week 12 in the placebo group compared to the 10/5 group (40% versus 19% in FAS). Subject # [b] (6) (placebo group) and one subject in the 10/5 group were considered to have new HO by primary read, but no new HO by Global Read. Three other subjects (one in placebo group, two in 5/2.5 group) were considered to have no new HO by primary read, but new HO by Global Read (Table 18).

L1248: ## Study 201 Secondary Endpoints: Volume of New HO at Flare-up Sites
L1249: In Study 201, about half of subjects had HO present at baseline at the flare-up site by CT (Table 19). At Week 12, the mean volume of new HO in the placebo group (averaged across all subjects, including those with new HO volume=0) was 16.2 cm3, which was numerically higher than in the two palovarotene groups. This was mainly attributable to one placebo recipient (subject # [b] [6]) with a left hip flare-up that resulted in a large volume of new HO at Week 12 (131.7 cm3). The other flare-ups resulting in new HO &gt;10 cm3 also involved the hip: a placebo subject with new hip HO of 29.5 cm3; and three subjects in the palovarotene 10/5 group with new hip HO of 48.4 cm3, 15.9 cm3 and 11.1 cm3, respectively. The lower mean volume of new HO in the palovarotene 5/2.5 group (and lack of dose-response overall) may be in part related to the lack of flare-ups at the hip with new HO in this 5/2.5 group, and lower proportion of hip flare-ups overall in this group (22%, versus 43% and 50% in the other groups).

L1257: ## Other Study 201 Secondary Endpoints
L1258: Among eight subjects with no edema at the flare-up site at baseline by MRI, none developed new HO at Week 12. Among 20 subjects with baseline edema, nine developed new HO, including 3/6 in the placebo group, 4/6 in the 5/2.5 mg group and 2/8 in the 10/5 mg group.
L1259: Among subjects who maintained diary entries, the mean number of days to resolution of flare-up symptoms was 64, 46 and 36 days for the placebo, 5/2.5, and 10/5 groups, respectively.
L1260: Flare-up pain, as assessed by the NRS (or FPS-R for age &lt;8 years), tended to decline from baseline to Week 12 in each group. Mean changes were -2.2, -1.9 and -3.6 in the placebo, 5/2.5 and 10/5 groups, respectively. The mean changes in NRS score for flare-up swelling were -2.3, -2.5 and -2.1 in these groups.
L1261: The range of motion at the joint nearest the flare-up site, as measured by goniometry, showed minimal changes from baseline to Week 12; mean percent change was -2.3, -4.2 and +0.6 in the
L1262: placebo, 5/2.5 and 10/5 groups, respectively. There were no significant differences between subjects with or without new HO, regardless of treatment group.
L1263: Patient reported scores for physical function (FOP-PFQ) and global health (PROMIS Global Physical and Global Mental Health scales) showed small changes which were not significantly different between treatment groups.
L1264: ## Flare-up Site Outcomes Across Studies (201, 202A/B, NHS)
L1265: All 40 subjects enrolled in Study 201 completed the 12-week study and enrolled in the initial Part A of the extension study (Study 202A). During Study 202A (mean duration of participation =11.3 months), 20/40 subjects did not experience a qualifying flare-up and received no treatment, while the other 20 subjects underwent evaluation and treatment (with 10/5 regimen) of a total of 28 new flare-ups. Subjects who had received the 10/5 regimen in Study 201 were more likely to have another flare-up treated in Study 202A (14/21 subjects, 67%), compared to subjects who had received the 5/2.5 regimen (3/9 subjects, 33%) or placebo (3/10 subjects, 30%).
L1266: When the Study 202 Part B protocol was implemented with revised treatment regimens, 36/40 subjects from Part A enrolled and 18 new subjects (including 13 from the NHS) entered the study, for a total of 54 subjects. During Study 202B (mean duration of participation =19 months), 33 of these subjects were treated and evaluated for a total of 52 new qualifying flare-ups. Among 10 subjects who withdrew from either Part A (n=4) or Part B (n=6), none were attributed to adverse effects (Table 20).

L1273: Across these phase 2 studies and the NHS, a total of 160 flare-ups with imaging data at baseline and Week 12 comprised the IF-FAS. These events were pooled by treatment group as follows:
L1274: - Placebo/untreated (total N=42 subjects, M =50 flare-ups): 10 flare-ups treated with placebo in Study 201, combined with 40 untreated flare-ups in the NHS
- Palovarotene 5/2.5 mg (N=9, M =9): 9 flare-ups treated with 5/2.5 regimen in Study 201
- Palovarotene 10/5 mg (N=27, M =49): 21 flare-ups in Study 201, and 28 flare-ups in Study 202A, treated with 10/5 regimen
- Palovarotene 20/10 mg (N=12, M =18): 18 flare-ups in Study 202B treated with 20/10 flare-up-only regimen (no prior chronic dosing) in skeletally immature subjects
- Palovarotene chronic/flare-up 20/10 (N=23, M =34): 34 flare-ups in Study 202B treated with 20/10 mg regimen (with prior chronic 5 mg dosing) in skeletally mature subjects
L1275: Because treatment compliance was &lt;80% in only 2/160 flare-ups, the ISE presents analyses of the IF-FAS (all imaged flare-ups), without analyses of a “per-protocol” population. The maximum number of imaged flare-ups in any individual subject/treatment group was 4. In addition to the flare-ups imaged in Study 202B (18 without prior chronic dosing, 34 with prior chronic dosing), there were 14 others (5 without/9 with chronic dosing) that were treated but not imaged; in most cases this was related to the pending transition to Study 202C in which flare-up site imaging was not conducted.
L1276: Demographic data for the groups contributing these data are presented in Table 21. As expected, the group receiving only 20/10 mg flare-up dosing was younger (mean age 13.6 years) than the other treated groups (mean 18 to 25 years). Untreated/imaged subjects in the NHS were also somewhat younger (mean 16.7 years) and had a higher proportion of males (56%) than the other groups. Demographic data for the F-FAS, i.e., including subjects with flare-ups that were not imaged (mostly in the NHS), were similar to the IF-FAS data.

L1291: The use of glucocorticoids to treat the flare-up was similar among the treatment groups (78 to 90%). In the flare-up-only 20/10 and chronic/flare-up 20/10 treatment groups, palovarotene doses were reduced based on tolerability in 23% of subjects at the higher flare-up dose of 20 mg, and in 11% of subjects at the lower flare-up dose of 10 mg, and three subjects (9%) discontinued the drug during flare-up dosing. (Note that all doses were reduced by weight in skeletally immature subjects, prior to any reductions based on tolerability.) In the 10/5 mg and 5/2.5 mg groups, no subjects required dose reduction or discontinuation related to tolerability.
L1292: Flare-ups in the NHS that are included in the IF-FAS (m =40) represent only a small fraction of all reported NHS flare-ups (m =228 in the F-FAS). Most of the other NHS events (m =174) were followed by Telephone Contact (TC) and were not imaged. Flare-ups of the upper back, which comprised 18% of this NHS TC group, were excluded from treatment by protocol from phase 2 studies and from the IF-FAS. Of the remaining flare-up locations, the most frequent among NHS TC flare-ups were hip (18%), lower spine/abdomen (13%), shoulder (13%), distal extremities (12%), upper spine/chest (9%) and knee (8%). The mean number of symptoms was slightly lower in the TC group compared to imaged (IF-FAS) NHS flare-ups (2.7 versus 3.9), and the proportion with only one symptom was higher (15% versus 5%).
L1293: ## Flare-ups Across Phase 2/NHS Studies: Incidence and Volume of New HO at Flare-up Sites
L1294: At Week 12, the ISE states that new HO had developed at the flare-up location in 13/40 (33%) NHS (untreated) flare-ups, and 4/10 (40%) placebo recipients in Study 201, or 17/50 (34%) overall for placebo plus untreated flare-ups. The mean volume of new HO (including all subjects, with or without new HO) was higher with placebo versus NHS (18.0 versus 9.1 cm3); this may be related to a greater proportion of hip flare-ups (50% versus 15%). The mean new HO volume was 10.8 cm3 for the combined placebo/untreated group.
L1295: Data for new HO at Week 12 in the 160 imaged (IF-FAS) flare-ups by pooled treatment group are summarized in Table 23. The proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects with new HO (21 to 41%) was in general not markedly different from placebo/untreated subjects (34%), but the mean volume of new HO was lower at each palovarotene dose level (1.2-5.6 cm3 treated, compared to 10.8 cm3 untreated), albeit with no apparent dose-response effect.

L1329: ## Efficacy of Flare-up Dosing in “Target” Population (\ge 8 Years for Females/\ge 10 Years for Males)
L1330: Based on the safety issue of PPC and risk/benefit considerations (see Section 7.7.1), the Applicant seeks approval only for this “\ge 8F/\ge 10M” population of FOP patients. Among the flare-ups evaluated in the NHS and phase 2 studies, only 10 occurred in younger subjects (i.e., &lt;8-year-old girls, &lt;10-year-old boys): four events in the NHS; and two, three, and one events, respectively, in the palovarotene 5/2.5, 10/5 and 20/10 flare-up groups. Because the majority of flare-ups (150 of total 160 IF-FAS events, 94%) occurred in this “target” population, the baseline data are similar to the overall F-FAS and IF-FAS except for slightly older mean ages, and the efficacy data are also similar (see ISE Table 14.2.11.2.1).
L1331: ## Efficacy of Flare-up Dosing by Age Group
L1332: Because of the variability of new HO volume data and small size of subgroups, evaluation of subgroups is challenging. Table 28 summarizes integrated flare-up HO volume data in two prespecified age subgroups. In the \ge 12- to &lt;17-year-old subgroup, mean volume of new HO in untreated flare-ups was high (mean 25.6 \text{cm}^3), due in part to three events with new HO volume &gt;100 \text{cm}^3 at Week 12 (representing all such events in the overall IF-FAS); mean volume was substantially lower in each palovarotene treatment group. In adults (\ge 18 years), who contributed more than half of the overall flare-up data, the volume of new HO in untreated flare-ups was much lower (mean 4.5 \text{cm}^3), therefore the relative reductions in palovarotene groups were smaller.

L1339: ## Efficacy of Flare-up Dosing by Sex
L1340: Among subjects with imaged flare-ups (IF-FAS), males and females were generally balanced with respect to demographic characteristics, prior FOP history, flare-up symptoms and distribution of flare-up locations. However, new HO data were strikingly different between the sexes. Mean volume of new HO at Week 12 was higher (20.2 \text{cm}^3) in females with untreated flare-ups, due in large part to two hip flare-ups with new HO of 137.0 and 131.7 \text{cm}^3 and two shoulder flare-ups with new HO of 107.0 and 87.3 \text{cm}^3. Mean new HO volumes in palovarotene
L1341: treated females were much lower (0.3 to 3.5 cm3). In males, mean new HO volume was very low in untreated flare-ups (mean 0.1 cm3), and was also low with palovarotene treatment except for the chronic/flare-up 20/10 group (mean 19.8 cm3), which was influenced by two hip flare-ups with new HO of 92.0 and 78.3 cm3 (Table 29).

L1348: ## Efficacy of Flare-up Dosing by Race
L1349: Most subjects with IF-FAS flare-up data were White. The remainder were described by race as Asian (n=2), Black or African American (n=2), “multiple” (n=4), “other” (n=1), and “not available” (n=9). The latter nine subjects were enrolled in France where regulations prohibit collection of race data (at least some of these subjects were probably White). In the ISE, all these groups not designated as White were pooled for analysis and the data were widely variable. Therefore, the evidence does not support any conclusions regarding flare-up efficacy in non-White groups.
L1350: ## Other Flare-up-Based Endpoints
L1351: Flare-up pain by NRS was assessed in all FOP studies, though it should be noted that subjects were unblinded to treatment except in Study 201. Mean pain scores ranged from 3.2 to 4.3 (on 0 to 10 scale) among the various treatment groups at baseline and declined in each group with mean changes at Week 12 ranging from -1.9 to -3.0. NRS scores for flare-up swelling also declined over 12 weeks, with similar changes between treatment groups. There were no consistent trends of change in range of motion at the joint nearest the flare-up site or in FOP-PFQ scores.
L1352: A variety of biomarkers were assessed during flare-ups, including markers of bone formation (P1NP, BSAP, osteocalcin) and bone resorption (CTX); angiogenesis (FGF); and inflammation/muscle degeneration (ESR, IL-6, TNF, LDH, CRP, IL-1 beta, CPK). No notable changes were seen in any of these markers through flare-up Week 12.
L1353: ## Summary of Efficacy of Flare-up Dosing with Respect to the Flare-up Site
L1354: A total of 160 flare-ups were evaluated across studies, including 110 events treated with palovarotene in Studies 201 and 202A/B, 10 events treated with placebo in Study 201 and 40 events untreated in the NHS. There was no evidence that the incidence of new HO at the flare-up site (the prespecified primary endpoint in Study 201) was reduced by palovarotene treatment. There were trends of reduced volume of new HO at the flare-up site with each regimen (5/2.5 mg, 10/5 mg, 20/10 mg) compared to untreated flare-ups. However, this finding is not conclusive because of several factors, including insufficient quantity of placebo-controlled data in Study 201; lack of control and randomization in Study 202; differences in design and population across studies; and lack of positive dose response across treatment regimens.
L1355: Among secondary and other clinical endpoints (not based on HO assessments) in these studies, there was no clear evidence of improved outcomes in treated versus untreated flare-ups. In the randomized, blinded Study 201, subjects receiving the 10/5 mg regimen exhibited trends of greater reduction in flare-up pain severity and improved ROM at the flare-up site, compared to 5/2.5 mg and placebo. However, the differences were not statistically significant and appear unlikely to be clinically meaningful.
L1356: ## Non-Flare-up-Based Outcomes of Chronic/Flare-up Dosing (Studies 202B/C)
L1357: There were 48 phase two subjects who received the chronic/flare-up treatment regimen and who participated in Study 202 Parts B and/or C for a mean of 19 and 20 months, respectively, prior to the February 28, 2020, cutoff date (Table 30). Like Study 301, Study 202C has been on partial clinical hold since December 2019 for treatment of pediatric subjects &lt;14 years old due to risk of PPC, and treatment was paused in older subjects in January 2020; restart data will be available on some of these subjects at a later date (see Section 6.2.1.4).

L1368: ## Study 202B/C: Whole-Body HO results With Chronic/Flare-up Dosing
L1369: Whole-body CT was conducted to assess baseline whole-body HO at the initiation of chronic palovarotene dosing, which occurred either in 202 Part B (Adult Cohort) or in Part C (Pediatric Cohort). L1370: As indicated above, the primary endpoint of Study 202, as per protocol amendment 4 (initiation of Part C), was the annualized change in whole-body HO volume in Parts B and C, as compared to the NHS; and secondary endpoints included percent of subjects with new HO at months 12, 24, 36 and overall. The NDA did not include these analyses with the rationale that 202C was ongoing as of the February 28, 2020, efficacy cut-off date.
L1371: In lieu of these analyses, the ISE only reported WBCT new HO data for the overall Study 202B/C FAS (N=48), and for the following three subgroups based on clinical review of flare-up symptoms and treatments received (including palovarotene and corticosteroids) in Part B:
L1372: - All treated flare-ups (n=9): subjects with all reported flare-ups and flare-up symptoms treated
L1373: - Untreated/undertreated flare-ups (n=30): subjects with at least one event in Part B with symptoms consistent with a flare-up that did not meet the criteria to initiate flare-up dosing (reported as adverse event (AE) of “condition aggravated”)
- No flare-ups or flare-up symptoms (n=9)

L1393: ## 6.3. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L1394: ## 6.3.1. Phase 3: Appropriateness of Reliance on Post Hoc Analyses To Support Efficacy
L1395: ## Issue
L1396: Phase 3 study: appropriateness of reliance on post hoc analyses to support efficacy
L1397: ## Background
L1398: The prespecified primary analysis for the primary endpoint was based on a Bayesian compound Poisson model. Three early interim analyses and one final analysis were prespecified in the protocol of Study 301. The trial crossed the futility boundary at the second interim analysis and the study was paused for dosing. However, additional post hoc analyses, including the Bayesian compound model without square root transformation, found evidence of clinically meaningful benefit of palovarotene.
L1399: Therefore, the submission relies on post hoc analyses to support the efficacy of palovarotene.
L1400: ## Assessment
L1401: Post hoc analyses are generally considered to be hypotheses generating, as they may inflate type-I error and raise concerns for potential bias caused by selection of analyses toward an intended favorable outcome. However, in this specific context, we recognize that the prespecified primary analysis may not have been appropriate for analyzing the primary endpoint, making the results challenging to interpret. Acknowledging the limitations of the prespecified analyses, we think it is reasonable to consider whether alternative, more appropriate analyses may provide evidence of efficacy.
L1402: ## Assessment of the Impact of Square Root Transformation
L1403: The primary endpoint was annualized new HO. However, the rate of growth in HO volume was estimated based on the square root transformation of each incremental change in HO by region between scans. Since WBCT scans were not performed at the same interval in the two studies (scheduled every 6 months in study 301 and every 12 months in the NHS), the prespecified analysis involves summing the square root of each incremental change to compare the square root of the sum of each change, which is problematic as they are not equivalent. This could have resulted in a bias against palovarotene due to the differential schedule of new HO assessments between study 301 and the NHS, which thus might have contributed to the failure of the primary analysis.
L1404: Table 35 illustrates how more frequent assessment could lead to a bias against palovarotene under the prespecified Bayesian analysis using the square root transformation. Assuming a new HO volume of 200 occurs in a body region before Month 6 and subsequently the region grows 200 more in HO volume during Month 6 to Month 12, the annual new HO will be 400. With the prespecified statistical model, it will be counted as two events with growth rate of \sqrt{200} per event under the square root transformation in study 301 and one event with growth rate of \sqrt{400} in the NHS. Therefore, the estimated annual new HO will be 2 \times \sqrt{200} = 28.3 in study 301 and \sqrt{400} = 20 in the NHS, respectively. This example illustrates that the prespecified approach may lead to a nonsensible difference in the estimated annualized new HO and a bias against more frequent assessment.
L1405: **Table 35. An Illustrative Example of Impact of Square Root Transformation on Annualized New HO**
L1406: Study	Month 6 Change	Month 12 Change	From Month 6	Total Change	Estimated Annual New
HO#
301	200	200	400	2 \times \sqrt{200} = 28.3
NHS	Not assessed	400	400	\sqrt{400} = 20

L1408: #Estimated annual new HO is annual number of events times the average amount of new HO per event. Each occurrence of a new HO is counted as an event.
L1409: Abbreviations: HO, heterotopic ossification
L1410: ## FDA's Assessment of Post Hoc Bayesian Analysis Without Square Root Transformation
L1411: The Applicant's post hoc Bayesian analysis without square root transformation resulted in a high posterior probability in support of efficacy. We note that inference from the Bayesian model could be affected by different specification of prior distributions of the multiple parameters in the model and the results could differ if influential priors are specified. FDA's analyses will focus on
L1412: frequentist methods that directly analyze the annualized new HO of each subject with minimal assumptions.
L1413: ## **FDA's Assessment of Applicant's Post Hoc wLME Analyses**
L1414: As noted in the previous section, the Applicant's post hoc wLME analysis, based on the CT scan associated with the longest follow-up and without square root transformation, achieved nominal statistical significance. However, results from the Applicant's wLME could be difficult to interpret as the annualized new HO for each subject was based on various length of follow-up. As most subjects had WBCT assessments on Month 12 (Table 10), we compared the changes in HO volume between study 301 and NHS subjects during a 12-month observation period as a landmark analysis, which does not rely on assumptions on a constant rate of change. Some subjects did not have changes in HO through a 12-month period (four subjects in study 301 and 11 subjects in NHS). Depending on how subjects with no 12-month HO change could be handled, there are different ways for performing the landmark analysis.
L1415: We performed the landmark analyses using different methods for subjects who did not have 12-month data to investigate the consistency of findings. For all these analyses, a robust sandwich variance estimator was used to account for heteroscedasticity in variance. Results from these landmark analyses with different ways of handling subjects without 12-month data and including different covariates were consistently in favor of palovarotene (Table 36). In addition, our analyses did not transform negative new HO values to zero.
