L1424: ## Conclusion
L1425: The prespecified Bayesian compound Poisson model incorporating square root transformation appears to have a bias against palovarotene due to the more frequent assessment in study 301. FDA identified more appropriate methods to compare the annualized new HO between study 301 and NHS subjects and conducted them post hoc.
L1426: Although these post hoc analyses support that the annualized new HO of study 301 subjects was lower than that of NHS subjects, post hoc analyses should be interpreted with caution.
L1427: ## 6.3.2. Phase 3: Use of an External Control Group (NHS) for Evaluation of Efficacy of the Chronic/Flare-up Regimen
L1428: ## Issue
L1429: Phase 3 study: Use of an external control group (NHS) for evaluation of chronic/flare-up regimen
L1430: ## Background
L1431: Because of a paucity of published data regarding FOP disease characteristics and progression over time, the Applicant initiated the natural history study (NHS, Study PVO-1A-001) in 2014 and enrolled 117 subjects, a relatively large proportion of the known global population of approximately 800 FOP patients. During the subsequent planning of the phase 3 study, 301, the Applicant considered that the NHS study population and assessments were suitable to serve as an external control group, as the two studies would be conducted at the same centers, with generally consistent standards of care and associated background treatment, such as use of prednisone for flare-ups. The relative objectivity and blinded assessment of the primary outcome measure, change in HO volume, was considered to minimize the potential for bias. Based on these considerations and the small number of FOP patients available for recruitment, Study 301 was designed as an open-label, single arm study. The Applicant also anticipated that about 40% of NHS subjects would go on to participate in Study 301, adding further consistency between the respective study populations.
L1432: ## Assessment
L1433: ## General Consideration
L1434: Despite the limitations associated with using an external control rather than a randomized concurrent control, FDA recognizes that support for effectiveness can emerge using an externally controlled trial when the following are met:
L1435: - Natural history of the disease is well defined
- External control population is very similar to that of the treatment group
L1436: - Concomitant treatments that affect the primary endpoint are not substantially different between the external control and the trial population
- Results provide compelling evidence of a change in the established progression of disease (December 2019)
L1437: The concomitant treatments in this population are not expected to affect the outcome of interest. The NHS study was performed to characterize the disease process and outcome. The focus here is whether the difference between the study populations in the NHS and study 301 impacted the conclusion regarding efficacy and whether the results are compelling enough to overcome the general concerns of potential confounding factors.
L1438: ## **FDA's Assessment of Comparability of Study Populations**
L1439: The enrollment criteria for the NHS and Study 301 were generally similar. Because NHS was restricted to subjects with the classic R206H mutation, which represents ~97% of FOP patients, the principal analysis population of Study 301 excluded a small number of participants with other mutations.
L1440: Allocation of subjects into these studies was sequential, as NHS enrollment was complete before Study 301 was initiated. All NHS sites also participated in Study 301, and a total of 39 subjects transferred from the NHS into Study 301 and contributed efficacy data to both studies. Any NHS subject who met enrollment criteria (e.g., without retinoid-safety-related exclusions) was eligible for this transition. According to the Applicant, Study 301 enrollment occurred rapidly, exceeding original projections, which resulted in the capping of enrollment at one site (1001, UCSF) which enrolled nine subjects from the NHS. Although the selection process for transition was not random, the Applicant did not assess reasons for not enrolling in 301 among those who were eligible but did not transition. In addition to NHS-to-301 transitions, eight subjects left the NHS to enroll in phase 2 study, 201, at the onset of a flare-up, and many other subjects left the NHS to enroll in other interventional studies. These transfers out of NHS were likely driven at least in part by clinical factors, which are largely unknown.
L1441: Table 37 presents baseline data for three cohorts within the Principal FAS: the 39 transition subjects who contributed efficacy data to both the NHS and Study 301; 62 NHS subjects who did not enroll in Study 301; and 58 subjects in Study 301 who had not participated in the NHS. Transition subjects' data at both NHS baseline and Study 301 baseline (at an average of 2.2 years later) are presented.
L1442: As shown, NHS subjects who remained in the NHS were older (mean age 20.0 year) than subjects who transitioned to Study 301 (mean 13.1 year) and other Study 301 subjects (mean 14.2 year). Consistent with older age, the NHS-only subjects tended to have more advanced disease, with generally higher whole-body HO volumes, greater number of body regions with HO, and higher scores on CAJIS and FOP-PFQ, indicating more severely impaired range of motion and physical function. Transition subjects reported a higher number of flare-ups prior to NHS enrollment (mean 3.8 within 12 months) than the other groups; this was driven by two outliers as discussed above (Section 6.2.1.4).

L1461: The FDA review team performed landmark analyses on the P-FAS population using propensity score weighting, matching, and targeted maximum likelihood estimation methods that are commonly used for causal inference for nonrandomized studies. Results from these analyses are also consistent (Table 40). Balance assessments showed the covariates were well balanced after weighting and matching (Section 16).
L1462: Results from the propensity score-based weighting and matching did not consider that some NHS subjects crossed over to Study 301 in the weighting or matching process, although the within-subject correlation was accounted for in the analysis after matching. The application of a propensity score based matching method needs to consider a bias-variance tradeoff and whether the matched subset is still representative of the target population. When tighter matching on more covariates is requested, the number of matched subjects is much smaller. The targeted maximum likelihood estimation method is generally believed to be robust for inferring the treatment effect for nonrandomized studies, with results that are consistent with results from analyses based on the propensity score weighting and matching. However, validity of conclusions on treatment effects from these analyses relies on the unverifiable assumption that there are no unknown or unmeasured confounding factors that could impact the difference between study 301 and NHS subjects.
L1463: Although loss to follow-up may remain an issue, the majority of subjects in these analyses completed the 12-month follow-up, so results may not be substantially changed. However, because the pattern of losses to follow-up may vary at different follow-up intervals between the two studies, the impact of differential loss to follow-up on results beyond 12 months is unknown.

L1480: Interpretation of results from this analysis should consider to what extent the disease is expected to progress similarly to what was observed in the NHS after these subjects transitioned to study 301. However, the impact of disease progression when enrolled into study 301 could not be fully assessed without a concurrent control.
L1481: ## Conclusion
L1482: When an external control is used, there will be a lack of assurance of comparability between treated and untreated subjects given the lack of randomization. To address the potential impact of measured confounding factors, various analyses using methods that are commonly used for nonrandomized studies were performed and these analyses provided consistent results. However, there is a residual uncertainty on the impact of unknown confounding factors and potential bias (e.g., differential loss to follow-up) on the study conclusion.
L1483: An issue related to differential loss to follow-up is the nonrandom enrollment of NHS subjects into study 301, which may have a potential selection bias if the enrollment was due to clinical outcome observed in NHS. Study 301 subjects were enrolled after NHS enrollment was complete at the same centers. Thus, there was no period of overlap in enrollment, during which clinical factors might have influenced the choice of studies in which to enroll. The enrollment of 39 NHS subjects to transition to Study 301 was non-random and yielded a cohort of subjects who were younger and with less severe disease than other NHS subjects, and who developed somewhat less new HO both off- and on-treatment compared to other subjects. This process could create bias, although the consistency of new HO data (palovarotene versus untreated) among both transition and non-transition subjects tends to support efficacy of the chronic/flare-up treatment regimen, and the transition subjects' data provide some "baseline-controlled" data within a specific group. Ultimately, however, the Applicant did adequately address the concern regarding potential bias caused by non-random enrollment of NHS subjects into Study 301. A randomized control group would have provided more reliable phase 3 results.
L1484: ## 6.3.3. Phase 3: Uncertain Clinical Implications of Negative New HO Volume Data
L1485: ## Issue
L1486: Negative new HO volume data: clinical significance, and implications for primary phase 3 efficacy analysis
L1487: ## Background
L1488: FOP is characterized by accumulation of HO, which is considered to be irreversible. As noted above (Section 6.2.1.3), the prespecified analysis of the phase 3 primary endpoint (volume of new HO per year in Study 301 versus NHS) used a Bayesian compound Poisson model that required any negative new HO data by region to be reset to 0. It was anticipated that the extent of negative HO data would be limited. However, results of these studies showed substantial declines in HO volume in some instances, raising questions about the clinical significance of such changes.
L1489: The negative changes in HO volume had substantial impact on the reduction in annualized new HO in treated subjects. Most post hoc analyses, which were performed by retaining negative HO volumes and produced nominally significant results, would lose nominal significance should negative changes be set to 0.
L1490: ## Assessment
L1491: In Studies 301 and the NHS, postbaseline WBCT scans were compared to the previous scan. If any new HO was qualitatively present in a certain body region, all HO in that region was remeasured. In many cases, the net change in HO was negative (&lt;0 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}) for a specific body region. There were more palovarotene-treated versus untreated subjects (47% and 24% in Study 301 and the NHS, respectively) with negative changes in new HO volume in at least one body region at the last measured timepoint. Net negative changes for total body HO also occurred more frequently in Study 301 (29% in Study 301 versus 5% in the NHS); Figure 10 shows a preponderance of palovarotene-treated patients (in red) with negative new total body HO compared to NHS patients (in gray).
L1492: Figure 10. Studies 301 and NHS: Distribution of Annualized Change in Total Body HO Volume, by Individual Patient
L1493: Source: Study 301 CSR Figure 5
L1494: Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; HO, heterotopic ossification; NHS, natural history study; PVO, palovarotene
L1495: This phenomenon is illustrated in the following WBCT images from a 14-year-old female. The patient received placebo treatment in Study 201 for a left hip flare-up, resulting in new HO at Week 12 (frames b,e) that was not present at baseline (a, d). Subsequently, she received palovarotene 10/5 mg treatment for a knee flare-up, and a 1-year follow-up scan of the left hip (c,f) appeared to show the areas of new HO at Week 12 becoming smaller over time while increasing in radiodensity. The measured difference in volume for the left hip region over this interval was substantial (-46 \text{ cm}^3).
L1496: **Figure 11. Images of Heterotopic Ossification in Hip Over Time**
L1497: Source: Study 301 CSR, Figure 2
L1498: Literature reports indicate that shrinkage of HO lesions may occur in untreated FOP patients, as well as in nongenetic forms of HO. While the mechanism is unknown, it is plausible that this may be related to resolution of edema in newer lesions with progressive calcification and consolidation to mature cortical bone, analogous to the remodeling of callus around a fracture. (per the Applicant's response to IR submission to the NDA on August 5, 2021).
L1499: Because negative HO volume changes were reported more frequently in Study 301 than in the NHS, the Applicant contends that palovarotene treatment may cause HO regression. However, it is important to note that all HO volume measurements in these studies were by body region,
L1500: therefore shrinkage in individual lesion(s) could be offset or masked by increasing size of other lesions within the same region. NHS subjects generally had more HO lesions that were growing in size; therefore, negative changes would tend to be underestimated in these untreated patients to a greater extent than in palovarotene recipients. Because of the lack of data on individual HO lesions in these studies, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the negative new HO data resulted from palovarotene-related regression of existing lesions as seen radiographically (perhaps due to consolidation of the lesion or decreased inflammation), in addition to inhibition of new HO formation.
L1501: The most plausible rationale for excluding negative HO changes from the primary analyses (i.e., resetting to zero as was done in the prespecified analyses) would be that such changes may represent artifact due to measurement variation. The HO volume calculations were in part dependent on subjective assessments and varying orientation of axial slices on different CT scans, however, given the processes of double read and adjudication, measurement error is unlikely to explain some of the larger HO volume declines observed, as described above. Moreover, measurement error would apply equally to scans from treated and untreated subjects, therefore this mechanism alone cannot explain the disproportionate number of treated subjects with net negative HO.
L1502: Thus in at least some instances, negative new HO volume changes are likely to reflect actual shrinkage of lesions, possibly as a natural process of lesion maturation or due to a decrease in inflammation, rather than a decrease in HO itself. The data are insufficient to conclude that palovarotene promotes this process. However, regardless of the exact mechanism, there does not appear to be a plausible rationale for excluding negative HO changes from analyses. On the other hand, if the reduction in volume was due to consolidation or a decrease in the underlying inflammatory process rather than inhibition of the growth of new HO, it is unclear whether the occurrence of negative new HO should be viewed as a treatment benefit, given that neither lesion consolidation nor decrease in inflammation have been associated with improvement in functional status in patients with FOP.
L1503: ## Conclusion
L1504: More frequent occurrence of negative new HO was observed in treated subjects and contributed substantially to the reduction of annualized new HO. However, it remains unclear what could physiologically account for negative HO volume changes or whether the occurrence of negative new HO volume is beneficial to a patient. If negative HO volume is not beneficial (i.e., does not improve functional outcomes), the clinical meaningfulness of the difference in annualized new HO as measured by regional WBCT scan is questionable. Together, these uncertainties regarding how to handle negative changes in HO volume when assessing drug effect bring into question that reliability of the Applicant's pre-specified and post hoc analyses, and thus render any interpretation of a potential benefit of palovarotene on total HO volume problematic.
L1505: ## 6.3.4. Phase 2 Studies: Efficacy of Flare-up-Only Dosing Was Not Established; Efficacy Data Pertaining to Chronic/Flare-up Dosing Were Generally Not Consistent With Phase 3 Data
L1506: ## Issue
L1507: Phase 2 studies: Efficacy of flare-up-only dosing was not established; efficacy data pertaining to chronic/flare-up dosing were generally not consistent with phase 3 data.
L1508: ## Background
L1509: The initial phase 2 studies were designed to demonstrate the potential of palovarotene to prevent formation of new HO at flare-up sites (Studies 201, 202A, 202B). The primary endpoint in this phase was the proportion of flare-ups resulting in significant new HO; this endpoint was not met with palovarotene treatment, although there were trends of reduced volume of new HO at the flare-up sites, a secondary endpoint. These findings are discussed in Section 6.2.2.4 above.
L1510: Subsequently (Studies 202B, 202C), chronic daily dosing was introduced, and the goal of treatment was changed to the reduction of new whole-body HO (annualized volume) as compared to untreated patients in the NHS, similar to the primary endpoint of Study 301. Unlike Study 301, Study 202 had no prespecified interim analyses, and because Study 202C was ongoing at the cutoff date for the NDA, few analyses of the 202B/C data were presented, and none involved the primary endpoint comparison to NHS data.
L1511: ## Assessment
L1512: Overall, the annualized rate of new whole-body HO was relatively high in Study 202B (mean 28.0 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) and Study 202C (mean 24.3 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}), compared to Study 301 (mean 9.4 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) and the NHS (23.7 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) (raw data, negatives included, no square root transformation).
L1513: The palovarotene chronic/flare-up regimen was the same in Studies 202B/C and 301: daily 5 mg with increase to 20/10 mg for flare-ups for 12 weeks, extended in 4-week increments for persistent symptoms, with weight-based dose reductions for skeletally immature patients. However, as described in Section Error! Reference source not found., flare-up dosing was used less extensively in Study 202B compared to Studies 202C and 301 based on different flare-up qualifying criteria specified in the protocols. An analysis of subgroups in the ISE suggests that this resulted in undertreatment (i.e., only the 5 mg chronic daily dose) of at least some flare-up symptoms in a large proportion of subjects (30/48) in Study 202B and an especially high mean volume of new HO (33.5 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) in this subgroup, compared to the 9/48 subjects in whom all flare-up symptoms were treated with flare-up dosing (mean new HO -3.0 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}). However, this observation is inconsistent with the data specific to Part C, in which all flare-up symptoms were treated but rates of new HO remained high.

L1515: Another issue is that the data from the “undertreatment of flare-up symptoms” subgroup of 30 subjects in Study 202B does not tend to support the effectiveness of the chronic 5 mg dose. In addition, the 9/48 subjects who had no reported flare-up symptoms in Study 202B/C experienced high levels of new HO (mean 25.1 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) despite continuous 5 mg dosing. This finding is not
L1516: consistent with data from other studies indicating that subjects without any flare-up symptoms generally develop relatively smaller quantities of new HO: among such patients, mean new HO volumes were 2.9 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in Study 301 and 6.7 \text{cm}^3/\text{year} in the NHS.
L1517: Comparisons across these studies are confounded by known and unknown differences in the respective study populations. Subjects in Study 202B/C were approximately 3 to 5 years older on average than Study 301 or the NHS because skeletally immature patients began chronic treatment later (in Study 202C rather than 202B) and were excluded from the group of additional patients who enrolled in the study at Part B.
L1518: Per protocol, subjects who enrolled de novo in Study 202B, and all subjects in Study 301 and the NHS, had not had any flare-up symptoms within 4 weeks of enrollment, and were therefore unlikely to develop substantial quantities of new HO at the site of any recent flare-up following the baseline whole-body CT. This did not apply to the other group of 202B/C subjects, who had participated in Studies 201 and 202A and may have begun chronic treatment in 202B immediately following a flare-up. In addition, the Applicant believes that this cohort may not be comparable to the other groups/studies because their initial enrollment (in Study 201) was prompted by an acute flare-up. Indeed, this cohort did exhibit larger quantities of new whole-body HO in 202B/C compared to the “de novo” cohort (mean new HO, 121.3 versus 57.8 \text{cm}^3 at month 36 by clinical reviewer calculation).
L1519: ## Conclusion
L1520: Because of the apparent inconsistency of the Study 202B/C versus Study 301 data and these complicating factors of protocol changes and differences in study populations, a more complete assessment of palovarotene efficacy in FOP will require further analysis of the 202B/C data, including comparisons to untreated NHS subjects and control of covariates; analysis of subjects who transferred from the NHS to Studies 202B/C or 301; and discussion of differences in WBCT interpretation procedures that were used in these studies. A detailed request for additional data and analyses was communicated by DGE to the Applicant on October 28, 2022, and discussed in a teleconference on November 18, 2022. The Applicant now has access to all WBCT scans collected up to the last-patient-last-visit for Studies 202 and 301, with a cut-off date of September 2022. The requested additional data and analyses, which will include post restart data from subjects who resumed palovarotene following the treatment pause in 2020, will not be available during this review cycle and will be submitted at a later date.
L1521: Recognizing that whole-body HO data from Study 202 Part C is most comparable to Study 301 based on use of the same treatment protocol, the Applicant will conduct separate analyses for Part C, using as baseline the first WBCT scan in Part C that was not obtained during or within 1 month after the end of a flare-up, for consistency with the Study 301 and NHS data to be compared. Combined Part B/C data will also be analyzed, using each subject's baseline WBCT scan at the time of initiating chronic therapy (either in Part B or Part C). Although there was less extensive use of flare-up dosing in Part B, analysis of the combined 202B/C HO data (as prespecified in the primary study endpoint) is important because the chronic 5 mg dose remained the same throughout, and because the combined data represent the longest duration of treatment (WBCT data are available through month 36 for most subjects in 202B/C versus month 18 for most subjects in 301).
L1522: ## 7. Risk and Risk Management
L1523: ## 7.1. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Nonclinical Data
L1524: Toxicological characterization of palovarotene was conducted in a battery of studies consistent with the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH)-M3(R2) guidance for industry (January 2010). A series of pharmacology, pharmacokinetics (PK)/absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME), repeat dose general toxicology studies of up to 26- and 39-week duration in rats and dogs, respectively, as well as reproductive toxicology (male and female fertility and early embryonic development (FEED), single species (rat) embryofetal development (EFD) and juvenile animal toxicity studies were conducted. Additional subchronic studies were completed in rabbits, rat, and dogs. As palovarotene adversely affected fetal development in pregnant rats, and retinoids as a class are known to carry a risk of affecting fetal development, neither an EFD study in pregnant animals of a second species nor a pre-/postnatal developmental toxicity study were warranted. A complete battery of genotoxicity studies was conducted. The Applicant provided a “weight-of-evidence”-based assessment of the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene. Nonclinical toxicity studies were also performed separately to qualify metabolites (M2, M3, M4a and M4b) for genetic toxicity and in vivo toxicity in rats and dogs.
L1525: Notable toxicities with potential clinical relevance will be discussed in more detail below.
L1526: ## Skeletal Toxicity
L1527: Palovarotene adversely affected the skeletal system in rats but not dogs. In juvenile rats (aged 3 weeks at initiation), changes were noted in the growth plates, cartilage/joints, and bones at doses \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day (below clinical exposure, based on AUC). In long bones and vertebrae, physes were either widened due to an expanded zone of hypertrophy/maturation (accompanied by chondrodystrophy), narrowed, or partially/completely closed. Effects of palovarotene were also extended to hyaline and articular cartilages. Additional changes included avascular necrosis, sometimes with microfracture of trabeculae and severe malformation of the head and/or neck of the femur at 1.2 mg/kg/day (below clinical exposure). The skeletal effects occurred with correlative decreases in biochemical bone formation markers (OC and PINP), and impacted bone size, shape, mass, geometry, and growth in general. Recovery was not attained for the majority of the skeletal and growth plate effects. Premature phyeal closure is also a risk noted in the palovarotene clinical program. In adult rats, skeletal effects were limited to chondrodystrophy in the epiphyseal growth plate of knee/stifle joint, which remains active throughout life in this species, with fractures near the long bone growth plates in a few rats at the highest dose level of 5 mg/kg/day (~1-fold MRHD by AUC) but not at \le 1 mg/kg/day (below clinical exposure). Chondrodystrophy was partly reversed when mild or minimal but persisted when severe, which is expected based on the biology and time-dependence of the endochondral bone formation process.
L1528: ## Mucocutaneous Effects
L1529: Mucocutaneous toxicity occurred in a dose and time-related manner in adult rats, rabbits, and dogs that involved mainly the skin. The skin changes were characterized by hair coat changes,
L1530: skin erythema, edema, scaling, epithelial hyperplasia (acanthosis), acute/chronic inflammation, hyperkeratosis, and/or hypergranulosis in the epidermis. In juvenile rats, skin lesions were limited to dry skin, thin fur cover, and/or scab. Squamous epithelium effects in other tissues, such as nonglandular mucosa of the stomach (forestomach), esophagus (rabbits only), and conjunctivae of the eye and surface of inner ear (dogs only), were also noted and thought to be related to skin toxicity. Mucocutaneous effects were reversible when dosing stopped. Skin effects have long been known to occur in response to retinoids and similar mucocutaneous changes are the most reported adverse reactions across all palovarotene clinical programs.
L1531: ## Reproductive Toxicity
L1532: ## Teratogenicity
L1533: Administration of daily oral doses of palovarotene to pregnant rats during the period of organogenesis resulted in multiple fetal external, visceral, and skeletal malformations at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day (below clinical exposures), consistent with the pattern of retinoid-mediated embryopathy. While maternal toxicity was evident by reductions in body weight gains at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day and lower food consumption at 1.25 mg/kg/day, the teratogenic findings with palovarotene are consistent with malformations noted with the retinoid class and were considered unrelated to maternal toxicity.
L1534: The Applicant measured palovarotene levels in human semen samples as an indirect measure of male-mediated embryo and fetal development risk. The data showed that the maximal estimated level of palovarotene in single ejaculate (33 ng or \sim 0.00017\% of the daily dose 20 mg administered) at 3 hours postdose resulted in a very low (2.7%) semen to plasma ratio. The maximum potential fetal exposure to palovarotene through semen is estimated to be 0.0066 ng/mL, which is 100-fold lower than exposure at the NOAEL (0.7 ng/mL) for effects on fetal malformations. Based on the absence of genotoxicity, testicular toxicity upon chronic exposure, and low transfer of the drug to human serum, palovarotene is considered unlikely to affect the development of an embryo or fetus carried by a pregnant female partner exposed to palovarotene via the patient's semen.
L1535: ## Testicular Toxicity
L1536: In the 4-week rat toxicity study, evidence of testicular toxicity including testicular degeneration, hypospermia, cellular debris in the epididymides and reduced sperm motility were seen in male rats given palovarotene at daily oral doses that exceeded maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of 5 mg/kg/day (\sim 1-fold MRHD by AUC). Though testicular changes were previously reported with retinoids, similar effects were not recapitulated in the pivotal 26-week repeat dose rat toxicity or male fertility studies and palovarotene had no effect on male rat fertility.
L1537: ## Genotoxicity and Carcinogenicity
L1538: Palovarotene was not genotoxic when tested in a battery of genotoxicity studies. Dedicated rodent carcinogenicity studies to assess the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene have not been conducted; instead, the Applicant assessed the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene using a WoE approach using data from the completed nonclinical studies, published literature and the intended patient population. The nonclinical reviewer concluded that the human carcinogenicity potential of palovarotene is uncertain based on the target signaling pathway, preneoplastic
L1539: changes observed in chronic rat and monkey studies, and tumor findings noted in rodent carcinogenicity studies with other retinoids. Carcinogenicity assessment in two rodent species is considered necessary as a post marketing requirement. Late in the review cycle, the Applicant submitted an amendment with additional nonclinical information requesting reconsideration of the postmarketing requirement for carcinogenicity studies. The nonclinical team will fully review the information amendment and request consultation from the Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee upon NDA resubmission. Details are included in Sections 13 and 22.
L1540: ## Impurities
L1541: The Applicant proposed a high acceptance criterion (originally (b) (4) and current plan (b) (4)%) for a drug substance impurity, (b) (4), which was present at very low levels (up to (b) (4)%) in palovarotene batches used for pivotal nonclinical toxicity studies. In order to qualify the drug substance impurity (b) (4), the Applicant conducted genotoxicity assessments (QSAR, in vitro Ames and chromosomal aberration) and a 4-week oral repeat dose general toxicity study in rats. (b) (4) was not genotoxic and no safety issue was identified in the rat toxicity study (see detailed discussions in Sections 7.7 and 13).
L1542: ## Conclusion
L1543: The safety issues identified in the nonclinical studies, including skin lesions, growth suppression, and premature closure of physis in juveniles, have been observed in humans treated with palovarotene. The skeletal findings are consistent with the retinoid class and are consistent with the desired pharmacological effect of palovarotene i.e., inhibition of chondrogenesis in the indicated FOP population. Risk of fetal malformations are based on the palovarotene rat EFD study and the class. Because of the exaggerated pharmacology in healthy animal models, no safety margins were established at the palovarotene NOAEL doses of &lt;0.03 mg/kg/day and &lt;12 mg/kg/day in the 26-week rat and 39-week dog toxicity studies, respectively (Table 42). The human risks might be manageable through various clinical interventions, including use of skin ointment for skin changes, growth monitoring in pediatric patients, labelling (e.g., contraindication and pregnancy testing before/during/after treatment) and other risk mitigation strategies, as appropriate. The available nonclinical database addressed all identified nonclinical safety issues. The nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology team identified no issues precluding approval of palovarotene in the indicated FOP population and considers postmarket studies necessary to characterize the long-term carcinogenicity risk with chronic palovarotene exposure.

L1549: Abbreviation: NOAEL, no observed adverse effect level
L1550: ## 7.2. Potential Risks or Safety Concerns Based on Drug Class or Other Drug-Specific Factors
L1551: Retinoids are associated with numerous class-related adverse effects. For palovarotene, the two most serious concerns are PPC and embryo-fetal toxicity, which have been reported with other retinoids and are discussed below (Sections 7.7.1 and Error! Reference source not found. respectively). By June 25, 2020, a total of 24 events of PPC were reported in 96 pediatric subjects aged &lt;17 years at enrollment, which was approximately 30% in patients ≥8/10 to 11 years of age (4 of 12 (33%) boys aged 10 to 11 years and 5 of 17 (29%) girls aged 8 to 11 years). Reduced bone mineral density appears to be associated with palovarotene and other retinoids and is discussed in Section 7.7.4. Other potential retinoid class effects include neuropsychiatric effects including depression, suicidality, seizures and pseudotumor cerebri; mucocutaneous adverse effects; serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome; musculoskeletal effects including arthralgia and back pain; hypersensitivity reactions; acute pancreatitis; hepatotoxicity; elevated triglycerides; inflammatory bowel disease; hearing impairment; and eye abnormalities including decreased night vision.

L1553: ## 7.3. Potential Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L1554: Not applicable; palovarotene has not been marketed in any country.
L1555: ## 7.4. FDA Approach to the Safety Review
L1556: The bulk of the FOP/palovarotene safety data involves the 5 mg chronic nonflare dose or the 20/10 mg flare-up regimen (all doses weight adjusted) in Studies 202B, 202C and 301. For this review, Clinical Data Scientist staff analyzed the pooled safety data from these studies for each of these regimens (chronic and 20/10 flare-up) in the Applicant's intended target population (females \ge 8 years of age, males \ge 10 years of age). These data are presented in this section alongside a Palovarotene (PVO) Total group consisting of all PVO-exposed subjects age \ge 8F/10M from all interventional FOP studies (201, 202A/B/C, 301), including the lower-dose flare-up regimens (10/5 mg, 5/2.5 mg) for which total exposure (including treatment duration) was relatively limited.
L1557: The safety data cutoff dates were February 28, 2020, for the initial NDA submission; July 30, 2021, for the NDA resubmission; and January 31, 2022, for the 90-day Safety Update. Although no subjects &lt;14 years of age have received palovarotene since the partial clinical hold issued on December 4, 2019, some off-treatment data pertaining to bone safety have been collected in these subjects. Subjects \ge 14 years of age also interrupted treatment starting on January 24, 2020, because of findings of the Study 301 interim analysis #2. Many of these subjects have since resumed treatment following treatment interruptions lasting 3 to 19 months, and some younger subjects also resumed treatment after reaching age 14.
L1558: The FOP full analysis set (FOP-FAS) includes all subjects enrolled or dosed in FOP clinical studies, including the NHS. The FOP flare-up (F) full analysis set (FOP-F-FAS) includes all subjects with at least one flare-up in the NHS (monitored either by phone contacts, or by in-clinic evaluation), or at least one palovarotene- or placebo-treated flare-up while on-study in a FOP interventional study.
L1559: Safety data are also included in the NDA for pediatric patients with multiple osteochondromas (MO) in study PVO-2A-201 (MO-FAS); six phase 1 and 2 studies in adults with COPD (COPD-FAS); and 12 single- and multiple-dose studies in healthy volunteers (HV-FAS). These datasets were not pooled with the FOP data based on differences in study designs and populations.
L1560: In addition to routine safety assessments (AEs, concomitant medications, vital signs, ECG, physical exam, safety labs), the FOP palovarotene studies included frequent pregnancy testing, the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS), and assessments related to bone safety and growth; the latter are discussed in Section 7.7.1. Because patients in the NHS were not treated, AE collection was limited to events resulting from study procedures.
L1561: No major data quality or integrity issues were identified that would preclude performing a safety review for this NDA. There were no major identified issues with respect to recording, coding, and categorizing AEs. The Applicant's translations of verbatim terms to MedDRA preferred terms for the events reported in Studies 201, 202A/B/C and 301 were reviewed and found to be acceptable. Treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) were protocol-defined as AEs that developed or worsened after administration of the first dose to 7 days after the last dose of study drug. All AEs in the reviewed trials were coded using MedDRA version 22.0 and reported according to standard criteria for mild, moderate or severe. These methods were found to be acceptable.
L1562: ## 7.5. Adequacy of Clinical Safety Database
L1563: The NDA 215559 safety database for palovarotene is adequate for the proposed FOP indication and dosage regimens. The FOP phase 2 and 3 studies enrolled a relatively large proportion of the known patients with this disease globally. Although comparison safety data in untreated FOP patients is very limited, there is substantial placebo-controlled data available for palovarotene in prior COPD studies (adults) and a multiple osteochondromas study (pediatric), and the safety profile of retinoids as a drug class is well known from extensive experience with other retinoids.
L1564: A total of 164 patients with FOP received at least one dose of palovarotene, including 139 patients in the Applicant's intended target population (age \ge8/10 years). L1595: ## 7.6.1.1. Overall Treatment-Emergent Adverse Event Summary
L1596: The following table presents an overview of treatment-emergent adverse events for the ≥8- to 10-year-old study population. There were no deaths during treatment or related to a TEAE. These two regimens were also similar with regard to overall AEs (97% versus 94%) and AEs leading to drug interruption or discontinuation. L1605: ## 7.6.1.2. Deaths
L1606: No deaths were reported during palovarotene treatment or for 30 days post-treatment in the FOP-FAS. In Study 301, a 13-year-old subject with a history of restrictive lung disease died 2.5 months after discontinuing palovarotene treatment because of disease progression and difficulty traveling. A postmortem exam determined the cause of death as restrictive lung disease from complications of FOP.
L1607: A 38-year-old female in the FOP NHS, with substantial disease burden based on high CAJIS score, died of a cardiac arrest. This subject never received palovarotene.
L1608: There were no deaths reported in the MO-FAS or HV-FAS.
L1609: In the COPD-FAS, most deaths were from cardiovascular or respiratory events and were related to the subjects' age and underlying disease. None of the deaths in the COPD-FAS were assessed as related to study treatment by the Investigator.
L1610: ## 7.6.1.3. Serious Adverse Events
L1611: Serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 36% of palovarotene-treated FOP subjects age \ge8/10 years. This high incidence is not unexpected given the severe morbidity related to the underlying disease. The most common SOC classes of serious adverse events were musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders (13.7% of subjects) and infections and infestations (10.1%). These included musculoskeletal events associated with FOP and/or retinoid use including premature physeal closure (PT: epiphyses premature fusion, which is discussed in Section 7.7.1), arthralgia, back pain and pain in extremity. SAEs of “condition aggravated” represent FOP flare-ups that did not meet protocol criteria for treatment; this issue is discussed in Section 7.7.3.

L1622: Abbreviations: AE, adverse event; FAS, full analysis set; FOP-FAS, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva full analysis set; N, number of patients in treatment arm; n, number of patients with adverse event; PVO, Palovarotene; SAE, severe adverse event; SOC, system organ class; TEAE, treatment-emergent adverse event
L1623: Retinoids, and hypervitaminosis A, have been associated with CNS adverse events including headache, benign intracranial hypertension/ pseudotumor cerebri and seizures/convulsions. In the FOP-FAS, two subjects (16 y/o female and 32 y/o male) experienced SAEs of tonic-clonic seizure or epilepsy during treatment with 20/10 mg flare-up dosing in Study 202B/C. In both cases, the subject had no prior history of a seizure and was begun on anticonvulsant treatment. In Study 301, a 15-year-old female with prior history of febrile convulsions experienced an SAE of syncope and later a nonserious syncopal seizure during flare-up treatment. In the MO study, a 7-year-old male with a history of febrile seizures experienced an SAE of status epilepticus on Day 199 of treatment with palovarotene 5 mg. Each of these subjects continued palovarotene treatment. A prior history of seizures was reported by 11% of subjects in the FOP NHS, and by 4% of Study 301 subjects at enrollment. In COPD studies, one subject (out of 458) treated with palovarotene 5 mg experienced an SAE of epilepsy, considered not related to treatment by the investigator. Based on a high background incidence of seizure in patients with FOP, these data do not support an association of palovarotene with seizures. One subject in Study 202, a 24-year-old female with a long history of myoclonus, discontinued the study due to an SAE of myoclonus, which appears to be associated with FOP.
L1624: ## 7.6.1.4. Dropouts and/or Discontinuations Due to Adverse Events
L1625: Among FOP subjects age \ge 8/10 years, treatment was discontinued due to an AE in 11 subjects (8%) and the incidence was similar between chronic and flare-up regimens (5% each). Infections and infestations were most common (4 discontinuations, 3% of subjects). Mucocutaneous AEs, such as dry skin, generally responded to dose reduction and resulted in only 2 discontinuations.

L1634: ## 7.6.1.5. Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events
L1635: Mucocutaneous adverse effects are characteristic of retinoids and hypervitaminosis A and were reported by most subjects. L1660: Severe mucocutaneous AEs were reported in 51% of FOP subjects and included skin exfoliation (31%), drug eruption (i.e., retinoid dermatitis, 18%) and blisters (7%). Mucocutaneous events were the most common reason for dose reductions, especially at the higher 20/10 mg flare-up doses; in almost all cases, subjects were able to continue treatment with lower doses and/or supportive measures such as skin lotions, lip balm, artificial tears, etc.
L1661: Because of the association of retinoids with depression and potential suicidality, the C-SSRS was administered to all study participants age \ge 8 years in Study 301 as well as the NHS. There was no evidence of an increase in suicidal thoughts or behavior. The FMQ for depression identified 11% of subjects, and one subject discontinued treatment after 1 month due to “non-suicidal/intentional self-injury.”
L1662: Hearing impairment is a common feature of FOP and was reported by 43% of NHS subjects. Audiometry in Study 301 confirmed high rates of hearing loss at baseline; the incidence and type of abnormal clinically significant findings at 12 months was similar to baseline. Hearing impairment TEAEs were reported in 12% of palovarotene-treated subjects in the FOP-FAS, with similar incidence during chronic and flare-up treatment (7% versus 8%, respectively); none of these events were considered severe or led to discontinuation of treatment. AEs of hearing impairment were much less frequent in subjects with MO or COPD, with no imbalances between palovarotene and placebo.
L1663: In Study 201, the only FOP study with a randomized, placebo-controlled design, the highest dose group (10/5 mg), compared to 5/2.5 mg or placebo, reported higher incidence of AEs of pruritis, dry skin and arthralgia; no other apparent imbalances were noted. There were no AEs that led to discontinuation, and only one SAE (vessel puncture site pain, in 10/5 study arm). A summary of AEs among subjects age \ge 8/10 in this study is included in Section 17.
L1664: ## 7.6.1.6. Laboratory Findings
L1665: Clinical laboratory evaluations including hematology, serum chemistry and urinalysis showed no clinically meaningful changes from baseline in mean or median values.
L1666: ## Triglycerides
L1667: Marked elevations have been reported in patients treated with other retinoids. In the FOP-FAS, hypertriglyceridemia AEs were reported in four subjects at the 20/10 regimen and two subjects during the chronic 5 mg period. Levels over 400 mg/dL were reported in just one subject with baseline high triglyceride (217 mg/dL) and a level of 428 mg/dL at 15 months of treatment with the chronic 5 mg dose. There were no significant trends in mean lipids during chronic or flare-up periods of the FOP studies, or in the prior COPD studies.
L1668: ## Lipase/Amylase
L1669: Acute pancreatitis has been reported with other retinoids, sometimes in association with elevated triglycerides. In palovarotene studies in FOP and COPD, the incidence of lipase elevations was similar between the palovarotene and placebo or untreated subjects. Lipase elevations in the FOP-FAS were transient and generally resolved while remaining on palovarotene treatment.
L1670: No TEAEs of pancreatitis were identified in the FOP-FAS, MO-FAS or the COPD-FAS populations. However, a 23-year-old white male in the HV-FAS had a SAE of pancreatitis during a DDI study with palovarotene and ketoconazole. The subject had asymptomatic mildly
L1671: elevated lipase on Day 2, received paracetamol on Day 14 for headache and initiated ketoconazole on Day 15. Lipase increased to 1084 U/L and the subject was hospitalized with mild abdominal pain. Triglycerides were normal. Palovarotene and ketoconazole were discontinued. The Investigator considered the event of pancreatitis to be possibly related to palovarotene and to paracetamol, with a possible contribution of ketoconazole by way of increasing palovarotene levels
L1672: ## Liver Function Tests
L1673: Other retinoids have been associated with moderate elevations of liver enzymes. In FOP studies, TEAEs of elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT)/aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and GGT were more common during the palovarotene 20/10 mg flare-up treatment compared with chronic treatment and placebo, indicating a possible dose effect. No subjects met Hy's Law criteria for liver transaminases (AST, ALT) or AST/ALT values &gt;3\timesULN and total bilirubin values &gt;2\timesULN. Hepatic steatosis was identified in the FOP-FAS and COPD-FAS but with a similar incidence between the palovarotene and placebo/untreated groups.
L1674: Vital sign measures including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature showed no consistent or clinically meaningful changes from baseline associated with palovarotene treatment.
L1675: ECG parameters in FOP studies showed no clinically meaningful changes in intervals including QT, QTcF and QTcB. In addition, a thorough QT study was conducted evaluating the effect of therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses of palovarotene on ECG parameters.
L1676: Hearing was tested in Study 301. Hearing impairment TEAEs were reported in 12% of palovarotene-treated subjects in the FOP-FAS, none of which were severe or lead to discontinuation of treatment. Almost half of FOP subjects had a history of hearing impairment.
L1677: ## 7.7. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L1678: ## 7.7.1. Premature Physeal Closure in Growing Children, With Potential for Adverse Effects on Growth
L1679: ## Issue
L1680: Premature physeal closure was reported in many pediatric subjects treated with palovarotene, with potential for adverse effects on growth
L1681: ## Background
L1682: Systemic retinoids, as well as vitamin A toxicity, have long been associated with a variety of adverse musculoskeletal effects. Among these are published case reports of PPC occurrence and impaired growth in children with prolonged exposure to various retinoids prescribed for the treatment of dermatologic conditions or cancer. Growth plate abnormalities and premature closure were also observed in juvenile rats exposed to palovarotene and were consistent with retinoid class effects (see Section 7.1). Prior to palovarotene studies, PPC had not been reported in patients with FOP.
L1683: Because of the potential risk, palovarotene FOP studies included a Bone Safety Management Plan (BSMP) in pediatric subjects (&lt;18 years of age). Based on hand/wrist x-rays at screening to assess growth plates, subjects with &lt;90% skeletal maturity (i.e., had achieved &lt;90% of adult height), defined as bone age &lt;12 years (girls) or &lt;14 years (boys), received weight-adjusted dosing and continued monitoring. This included scheduled PA hand/wrist and AP knee radiographs to monitor growth plates and bone age; measurements of standing height (stadiometry) and knee height (knee caliper); and use of whole-body CT scans to measure femur and tibia length and further assess growth plates. In addition, WBCT scans were used (in all subjects, pediatric and adult) to assess potential avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, due to the association of AVN with corticosteroid use and the reported occurrence of AVN with palovarotene in a rat study. These assessments were conducted every 6 months in Study 301 and every 6 to 12 months in Study 202B/C. Growth assessments were conducted every 12 months in the NHS. Similar monitoring was included in a pediatric study of palovarotene treatment for a different indication, multiple osteochondromas (MO).
L1684: Study 301 began enrollment in November 2017. In 2019, multiple instances of PPC among pediatric subjects in this study were reported based on scheduled radiographs. In December 2019, a partial clinical hold was imposed for the dosing of any children under age 14 years in all palovarotene studies, including the FOP Studies 301 and 202C and the MO study. This partial clinical hold remains in effect, and dosing was never resumed except for children who subsequently reached age 14. Protocol amendment 5 added an extended 2-year safety follow-up for pediatric subjects, including annual assessment of growth, hand/wrist radiograph and WBCT.
L1685: ## Assessment
L1686: Regarding *bone safety*, 3 pediatric age categories were evaluated in the ISS:
L1687: - &lt;8 years (girls)/&lt;10 years (boys), representing a prepubertal population;
- ≥8/10 to &lt;14 years of age, representing an early adolescent population (generally early-to-mid pubertal) which has, on average, attained approximately 80 to 90% of adult height;
- ≥14 to &lt;18 years, representing a late adolescent population.
L1688: In Study 301 at baseline, pediatric patients with FOP exhibited generally normal skeletal maturation: mean chronologic age and bone age by x-ray were closely matched (11.4 and 11.5 years, respectively), and all adolescents age ≥14 years had achieved ≥90% skeletal maturity, i.e., bone age ≥12 (girls) or ≥14 (boys). During palovarotene treatment, mean increase from baseline in bone age (BA) was slightly greater than mean increase in chronologic age (CA): mean ratios of \Delta BA/\Delta CA were 1.2-1.4 at months 6, 12, 18 and 24. Individual changes were highly variable. Growth plate x-rays were not obtained in FOP NHS patients for comparison.
L1689: Standing height was also in the normal range at baseline in most children with FOP. Table 51 presents mean height Z-scores, which ranged from -0.50 to +0.44 at baseline across the three pediatric age categories in Studies 301 and the NHS. Although there was great variability among individual subjects, these data showed a trend toward lower height Z-scores in adolescents compared to younger children at baseline; this may reflect the development of spinal deformities in some adolescents with FOP. At month 12, mean height Z-scores declined moderately from baseline among palovarotene-treated subjects &lt;14 years old; there were slightly smaller mean
L1690: declines among untreated NHS subjects. Differences in growth between treated and untreated subjects were most apparent in subjects who developed PPC, as discussed below.

L1696: Across Studies 301 and 202B/C, there were 25 subjects in the youngest group (age &lt;8/10 years at study entry) who were treated with palovarotene; among these, 14 (56%) developed PPC. There were 39 early adolescent subjects (age ≥8/10 to &lt;14 years); among these, 10 (26%) developed PPC as of the ISS cutoff date (July 31, 2021), and 3 others were reported as of the Safety Update cutoff (January 31, 2022), for a total of 13/39 in this age group (33%). Among 38 older adolescents (age ≥14 to &lt;18 years) in these studies, none were reported to develop PPC.
L1697: The mean age at enrollment of subjects who went on to develop PPC was 8.0 years, compared with 12.3 years for subjects &lt;18 years of age who did not develop PPC. There was a similar distribution of females and males in subjects with and without PPC. With one exception, all cases of PPC became first apparent on x-rays of the knee (partial or complete closure of distal femur and/or proximal tibia growth plates), typically on the scheduled x-rays at month 12 of treatment. PPC appeared to be bilaterally symmetric and synchronous at other joints, based on a very limited number of subjects with bilateral or additional x-rays; this issue was not systematically evaluated. Advances in bone age at the hand/wrist were generally similar in subjects with and without PPC. In the ISS, the Applicant evaluated palovarotene exposure (cumulative dose, duration of chronic or flare-up dosing, AUC for concentration versus time curve) for pediatric subjects with and without PPC; no consistent trends were apparent.
L1698: Table 52 shows that while palovarotene treatment was associated with trends of slower growth overall in comparison to NHS subjects, the subset that developed PPC accounted for most of the difference, especially among early adolescent subjects (age ≥8/10 to &lt;14 years). In Study 301, mean standing height increase was 1.2 cm/year in this age group with PPC, compared to 3.5 cm/year in treated subjects without PPC and 4.2 cm/year in untreated subjects, and the proportion with growth velocity &lt;4 cm/year was greater (86%, 54% and 41% in these respective groups). It should be noted that this is a small subgroup (seven subjects age ≥8/10 to &lt;14 years with PPC).

L1708: Table 54 lists the 27 study subjects with reported PPC: 3 who received palovarotene in the phase 2 study, 202B/C, and 24 treated in the phase 3 study, 301. There were five subjects (marked with * in the table) who received only chronic dosing, and the remainder received both chronic and flare-up dosing. All of these subjects received weight-based dose reductions at enrollment based on bone age indicating &lt;90% skeletal maturity. As shown in the table, almost all the subjects who developed PPC experienced declines in height Z-score during treatment, but individual changes were highly variable. The challenges of growth assessment in FOP patients are illustrated in the data for subject # (b) (6), who exhibited a large decline in height Z-score (-4.9) that resulted from an absolute height decline of 17 cm, no doubt reflecting changes in posture and/or deformities.
L1709: Following the interruption of palovarotene treatment on or before initiation of the PPC-related clinical hold, growth data are available for up to 2 years off treatment in numerous subjects (and
L1710: are included in Table 54 for these subjects). In general, trajectories of height Z-score and other growth parameters continued unchanged in subjects with and without PPC, showing no evidence of a rebound in growth following palovarotene discontinuation.
L1711: In addition to the risk of reduced stature based on growth slowing or arrest, PPC at the distal femur and/or proximal tibia has the potential to create leg length discrepancy due to asymmetric effects on the right and left leg, or abnormal knee angulation due to differential growth of medial and lateral aspects of the growth plate. Two parameters included in Table 54 are relevant to these potential risks. The difference between right and left leg length was derived from the sum of femur and tibia length, as measured by whole-body CT scans, on each side. The Applicant postulated that a change from baseline of &gt; +1.5 cm or &lt; -1.5 cm in the R-L difference may be of concern; only one of the PPC subjects (among those with available data) exceeded this threshold (subject # [b] (6)), with an apparent change of -1.9 cm from baseline R-L difference but nearly equal R-L length at final assessment (\Delta -0.1 cm). Data from palovarotene-treated subjects without PPC and from NHS subjects were similar to these subjects with PPC in not showing evidence of developing leg length discrepancies. The other parameter listed in the table, lateral distal femoral angle, was measured on AP knee radiographs; normal range for this angle in healthy children is approximately 79 to 85°, representing mild valgus. As indicated, all the subjects with PPC had values within or close to this range at last measure, with changes from baseline that were generally small and probably within the normal variability of the measure, which is susceptible to rotation of images; data from subjects without evidence of PPC were similar.

L1718: The Applicant's study of pediatric patients with multiple osteochondromas (MO) enrolled 193 patients ages 2 to 14 years (mean 7.7 years) into 3 randomized groups of palovarotene 2.5 mg and 5 mg, and placebo (N=66, 65 and 62, respectively). During treatment, height changes were generally similar between groups, and height Z-scores showed little change over time with no notable trends. One subject in each dose group had physeal closure by radiograph in some joints; each of these subjects was ≥11 years old and the changes were attributed to normal physiologic closure. Changes in bone age were similar between the treatment groups. Because this study was prematurely stopped due to the PPC findings in FOP studies, most subjects did not have data beyond 6 months.
L1719: Review of whole-body CT scans in all palovarotene-treated and untreated (NHS) subjects with FOP showed no evidence of femoral head abnormalities related to AVN, through the safety update cutoff date of January 31, 2022.
L1720: Further ER analyses were conducted to assess the impact of palovarotene exposure on PPC risks. The results show that the risk of PPC is increased at higher palovarotene AUCs (Figure 12). However, this result is likely to be driven by patients &lt;8 years old. When only considering patients 8/10 to 13 years, there is absence of a clear relationship between the proportion of subjects with PPC and AUCs (Figure 13).

L1727: In general, there is no ER relationship for palovarotene exposure and proportion of patients with PPC events for subjects greater than 8 years of age. Lowering dose of palovarotene dose for subjects younger than 12 years of age is not predicted to reduce risks of PPC for pediatrics. The reviewer acknowledged that this conclusion is limited by the small number of reported PPC events in the clinical studies.
L1728: ## Conclusion
L1729: The review team agrees with the Applicant that palovarotene treatment of pediatric patients with FOP is associated with a serious risk of PPC. Premature physeal closure development was most apparent at the active growth plates of the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia), which is consistent with literature reports involving other retinoids. Premature physeal closure was not generally associated with rapid advances in bone age as assessed by x-rays of the hand/wrist.
L1730: All patients with open growth plates are likely to be at risk of PPC. Younger children (\le 8/10 years) may be at greatest risk, but 33% of older pediatric patients (age \ge 8/10 to &lt;14 years) also showed evidence of PPC in the clinical studies. The Applicant could not identify specific risk factors or a safe level of palovarotene exposure. PPC was not reported in any subjects \ge 14 years of age; this may result from difficulty distinguishing premature versus physiologic physeal closure in this age group.
L1731: Because PPC involved the knee and appeared to be irreversible, reduced height is expected to result. Growth data in the palovarotene studies were highly variable, which is due in part to measurement difficulty in some FOP patients. While some study subjects with developing PPC were continuing to grow at near-normal rates, others showed near-cessation of growth and sharp declines in height Z-score. Overall, there were trends of reduced growth velocity and declining height Z-score, and greater variability, among palovarotene-treated compared to untreated NHS patients, particularly in early adolescents (age \ge 8/10 to &lt;14 years at study onset) who developed PPC. Measurements of knee height, and of femur and tibia length (CT), were generally consistent with standing height data.
L1732: In addition to reduced stature, and potentially disproportionate growth (e.g., short legs relative to trunk), PPC of growth plates at the knee poses a potential risk of leg length discrepancy or abnormal knee angulation. Radiographs have shown no evidence of such effects in study subjects to date, but the duration of treatment and/or follow-up has been limited in most cases, and longer-term data are needed.
L1733: PPC and impaired growth represent a major safety risk of palovarotene treatment in children with FOP and open growth plates. Product labeling should include a boxed warning and recommendations for patient monitoring, including height measurements and imaging of growth plates.
L1734: ## 7.7.2. Teratogenicity Potential Consistent With the Retinoid Drug Class
L1735: ## Issue
L1736: Embryo-fetal toxicity (retinoid class effect)
L1737: ## Background
L1738: Embryo-fetal toxicity has been reported with multiple retinoids and may result in irreversible fetal malformations, adverse pregnancy outcomes and stillbirths. The labeling of all approved retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin, tretinoin, bexarotene) includes Boxed Warnings for pregnancy and teratogenicity.
L1739: ## Assessment
L1740: Embryo-fetal toxicity consistent with retinoid effects was observed in fetal rat studies of palovarotene (Section 7.7.1).
L1741: The disease burden of FOP appears to result in low reproductive fitness, and there are only rare reports of pregnancy in women with FOP (almost all known cases of FOP result from new spontaneous mutations). FOP poses life-threatening risks for both the mother and fetus, including cardio-respiratory complications, thromboembolism, delivery complications, fetal distress, and premature birth. Consensus guidelines for FOP advise of these life-threatening risks and urge serious consideration and family planning before attempting a pregnancy. As a result of the high-risk nature of pregnancy to both mother and fetus, reports of miscarriage are fairly common amongst the small number of FOP pregnancies documented in case reports. The risk of embryo-fetal toxicity from palovarotene would potentially add to the incidence of these events in the population likely to use the drug.
L1742: Clinical studies of palovarotene included frequent pregnancy testing and contraception requirements as a precaution. To date, there are no reports of pregnancy or in utero exposure to palovarotene. Based on a phase 1 study showing very low palovarotene levels in semen, administration to a male is considered to be of low risk to female partners who become pregnant.
L1743: ## Conclusion
L1744: The risk of teratogenicity, and other pregnancy-related risk in FOP patients, warrants a Boxed Warning. The Applicant has proposed a risk management plan with the goal of educating prescribers, pharmacists and patients, which does not include a REMS. This is a reasonable approach based on the following: the FOP patient population is very small and is largely managed by experts in the disease; the pregnancy risks of FOP and importance of family planning discussions are already included in consensus guidelines; pregnancy is very infrequent in FOP patients due to low reproductive fitness; and off label use of palovarotene for other indications such as acne is not expected to occur.
L1745: ## 7.7.3. Increased Rate of Reported Flare-ups During Palovarotene Treatment; Potential for Retinoid-Induced Myositis
L1746: ## Issue
L1747: Increased rate of reported flare-ups during palovarotene treatment; potential for retinoid-induced myositis
L1748: ## Background
L1749: The rate of new FOP flare-up episodes was assessed in the NHS and palovarotene studies and is relevant to both efficacy and safety. Flare-up incidence and rate were designated in phase 3 as secondary efficacy endpoints to assess whether chronic palovarotene treatment may suppress the initiation of new flare-ups, in addition to potentially suppressing formation of new HO. However, retinoids, and vitamin A in toxic doses, have been associated with hyperostosis and calcification of ligaments and tendons; musculoskeletal adverse effects including back pain,
L1750: arthralgia, myalgia; and rare reports of severe myositis, sometimes associated with strenuous physical activity. Because FOP flare-ups are frequently triggered by local inflammation or trauma and are characterized by ossification of muscle and other soft tissues, there is a theoretical concern for induction or exacerbation of flare-ups by palovarotene.
L1751: ## Assessment
L1752: In all FOP studies, subjects were instructed to call the site immediately for potential flare-up symptoms. The process by which flare-ups were treated and reported varied among the FOP studies.
L1753: ## NHS
L1754: Subjects reporting potential flare-ups were evaluated in clinic or monitored with weekly phone contacts. Subjects were also contacted by phone every 6 months between the yearly clinic visits but were not systematically asked about new flare-ups at visits and did not record symptoms in diaries.
L1755: ## Phase 2 Studies 201/202A/B
L1756: In these studies, flare-ups were treated if they met the following criteria: had at least 2 out of 6 predefined symptoms (pain, soft tissue swelling, decreased ROM, stiffness, redness and warmth), were within 7 days of symptom onset, symptoms were consistent with the subject's previous flare-ups, and flare-ups were confirmed by the investigator. Flare-ups that were not treated (i.e., not meeting these criteria, or intercurrent flare-ups at a different location during flare-up treatment) were recorded not as flare-ups *per se*, but as AEs under the MedDRA preferred term of "condition aggravated."
L1757: ## Phase 3 Study 301 and Phase 2 Study 202C
L1758: In these studies, the criteria for initiating flare-up treatment were expanded such that only one symptom (or traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up) was required, if consistent with previous flare-ups and confirmed by the investigator, with no requirement to start treatment within 7 days of onset. Intercurrent (or markedly worsened) flare-ups were recorded as new flare-ups and treated as such, so that there were no AEs of "condition aggravated."
L1759: ## Flare-up Incidence and Rate in Phase 2 Studies
L1760: During the 12-week period of treatment/follow-up of the index flare-up in Study 201, new symptoms consistent with a flare-up (i.e., condition aggravated AEs) were reported by more subjects randomized to the palovarotene 10/5 mg regimen (13/21, 62%) in comparison to the 5/2.5 mg regimen (2/9, 22%) or placebo (3/10, 30%). In addition, some of the subjects treated with the 10/5 mg regimen experienced more than one new flare-up event within the 12-week observation period, therefore the rate of new events was highest in this treatment group. The majority of these events occurred at a new location rather than at the original flare-up location. New events, particularly those involving a new location, occurred somewhat more frequently in the first 4 weeks of treatment, compared to Weeks 5-8 or Weeks 9-12. Two of the events in the 10/5 group were categorized as SAEs of condition aggravated.

L1778: ## **Flare-up Incidence and Rate in Phase 3 Study**
L1779: For the Study 301 secondary endpoints of flare-up incidence and rate in comparison to the NHS, the SAP defined qualifying flare-ups as the presence of at least 2 flare-up symptoms. As noted above, this criterion had been used to determine treatment in earlier phase 2 studies, but any number of symptoms (\ge 1) was sufficient to define a flare-up in the NHS or Study 301, and upon request the Applicant submitted analyses based on \ge one symptom and on \ge two symptoms. These two studies were similar with regard to the number of reported symptoms per event (mean and median were 3.0 in both studies), and the proportion of flare-ups with only one reported symptom (13%, 14% respectively).
L1780: Flare-ups were reported by a slightly greater proportion of palovarotene-treated versus untreated subjects through month 12: 67% in Study 301 and 56% in the NHS, based on \ge one relevant symptom (Table 56). The proportions based on \ge two symptoms were slightly lower: 65% and 54%, respectively. Among subjects with \ge one flare-up event, the number of reported events per subject (based on \ge one symptom) was also greater in Study 301 (mean 4.2, range 1-23) versus the NHS (mean 2.5, range 1 to 9). Therefore, among all patients (with or without flare-ups), the rate of flare-ups per month of study participation was greater in Study 301 compared to the NHS (0.15 versus 0.07 per subject-month, respectively). Data were similar for the subset of 39 subjects who crossed over from the NHS to Study 301.

L1786: As noted by the Applicant, these differences in flare-up rate may be explained, at least in part, by differences in reporting related to study design and conduct. NHS subjects generally had less frequent contact with study staff compared to Study 301 subjects. Phone contacts were primarily every 6 months in the NHS; in Study 301, subjects were contacted every 3 months during chronic dosing and every 4 weeks during flare-up dosing. Study 301 subjects were asked to maintain daily symptom diaries, which were reviewed at clinic visits; NHS subjects did not use diaries and may have been less motivated to report symptoms that were not intended for any treatment. In addition, worsening of flare-ups was not systematically recorded in the NHS, unlike Study 301. Other aspects of care, such as the use of high-dose prednisone to treat flare-ups, were generally similar between the two studies.
L1787: There are limited data supporting the Applicant's position that flare-ups were under-reported in the NHS. Among the 39 crossover subjects, the mean number of flare-ups recorded prospectively in the last 12 months of the NHS was 0.6; at the time of enrollment in Study 301, the same 39 subjects reported (retrospectively) a mean of 1.1 flare-ups during the previous 12 months (the same time period) (Table 20.1.35.1 in ISE resubmission)
L1788: In Study 301, many subjects experienced multiple flare-ups, often in succession, whereby a new event within 12 weeks of the onset of the last event would restart the 20/10 dosing regimen before chronic dosing (5 mg) could resume. Thus, a flare-up "cycle" could include one or multiple flare-ups; the mean number of flare-ups per cycle in the study was 2.2 and the maximum was 23. Table 59 compares the rates of new flare-ups occurring during chronic dosing (i.e., the first or index flare-up of a new cycle) and during flare-up dosing (any subsequent flare-ups within a cycle). The rate of reported new flare-ups was greater during the higher dosing periods (0.33 versus 0.12 events/month). Among these follow-on events within a flare-up cycle, 82 (42%) were categorized as worsening of the initial flare-up, and 114 (58%) were categorized as intercurrent flare-ups at a new location. New events were generally distributed evenly by time interval throughout the flare-up treatment cycle.
