L1795: The clinical significance of the number of flare-ups in these studies with regard to disease progression is unclear. Subjects reporting \ge one flare-up, compared to subjects reporting no flare-ups, developed larger quantities of new whole-body HO, both in the NHS (mean 40.8 versus 6.7 \text{cm}^3 at month 12), and also in Study 301 (mean 9.0 versus 2.9 \text{cm}^3) (ISE Table 30). Otherwise, however, the number of flare-ups did not appear to be closely related to the quantity of new whole-body HO in these studies. Among the five subjects in either NHS or Study 301 with annualized new HO &gt;100 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year}, 3 of the 4 NHS subjects had reported only 1 or 2 flare-ups. The only Study 301 subject (# [b] [6]) with &gt;100 \text{ cm}^3/\text{year} of new HO (236.8 \text{cm}^3/\text{year}) was an exception, having reported 13 flare-ups.
L1796: Among the 39 subjects who transferred from the NHS to Study 301, the change in number of flare-ups for a given subject did not appear to predict the change in new HO. The two subjects (# [b] [6] and # [b] [6]) with the largest increases in number of flare-ups between NHS and Study 301 (one event to 18 events, and one event to 14 events, respectively) nevertheless had large declines in rates of new HO from the NHS to Study 301. In such cases, extended high-dose treatment of the numerous flare-ups (encompassing nearly all of these two subjects' time of participation in Study 301) may have suppressed the formation of new HO, if not the rate of clinical events or symptoms.
L1797: ## Conclusion
L1798: FOP flare-up episodes were reported by a greater proportion of palovarotene-treated subjects in the phase 3 study, 301, compared to untreated subjects in the NHS, and at a higher frequency (0.15 versus 0.07 per month). However, flare-ups appear to have been under-reported in the NHS based on the study design. This may be supported by findings of a published survey in which untreated FOP patients reported an average of 1.9 flare-ups in the preceding 12 months, which is a rate of 0.16 events per month (*J Bone Miner Res.* 2016; 31:650).
L1799: Within Study 301, flare-ups were reported at higher rates during cycles of flare-up treatment (0.33 new events per month, versus 0.12 per month during chronic dosing). Data from Study 202B/C subjects receiving the chronic/flare-up regimen were consistent with this finding, with 0.20-0.29 new events per month during flare-up dosing, versus 0.10 per month during chronic dosing. In the randomized Study 201, more new events (condition aggravated AEs, mostly at a new location) were reported in subjects receiving the highest dose flare-up regimen (10/5 mg) compared to 5/2.5 mg or placebo.
L1800: There are several possible explanations for these findings. According to the Applicant, some FOP experts have reported anecdotally that flare-ups may occur in clusters or in rapid sequence, although this is not well documented in the literature. Higher palovarotene doses may trigger inflammatory processes leading to new flare-ups, or could result in musculoskeletal adverse
L1801: events related to retinoid effects that could be misinterpreted as flare-up symptoms, or could potentially result in musculoskeletal adverse events that trigger new flare-ups. Flare-up symptoms may rebound following withdrawal of the high dose corticosteroids which are administered during most flare-ups. Additionally, patients may have a tendency to over-report symptoms during treatment, perhaps related to frequent contacts with study staff and questioning about possible adverse events while already experiencing symptoms of the initial flare-up in the cycle.
L1802: The clinical significance of the apparent increase in flare-ups in these studies is uncertain, given that the overall rate of flare ups in Study 301 of 0.15 events per month is similar to the reported rate for untreated FOP patients in the literature (approximately 2 per year). To gain further insight, DGE has asked the Applicant to analyze the relationships between flare-ups (“index” and subsequent events during flare-up dosing) and new HO (both at and away from flare-up sites), in Studies 301, 202B, 202C and the NHS. This information is not available during this review cycle and is planned to be submitted at a later date.
L1803: ## 7.7.4. Apparent Adverse Effects of Palovarotene on Vertebral Bone Mineral Density, Bone Mineral Content, and Fractures
L1804: ## Issue
L1805: Apparent adverse effects of palovarotene on vertebral bone mineral density (BMD), bone mineral content (BMC), and fractures.
L1806: ## Background
L1807: Literature reports indicate that retinoids and vitamin A toxicity may cause bone demineralization, osteoporosis, or “slender long bones” in children. Labeling for isotretinoin in the treatment of acne includes a Warning for negative effects on BMD seen in clinical trials. There is no definitive evidence of an increase in fractures related to retinoid use.
L1808: ## Assessment
L1809: Assessments of BMD and BMC by DXA were not included in the palovarotene FOP studies because of the likely confounding effects of extensive HO in overlying soft tissues. DXA was conducted on subjects with MO (age 2 to 14 years) in study PVO-2A-201. Although treatment duration was limited in most subjects due to early termination of the trial, there were discernable trends of reduced BMC accrual in the palovarotene 5 mg treatment group compared to the 2.5 mg and placebo groups. Figure 14 shows that lower BMC in the 5 mg group appeared to persist at the follow-up visit 6 months after discontinuation of the drug.
L1810: **Figure 14. Lumbar Spine BMC, Percent Change From Baseline, in Subjects With MO Who Completed 12 Months of Treatment (Study PVO-2A-201)**
L1811: Source: Study PVO-2A-201 CSR Figure S27B.1C
Abbreviations: BMC, bone mineral content; MO, multiple osteochondromas; PVO, palovarotene; SD, standard deviation
L1812: Because of this adverse BMC trend in the MO trial, the FOP DMC requested retrospective re-evaluation of the WBCT scans from FOP Studies 301 (palovarotene treated) and the NHS (untreated), which had been obtained to measure HO, for the assessments related to vertebral structural integrity listed below. It should be noted that these measures have not been validated by FDA for assessment of fractures or estimation of fracture risk in clinical trials; standard radiographs are considered the gold standard for assessment of vertebral fractures. In addition, as discussed above (see Section 6.3.3), the populations of Studies 301 and the NHS differed in age and possibly other factors due to the lack of randomization.
L1813: Biomechanical CT (BCT) analysis was conducted at L1, L2 or adjacent vertebrae (i.e., T12 if either L1 or L2 was not evaluable) to derive the following parameters:
L1814: - Estimated bone compressive strength (Newtons) by finite element analysis
- Trabecular volumetric BMD (\text{mg}/\text{cm}^3) of the central vertebral body
- BMC (g) of the entire vertebral body
L1815: The Applicant analyzed the data for changes from baseline, with adjustments for covariates, and reported nominally significant associations of palovarotene treatment with lower values for each of these parameters.
L1816: Vertebral fracture analysis (VFA) of T4 through L4 vertebrae was conducted using automated placement of 6 points to outline vertebral morphometric shape, which were used to calculate deformity ratios for grading using established criteria of Genant:
L1817: - Normal (Grade 0; deformity &lt;20%)
- Mild (Grade 1; deformity \ge 20\% to &lt;25%)
- Moderate (Grade 2; deformity \ge 25\% to &lt;40%)
- Severe (Grade 3; deformity \ge 40\%)
L1818: The prevalence of these fractures on baseline imaging was 21.5% in palovarotene-treated subjects (Study 301) and 23.6% of untreated subjects (NHS). At 12 months, 28.4% of palovarotene-treated subjects (Study 301) and 11.6% of untreated subjects (NHS) were found to have at least one new-onset vertebral fracture that was not present at baseline. For the target \ge 8/10-year-old population, these proportions were 24.2% and 11.8%, respectively. The 12-month incidences of at least one new-onset moderate/severe fracture (Grade 2 or 3) were 8.6% (palovarotene) and 4.7% (untreated) overall, or 9.1% and 4.4% for the \ge 8/10 population. The report indicates that all of these apparent fractures were asymptomatic.
L1819: The Applicant also analyzed clinical fracture AEs in the FOP-FAS: normotopic bone fractures were reported in 13/164 subjects (7.9%), including 2/23 subjects (8.7%) in the placebo arm.
L1820: ## Conclusion
L1821: The results of the BCT analysis suggest that palovarotene treatment may be associated with decreases in vertebral bone strength, BMC and BMD. Prior vertebral fractures appeared to be highly prevalent at baseline in FOP studies given the young age of the population, which may be disease related, and new abnormalities occurred at a higher rate in palovarotene-treated versus untreated patients over 12 months. These effects are consistent with some data involving other retinoids, but do not establish a definitive causal association due to the post hoc nature of the analyses, use of nonvalidated measures, and differences between the populations of the two nonrandomized studies.
L1822: ## 8. Therapeutic Individualization
L1823: ## 8.1. Intrinsic Factors
L1824: ## Hepatic Impairment
L1825: FOP is an ultrarare disease with approximately 800 known patients worldwide. The median lifespan of FOP patients is 56 years. The Applicant claimed that hepatic impairment is not a known complication of patients with FOP. In the NHS, none of the 114 patients with FOP with available hepatic medical history had cirrhosis, and only one of 114 subjects (0.9%) reported a history of mild hepatitis. The effect of hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene has not been evaluated in a dedicated study. According to the Applicant's population PK analyses, there was no evidence that serum albumin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), or bilirubin affected palovarotene PK.
L1826: Per the Applicant, in an exploratory covariate analysis of the population PK analyses, mild and moderate hepatic impairment did not affect palovarotene PK. However, most subjects (healthy subjects and patients) in the population PK dataset (N=577) had normal hepatic function and only a small number of subjects (~2%) had elevated baseline AST (40-75 U/L) or ALT (50-90 U/L), with a total of five subjects classified as moderate hepatic impairment and none of subjects classified as severe hepatic impairment. Therefore, due to limited sample size of subjects with moderate hepatic impairment, the effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) hepatic impairment on the PK of palovarotene is not conclusive from the submitted population PK analyses.
L1827: The Applicant also conducted a physiological based PK (PBPK) analysis and concluded that the moderate hepatic impairment status would not significantly affect the PK of palovarotene. The review team, however, concludes that the PBPK analyses are inadequate to evaluate the effect of hepatic organ impairment, as the metabolic pathways of palovarotene have not been well characterized. Specifically, six unidentified metabolites accounted for approximately 28.4% of the dose in feces according to the human mass balance study, and there is uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 to the elimination pathway of palovarotene (see Section 14.4 for more detailed assessment). Since palovarotene is significantly metabolized in the liver, the exposure may be expected to be higher in moderate-to-severe hepatic impaired patients. Due to the lack of PK data, the use of palovarotene in patients with moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment is not recommended. The Applicant should conduct a hepatic impairment study to evaluate the effect of moderate (Child-Pugh B) and severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) on the PK of palovarotene to inform the dosing recommendations in patients with hepatic impairment.
L1828: ## Renal Impairment
L1829: Renal impairment is not a known complication of FOP patients. None of the 114 subjects in the NHS with available renal medical history reported renal impairment. Furthermore, in the mass balance study, only 3% of radioactivity was recovered in urine, indicating renal excretion is a minor elimination route of palovarotene. No dedicated PK study was conducted in subjects with renal impairment. According to the Applicant's population PK analyses, there was no evidence that serum creatinine affected palovarotene PK. Most subjects in the population PK dataset (N=577) had baseline serum creatinine &lt;1.2 mg/dL and only &lt;5% of subjects had baseline serum creatinine between 1.2 – 1.6 mg/dL. Due to the minor role of renal excretion in palovarotene elimination, an increased palovarotene exposure is not expected in patients with mild-to-moderate renal impairment. However, since severe renal impairment may potentially affect the drug's hepatic metabolism, there is a concern of increased exposure in severe renally impaired patients. While no dose adjustment is needed for patients with mild-to-moderate renal impairment, the use of palovarotene in patients with severe renal impairment is not recommended.
L1830: ## Body Weight
L1831: According to the population PK analysis, body weight has a significant impact on palovarotene PK, resulting in increasing exposure with decreasing weight at the same dose. For the range of body weights in the analysis population (13-130 kg), CL/F ranged from 8.85-26.8 L/h, which was 56% lower to 35% higher compared to the typical value of CL/F (19.9 L/h) for a 70-kg subject. The simulation results showed that following 20 mg daily dosing under fed state, steady-state AUC was 8% higher for a 51 kg subject and 18% lower for a 98 kg subject compared to a 70 kg subject, respectively. (Table 60).

L1834: (b) (4)
L1835: The PK data from Study 202 showed that skeletally immature patients receiving weight-adjusted doses had systemic exposure comparable to that in adults receiving chronic 5 mg and flare-up 10/20 mg doses (Refer to Appendices 14.3). Consistently, population PK simulations showed comparable palovarotene exposure between patients &lt;14 years and patients ≥14 years who are greater than 60 kg (Figure 15). However, the exposures of palovarotene in patients ≥14 years were higher than that in subjects &lt;14 years in the same body weight categories (i.e., body weight 30 kg–40 kg, 40 kg–50 kg, and 50 kg–60 kg). Since body weight rather than age is a significant covariate affecting palovarotene PK in the population PK model, there is not sufficient rationale supporting 14 years of age to be included in the weight-adjusted dosing regimen. In addition, in phase 3 clinical studies, patients ≥18 years of age received orally administered 5 mg palovarotene once daily and 20 mg/10 mg dosing at flare-up, whereas weight-adjusted dose was used for skeletally immature subjects under 18 years of age.
L1836: Based on this information, the review team recommends that the weight-adjusted doses be applied for FOP patients &lt;18 years of age, while patients ≥18 years of age receive orally administered 5 mg palovarotene once daily and 20 mg/10 mg dosing at flare-up. This recommendation follows the same recommendations as in Study 301.

L1841: ## Age, Sex, Race, and Health Status
L1842: In a single-dose PK study (Study NP17726), no significant difference in palovarotene exposure was observed between young males (21 to 40 years) and elder males (65 to 74 years). The geometric mean AUC of palovarotene in elder women (65 to 73 years) was 20% higher than that in elder males. The difference in palovarotene exposure between elder males and females can be explained by the differences in body weight. In another single-dose PK study (Study PVO-1A-101), the PK parameters of palovarotene were similar between Japanese and non-Asian groups at either the 10 mg or 5 mg dose. Based on a population PK analysis of palovarotene plasma concentration data from 577 subjects with baseline age ranging from 2 to 85 years, there was no evidence that age affected palovarotene pharmacokinetics. Similarly, population PK analysis showed that neither sex, race (Asian, black, white, and other), nor health status (healthy volunteers, FOP, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and multiple osteochondromas) were significant covariates on the PK of palovarotene.
L1843: ## 8.2. Extrinsic Factors
L1844: ## Food Effects
L1845: The food effect study (Study PVO-1A-102) was conducted in healthy volunteers using the to-be-marketed formulation (TBM) of palovarotene. In addition to the effect of food on the PK of palovarotene capsules, the study evaluated the effect of swallowing intact capsule versus sprinkling the contents on apple sauce on the PK of palovarotene. Following oral administration of two 10 mg palovarotene capsules after a high-fat breakfast, palovarotene C_{max} and AUC_{0-inf} were 15% and 39% higher, respectively, when compared to exposures under fasting conditions (Table 61). Following administration of the palovarotene capsules by sprinkling the contents onto one teaspoon of apple sauce after a high-fat breakfast, both AUC and C_{max} were comparable to when the capsules were swallowed whole after a high-fat breakfast (Table 61).
L1846: In Study 301, patients were instructed to take palovarotene capsules with a full meal. For FOP patients with difficulty swallowing intact capsules due to ankylosis of the jaw, the contents of capsules were sprinkled on soft foods (i.e., apple sauce) and administered with a meal. In the drug label, the Applicant proposed that palovarotene should be administered with food, preferably at the same time each day. If a patient cannot swallow whole capsules, he/she can sprinkle the contents of capsules onto a teaspoon of soft food and take with a meal. The Applicant's dose administration instructions are supported by the food effect data and phase 3 trial.

L1851: ## Smoking
L1852: In Study RB16327, a single dose of 5 mg palovarotene was administered to smokers (N=6) and nonsmokers (N=6) under fed state. Compared to nonsmokers, smokers showed a 22% increase in mean AUC(271\pm 75 ng\cdoth/mL versus 222\pm 29 ng\cdoth/mL), and 32% increase in mean C_{max} (39.7\pm 9.83 ng/mL versus 30.1\pm 8.21 ng/mL) (refer to Section 14.2.1 for more information of Study RB16327). Population PK analysis based on the PK data of 66 smokers and 370 nonsmokers did not detect smoking status as a significant covariate on the PK of palovarotene. No dose adjustment is needed for smokers.
L1853: ## Drug-Drug Interaction (DDI)
L1854: In vitro drug interaction studies showed that palovarotene is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4 and metabolized by CYP2C8 and 2C19 to a minor extent. At clinically relevant plasma concentrations, palovarotene did not significantly inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6 or CYP3A4 in vitro. Palovarotene at clinically relevant concentration (0.32\mu M) did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, but induced CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 mRNA expression by 3.8 – 5.0 folds and 1.8 – 2.4 folds in vitro, respectively.
L1855: The Applicant submitted four clinical DDI study reports and a physiological based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model report that evaluated the DDI liability of palovarotene as a victim of CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and CYP2C19.
L1856: ## Effect of CYP3A4 Inhibition and Induction on Palovarotene PK
L1857: Study 17041B showed that co-administration of ketoconazole 400 mg QD (a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor) and palovarotene 1 mg QD caused an increase of palovarotene AUC by 3.1-fold. Study NP17040 showed co-administration of rifampin 600 mg QD (a strong inducer of CYP3A4, 2C8, 2C19 and several transporters) and palovarotene 1 mg QD caused a decrease of palovarotene AUC by 89%. The PBPK model simulated the scenarios of single oral doses of 5 mg and 20 mg palovarotene in the absence of any perpetrator and on the 15th day of 21 days of dosing of erythromycin (moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor) or efavirenz (moderate CYP3A4 inducer) in healthy subjects. The simulated geometric mean ratios of AUC_{0-inf} and C_{max} for palovarotene in the absence and presence of erythromycin (500 mg QID) are 2.54 (90%CI of 2.39, 2.69) and 1.64 (90% CI of 1.59, 1.69), respectively, and for efavirenz (600 QD) are [REDACTED] (b) (4) and [REDACTED] (b) (4) respectively.
L1858: The review team agrees that the Applicant's PBPK analyses are adequate to evaluate the effects of the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin on the PK of palovarotene. However, the review team concluded that the PBPK analyses are inadequate to evaluate the effect of the moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz on the PK of palovarotene for the following reasons: (1) The PBPK model underpredicted the effect of the strong CYP3A inducer rifampin on the AUC and C_{max} of palovarotene by [REDACTED] (b) (4) (the reason for the underprediction is unclear), thus, the ability of the palovarotene model to predict the effect of other inducers is in question; (2) efavirenz is also a clinical inducer of CYP2C19; however, the current efavirenz PBPK model is not validated for CYP2C19 induction predictions; and (3) there is uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C19 in the elimination of palovarotene (see Section 14.4 for more detailed assessment).
L1859: The Applicant proposed to avoid concomitant use of moderate-to-strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers. The review team agrees with the proposal to avoid concomitant use of moderate-to-strong CYP3A inhibitors and moderate CYP3A inducers. However, since rifampin decreased the AUC of palovarotene by 89%, the review team recommends that the use of strong CYP3A inducers with palovarotene should be prohibited. Since a moderate CYP3A inhibitor is expected to increase the AUC of palovarotene by approximately 2.54-fold based on the PBPK simulation using erythromycin, the dose of palovarotene should be reduced by half (Table 62). Since the effect of moderate CYP3A inducer on the PK of palovarotene is unknown, the concomitant use of palovarotene with moderate CYP3A inducers is not recommended.
L1860: During the late cycle communication, the review team recommended the Applicant to conduct a clinical DDI trial to evaluate the effect of a moderate CYP3A4 inducer on the pharmacokinetics of palovarotene in healthy adult subjects, to assess the magnitude of exposure change of palovarotene, and to determine the appropriate dosing recommendations for palovarotene when used concomitantly with a moderate CYP3A4 inducer. However, the Applicant indicated that common CYP3A moderate inducers are not expected to be routinely co-administrated with palovarotene in patients with FOP. The Applicant prefers to keep the current recommendation in the USPI to “avoid the concomitant use of moderate CYP3A4 inducers with SOHONOS”, rather than to conduct a clinical DDI trial. The review team agrees with the Applicant’s approach.

L1864: In Study NP21025, a single oral dose of 40 mg prednisone decreased the AUC of co-administered palovarotene by 14%. However, maximum induction of CYP3A4 was not achieved with a single dose of prednisone. The results from Study NP21025 cannot be used to justify that co-administration of multiple-dose prednisone does not affect the PK of palovarotene. Population PK analyses of the PK data of 59 subjects concomitantly taking prednisone did not detect the use of prednisone as a significant covariate on the PK of palovarotene. The review team agrees that no dose adjustment is needed for palovarotene in patients who concomitantly use prednisone.
L1865: ## Effect of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 Inhibition and Induction on Palovarotene PK
L1866: The Applicant conducted PBPK modeling to predict the scenarios of single oral doses of 5 mg and 20 mg palovarotene in the presence of gemfibrozil (strong CYP2C8 inhibitor), fluoxetine (strong CYP2C19 inhibitor) and fluconazole (moderate CYP3A inhibitor and strong CYP2C19 inhibitor) in healthy subjects. However, the review team concluded that the PBPK analyses are inadequate to evaluate the effects of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 inhibitors on the PK of palovarotene due to the uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 to elimination of palovarotene (see Section 14.4 for more detailed assessment). Considering the strong CYP3A4 inhibitor ketoconazole increased the AUC of palovarotene by 3.1-fold, (b) (4)
L1867: , it is reasonable to expect that coadministration of a specific inhibitor of CYP2C8 or CYP2C19 would result in a weak interaction effect (i.e., increase on the AUC of palovarotene by (b) (4)). Additionally, in the phase 3 trial, concomitant use of strong inhibitors of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 was allowed and the intersubject variability in AUC was 40%. The review team agrees with the Applicant that no dose adjustment is needed for palovarotene when patients concomitantly use a specific strong CYP2C8 or 2C19 inhibitor. However, concomitant use of palovarotene with a dual strong CYP2C19 and moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor (e.g., fluconazole, fluvoxamine) should be avoided. If co-administration is unavoidable, the dose of palovarotene should be reduced by half (Table 63).
L1868: ## Effect of Palovarotene on Other Drugs
L1869: ## Prednisone
L1870: Study NP21025 showed that co-administration palovarotene 5 mg QD did not change the PK of prednisone. However, the effect of palovarotene 10 mg or 20 mg QD on co-administered prednisone was not evaluated.
L1871: ## Midazolam
L1872: In Study PVO-1A-102, palovarotene 20 mg QD reduced the AUC and C_{max} of co-administered midazolam by 14% and 10%, respectively. Palovarotene is not a clinical inducer of CYP3A4. The review team agrees with the Applicant that no dose adjustment is needed for concomitantly used CYP3A4 substrates.

L1879: ## Transporter-Mediated Drug Interactions
L1880: In vitro data showed that palovarotene is not a substrate of P-gp, BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3 or OCT1. Substrate interaction assessments with renal transporters OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1 and MATE2-K transporters were not conducted because only 3.2% of the dose was recovered in urine. Palovarotene is not an in vitro inhibitor of P-gp, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, or MATE2-K transporters. Palovarotene inhibited BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and BSEP transporter with IC50 values of 9.69µM, 1.83µM, &gt;3µM, &gt;3µM, and 14.7µM, respectively. The steady-state Cmax of palovarotene following 20 mg QD oral dosing was 0.333µM to 0.487µM. At the recommended maximum dose (20 mg QD), palovarotene does not pose a clinically relevant risk with respect to the inhibition of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, or BSEP transporters. Also, the Applicant measured the solubility of palovarotene in fed-state simulated intestinal fluid at 37°C and pH 5, which was 2.37±0.23 µg/mL or 5.8µM. The ratio of Igut/IC50 (Igut: the intestinal luminal concentration of the interacting drug calculated as the dose/250 mL) for intestinal BCRP transporter is 0.60 and the calculated palovarotene R value is 1.60, which is below the threshold value of 11. No BCRP-mediated DDI is expected for palovarotene at 20 mg QD.
L1881: ## 8.3. Plans for Pediatric Drug Development
L1882: Palovarotene is indicated for the treatment of adults and children (females 8 years and older, and males 10 years and older) with FOP. A six-week toxicity study was conducted in juvenile rats with oral palovarotene administered daily at 0.1, 0.5 or 1.2 mg/kg/day from postnatal Weeks 3 through 9 (prior to the closure of epiphyses, which normally occurs between Weeks 15 to 16). Palovarotene adversely affected skeletal growth and development resulting in abnormal bone size, shape, mass and/or geometry in juvenile rats treated at ≥0.5 mg/kg/day (below the clinical exposure, based on AUC). Palovarotene caused dose-related thinning/closure of the physis, physeal hypertrophy and chondrodysplasia in multiple bones, decreased endochondral ossification and hypertrophic hyaline cartilage, and hypertrophy and chondrodysplasia in articular cartilage. Additionally, decreased bone density, avascular necrosis in the femoral head and neck region, and microfractures were notable at 1.2 mg/kg/day. These changes occurred with correlating decreases in bone formation markers, radiological changes (abnormal shape, diffuse bone loss, increased/decreased physis thickness, and increased space between bones). No recovery for effects on thinning/closure of the physis or chondrodysplasia were observed at ≥0.5 mg/kg/day; partial to complete recovery of decreased bone growth were seen in animals at 0.5 mg/kg/day.

L1888: ## 8.4. Pregnancy and Lactation
L1889: ## Animal Data
L1890: The Applicant conducted fertility and early embryonic development studies in male and female rats and an embryofetal development study in a single species (rat). The Agency agreed that there was no benefit in conducting an EFD study in pregnant animals of a second species, as palovarotene adversely affected fetal development in pregnant rats, which was consistent with the retinoid class known to carry fetal development risks.
L1891: The following section summarizes the outcomes and conclusions of these studies. Greater details of the reproductive toxicity studies are provided in the Section 13.1.
L1892: **Table 65. Nonclinical Data Supporting Labeling on Fertility, Pregnancy, and Lactation**
L1893: Labeling Section	Nonclinical Data
8.1 Pregnancy	
In an embryo-fetal developmental toxicity study in rats, palovarotene was administered orally during the period of organogenesis (gestation day 6 to 17) at doses of 0.01, 0.25 and 1.25 mg/kg/day. Palovarotene caused multiple fetal malformations including cleft palate, protruding tongue, eye defects (anophthalmia, microphthalmia), skull abnormalities (exencephaly, abnormal head shape, dilated cerebral ventricles, misshapen brain), abnormalities of blood vessels, kidney, ureter, and skeletal malformations and variations (short, unossified/incomplete ossification of bones) at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day (below clinical exposure). Maternal toxicities in the form of reductions in body weight gains were noted at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day and lower food consumption at the 1.25 mg/kg/day.
The teratogenic findings with palovarotene are consistent with malformations noted with the class (retinoids).
The NOAEL for effects on fetal development was 0.01 mg/kg (AUC_{0-24h}=8.7 ng.h/mL, below clinical exposure).

8.2 Lactation	
The partitioning of palovarotene into animal milk was not studied.

13.1 Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility	
In a male fertility and early embryonic development study, palovarotene was administered orally to male rats prior to and during mating for total of 11 weeks at doses of 0.3, 1 and 3 mg/kg/day. Males did not tolerate 3 mg/kg/day and this group was terminated prematurely on Day 39 due to the death of a male on Day 30, with adverse skin and hair coat related clinical signs, and substantially reduced BW gain. Paternal toxicities including significant reduction (up to 18%) in BW gains and skin changes (thin cover, red skin and scab) were seen at 0.3 and 1 mg/kg/day. Therefore, the NOAEL for paternal general toxicity was not identified. Palovarotene did not affect mating, fertility indices, or reproduction parameters. The NOAEL for reproductive effects in males was 1 mg/kg/day (AUC_{0-24h}=421 ng.h/mL) based on the absence of adverse effects on fertility and reproduction parameters.
In a female fertility and early embryonic development study, palovarotene was administered orally to female rats 14 days prior to mating with drug naive males and up to GD 7 at dose levels of 0.3, 1 and 3 mg/kg/day. Palovarotene caused prolonged periods of diestrus, slightly lower ovulation rates, fewer implantation sites, and reduced numbers of live embryos at 3 mg/kg/day. No effect was observed on mating and fertility indices or the conception rate in females at any dose level. Maternal toxicities, including skin, hair/coat related clinical signs, reduced BW gain and lower food consumption were noted at \ge 1 mg/kg/day. The NOAEL for female fertility was 3 mg/kg/day (AUC_{0-24h}=918 ng.h/mL).

L1904: ## 9. Product Quality
L1905: ## Drug Substance
L1906: The Palovarotene drug substance is a new chemical entity. It is a poorly soluble achiral compound with a molecular formula of C27H30N2O2 and a molecular weight of 414.5 g/mol. It is manufactured as a single crystalline form. The review confirmed the identity of the drug substance based on infrared (IR) spectroscopy, 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, mass spectroscopy (MS), ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy, elemental analysis and x-ray powder differentiation (XRPD) data. The review also assessed starting material design, manufacturing process, in process controls, characterization, impurities, and physicochemical properties as adequate to support the quality of the drug substance. The drug substance specification includes appropriate tests and acceptance criteria to support the identity, strength, purity, and quality of the drug substance. Related substances are limited at levels recommended in ICH Q3A, except for, which is proposed at a limit of ≤(b)(4)%. This limit has been determined to be reasonable by the Pharmacology/Toxicology review team. Solvents used during the manufacturing process are controlled as per the ICH Q3C Guidelines. The risks associated with potential genotoxic impurities in the drug substance were assessed following ICH M7 and were determined to be extremely low. A retest date of (b)(4) months is granted for palovarotene drug substance when stored at (b)(4).
L1907: The Applicant proposed high acceptance criteria (original plan (b) (4) and current proposal (b) (4)%) for the impurity (b) (4) in the drug substance as compared to the qualification threshold (0.15%) established, as per ICH Q3A recommendations. (b) (4) is a process impurity of the drug substance which persists in the final drug substance at levels exceeding the ICH qualification threshold of 0.15%. It is (b) (4). It was identified in palovarotene batches late in the drug development phase and it was not present in drug substance batches used for pivotal repeat dose 26-week rat and 39-week dog toxicity studies. The toxicology batch (R0042674) used for the male and female fertility and early embryonic development (FEED) studies contained (b) (4), but at a much lower level ((b) (4)%) than in the proposed specification. Moreover, the toxicity endpoints assessed in the FEED study were limited compared to standard toxicity studies. On the other hand, (b) (4) was detected (b) (4)% in drug substance material used for clinical studies PVO-1A-202/204, PVO-2A-201 (MO-Ped) and PVO-1A-301 (Study 301). Based on the absence of an already established PDE, comprehensive toxicology data from the palovarotene nonclinical program or published studies, the safety of this impurity was not considered qualified at the time of the initial palovarotene NDA submission. In the NDA resubmission, the Applicant conducted and submitted nonclinical studies with (b) (4) and implemented manufacturing process changes and proposed a new acceptance limit of (b) (4)% for the commercial product.
L1908: Nonclinical toxicology studies to assess the safety profile of (b) (4) consisted of genotoxicity studies (QSAR in silico analyses and in vitro bacterial Ames and chromosomal aberration in human lymphocyte assays) and a dedicated 4-week oral general repeat dose toxicity study with the purified impurity, (b) (4). No structural alert for mutagenicity was detected on (b) (4) when tested by QSAR performed with expert- and statistical-based models (DEREK and SARAH). (b) (4) was neither mutagenic nor clastogenic in the in vitro Ames and chromosomal aberration assays in the presence and absence of metabolic activation. In the rat oral repeat dose general toxicity study, there was no (b) (4)-induced toxicological finding noted up to the highest dose tested (b) (4) mg/kg/day (\ge 10-times maximum clinical exposure). Moreover, no finding of concern was reported up to (b) (4) mg/kg/day in the DRF 7-day rat toxicity study.
L1909: Overall, no safety hazard was identified in (b) (4) toxicology studies. The NOAEL dose identified in the confirmatory 4-week rat toxicity study with (b) (4) was (b) (4) mg/kg/day, providing &gt;10-fold the maximum level of (b) (4) calculated at the MRHD using the (b) (4)% specification limit. The completed nonclinical studies support the proposed impurity acceptance criteria of (b) (4)% and the safety of (b) (4) is considered qualified nonclinically.
L1910: ## Drug Product
L1911: The drug product is an immediate release capsule composed of the drug substance and inactive ingredients, including croscarmellose sodium, lactose monohydrate, magnesium stearate, microcrystalline cellulose, povidone, and sodium lauryl sulfate. The hard gelatin capsule (size 0) is composed of titanium dioxide ((b) (4)) and gelatin ((b) (4)). The formulation contains no phthalates. The drug product was assessed with respect to its critical quality attributes and risks associated with drug product formulation, specification for quality control, stability for shelf-life determination, impurities, packaging, and compatibility with soft food for a pediatric patient population.
L1912: The review assessed the physicochemical risks to the drug product such as possible degradation during manufacturing and product shelf-life source of impurities in the drug product, and
L1913: compatibility with soft food. Absence of drug product compatibility data with soft food, and risk of nitrosamine impurity were identified during the review cycle. These issues were satisfactorily addressed by the Applicant. Labeling was revised as follows: “*SOHONOS may be swallowed whole, or capsules may be opened, and the contents emptied onto a teaspoon of soft food and taken within 1 hour of opening provided it was maintained at room temperature and not exposed to direct sunlight.*”
L1914: The drug product specification included acceptable tests and acceptance criteria to assure the identity, strength, purity, and quality of all strengths of the drug product. Analytical method validations for all tests were found to be acceptable. The shelf-life of 36 months is supported based on 36 months of long-term, 36 months of intermediate and 6 months of accelerated stability data. Photostability study shows that the drug product is sensitive to light. Therefore, appropriate instruction on container closure has been added. Finally, the in-use stability results show that drug product stays within the specification when blisters are exposed for 10 minutes to fluorescent light for 28 consecutive days.
L1915: ## Quality Labeling
L1916: The quality aspects of the labeling were reviewed and found to be adequate.
L1917: ## Manufacturing
L1918: ## Process
L1919: Manufacturing process utilizes [REDACTED] (b) (4). The reviewer identified absence of certain critical manufacturing information such as reconciliation data for each manufacturing unit operation, in-process controls for [REDACTED] (b) (4). L1920: ## Facilities

L1922: ## Biopharmaceutics
L1923: The biopharmaceutics review focused on the acceptability of the in vitro dissolution test method and acceptance criteria. No biowaiver for lower strengths of the drug product was requested as clinical and TBM (to be marketed) drug product batches were administered in various clinical safety/pharmacokinetic studies.
L1924: Bridging of clinical and TBM drug products manufactured at different manufacturing sites is supported by pharmacokinetic (PK) data in healthy and FOP patient populations that were assessed by the Office of Clinical Pharmacology (OCP). In response to several information
L1925: requests, the Applicant provided adequate justification for the final test method parameters and acceptance criteria, as well as data to support the discriminating power of the method with respect to variations in manufacturing and drug substance particle size variation. Because the drug is a BCS class II compound, the Applicant Team Lead (ATL) initiated a discussion between the OPQ sub discipline reviewers regarding the acceptability of the drug substance particle size distribution (PSD) limit and its possible impact on bioavailability (BA). Both the biopharmaceutics and drug substances reviewers agreed with the Applicant's proposed PSD limit of D90-NMT ^{(b)}_{(4)} \mum for the drug substance specification.
L1926: ## Life-Cycle Considerations
L1927: Palovarotene is a BCS class II drug. Therefore, any change in the drug substance particle size distribution and polymorphism may require appropriate bridging to establish bioequivalence and a prior approval supplement (PAS).

L1934: ## 10. Human Subjects Protections/Clinical Site and Other Good Clinical Practice Inspections/Financial Disclosure
L1935: The clinical studies (NHS, 201, 202A/B/C, 301) were conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and that are consistent with the ICH Good Clinical Practice (GCP) and FDA regulations.
L1936: The original NDA submitted on March 31, 2021, was withdrawn on August 21, 2021, due to issues of data quality and integrity involving missing WBCT scan readings, which were identified during the review cycle and required extensive updating of the datasets and efficacy analyses. The resubmission includes a Data Integrity Quality Review Report which outlines the steps that were taken to assure the accuracy and reliability of the data. During this second review cycle, no additional issues involving data quality or integrity were identified.
L1937: Financial disclosure information was provided (in the original NDA submission) for the covered clinical studies 001, 201, 202A/B/C and 301, as defined by 21 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 54.2(e), which establish the effectiveness and safety of palovarotene (See Section 23). No concerns are raised about the integrity of the data.

L1940: ## III. Appendices
L1941: ## 12. Summary of Regulatory History
L1942: The investigational new drug (IND) 120181 was submitted by Clementia Pharmaceuticals Inc. (Clementia) on March 28, 2014, to investigate palovarotene for the treatment of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). Palovarotene was previously under development by Roche Pharmaceuticals Inc. (Roche) under IND
L1943: . Clementia licensed palovarotene from Roche
L1944: On July 21, 2014, U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) designated palovarotene as an orphan drug product for the treatment of FOP. Fast Track designation was subsequently granted on November 25, 2014, for prevention of heterotopic ossification following preosseous flare-ups in patients with FOP. In a meeting held on May 14, 2015, Clementia updated FDA on the development of palovarotene for the treatment of FOP as it pertained to the pediatric population and discussed the overall development plan to support product registration. During this meeting FDA reiterated concerns with Clementia's methodology for selecting doses for pediatric patients and suggested that Clementia could use nonclinical data on the reversibility of growth effects to help justify their pediatric dose selection.
L1945: A subsequent type C meeting was held on March 1, 2017, to gain agreement on the formation of new heterotopic ossification (HO) as a clinically meaningful outcome that would be appropriate as the primary endpoint in a phase 3 study, and the potential to utilize Clementia's natural history study (NHS) as a control group. During the meeting, FDA conveyed that in principle, they agreed with the use of new HO for the primary endpoint; however, FDA requested additional clarification on the specifics of how new HO data would be obtained for use as the primary efficacy endpoint. FDA also stated that additional discussion would be needed regarding the use of the NHS as an external control group for the phase 3 study.
L1946: An end-of-phase 2 (EOP2) meeting was held on June 27, 2017, to discuss key design features of the phase 3 study, including enrollment criteria, dosing regimen, control group, and safety monitoring. FDA conveyed that use of the NHS study as an external control group may be acceptable; however, the FDA reiterated the preference for randomized controlled data. FDA further noted that the acceptability of NHS data and comparability of NHS and phase 3 patients will be review issues. With regards to dosing, FDA commented that chronic dosing for adult patients appeared reasonable, but the chronic dosing regimen for the pediatric population, especially skeletally immature children, was a safety concern. FDA conveyed to Clementia that the phase 3 protocol should have clear criteria, schedules, and algorithms for dose interruption and dose de-escalation. Additionally, FDA recommended stringent safety monitoring, including the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) and evaluation of growth in the pediatric population. During this meeting, FDA also noted that a food effect study was conducted in the COPD program; Clementia agreed to perform a food effect study with the to-be-marketed formulation specific for the FOP program. Breakthrough Therapy designation for the prevention of HO in patients with FOP was granted on July 11, 2017.
L1947: At a type B meeting held on October 23, 2018, under the Breakthrough Designation program, Clementia requested FDA concurrence for the potential of the phase 2 outcomes data for the episodic flare-up 20/10 mg palovarotene regimen to support a New Drug Application (NDA) for full approval of this dosing regimen for the treatment of FOP in children and adults. It was agreed that the available phase 2 data would support the filing of an NDA for prevention of heterotopic ossification associated with flare up symptoms in patients with FOP. Clementia proposed, and FDA agreed, that the ongoing phase 3 trial could be submitted as a supplemental NDA for a chronic dosing regimen. This meeting also included discussion about the different imaging modalities that were used in the studies and the image acquisition guidelines and adjudication processes.
L1948: Another type B meeting held under the Breakthrough Designation program on February 5, 2019, focused discussion on nonclinical aspects of the planned NDA. FDA stated that nonclinical studies to assess the effects of palovarotene on female fertility, early embryonic development, and male fertility, would be required. Clementia responded with a request to conduct these studies as a postmarketing commitment. The requested studies were conducted subsequently and submitted with the NDA.
L1949: Rare Pediatric Disease designation was granted on February 7, 2019. Pre-NDA meetings were held with CMC and clinical on February 7 and February 14, 2019, respectively. During the February 14, 2019, meeting, the format and content of the planned NDA for all relevant disciplines was discussed. FDA recommended that a thorough QT (TQT) study should be conducted, as the available nonclinical data might not support waiver of a TQT study. FDA also continued to recommend that Clementia conduct a food effect study with the to-be-marketed formulation of palovarotene to support labeling that the drug may be swallowed whole or sprinkled on soft foods. There were no agreements made for late submission of application components.
L1950: In April 2019, Clementia was acquired by Ipsen. Ipsen Biopharmaceuticals, Inc. is the US commercial branch of Ipsen. On December 4, 2019, a teleconference was held during which a partial clinical hold (PCH) was issued by the FDA for children under 14 years of age participating in the palovarotene clinical trials following reports of premature epiphyseal closure. Ipsen submitted a complete response to the PCH on April 16, 2020. FDA issued a correspondence on May 15, 2020, to continue the PCH. This partial clinical hold remains in effect.
L1951: A subsequent pre-NDA Meeting was held on July 28, 2020, to discuss the adequacy of Ipsen's drug development program to support their future NDA. Ipsen's updated proposal included changes to the following: indication (b) (4)
L1952: dosing regimen (to include chronic and flare-up dosing regimens), and the proposed safety and efficacy data to be included in the submission. During this meeting, FDA communicated the need to review bone safety and other safety data on pediatric subjects \ge 12 years old. There were no agreements made for late submission of application components.
L1953: Ipsen submitted NDA 215559 on March 31, 2021, and the application was filed on May 30, 2021. An informal teleconference was held with Ipsen on August 6, 2021, to discuss FDA concern about the reliability of the data submitted with the NDA. The concerns stemmed from the issues regarding the imaging vendor wherein Ipsen informed FDA that rereads for one or multiple timepoints for subjects in the trial were required. Due to these concerns, FDA
L1954: recommended that Ipsen withdraw their NDA and resubmit following further investigation with the imaging vendor to include a complete root cause analysis of the processes that may have led to the issues described. On August 12, 2021, Ipsen submitted a request for withdrawal of the application. The NDA was subsequently resubmitted on April 29, 2022, and filed on June 28, 2022.
L1955: ## 13. Pharmacology Toxicology: Additional Information and Assessment
L1956: ## 13.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted Under the IND
L1957: Data from a series of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies completed with palovarotene and published scientific literature cited by the Applicant support the mechanism of action and potential benefits of palovarotene for the proposed indication in FOP patients.
L1958: ## 13.1.1. Primary Pharmacology
L1959: Data from a series of in vitro and in vivo nonclinical pharmacology studies completed with palovarotene and published scientific literature cited by the Applicant support the mechanism of action and potential benefits of palovarotene for the proposed indication in FOP patients.
L1960: **Table 67. In Vitro Pharmacological Studies of Palovarotene**
L1961: Study	Findings
Receptor binding and transactivation assay	Palovarotene is selective for binding to RAR\gamma (6 to 10-fold) as compared to RAR\alpha and RAR\beta, based on IC50 values (450, 4700, and 2900nM, respectively).
Palovarotene demonstrated 3 to 12-fold greater in vitro functional activity at RAR\gamma as compared to RAR\alpha and RAR\beta, with EC50 values of 8.0, 94.2 and 25.0nM, respectively).
The main metabolites M2, M3, M4a and M4b demonstrated reduced RAR\gamma activity (1.2, 1.7, 14, and 4.2% of parent, respectively).
Effect of RAR\gamma agonist on cell differentiation and Smad signaling	Published study provided evidence that treatment with RAR\gamma agonists (e.g., CD1530) inhibited BMP-induced differentiation of chondrogenic (ATDC5) cells. In the treated ATDC5 cells, reductions (>80%) in the levels of phosphorylated Smad (pSmad 1, 5, and 8) and decreases in Smad proteins were noted.
The response in ATDC5 cells was abrogated in the presence of proteasome inhibitors, suggesting that RAR\gamma agonists might potentially promote proteasome mediated Smad protein degradation.
Similarly, palovarotene also reduced BMP-induced pSmad1/5 proteins in human FOP fibroblast cell line carrying an overactive ALK2R206H mutation (replicates the codon 206 mutation present in most patients with FOP).

Abbreviation: BMP, bone morphogenetic protein; EC50, dose at half-maximum response; FOP, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva; IC50, half-maximal inhibitory concentration; RAR, retinoic acid receptor
L1963: The in vivo efficacy of palovarotene was evaluated by the Applicant and in published research studies in three distinct injury-based (BMP-implant, ALKQ207D and ALK2R206H) and one spontaneous (Prrx1-R206H) mouse models of HO.
L1964: **Table 68. In Vivo Activity of Palovarotene**
L1965: Study	Findings
Injury-based HO models
BMP-2 implant mouse model	
In BMP-implant mouse model, a wild-type mouse was implanted with matrigel containing skeletogenic factor recombinant rBMP-2 inside the calf muscle to induce injury. Mice received various daily doses of retinoids and palovarotene by oral gavage for 12 days. Suppression of HO was evaluated by measuring bone volume/total volume in ectopic masses by microcomputed tomography (microCT) on Day 12.
In general, activation of the RAR receptor including by palovarotene at 0.12 to 4 mg/kg or HED 0.6 to 19 mg was effective in preventing the formation of ectopic mineralized tissue masses at the operation sites.
The effectiveness of retinoids was highest for RAR\gamma selective agonists (CD1530, palovarotene). The pan-agonist, all-transretinoic acid, and RAR\alpha agonist (NRX185183) inhibited HO as well, but their effectiveness was partial and required high doses. This was likely attributed to the high expression of RAR\gamma in chondrogenic cells and chondrocytes as compared to other RAR members (Koyama et al. 1999).
Mice treated with various doses of palovarotene showed dose-dependent HO inhibition.
Inhibition of HO was mediated exclusively via the RAR\gamma as the effect was completely abolished in RAR\gamma null mice.

ALKQ207D mouse model	
The ALKQ207D transgenic mice carry Cre-inducible Q207D mutant (change in amino acid residue 207 from glutamine to aspartic acid) that constitutively activates ALK2 in the absence of ligand. HO was induced in homozygous ALKQ207D mice at 16 days of age by intramuscular injection with adenovirus expressing Cre- recombinase (Adeno-Cre) into the posterior femoral muscle region to activate the transgene plus cardiotoxin to initiate an inflammatory triggering event (i.e., muscle injury).
Oral administration of palovarotene to ALKQ207D mice starting from the day of muscle injury and for 15 consecutive days resulted in dose-dependent reductions in injury-induced HO volume (75 to 100%) at the injury site, with ED50 of 2 mg/kg/ day (HED =7 mg/day).
Treatment with palovarotene is most effective (up to 93.5% HO inhibition) when initiated early (prior to and up to 3-days post injury), but effectiveness was decreased to 71% inhibition of heterotopic bone volume when initiating treatment 7-days post injury.
The data suggest that RAR\gamma agonists block HO by preventing chondrogenic cell differentiation and cartilage formation, but are not effective in the osteogenic phase of HO.
L1966: Study	Findings
ALK2R206H mice model	
The conditional-on knock-in ACVR1/ALK2R206H mouse was developed to encode mildly activating gain-of-function classical FOP R206H mutant allele (substitution of arginine with histidine in codon 206). One month old ALK2R206H mice were treated with doxycycline to induce global expression of the mutant allele and cardiotoxin into quadriceps muscle to induce local inflammation and HO. HO volume was measured by microCT and 3D image reconstruction at Day 14.
Treatment with oral palovarotene starting from Day 1 to Day 3 of injury at 4 mg/kg (HED =19 mg) followed by 0.6 mg/kg (HED =3 mg) from Day 4 to Day 14 diminished heterotrophic bone formation by more than 86%, based on bone volume/total volume quantification.
In vehicle-treated ALK2R206H mice movement of the HO-affected leg was impaired whereas in drug treated group joint mobility of the HO-affected leg was maintained.
Moreover, histochemical analysis showed that newly formed heterotopic cartilaginous tissue and endochondral bone were present in vehicle-treated but not in palovarotene-treated ALK2R206H mice.

Spontaneous HO models
Prrx1-R206H spontaneous HO mice model	
Additional studies were conducted in Prrx1-R206H mice, that contain the R206H mutation in a tissue specific manner in skeletal mesenchymal progenitor cell (Prrx1+). Prrx1-R206H mice recapitulate many of the phenotypic features of FOP patients (e.g., malformed hindlimb at birth and spontaneous postnatal development of HO in the absence of injury).
Palovarotene blocked spontaneous HO in pups when nursing dams were dosed orally with 50 µg/mouse/day from birth to 14 days and pups were dosed orally with 20µg Q2D from Day 15-30.
It also prevented skeletal defects and improved mobility with markedly reduced HO.
It also reversed histologic growth plate abnormalities compared to those observed in untreated Prrx1-R206H mice.
L1967: Source: Reviewer derived from Study # CLM001-PD-002, Study # 001,
Abbreviations: ACVR1, Activin receptor IA/ also known as ALK2, activin-I ke kinase 2; EC50, dose at half-maximum response; HED, human equivalent dose; HO, heterotopic ossification; microCT, microcomputed tomography; Q2D, every 2 days; RAR, retinoic acid receptor; rBMP-2; recombinant bone morphogenetic protein-2
L1968: ## 13.1.2. Secondary Pharmacology
L1969: Screening for off-target binding sites indicated interaction with adenosine A3, benzodiazepine and the delta opioid receptor with high IC50 values of 3.94, 2.12, 1.85µM, respectively, when tested up to 10µM. Of note, the IC50 for RAR\gamma binding is 450nM. Inhibition (&gt;10%) of phosphodiesterase I, phosphodiesterase IV, cathepsin G, human immunodeficiency virus type 1 protease and increased guanylate cyclase activity were noted at high concentrations (30-fold higher than human exposure observed at MRHD). Therefore, palovarotene is not considered to possess clinically relevant secondary pharmacology activity.
L1970: ## 13.1.3. Safety Pharmacology
L1971: Based on safety pharmacology studies conducted to assess the potential for cardiovascular, neurobehavioral, gastrointestinal and urinary effects, palovarotene did not appear to pose any
L1972: acute safety concerns at clinically relevant exposures. A respiratory safety pharmacology study was not conducted; however, no evidence of adverse respiratory function was noted in repeat dose toxicity studies.
L1973: **Table 69. Summary of Safety Pharmacology Studies**
L1974: Study/ Study No.	Findings
hERG assay in CHO cells	
The effect of palovarotene on hERG current was tested on CHO cells expressing hERG potassium channel at concentrations ranging from 1 to 10\muM using whole cell patch clamp method.
Palovarotene significant reduced inward and outward K+ currents, with IC50 of 7.2\muM (~2985 ng/mL), which results in wide safety margin (>30-fold between hERG IC50 and the free Cmax at the MRHD).
Based on the absence of in vivo CV effects, low in vitro potency, and absence of effects on hERG or action potential in the subsequently conducted assays, palovarotene is unlikely to affect CV functions in patients.

hERG assay in HEK293 cells	
The effects of palovarotene and its major metabolites (M2, M3, M4a and M4b) on hERG current were tested on HEK293 cells expressing hERG potassium channel at 0.3, 1, 3, 10 and 30\muM.
Palovarotene and its metabolites did not produce more than 38% reduction in hERG current.
IC50 could not be calculated, but it is >30\muM.
The discrepancy in blocking hERG channel may be due to the differences in the hERG receptor structure between the cell lines. The positive controls in both test systems blocked hERG current, which confirmed the sensitivity of the test systems.

Action potential assay in Canine Purkinje fibers	
In ventricular cardiac fibers isolated from dogs, palovarotene had no effect on resting membrane potential, depolarization rate, upstroke amplitude, or action potential duration at concentrations up to 10\muM (30-fold Cmax at MRHD).

Potential neurobehavioral effects in male Wistar rats	
Wistar Han rats were administered with a single oral dose of palovarotene at 0.2, 1 or 5 mg/kg. Irwin-type assessments were conducted at 0.5 to 5 h postdose.
Palovarotene did not affect central or peripheral nervous system endpoints.

Potential cardiovascular effects in male beagle dogs	
Conscious and telemetered dogs were administered with a single oral dose of palovarotene at 0.04, 0.2, 1 or 10 mg/kg. Cardiovascular parameters (heart rate, blood pressure, and electrocardiograms) were monitored through 8 hours postdose.
Palovarotene did not cause any changes in heart rate, blood pressure or ECG parameters up to 10 mg/kg (1-fold Cmax and 28-fold AUC at MRHD).

L1978: ## 13.1.4. ADME/PK
L1979: Palovarotene absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME) and PK parameters were characterized in humans, rats, dogs, and monkeys. Palovarotene was quantified using protein precipitation extraction HPLC/MS/MS assay with solid phase extraction. Metabolites were assayed by HPLC/UV or HPLC/MS/MS.
L1980: ## Absorption
L1981: - Contrary to humans, food did not significantly affect the pharmacokinetics of palovarotene in the animal species evaluated.
- In both fasted and fed animals, oral bioavailability (BA) was medium in mouse (44 to 56%), rat (28 to 32%), dog (63 to 70%) and low in monkey (8 to 13%). Relative and absolute BA were not determined in human.
- Palovarotene was rapidly absorbed in mice, rat and dog (Tmax=0.25 to 2 h) and slightly slower in monkeys (Tmax=5 to 13 h) and 8 h in human.
- Palovarotene had a high apparent volume of distribution in human (237 L), rats and monkeys (1.5 to 4.2 L/kg) and low in dogs (0.3 L/kg).
- The terminal elimination half-life (t1/2) values were 3 h in rats, 4 h in rat and dog, 8 h in monkey and 9 h in human.

L1987: ## Distribution
L1988: - In autoradiography tissue distribution studies, palovarotene exhibited a slow but extensive distribution into the tissues.
- Maximal blood and tissue levels were attained 4 to 8 hours post-dose in the adrenal cortex, adrenal medulla, liver, and the walls of the small intestine and caecum.
- The mean blood to plasma ratios of palovarotene in mouse, rat, dog, monkey and human ranged from 0.52 to 0.63, indicating that palovarotene did not partition into erythrocytes
- There was no evidence of retention in, or affinity for, melanin-containing tissues.
- Palovarotene was highly (97 to 99%) bound to proteins in mouse, rat, dog, monkey and human plasma.
L1989: ## Metabolism
L1990: - Palovarotene is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, and to a minor extent by CYP2C8 and CYP2C19.
- The in vitro metabolic profiles of palovarotene in liver microsomes and hepatocytes from mice, rats, dogs, monkeys, and humans were qualitatively similar but quantitatively different across species. The in vivo metabolite profiles were similar in rats and dogs. No metabolites unique to humans were identified.
- The four major metabolites identified were: M2 (6-OH) and M3 (7-OH) which are further metabolized to M4a (6-oxo) and M4b (7-oxo), M5, the carboxyl \beta-glucuronide of the
L1991: parent compound, was also detected after incubation with cryopreserved hepatocytes. Exposure to each of the metabolites, M2, M3, M4a and M4b was much lower than the parent in all species. The in vivo metabolite-to-parent drug ratios were 2 to 13% in rats and 1 to 27% in dogs.
L1992: - The pharmacological activity of main metabolites M2, M3, M4a, M4b was lower than that of parent (1.2%, 1.7%, 14%, and 4.2% of parent activity, respectively) in an in vitro RAR\gamma transactivation assay.
L1993: ## Excretion
L1994: In rats and dogs, palovarotene was primarily eliminated through the biliary and fecal routes, and recovery was complete within 7 days, with most of the administered radioactivity recovered within the first 24 hours. In both species, small fractions of the dose (&lt;1%) were recovered in urine.

L2001: ## Pharmacokinetic drug interaction and transporter studies
L2002: - Palovarotene is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4, and its in vitro biotransformation could potentially be influenced by strong inhibitors and inducers of CYP3A4.Ketoconazole (a strong inhibitor of CYP3A4) competitively inhibited the metabolism of palovarotene, with Ki of 0.2\muM.
- Palovarotene's exposure was increased (3-fold) and decreased (9-fold) in the presence of ketoconazole and rifampin (strong induced of CYP3A4) and human DDI studies.
- In vitro, palovarotene did not significantly inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6. For CYP3A4, IC50 values of palovarotene and its metabolites
- (M1 through M4) were &gt;100\muM (300-fold Cmax at the MRHD), suggesting that palovarotene is not likely to inhibit the CYP3A4-dependent elimination of other drugs.
- Palovarotene was not an inducer of CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 but induced CYP2B6 and CYP3A4. A clinical DDI study was conducted and has
L2003: demonstrated that palovarotene is not a CYP3A4 inducer in vivo. For CYP2B6, the risk assessment of all available data suggests that the likelihood of palovarotene to induce CYP2B6 in vivo is negligible.
L2004: - Palovarotene does not appear to be a significant substrate of UGTs and does not pose a clinically relevant risk with respect to their inhibition.
- Palovarotene was not a substrate of the following efflux and uptake transporters: P-gp, BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3 and OCT1.
- As palovarotene is essentially excreted by biliary route, the interaction with renal transporters (OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1 and MATE2-K) was not warranted. Of the transporters tested, palovarotene inhibited BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and BSEP, with IC50 values of 9.69µM, 1.83µM, &gt;3, &gt;3µM, and 14.7µM, respectively. An evaluation of the DDI risk was performed and showed that clinically significant interaction of palovarotene with other drugs was unlikely.

L2035: ## 13.1.6. Toxicology
L2036: ## 13.1.6.1. General Toxicology
L2037: ## 13.1.6.1.1. 26-Week Toxicity Study in Rats, Study 1013603
L2038: ## Key Study Findings
L2039: - Groups of Wistar rats were given oral daily doses of vehicle (Miglyol 812 with 0.01% BHA and 0.01% BHT), or palovarotene at 0.3, 0.6 and 1 mg/kg/day for 26 weeks, including groups terminated after 13-weeks. Recovery was assessed for an additional 8 weeks.
- Adverse drug-related skin lesions lead to early termination of one male and two females treated at 1 mg/kg/day.
- The target organs were the skin, growth plate of stifle or knee joints and sternum, and nonglandular forestomach during the interim and terminal sacrifices at all doses.Skin: Lesions including hypergranulosis, epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis), chronic active skin inflammation and skin ulceration were noted at all doses.
- Growth plate: Dose-dependent chondrodystrophy in the growth plate of knee joints were observed at all dose levels. Chondrodystrophy in the growth plate in sternum was seen in both sexes at 1 mg/kg/day.
- Forestomach: Degeneration/dyskeratosis and acute keratin layer inflammation of nonglandular stomach epithelium were noted in both control and treated animals but with increasing incidence and severity at \ge 0.6 mg/kg/day. The lesion in rat forestomach was considered rodent-specific and not clinically relevant due to the absence of comparable structure in human.
- The growth plate chondrodystrophy and forestomach lesion were still present in recovery animals.
- In general, the findings in this study were consistent with the class and those noted in subchronic studies in this species.
- Based on area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) ratios, exposure to each of four metabolites (M2, M3, M4a, and M4b) was generally &lt;13% of the exposure to palovarotene itself.
- While evidence of testicular toxicity was seen in male rats given daily oral doses at 5 mg/kg in the 4-week study, this dose level produced severe toxicity and deaths, so it is possible that the findings were related to the underlying poor conditions of the animals rather than a direct palovarotene effect. There was no evidence of testicular toxicity in rats or dogs in chronic toxicity studies
- The NOAEL was not established and was considered &lt;0.3 mg/kg/day (AUC_{0-24h} &lt;168 ng.h/mL) due to only partially recoverable growth plate chondrodystrophy of the stifle joint and persistent forestomach degeneration/dyskeratosis observed at all doses. Adverse findings in the animals were considered consistent with exaggerated pharmacology.

L2045: **Table 78. Observations and Results of 26-Week Oral Toxicity Study in Rats**
L2046: Parameter	Major Findings
Mortality	
Palovarotene caused deaths in three animals treated at 1 mg/kg/day. One HD male sacrificed on Day 94 due to drug-related limb injury and present with histological slight hemorrhage and moderate inflammation in the right humeroradial joint.
One HD male and female HD sacrificed in moribund condition during Week 22 due to skin lesions (sores/scab on the skin, red focus areas and dark red and drug crusted areas, epidermal hyperplasia, chronic active inflammation, ulceration, hemorrhage and hypergranulosis).
Deaths in four animals (control male, LD female, MD male and female) was considered incidental as these died on Days 92, 24, 23 and 92 following blood collections.

Clinical signs	
Skin and pelage lesions (red/rough hair coat, red skin and sores/scabs) were seen in all treated males and females at \ge 0.6 mg/kg/day: The onset time ranges from Days 6 to 13 across groups. Incidences was higher during the first 13 weeks (interim) and decreased over the course of the treatment period.
The head, mouth, and dorsal-cervical and thoracic regions were most affected. Skin findings resolved largely during the recovery period.

Body weights	
Lower mean BW (9 to 15%) were observed in males and females treated at 1 mg/kg/day. All treated males (6 to 22%) and females (12 to 18%) at \ge 0.6 mg/kg/day had a reduced BW gain.
BW changes were considered adverse based on >10\% and the absence of any change in food consumption at the end of dosing.
Body weight loss did not fully recover in HD males and females.
There was a transient decrease (up to 9%) in FC noted at 1 mg/kg/day during the first 3 months but not at the end of dosing.

Ophthalmoscopy	Unremarkable
ECG	Not measured
Hematology	
Modest increases in neutrophil counts were seen throughout dosing, predominately in males (33 to 88%), and females (13 to 80%) at 1 mg/kg/day. The neutrophil changes suggest immune or inflammatory change and correlate with skin lesions observed clinically or inflammatory stomach lesions observed microscopically or both.
All hematological changes were reversible.

Coagulation	Unremarkable

L2049: Parameter	Major Findings
Histopathology	Drug-related histologic findings were observed in the skin, bone (sternum), stifle (knee) joint, and forestomach during the interim as well as terminal sacrifices. Skin ulcerations was notable in males treated at 1 mg/kg/day and females \ge 0.6 mg/kg/day only at terminal sacrifices.
All skin lesions cleared in recovery animals.
Forestomach:
Degeneration/dyskeratosis of nonglandular stomach epithelium was present in control and treated groups at the interim terminal, and recovery sacrifices, suggesting that it was a spontaneous finding.
However, palovarotene increases in the incidence and severity of these findings were noted at all doses.
Test article related acute keratin layer inflammation consisting of neutrophils and lymphocyte infiltration were seen in interim animals at \ge 0.6 mg/kg/day and all terminal males.
Stomach lesions persisted at the end of recovery.
The lesion in rat forestomach was considered species-specific and not clinically relevant as this organ has no human equivalent.

L2052: ## 13.1.6.1.2. 39-Week Oral Toxicity Study in Dogs,
## Study 1013980
L2053: ## Key Study Findings
L2054: - A group of male and female beagle dogs were orally treated with vehicle (Miglyol 812 with 0.01% BHA and 0.01% BHT) or palovarotene doses of 12, 25 or 40 \mug/kg/day for at
L2055: least 13 or 39 weeks. Due to the lack of significant toxicity, the mid dose was increased from 25 to 120 µg/kg/day for at least 39 weeks (Week 13 through Week 52). Recovery was assessed for an additional 13 weeks in animals treated at 12 and 40 µg/kg/day. Recovery was not evaluated in animals administered 25/120 µg/kg/day.
L2056: - Skin findings were noted at all dose levels, with frequency and severity increasing with doses.
- Adverse skin clinical signs at 120 µg/kg/day necessitated early euthanasia of seven dogs (two males and five females between Week 26 to 33 and Week 19 to 52, respectively) due to repetitive occurrences of clinical otitis externa, conjunctivitis, and severe skin lesions, which were manifested systemically with an inflammatory response and hypergranulosis of the skin.
- The surviving animals also presented with skin related clinical signs including aural discharge (black), ocular discharge, red conjunctivae, alopecia, black/red/broken skin and scabs, predominantly at ≥12 µg/kg/day.
- Drug-related conjunctivitis of the eye was noted after 39 and 52-weeks of treatment in one male at 120 µg/kg/day.
- Histological findings related to palovarotene were only noted in the skin, and included dose-related hypergranulosis at all doses, lymphohistiocytic/neutrophilic infiltrates, parakeratosis predominantly in animals treated at 40 and 25/120 µg/kg/day. Moreover, skin histopathology (erosion, epithelial hyperplasia, cell infiltrates, inflammatory exudate) occurred in limited number of animals treated at 12 and 25/120 µg/kg/day
- The skin findings were largely reversible except lymphohistiocytic infiltrates at 12 µg/kg/day and inflammatory exudate noted at 40 µg/kg/day.
- The NOAEL was &lt;12 µg/kg/day (AUC0-24h &lt;103 ng.h/mL) based on in-life and histological skin lesion (hypogranulosis) noted at all tested doses.

L2074: ## 13.1.6.3. Carcinogenicity
L2075: Palovarotene's nonclinical package did not include rodent carcinogenicity studies. Instead, the Applicant conducted a WOE assessment to address the carcinogenic potential of palovarotene using the available information from the completed nonclinical studies, published literature and the intended patient population. In brief, the Applicant argued that palovarotene is unlikely to pose a carcinogenic hazard to patients and lifetime rodent carcinogenicity studies are not necessary based on:
L2076: - Absence of preneoplastic and neoplastic lesions in palovarotene's nonclinical chronic toxicology program in rats and dogs,
- The lack of strong mechanism-based evidence linking RAR\gamma activation with increased risk of cancer from publicly available information, no significant risks identified from review of class effects of retinoids for nonchronic indications
- No evidence of hormonal effects or immunosuppression
- Negative overall genotoxicity assessment
L2077: The Agency review of the WOE assessment suggested that the human carcinogenic potential of palovarotene is uncertain considering:
L2078: - Target biology: RAR\gamma is a member of the nuclear receptor superfamily that act as transcription factors and mediate pleiotropic effects of retinoids in cellular hemostasis and early development (organogenesis). It has been shown to regulate the balance between cellular proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis of normal and malignant cells.
- Published studies provide evidence of the potential role of RAR\gamma in cancer both as an oncogene and tumor suppressor gene depending upon the type of cancer studied (Marinelli et al. 2007). Overexpression of RAR\gamma was shown in multiple human cancers such as hepatocellular carcinoma, esophageal cancer, and cholangiocarcinoma. In these models, RAR\gamma facilitated the progression of tumors through multiple signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt, NF-\kappaB, and Wnt/\beta-catene. On the other hand, treatment with retinoic acid, a RAR\gamma ligand, was shown to increase death of SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells and induce apoptosis of pancreatic cancer cells.
- Preneoplastic histological findings were noted in the skin, as epidermal hyperplasia in the context of chronic active skin inflammation in rats, which were supported by similar
L2079: findings in dogs at clinically relevant exposures. In addition, dyskeratosis/inflammation were seen in the stomach of rats in the 26-week study at clinically relevant exposures.

- The available tumor outcome data from rodent carcinogenicity studies with approved oral and topical retinoids described tumor findings in the skin, liver, blood vessels and adrenal glands.
- Indication: palovarotene is the first in class molecule for the treatment of chronic disease.
L2080: The initial nonclinical review of the WOE did not completely exclude the carcinogenic risk of palovarotene with high certainty, hence rodent carcinogenicity studies in two species were recommended as a post marketing requirement, should palovarotene be approved for the indicated FOP population. However, the Applicant submitted additional information late in the review cycle requesting reconsideration of the requirement for carcinogenicity studies. The nonclinical team will review the information amendment and request consultation from the Executive Carcinogenicity Assessment Committee upon NDA resubmission.
L2081: ## 13.1.6.4. Reproductive and Developmental Toxicity
L2082: ## 13.1.6.4.1. An Oral Gavage Fertility and Early Embryonic Development Study of Palovarotene in Male Rats, Study 9001429
L2083: ## Key Study Findings
L2084: - Palovarotene was orally administered to male rats prior to mating, during mating, and up to scheduled termination (approximately 11 weeks in total) at 0.3, 1 and 3 mg/kg/day.
- The high dose exceeded the MTD as it caused premature termination of the group on Day 39 due to death, adverse skin and hair coat-related clinical signs, and substantially (up to 70%) reduced BW gain.
- Significant nondose related reductions in BW gain (18%) and skin changes (thin cover, red skin and scab) were noted at both 0.3 and 1 mg/kg/day doses. Therefore, the NOAEL for paternal general toxicity was not identified.
- Palovarotene did not cause adverse effects on mating, fertility indices, conception rate, reproductive organ weights, or sperm parameters.
- No drug-related effects were observed on reproductive parameters (implantation sites, live embryos, dead embryos, early resorptions or the rate of pre- or postimplantation loss) in untreated females mated with treated males.
- The NOAEL for reproduction in males is 1 mg/kg/day (AUC_{0-24h}=569 ng.h/mL) based on the absence of adverse effects on fertility and reproduction parameters up to this dose level (the highest tolerated dose).

There was an increased frequency and/or incidence of males noted with hypersensitivity between Days 10 and 122 and vocalization between Days 56 and 108.
Body weights	Palovarotene caused nondose related reduction in BW gains (18%) and absolute BW (6%) at both 0.3 and 1 mg/kg/day doses. Marginal decreases in food consumption (3 to 5%) were noted at the same dose levels.
Gross pathology, organ weight and Histology	There were no effects noted on reproductive organ weight, gross pathologic and histopathologic finding in the testes or epididymides of males and 0.3 and 1 mg/kg/day.
Mating and fertility	Palovarotene did not affect the mean number of days to mating, fertility indices, conception rate, sperm motility, morphology or concentration when tested up to 1 mg/kg/day.

L2095: ## 13.1.6.4.2. An Oral Gavage Fertility and Early Embryonic Development Study of Palovarotene in Male Rats, Study 9001429
L2096: ## Key Study Findings
L2097: - Palovarotene was administered to female Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats for 14 days prior to mating with drug naïve male and up to GD 7 at the dose levels of 0.3, 1 and 3 mg/kg/day.
- Skin and hair coat related clinical signs, reduced BW gain and lower food consumption were noted at \ge 1 mg/kg/day.

- No effect on mating, fertility indices and conception rate were seen in females at any dose level.
- The NOAEL for reproduction in females was 1 mg/kg/day [AUC0-24h=421 ng.h/mL] based on adverse effects noted in estrus cycle and reduced embryofetal survival at 3 mg/kg/day.
