L2107: ## 13.1.6.4.3. Developmental Toxicity Study in Rats With Toxicokinetic Evaluation, Study 1003177
L2108: ## Key Study Findings
L2109: - Palovarotene was orally administered to pregnant female rats during the period of organogenesis (GD 6 to 17) at doses of 0.01, 0.25 and 1.25 mg/kg/day.
- Modest maternal toxicities characterized by reduced body weight gain (10% to 20% lower) were noted at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day and decreased food consumption (10%) was seen at 1.25 mg/kg/day.
- Palovarotene was teratogenic in rats as it caused multiple fetal external, visceral and skeletal malformations at \ge 0.25 mg/kg/day, consistent with the pattern of retinoid-mediated embryopathy.
L2110: - Fetal NOAEL = 0.01 mg/kg/day [AUC0-24h = 8.7 ng.h/mL] based on the increases in the incidence and severity of fetal malformations at ≥ 0.25 mg/kg/day.
- Maternal NOAEL = 0.01 mg/kg/day [AUC0-24h = 8.7 ng.h/mL] based on decrease in maternal body loss at ≥ 0.25 mg/kg/day.

L2122: ## 13.1.6.4.4. A 6-Week Oral Gavage Toxicity Study of Palovarotene in 3- to 9-Week-Old Rats, Followed by a 6-Week Recovery Period
L2123: Juvenile rats were treated orally with 0 (vehicle), or palovarotene at the doses of 0.1, 0.5 and 1.2 mg/kg/day from postnatal Weeks 3 through 9 (covering human development period of 2 to 12-year years old). Recovery was assessed for an additional 6 weeks.
L2124: - Palovarotene adversely affected skeletal growth and development in a dose-dependent manner in juvenile rats treated at \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day. The findings included the following:Decreases in bone formation markers (OC and PINP)
- Reduction in bone size (femur and tibia length/width)
- Decreases in bone densitometry area, BMC, and BMD at the proximal, mid and distal femur, total/cortical/subcortical femoral diaphysis, vertebral body
- Radiological changes in several bones (abnormal shape, diffuse bone loss, increased/decreased physis thickness, and increased space between bones)
- Dose-related increases in the incidence and severity of histopathologic findings were noted in phyeal, articular, hyaline cartilages and bone in animals treated at 0.5 and 1.2 mg/kg/day.Physis: Dose-related thinning/closure of the physis, phyeal hypertrophy, and chondrodysplasia were observed in multiple bones (humerus, radius, ulna, femur, tibia, hindpaw, vertebrae, and sternum)
- Hyaline cartilage (Vertebral epiphysis): Decreased endochondral ossification and hypertrophic hyaline cartilage
L2125: ## NDA 215559
## Sohonos, palovarotene capsules
L2126: - Articular cartilage: Hypertrophy and chondrodysplasia were seen in the sternebrae, osteochondral junctions, humeral/scapular, femoral/acetabular joints and proximal tibial articular cartilage.
- Bone: Decreases in bone was noted in all bones except nasal cavity and calvarium, and necrosis in the femoral head and neck region.
- Histomorphometry measurement: thickening of proximal tibial physis at \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day.
- These effects reflect the intended pharmacodynamic activity (inhibition of chondrocyte differentiation) of palovarotene. Changes in bone mass and geometry could be secondary to effect on skeletal growth.
- Effects on physeal closure and decreased vertebral epiphyseal bone did not reverse.
- Of note, skeletal effects chondrodystrophy were noted in 4 and 6 weeks repeat dose toxicity study conducted on adolescent rats (7 weeks old ~older than 12 years old human).
- The NOAEL is 0.1 mg/kg/day (AUC_{0-t}=681 ng.h/mL) based on the adverse pathologic changes observed in the skeleton at \ge 0.5 mg/kg/day.

L2158: ## 14. Clinical Pharmacology: Additional Information and Assessment
L2159: ## 14.1. In Vitro Studies
L2160: Four in vitro metabolism, two in vitro transporter, one in vitro plasma protein binding, one in vitro blood-to-plasma ratio, and five in vitro drug interaction study reports were submitted in current NDA.
L2161: ## 14.1.1. In Vitro Metabolism Studies
L2162: In Study 10008691, the metabolic stability of palovarotene was evaluated in pooled liver microsomes from multiple species. Over a 60-minute incubation interval, the percent conversion of palovarotene was 89.1%, 68.5%, 50.4%, 40.6%, 25.5%, and 25.3%, respectively, in microsomes prepared from a human donor, Balb/c mouse, cynomolgus monkey, Hanover-Wistar rat, beagle dog, and CD-1 mouse. Five metabolites, M1 (6,7-dihydroxy), M2 (6-hydroxy), M3 (7-hydroxy), M4a (6-oxo), and M4b (7-oxo), were detected and characterized. Incubation of palovarotene with cryopreserved hepatocytes from human, dog, monkey, and Sprague-Dawley rat showed conversion of palovarotene to six metabolites, M1, M2, M3, M4a, M4b and one beta-glucuronide conjugate.
L2163: In Study 1008690, incubation of single human CYP450 isoforms with palovarotene demonstrated that CYP3A4, 2C8, and 2C19 oxidized palovarotene to metabolites. The major route of transformation was by CYP3A4, which converted palovarotene to M1, M2, M3, M4a and M4b. In human liver microsomal proteins (2 mg/mL), the Vmax (the maximum initial velocity in the absence of inhibitor) of palovarotene was determined as 1.97 nmole/min/mg, the Km (the Michaelis-Menten constant) was 59\muM, and Vmax/Km (intrinsic clearance) was 0.033 mUmin/mg protein. The Km values is much higher than the steady-state Cmax (0.33 to 0.49\muM) of palovarotene following 20 mg QD oral dosing. In human liver microsomes, ketoconazole, midazolam, and erythromycin appeared to be competitive inhibitors of palovarotene with Ki of 0.184\muM, 37.5\muM, and 64.6\muM, respectively. Study CYP1933-04 investigated in vitro stability of palovarotene in an incubation with recombinant human CYP2B6 and no significant metabolism of palovarotene was observed.
L2164: In Study CYP1558R2A, palovarotene was incubated with recombinant UDP glucuronosyl transferases (UGT) enzymes. The half-life values of palovarotene in UGT1A1, UGT1A3, UGT1A9, UGT2B7 and UGT2B15 incubations were determined to be &gt;240 minutes. The half-life values of palovarotene in UGT1A4 and UGT1A6 incubations were determined to be 183 and 142 minutes, respectively. However, due to the absence of phase I enzymes in the incubation, no conclusion could be drawn regarding the role of UGT enzymes in the metabolism of palovarotene.
L2165: ## 14.1.2. In Vitro Transporter Studies
L2166: In Study CYP1933-01, bidirectional apparent permeability assays showed that palovarotene was not a substrate of P-gp or BCRP. Transporter-expressing HEK293 cell uptake assays showed that palovarotene was not a substrate of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1. In Study CYP1933-02, palovarotene was determined to be an in vitro inhibitor of BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, and bile salt export pump (BSEP) transporters with IC50 values of 9.69\muM, 1.83\muM, &gt;3\muM, &gt;3\muM, and 14.7\muM, respectively. Palovarotene did not inhibit P-gp, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1, or MATE2-K transporters in vitro.
L2167: *Reviewer's comments:* The steady-state Cmax of palovarotene following 20 mg QD oral dosing was 0.33\muM to 0.49\muM. At the recommended maximum dose (20 mg QD), plasma palovarotene does not pose a clinically relevant risk with respect to the inhibition of OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1, or BSEP transporters. Also, the Applicant measured the solubility of palovarotene in fed-state simulated intestinal fluid at 37°C and pH 5, which was 2.37\pm0.23 \mug/mL or 5.8\muM. The ratio of Igut/IC50 for intestinal BCRP transporter is 0.60 and the calculated palovarotene R value is 1.60, which is below the threshold value of 11. No BCRP-mediated DDI is expected for palovarotene at 20 mg QD.
L2168: ## 14.1.3. Plasma Protein Binding and B/P Ratio
L2169: Study 1008422 showed that palovarotene was highly bound (ranging from 97.9% to 99.6%) to human plasma proteins over the concentration range of 6 to 1 000 ng/mL. In Study 1008425, the in vitro mean whole blood-to-plasma ratios of palovarotene (100-1000 ng/mL) in male and female human subjects were determined as 0.62 and 0.61, respectively. Palovarotene did not partition into erythrocytes.
L2170: ## 14.1.4. In Vitro Drug Interaction Studies
L2171: In Study 1008423, the potential of palovarotene to inhibit major CYP450 enzymes was assessed using cDNA-expressed enzymes. The showed that the IC50 values of palovarotene on human CYP1A2, 2C8, 2C9, 2C19, and 2D6 were &gt;100µM, 4.7µM, 8.1µM, 7.9µM, and &gt;100µM, respectively. For CYP3A4, IC50 values of palovarotene and its major metabolites were &gt;100µM. Study CYP1933-05 showed that palovarotene inhibited CYP2B6 with an IC50 value of 55.9µM. Study CYP1558 R2B showed that palovarotene reversibly inhibited multiple UGT enzymes. The IC50 values of palovarotene against UGT1A1, UGT1A3, UGT1A4, UGT1A6, UGT1A9 and UGT2B7 were 3.90µM, 21.3µM, 1.98µM, 21.8µM, 4.76µM, and 20.1µM, respectively. The steady-state Cmax of palovarotene following 20 mg QD oral dosing is 0.33µM to 0.49µM. Therefore, at the recommended maximum dose, palovarotene is unlikely to inhibit major CYP450 or UGT enzymes.
L2172: In Study CYP1933-03, CYP450 enzyme induction potential of palovarotene was assessed in cryopreserved human hepatocytes from three separate human donors. Palovarotene at up to 1µM did not induce CYP1A2, CYP2C9, or CYP2C19 in any of the three donors. Using steady-state plasma palovarotene Cmax of 0.49µM and fu,p of 0.02, the maximal unbound plasma concentration of palovarotene in liver is estimated as 0.49 * 0.02 * 30=0.3µM. Palovarotene at 0.32µM induced mRNA expression of CYP2B6 by 1.8 – 2.4 fold compared to vehicle controls or 14% and 49% of the positive control in two donors, respectively but did not induce CYP2B6 in the third donor. Palovarotene at 0.32µM induced mRNA expression of CYP2C8 by 1.5 fold compared to vehicle controls or 55% of the positive control in one donor but did not induce CYP2C8 in the other two donors. Palovarotene at 0.32µM induced mRNA expression of CYP3A4 by 3.8 – 5.0 fold compared to vehicle controls or 1%, 1%, and 19% of the positive control in three donors.
L2173: *Reviewer's comments: Based on the 2-fold induction and 20% of the positive control threshold, in vitro data suggest palovarotene may potentially induce CYP3A4 and 2B6 at the recommended maximum dose. At 20 mg QD dose, the potential of in vivo CYP2C8 induction is low. Further clinical assessment of CYP3A4 induction is needed. In clinical DDI study (Study PVO-1A-102), following co-administration of midazolam with palovarotene 20 mg QD for 14 days, palovarotene did not alter the PK of midazolam. Therefore, considering the smaller magnitude of in vitro induction of CYP2B6 compared to CYP3A4, a clinical DDI study for CYP2B6 induction assessment is not needed.*
L2174: ## 14.2. In Vivo Studies
L2175: A total of 22 clinical study reports and one clinical study synopsis (Study PVO-1A-203) were submitted in current NDA (Table 94). Study PVO-1A-203 was an open-label extension study in FOP patients and was terminated early. Studies NP17124, NA17098, NB18332, NA17598, and NB19751 were conducted in chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) patients at doses of 0.2 – 5 mg QD. Study PVO-2A-201 was conducted in multiple osteochondromas (MO) patients at doses of 2.5 and 5.0 mg QD. Study NP17584 is a relative BA study conducted with two Roche's old formulations for COPD program. The formulations were not used in FOP patients. Study NP17055 is a clinical DDI study which assess the effect of palovarotene 1 mg QD on the PK of co-administered midazolam. The dose of palovarotene did not cover the recommended maximum dose for FOP indication (20 mg QD). Therefore, the five COPD studies, MO study,
L2176: Study PVO-1A-203, Study NP17584, and Study NP17055 were not reviewed. Only the 14 remaining clinical studies were reviewed in this section.

L2183: ## 14.2.1. Study RB16327: Single Ascending Dose Study
L2184: ## Study Design
L2185: Study RB16327 was a single-center, ascending single-dose, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study conducted in 40 healthy nonsmoking male subjects and eight healthy currently smoking male subjects aged 40 to 65 years. Six doses of palovarotene (oral solution or suspension) were studied. The number of subjects in each dose group is summarized in Table 95. A sequential food-effect study was performed with subjects in Group 5 to assess the influence of fasting on the PK of palovarotene. A washout period of approximately 3 weeks separated doses under fed (10 mg) and fasting conditions (5 mg) for Group 5 subjects. Except for subjects in the Group 5 fasted period, subjects were dosed approximately 10 minutes after consuming a standardized high-fat breakfast. Blood samples were drawn predose and 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168, 192, 216, and 240 hours postdose.

L2195: ## 14.2.2. Study RB16328: Multiple Ascending Dose Study
L2196: ## Study Design

In addition, morning trough samples were collected predose on Days 3, 7, 11, 14, 18, 21, and 24.

L2206: ## 14.2.3. Study NP17056: Mass Balance Study
L2207: ## Study Design
L2208: Study NP17056 was a phase 1, single-center, nonrandomized, open-label, single oral dose study of [^{14}C]-radiolabeled palovarotene absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion in six healthy male subjects aged 45 to 64 years. Enrolled subjects received 1.0 mg of [^{14}C]-radiolabeled palovarotene under fed conditions on Day 1. Blood, urine, and feces samples were collected daily until the limits of radioactivity recovery were met (Day 10 for five subjects and Day 14 for one subject). The formulation used in Study NP17056 was a hard gelatin capsule containing a solution. Measurement of the plasma concentrations of palovarotene and its major metabolites M2, M3, M4a, and M4b was determined using a validated LC-MS/MS method. Liquid scintillation spectrometry was used for plasma and urine samples.
L2209: ## PK Results
L2210: The mean plasma concentration versus time profile of palovarotene was characterized by a moderate absorption rate (T_{max} of approximately 4 hours) followed by a biphasic decline with a mean t_{1/2} of approximately 8 hours. In plasma samples, based on AUC_{0-\infty}, palovarotene accounted for approximately 14% of the mean radioactivity over the complete sample collection period. The four major metabolites, M3, M4b, M2, and M4a accounted for 10%, 7%, 5%, and 4% of the mean total radioactivity, respectively. The pharmacological activity of two active metabolites M3 and M4b was 1.7% and 4.2% of that of palovarotene based on *in vitro* RAR\gamma transactivation assay.
L2211: The whole blood to plasma radioactivity ratio ranged from 0.44 to 0.83 with a mean value of 0.61. The radioactivity in blood cells ranged from 1% to 33% with a mean value of 12%, indicating that most of the radioactivity was in plasma (88%).
L2212: For mass balance, the combined mean (SD) accumulative dose recovered in urine and feces was 97.0% (5.6%) over 168 hours postdose (7 days) and 100% (2.7%) over 312 hours postdose (13 days). Overall, 97.1% of the dose was recovered in the feces and 3.2% in the urine over 13 days postdose. Palovarotene and its four known major metabolites accounted for 67.2% of the dose (M4a and M4b 32.2%, M2 20.2%, M3 12.4%, and palovarotene 2.4%) in feces while six other unidentified metabolites accounted for 28.4% of the dose in feces. Metabolites were unsuccessfully profiled from the urine samples.
L2213: ## 14.2.4. Study NP17726: Effect of Age and Sex
L2214: ## Study Design
L2215: Study NP17726 was an open-label, parallel-group, nonrandomized study to investigate the influence of age and sex on the PK of palovarotene in healthy young adult male and healthy elderly male and female subjects. Twelve healthy subjects in each of the following three groups were recruited: Group 1 (young male group)—males aged 18 to 45 years; Group 2 (elderly male group)—males aged 65 to 74 years; Group 3 (elderly female group)—females aged 65 to 74 years. Enrolled subjects received a single 1.0-mg dose (2 × 0.5-mg soft gelatin capsules) of palovarotene on Day 1, within 30 minutes of completing a standardized breakfast. Blood samples were collected for PK analysis before and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, and 72 hours after study drug administration.
L2216: ## PK Results
L2217: As shown in Table 98, the PK parameters of palovarotene were similar in elderly males and young adult males. However, the geometric mean C_{max} and AUC_{0-t} in elderly females 36% and 20% higher than that in elderly males. Both CL/F and V/F were lower in elderly females compared with elderly males. However, when CL/F was adjusted for body surface area (BSA) and V/F was adjusted for body weight, no obvious differences in these PK parameters between elderly males and elderly females were observed. The differences in palovarotene exposure between elderly males and elderly females can be explained by differences in body size.

L2222: ## 14.2.5. Study PVO-1A-101: Effect of Race
L2223: ## Study Design
L2224: Study PVO-1A-101 was a single-center, double-blind, randomized, crossover, single-dose study comparing the PK profile of palovarotene in 10 healthy Japanese and 8 non-Asian subjects (two African American, five White and one other) aged 18 to 55 years. Of the 18 subjects, there were eight matched pairs of non-Asian and Japanese subjects matched by age, gender, and BMI. In Period 1, subjects were randomly assigned to receive either 5-mg or 10-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules under fed state. In Period 2, they received the alternate dose under fed state. A washout interval of 5 days separated the two doses. Blood samples were obtained predose and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 24, 48, and 72 hours postdose.
L2225: ## PK Results
L2226: The PK parameters of palovarotene are summarized in Table 99. The PK parameters of palovarotene were similar between Japanese and non-Asian groups at both dose levels. C_{max} and AUC values appear dose-proportional between doses in each racial group. Mean total body clearance (CL/F) values ranged from 22.7 to 24.2 L/h across doses and racial group confirming dose proportionality and similar PK between racial groups.

L2231: ## 14.2.6. Study PVO-1A-103: Thorough QT Study
L2232: ## Study Design
L2233: Study PVO-1A-103 was a single-center, randomized, partially double-blind, placebo- and positive-controlled, four-way crossover study to evaluate the effect of a therapeutic and a supratherapeutic dose of palovarotene on the QT interval in 32 healthy adult subjects aged 18 to 55 years. Subjects received the following single-dose treatments in random order under fed state:
L2234: palovarotene 50 mg, palovarotene 20 mg, placebo, and moxifloxacin 400 mg. A minimum washout interval of 5 days separated each dose. Blood samples were obtained 1.25, 1, and 0.75 hours predose and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24 hours postdose. The 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) were extracted from a continuous Holter recording by a central ECG laboratory at the following time points on Day 1 in each period: 1.25, 1 and 0.75 hours predose and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24 hours postdose.
L2235: ## PK Results
L2236: As shown in Table 100, the plasma PK of palovarotene was dose proportional from 20 to 50 mg in the fed state following a single dose.
L2237: In the concentration-QTc analysis, a linear model with an intercept was fitted for the palovarotene plasma concentrations, which represented the data in an acceptable way. The estimated slope of palovarotene plasma concentration in the concentration-QTc relationship was shallow and not statistically significant (-0.000087 ms per ng/mL [90% CI: -0.0058, 0.0056]) with a positive and not statistically significant intercept of 1.0 ms. The predicted QT effects (\Delta\Delta\text{QTcF}) using this model were 0.97 ms (90% CI: -0.80, 2.74) and 0.95 ms (90% CI: -0.98, 2.89) for palovarotene 20 mg (geometric mean C_{\text{max}}=134 ng/mL) and palovarotene 50 mg (geometric mean C_{\text{max}}=314 ng/mL), respectively. Based on this concentration-QTc analysis, an effect on \Delta\Delta\text{QTcF} exceeding 10 ms can be excluded within the range of observed palovarotene plasma concentrations up to ~500 ng/mL. There were no subjects with \text{QTcF} &gt; 450 ms and no subjects with \Delta\text{QTcF} &gt; 30 ms. There were no treatment-emergent T-wave morphology changes or U-waves.

L2243: ## 14.2.7. Study PVO-1A-104: Exposure in Seminal Fluid
L2244: ## Study Design
L2245: Study PVO-1A-104 was a single-center, randomized, open-label, single-period study to assess the relationship between oral doses of palovarotene and the transfer of palovarotene into seminal fluid following multiple oral doses in 24 healthy adult male subjects aged 18 to 55 years. Subjects were randomized to one of three postdose semen sampling times (3, 24, or 72 hours postdose on Day 5). Single doses of 20 mg (two 10-mg capsules) were taken orally, once daily, 30 minutes following a standardized high-fat, high-calorie breakfast for 5 days. Blood samples were obtained predose on Days 1 and 5 and at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours after palovarotene administration on Day 5.
L2246: ## PK Results
L2247: The geometric means of plasma C_{max} and AUC_{0-\tau} were 120 ng/mL and 876 ng\cdoth/mL, respectively, on Day 5 following daily doses of 20-mg palovarotene for 5 days. The mean t_{1/2} of palovarotene was 11 hours. The median T_{max} of palovarotene was approximately 4 hours and ranged from 1 to 8 hours postdose. Palovarotene levels in all seminal fluid samples collected at 24 hour and 72 hours postdose were below the limit of quantitation (5 pg/mL). In the eight subjects randomized to the 3-hour collection time point, the mean amount of palovarotene in ejaculate was 8.84 ng, which accounted for 0.0000442% of the dose. The time-matched ratio of semen to plasma concentration was 0.0273.
L2248: ## 14.2.8. Study PVO-1A-102: Food Effects and CYP3A4 Induction by Palovarotene
L2249: ## Study Design
L2250: Study PVO-1A-102 was conducted in two components. The DDI component was an open-label single sequence component to assess the induction potential of the highest proposed clinical dose of palovarotene (20 mg) on the PK of midazolam as a CYP3A4 substrate. The PK of palovarotene after single and multiple 20-mg doses was also evaluated as part of this DDI component. In addition, the food effect component evaluated the effect of food and the effect of swallowing the intact capsule versus sprinkling the contents on apple sauce on the PK/BA of palovarotene.
L2251: In the DDI component, in the morning of Day 1, 24 subjects received a single oral dose of 2-mg midazolam 30 minutes after the start of a standardized breakfast. On Day 2 through Day 15, subjects received oral QD dose of 20 mg palovarotene capsule in the morning, 30 minutes after the start of a standardized breakfast. A second dose of 2 mg midazolam was administered on Day 15 in the morning (immediately following the palovarotene dose). PK samples for midazolam and its metabolite 1-hydroxymidazolam were obtained at the following time points on Days 1
L2252: and 15: predose and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24 hours after midazolam administration. PK samples for palovarotene were obtained at the following time points on Days 2 and 15: predose and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, and 24 hours after palovarotene administration. An additional blood sample was collected at 48 hours after the palovarotene dose on Day 15.
L2253: The food effect component was an open-label, single-dose, randomized, 3-treatment, 3-period, crossover study design. A total of 24 healthy subjects were randomized 1:1:1 to one of three treatment sequences (n=8/sequence): Sequence A-B-C, Sequence B-C-A, or Sequence C-A-B. All subjects received three single oral doses of 20 mg palovarotene on Days 1, 6, and 11, separated by 5-day washout periods.
L2254: - Treatment A: 20 mg palovarotene whole capsule administered under fasting conditions
- Treatment B: 20 mg palovarotene whole capsule administered under fed conditions
- Treatment C: 20 mg palovarotene sprinkled on apple sauce, administered under fed conditions
L2255: PK samples for palovarotene in the food effect component were obtained at the following time points:
L2256: - Days 1, 6, and 11 at predose (Hour 0), and 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 16 hours postdose
- Days 2, 7, and 12 at 24 hours postdose
- Days 3, 8, and 13 at 48 hours postdose
L2257: ## PK Results
L2258: As shown in Table 101, co-administration of palovarotene 20 mg QD for 14 days reduced the AUC and C_{max} of midazolam by 14% and 10% respectively. The AUC and C_{max} of 1-hydroxymidazolam decreased by 8% and 9%, respectively.

L2278: ## 14.2.9. Study NP17041: CYP3A4 Inhibition by Ketoconazole
L2279: ## Study Design
L2280: Study NP17041 was an open-label study conducted to investigate the effect of ketoconazole on the PK of palovarotene in 18 healthy male subjects aged 18 to 64 years. Palovarotene 1 mg (2 × 0.5 mg soft gelatin capsules) was administered once daily for 21 days, within 30 minutes after completing a standardized breakfast. Palovarotene was co-administered with 400-mg ketoconazole once daily on Day 15 through Day 21. Blood samples for PK analysis were collected on Day 14 (palovarotene alone at steady state) and Day 21 (palovarotene + ketoconazole) predose and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, and 24 hours postdose.
L2281: ## PK Results

L2297: ## 14.2.11. Study NP21025: Drug Interaction with Prednisone
L2298: ## Study Design
L2299: Study NP21025 was an open-label, single sequence study to investigate the effect of prednisone, a weak CYP3A4 inducer, on the PK of palovarotene in 22 healthy male subjects aged 18 to 64 years. Within 30 minutes after completing a standardized breakfast, 5-mg palovarotene (2 \times 2.5-mg soft gelatin capsules) was administered once daily on Days 2 through 9 and a single 40-mg dose of prednisone was administered once daily on Days 1 and 9. On Days 1, 8, and 9, blood samples for the PK assessment of palovarotene and its metabolites and prednisone/prednisolone were taken before and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, and 24 hours after study drug administration. The effect of prednisone on palovarotene PK and the effect of palovarotene on prednisone PK were assessed.
L2300: ## PK Results
L2301: As shown in Table 106, co-administration of a single dose of prednisone 40 mg decreased the AUC and C_{max} of palovarotene by 13%, relative to treatment with palovarotene alone. On the other hand, co-administration of palovarotene 5 mg QD for 8 days did not change the AUC or C_{max} of prednisone.

L2306: Reviewer's comment: Complete induction of CYP3A4 was unlikely to reach with a single dose of prednisone. The results from Study NP21025 cannot be used to justify that co-administration of multiple-dose prednisone does not affect the PK of palovarotene. However, population PK analysis of the PK data of 59 subjects concomitantly taking prednisone did not detect concomitant use of prednisone as a significant covariate on the PK of palovarotene. The review team agrees that no dose adjustment is needed for palovarotene in patients who concomitantly use prednisone. Also, the palovarotene dose (5 mg QD) used in Study NP21025 did not cover flare-up doses (10 mg and 20 mg QD).
L2307: ## 14.2.12. Study PVO-1A-201: Phase 2 Study in FOP Patients
L2308: ## Study Design

Overall, 21 subjects received 10-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules once daily for 14 days followed by 5-mg once daily for 28 days (10/5-mg regimen), nine subjects received 5-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules once daily for 14 days followed by 2.5-mg once daily for 28 days (5/2.5-mg regimen), and 10 subjects received placebo for 24 days. L2327: Reviewer's comments: The elimination half-life of palovarotene observed in FOP patients (4.4 to 4.9 hours) was shorter than that (approximately 8 to 12 hours) observed in healthy adults in multiple phase 1 studies. In Study PVO-1A-201, plasma PK samples were collected from FOP patients at five time points only and the last time point was at 24 hours postdose. In contrast, more intense PK sampling was conducted in studies conducted in healthy subjects and the last sampling time point was at 48 hours or 72 hours post dose. The half-life of palovarotene in FOP patients may not be accurately characterized.
L2328: ## 14.2.13. Study PVO-1A-202: Phase 2 Study in FOP Patients
L2329: ## Study Design
L2330: Study PVO-1A-202 is an open-label extension of Study PVO-1A-201, comprising three parts: Parts A, B, and C. In Part A, all subjects received the 10/5-mg palovarotene regimen at the time of a subsequent eligible flare-up (weight adjusted for skeletally immature pediatric subjects). No PK sampling was performed in Part A. Part B included 18 new adult subjects who did not participate in Study PVO-1A-201 or Study PVO-1A-202/Part A. Adult and skeletally mature pediatric subjects (i.e., those with at least 90% skeletal maturity) received 5-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules daily for up to 24 months (chronic treatment). When a flare-up occurred, subjects received 20-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules daily for 4 weeks followed by 10-mg hard gelatin capsules daily for 8 weeks (20/10-mg regimen). This flare-up regimen was extended if the flare-up had not resolved after 12 weeks. Eight skeletally immature pediatric subjects received only flare-up treatment with weight adjusted-equivalents (Table 111) of the 20/10-mg regimen (i.e., no 5-mg chronic treatment).
L2331: The steady-state PK of palovarotene was assessed 7 days after treatment initiation and at the end of treatment for the first treated flare-up only. In Part C, all subjects received 5-mg palovarotene daily for up to 24 months, with dose escalation for flare-up treatment to 20-mg palovarotene for 4 weeks followed by 10-mg palovarotene for 8 weeks (20/10-mg regimen). This flare-up regimen was extended if the flare-up had not resolved after 12 weeks. Doses were weight-adjusted in skeletally immature subjects. In Parts B and C, blood samples for PK analysis were obtained once during chronic palovarotene treatment and twice during flare-up-based treatment: once during the 20-mg regimen and once during the 10 mg regimen. Blood samples were collected predose and 3, 6, 10, and 24 hours postdose.

L2355: ## 14.2.14. Study PVO-1A-301: Pivotal Phase 3 in FOP Patients
L2356: ## Study Design
L2357: Study PVO-1A-301 is a phase 3, multicenter, open-label study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of palovarotene in adult and pediatric subjects with FOP. Subjects receive chronic dosing with 5-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for up to 24 months with dose escalation to 20-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for 4 weeks followed by 10-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for 8 weeks (20/10-mg regimen) if the subjects experience a flare-up or a high-risk traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up. This flare-up regimen is extended if the flare-up has not resolved after 12 weeks. Doses are weight-adjusted in skeletally immature subjects. Blood samples for PK analysis are obtained once during chronic palovarotene treatment and twice during flare-up-based treatment: once during the 20-mg regimen and once during the 10-mg regimen. Blood samples are collected pre-dose and 3, 6, 10, and 24 hours post-dose.
L2358: ## PK Results
L2359: Mean (\pmSD) plasma concentrations of palovarotene versus time by treatment are presented in Figure 19. The overall shape of the mean plasma concentration versus time profile for palovarotene was similar across the treatment groups of 5 mg, 10 mg and 20 mg QD or weight-adjusted equivalent doses. As shown in Table 115, following chronic (5 mg or weight-adjusted) and flare-up (high dose 20 mg and low dose 10 mg or weight-adjusted) treatments, the mean steady-state palovarotene Cmax and AUC0-24h proportionally increased with dose. Across the dose cohorts, mean T1/2 of palovarotene was approximately between 4 to 5 hours. The mean CL/F values of palovarotene ranged from 16.5 to 17.8 L/h, across all the doses tested.

L2369: ## 14.3. Pharmacometrics Review
L2370: An NDA (NDA 215559, SDN 1) for palovarotene was previously submitted to the FDA on March 31, 2021, including a population PK report (pvo-popPK-001) based on phase 1-3 data and an exposure-response analyses report (pvo-fop-er-001) based on phase 2 data. The Applicant withdrew the original application on August 12, 2021, after discussions between the FDA to allow further adequate verification of data and integration of data updates into the NDA. On April 29, 2022, the Applicant resubmitted the NDA application (NDA 215559, SDN 29) with additional efficacy data from subjects with confirmed anatomy whole-body CT scan. An additional population PK report (pvo-poppk-003) exploring the effect of renal and hepatic status on palovarotene exposure, and an updated exposure-response analyses report (pvo-fop-er-002) based on both phase 2 and phase 3 data were provided in this resubmission. These reports were used to support palovarotene dose selection in general patient population and specific populations (e.g., pediatrics, patients with renal, and hepatic impairment).
L2371: In general, the Applicant's population PK and exposure-response (ER) analyses are considered acceptable in describing the observed palovarotene concentrations in healthy subjects and patients. The Applicant's analyses were verified by the reviewer, with no significant discordance identified.
L2372: More specifically, the developed model was used to support the current submission as outlined (Table 116).
L2373: **Table 116. Pharmacometrics Review and Summary**
L2374: Utility of the Final Model
Recommendation	Statement	Reviewer's Comments
Support the labeling statement for intrinsic factor of body weight	Section 12.3
"Body weight was found to have a significant effect on the pharmacokinetics of palovarotene resulting in increasing exposure with decreasing weight at the same dose."	The statement is acceptable. The covariate analysis demonstrates that the clearance of palovarotene was affected by weight, resulting in increasing exposure with decreasing weight at the same dose. Instead, age was not found to be a significant covariate affecting palovarotene exposure. Therefore, the reviewer determined that 14 years of age is not an appropriate age cut-off for determining weight-based dosing regimen.
Instead, we recommend following the same dosing instructions in phase 3 study that weight based-dosing regimen be used in skeletally immature (<90%) patients under 18 years, while patients ≥18 years of age used flat dose of 5 mg QD, with dose escalation for flare-up at 20 mg/10 mg.

L2378: ## 14.3.1. Population PK Analyses
L2379: ## 14.3.1.1. Applicant's Population PK Analyses
L2380: The population PK (popPK) analyses was based on PK data from 16 studies: nine studies in healthy volunteers (RB16327, NP17584, NP17726, PVO-1A-101, RB16328, NP17055, NP21025, PVO-1A-102 and PVO-1A-103), three studies (NA17598 [Tier 2], NP17124 and NB18332) in patients with symptomatic emphysema secondary to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), three studies (PVO-1A-201, PVO-1A-202 B and C and PVO-1A-301) in patients with FOP and one study (PVO-2A-201) in patients with multiple osteochondromas (MO).
L2381: Palovarotene was administered orally as a single or multiple once daily dosing either as a powder-filled hard gelatin capsule (to be marketed formulation), solution-filled hard gelatin capsule, soft gelatin capsule, or tablet formulation.
L2382: The analyses dataset included 9088 quantifiable concentration records from 701 subjects. Concentrations that were below the limit of quantification (BLQ) were excluded from the analysis (n=673). The majority of BLQ values (n=594) came from the two studies (RB16327 and RB16328) which had higher lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) (0.02 and/or 0.2 ng/mL) compared to all other studies (LLOQ of 0.01 or 0.0005 ng/mL). The impact of including the postdose BLQ concentrations was assessed during interim analyses by implementing the M3 method. However, these BLQ concentrations had no impact on parameter estimates or model predictions. Palovarotene PK samples following the administration of ketoconazole (study RB16328 [group 6]) were not included in the PopPK analyses. The planned timing of PK samples for palovarotene are presented in Table 117.
L2383: The summary statistics for the continuous and categorical covariates are presented in Table 118.

L2399: ## Base PK Model
L2400: The pharmacokinetics of palovarotene was described by a 2-compartment distribution model, with first-order absorption from an absorption compartment, six transit compartments to describe the delay in absorption, and first-order elimination. The PK model was parameterized in terms of apparent clearance (CL/F), apparent central and peripheral volumes of distribution (Vc/F and Vp/F respectively), apparent intercompartmental clearance (Q/F), absorption rate constant (Ka) and mean transit time (MTT), and relative BA (F) between fed and fasted status. Between-subject variability or interindividual variability (IIV) was estimated on all parameters, except the parameter F. A full variance-covariance matrix for random effects was included in the model. Between-occasion variability or interoccasion variability (IOV) was estimated on Ka and MTT. The residual error model consisted of a proportional error model.
L2401: ## Covariates Analysis
L2402: Covariate selection was based on plots of inter-individual variability (ETA) of different PK parameters versus covariates, univariate covariate analysis, and physiological rationale or clinical interest. Age, body weight, gender, race, smoking status, health status, administration with food, formulation, method of administration, administration of prednisone, albumin, ALT, AST, ALP, creatinine, and bilirubin were selected to be evaluated. The full covariate model with backwards deletion approach (at a significance level of 0.001) was utilized for covariate modeling.
L2403: The following covariates were included in the final model:
L2404: - Baseline weight on CL/F, Vc/F, Q/F and Vp/F, using a power model centered at 70 kg.
- Fasted conditions on MTT and F.
- Method of administration on MTT, when the content of the capsule was sprinkled on food.
L2405: ## Final Model
L2406: The parameter estimates from the final popPK model for palovarotene are listed in Table 119. CL/F, Vc/F, Q/F and Vp/F increased with body weight. For the range of weights in the analysis population (13-149 kg), CL/F ranged from 8.59-29.0 L/h (i.e., 57% lower to 46% higher compared to a 70-kg subject), Q/F ranged from 0.688-9.36 L/h (83% lower to 124% higher compared to a 70-kg subject), Vc/F ranged from 7.97-71.4 L (78% lower to 97% higher compared to a 70-kg subject), and Vp/F ranged from 19.7-143 L (75% lower to 85% higher compared to a 70-kg subject).
L2407: Under fasted state, the MTT was 64% shorter indicating that the appearance of palovarotene is expected to be quicker in the fasted state, and the relative BA was 23% lower compared to the fed state. The MTT was also 73% shorter when palovarotene powder-filled hard-gelatin capsule were sprinkled on food compared to capsule swallowed whole, suggesting a quicker appearance of palovarotene in the systemic circulation, but there was no difference on F, and thus in the overall exposure.

L2435: ## 14.3.1.2.1. Adequacy of the Model in Describing the Data

L2437: ## 14.3.1.2.2. Impact of Hepatic and Renal Impairment on Palovarotene PK

Both baseline and time-changing renal status was derived based on the following criteria:

L2479: The Applicant concluded that there is no relationship between palovarotene clearance and CRCL/hepatic status/renal status. No additional modelling to assess the impact of hepatic or renal status on palovarotene PK was undertaken.
L2480: Reviewer's comments: The Applicant proposed that no dose adjustment is recommended in patients with mild or moderate renal impairment. This conclusion is based on the above analysis showing no impact of mild or moderate renal status on ETA (CL/F) or CWRES based on the final PopPK model. A total of 181 subjects with mild renal impairment and 26 subjects with moderate renal impairment were included in this analysis. This sample size is considered sufficient to inform no impact of these covariate on major palovarotene pharmacometrics parameters in the PopPK model, and the model also appears to be unbiased without these covariates. Therefore, the Applicant's analyses regarding impact of renal impairment on palovarotene PK are acceptable.

L2486: ## 14.3.1.2.3. Palovarotene Exposures by Weight-based Dosing Regimen by Age Groups
L2487: ## Applicant's Proposed Dosing Regimen
L2488: The Applicant proposed that for patients \ge 14 years of age, the recommended dosing is 5 mg once daily (chronic treatment), with an increase in dose at the time of a flare-up to 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks for a total of 12 weeks (20/10 mg flare-up treatment), even if symptoms resolve earlier. For patients who are under 14 years of age, the Applicant's weight-adjusted dosage is proposed as shown in Figure 26.
L2489: **Figure 26. Weight-Adjusted Dosage for Children &lt;14 Years**
L2490: Weight	Chronic Dosing	Flare-up (Weeks 1 to 4)	Flare-up (Weeks 5 to 12)
\ge 60 kg1	5 mg	20 mg	10 mg
40 \le 60 kg	4 mg	15 mg	7.5 mg
20 \le 40 kg	3 mg	12.5 mg	6 mg
10 \le 20 kg	2.5 mg	10 mg	5 mg
L2491: 1 All children \ge 14 years of age and adults will receive the dose in the \ge 60 kg weight category.
L2492: (b) (4)
L2493: ## Reviewer's Analyses
L2494: PopPK analyses suggested that body weight has a significant effect on the exposure of palovarotene, whereas age was not included as a significant covariate in the model. Therefore, it is not clear why an age cut-off (i.e., 14 years) is needed for determining the use of weight-based dosing regimen.
L2495: In order to assess the impact of age cut-off for the proposed weight-based dosing regimen, the distribution of palovarotene AUC was simulated at different dose levels and body weight groups for patients both &lt;14 years of age and \ge 14 years of age (Figure 27).
L2496: **Figure 27. Simulated Palovarotene AUC at Steady-state (AUC_{ss}) by Different Body Weight and Age Categories**
L2497: Source: Reviewer's analyses
L2498: Abbreviations: AUC, area under the concentration versus time curve; POV, palovarotene; QD, once daily; ss, steady state
L2499: The results show that the proposed weight-based dosing (&lt;14 years old) provides comparable AUC_{ss} across body weight range from 10 kg to 100 kg. In addition, it is also noticed that subjects \ge14 years of age had higher exposure as compared to subjects &lt;14 years of age in the same body weight categories (i.e., 30 kg – 40 kg, 40 kg – 50 kg, and 50 kg – 60 kg). This suggests that patients \ge14 years old &amp; weight &lt;60 kg may also benefit from weight-based dose adjustment regardless of age.
L2500: In addition, in phase 3 clinical studies, patients greater or equal than 18 years of age received orally administered 5-mg palovarotene once daily and 20 mg/10 mg dose at flare-up, whereas weight-adjusted dose was used for skeletally immature subjects under 18 years of age.
L2501: As a result, we determined that 14 years of age is not appropriate to be used as the cut-off age for determining weight-based dosing regimen. Instead, we recommend following the same dosing regimen as studied in phase 3 trials with age cut-off at 18 years of age.
L2502: ## 14.3.2. Dose/Exposure-Response Analyses
L2503: ## 14.3.2.1. PK/PD Relationships for Efficacy
L2504: The primary endpoint for the palovarotene in this submission is the change from baseline [CFB] in HO volume. The objective of the dose/exposure-response analysis is to investigate the
L2505: relationship between palovarotene dose or exposures and its efficacy. This analysis was used to support the proposed dosing regimen for palovarotene in both pediatric and adult patients, specifically whether weight-based dosing regimen is acceptable for pediatrics and/or adults.
L2506: ## Applicant's Analyses
L2507: ## Data
L2508: Phase 2 trials: PVO-1A-001, PVO-1A-201, and PVO-1A-202
L2509: Phase 3 trial: (PVO-1A-301)
L2510: ## Methods
L2511: At phase 2 trials, several dosing regimens for palovarotene was explored as following:
L2512: - Palovarotene 5 mg once daily for 2 weeks followed by 2.5 mg once daily for 4 weeks (5/2.5 mg flare-up only regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation.
- Palovarotene 10 mg once daily for 2 weeks followed by 5 mg once daily for 4 weeks (10/5 mg flare-up only regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation.
- Palovarotene 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks (20/10 mg) within 7 days of flare-up initiation, with treatment extension in 4 week increments for persistent symptoms.
- Palovarotene 5 mg daily with increased dosing at the time of a flare-up to palovarotene 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks (chronic/flareup regimen) within 7 days of flare-up initiation, with treatment extension in 4-week increments for persistent symptoms.
- Weight-based dosing to achieve daily drug exposures equivalent to adult subjects were selected for skeletally immature children according to three weight categories (20 to &lt;40 kg, 40 to &lt;60 kg, and \ge60 kg).
L2513: For Study PVO-1A-301, subjects received chronic dosing with 5-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for up to 24 months with dose escalation to 20-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for 4 weeks followed by 10-mg palovarotene hard gelatin capsules or weight-adjusted dose for 8 weeks (20/10-mg regimen) if the subjects experience a flare-up or a high-risk traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up. This flare-up regimen is extended if the flare-up has not resolved after 12 weeks.
L2514: HO volume and relative change from baseline in HO volume versus exposure metrics (average daily dose, cumulative dose of palovarotene, average AUC and cumulative AUC of palovarotene) was assessed based on phase 2 (Day 84) and phase 3 clinical data (Month 12). Empirical Bayes estimates (EBEs) of individual pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters for individual subjects were obtained from the final palovarotene PopPK Model 082.

L2530: Reviewer's comments: In general, the Applicant's ER analyses between the change from baseline [CFB] in HO volume versus different palovarotene dose/exposure parameters. No significant ER relationship was observed based on phase 2 data for the change from baseline [CFB] in HO volume at Day 84, while there is a trend of decreasing change from baseline or relative change from baseline in HO volume with increasing assessed exposure metrics (cumulative dose, average daily dose, average daily AUC, and cumulative AUC), suggesting higher dose/exposure level might have better efficacy as measured by annualized change in new HO volume.
L2531: The results for ER analyses are different between phase 2 and phase 3 trials, possibility due to longer duration of new HO volume measurement in phase 3 study (12 months) and phase 2 trials (84 days). However, we should also consider that this ER analyses based on phase 3 trials have some limitations due to the study design as only one dosing regimen or placebo was tested in Study PVO-1A-301: (1) Patients with annualized change in new HO volume data were either treated with one dosing regimen (chronic 5 mg, flare-up 20/10 mg) or not treated with palovarotene; (2) patients with flare-ups were treated with high doses (20/10 mg QD) and patients without flare-ups were treated with the low dose (5 mg QD). In addition, we also noticed that placebo response mainly obtained from Study PVO-1A-001 has a large variability, in which HO volume change from baseline could range from -91300 mm to 391730 mm by Month 12 for the placebo group. This large variability limited the precision we interpreted for the placebo
L2532: *response, and therefore we have less confidence for the detected ER relationship as shown in Figure 28. In general, flare-up doses for controlling new HO formation seems to be appropriate. In summary, the exposure-response analyses in FOP patients support the effectiveness of the proposed chronic 5 mg and flare-up 20/10 mg dosing regimen. The primary support for the efficacy of the palovarotene chronic and flare-up dosing regimen is the clinical data of annualized new HO data generated in Studies PVO-1A-301 and the NHS.*
L2533: ## 14.3.2.2. PK/PD Relationships for Safety
L2534: ## Applicant's Analyses
L2535: No PK/PD (pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic) relationship for safety was performed.
L2536: ## Reviewer's Analyses
L2537: The main adverse effects reported for palovarotene is premature physeal closure (PPC). By June 25, 2020, a total of 24 events of PPC were reported in 96 pediatric subjects aged &lt;17 years at enrollment. To mitigate the risk of PPC, the Applicant proposed to limit target population to females \ge 8 years and males \ge 10 years (“\ge 8/10 population”). In order to further assess the impact of age on PPC, additional analyses were performed.
L2538: Figure 29 shows the number of pediatric subjects (boys or girls) with or without PPC by age at enrollment. PPC occurs in ~30% of patients \ge 8/10 years to 11 years of age, with 4 of 12 (33%) boys aged 10 to 11 years and 5 of 17 (29%) girls aged 8 to 11 years. The prevalence of PPC is higher with increasing palovarotene AUCss (Figure 30). However, this result is likely to be driven by patients &lt;8 years old. When excluding subjects younger than 8 years of age, there is absence of relationship between proportion of PPC and AUC in patients 8/10 to 13 years old (Figure 31).

L2549: ## 14.4. Physiological Based Pharmacokinetic (PBPK) Review
L2550: ## Executive Summary
L2551: The objective of this review is to evaluate the adequacy of the Applicant's physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) analyses to:
L2552: - evaluate the drug-drug interaction (DDI) potentials of palovarotene as a victim of moderate CYP3A inhibitors or inducers, strong CYP2C8 inhibitors, and strong CYP2C19 inhibitors.
- predict the PK of palovarotene in subjects with hepatic or renal impairment
L2553: The Division of Pharmacometrics has reviewed the PBPK analyses report (IPN-3B), the response to FDA's information request (rtq-fda-10june2022) submitted on July 8th (seq 0034), and the modeling supporting files to conclude that:
L2554: - The PBPK analyses are adequate to evaluate the effects of the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin on the PK of palovarotene. Drug interactions of palovarotene with erythromycin was approximately 2.5-fold increase in AUC, which is similar to the observed effect of the strong CYP3A inhibitor ketoconazole.
- Because the metabolic pathways of palovarotene have not been well characterized, the PBPK analyses are inadequateto evaluate the effects of strong CYP2C19 inhibitors, strong CYP2C8 inhibitors and moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz
- to evaluate the effects of organ impairment
L2555: ## Background
L2556: Palovarotene (also known as IPN60120, CLM-001, or RO3300074) is a retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR\gamma) selective agonist currently being developed for prevention of heterotopic ossification in adults and children (aged 8 years and above for females and 10 years and above for males) with FOP. The available dose strengths are 1 mg, 1.5 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg. Recommended dosages are 5 mg once daily for chronic treatment, with an increase in dose at the time of a flare-up to 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks, followed by 10 mg once daily for 8 weeks for a total of 12 weeks (20/10 mg flare-up treatment). The tablets should be taken with food preferably at same time each day.
L2557: Following oral administration of single- and multiple-dose of palovarotene, its C_{max} and AUC increased dose proportionally across the dose range of 0.02- to 50-mg after single doses and 0.4 to 20 mg after once daily dosing (QD) in healthy adult subjects, and no accumulation of palovarotene was observed (NP17726, RB16327, PVO-1A-102, POV-1A-301 and RB16328).
L2558: Steady state was reached by Day 3 (Report 1006914/RB16328). After a standardized FDA high-fat meal, the C_{max} and AUC of palovarotene increased 16% and 40%, and T_{max} delayed by approximately 2h, compared to the fasted state, following a single 20-mg dose.
L2559: Palovarotene has high permeability and low solubility (Quality Report 2.3.S.1.3). It is well-absorbed and is extensively metabolized primarily through CYP3A4 with minor contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 (study 1008690). In the human ADME study, approximately 3.2% and 97% of radioactivity dose were recovered in the urine (negligible amount of unchanged parent) and the feces (2.31% unchanged parent), respectively. Palovarotene is not a substrate of P-gp, BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or OCT1 (CYP1933_01). Palovarotene is determined in vitro to be a competitive inhibitor of CYP2C8, 2C9 and 2C19 with K_i values of 4.7, 8.1, and 7.9 \muM, respectively (1008423). Whether palovarotene is a time-dependent inhibitor of CYP enzymes has not been investigated. Palovarotene is an inducer of CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 in vitro; whether palovarotene is also an inducer of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 is inconclusive based on the in vitro study because the response of the positive controls was less than 2-fold (CYP1933_03). Palovarotene inhibited probe substrate transport mediated by BCRP, OATP1B1, OATP1B3, OCT1 and BSEP, with IC_{50} values of 9.69\muM, 1.83\muM, &gt;3\muM, &gt;3\muM, and 14.7\muM in vitro, respectively (CYP1933_02). Palovarotene is not an inhibitor of probe substrate transport mediated via P-gp, OAT1, OAT3, OCT2, MATE1 and MATE2-K (CYP1933_02). The Applicant conducted clinical DDI studies with ketoconazole, rifampin, and midazolam to evaluate some of the in vitro findings. Refer to the Clinical Pharmacology review section for detailed information on palovarotene regarding ADME properties, in vitro and clinical studies used in the PBPK modeling analysis.
L2560: ## Methods
L2561: Simulations were performed using the PK/PD Profiles mode in the Simcyp® Simulator (Versions 19 and 21, Certara, Sheffield, UK). Schemes of the PBPK modeling and simulation strategy are shown in Figure 32, which summarizes the studies used for palovarotene model development and verification, and model applications in predicting DDI and effects of organ impairment. The final model input parameters were summarized in Table 126. The palovarotene PBPK model consists of a first-order absorption model, a minimal PBPK model with a single adjustable compartment for distribution and an enzyme kinetics model for elimination. The Simcyp library files sim-ketoconazole-400 mg QD, SV-rifampin-MD, SV-Efavirenz, SV-Erythromycin_EC, SV-Fluconazole, and SV-Fluoxetine were used for DDI simulations without any modification unless otherwise noted. Simcyp population models of sim-Cirrhosis CP-A, -B and -C in Version 21 were used to simulate effects of organ impairment on palovarotene exposure. All other simulations were performed using Version 19.

L2583: ## **Can PBPK Analyses Predict the Effects of CYP Inhibitors and Inducers on the PK of Palovarotene?**
L2584: No. The palovarotene PBPK model could not be used to predict the effects of CYP inhibitors and inducers, except for the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin for reasons discussed below.
L2585: ## *Effect of the Moderate CYP3A Inhibitor Erythromycin*
L2586: The relative contributions of CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and CYP2C19 in the hepatic metabolism (f_{m,CYP}) were initially estimated to be (b) (4)
L2587: (Report 1008690). However, when these values were applied to the palovarotene PBPK model, the model overpredicted the effect of the strong CYP3A inhibitor ketoconazole on palovarotene PK. The f_{m,CYP3A} value in the palovarotene PBPK model was optimized to be 0.7 in order to reproduce the observed inhibitory effect of ketoconazole on palovarotene PK (Study NP17041B). In the human ADME study, metabolites formed by CYP3A represent for approximately 65% of the recovered dose, which is similar to the f_{m,CYP3A} value estimated from the ketoconazole DDI study. Therefore, the f_{m,CYP3A} value is considered verified and the predicted effects of erythromycin on palovarotene are considered adequate. Palovarotene AUC and C_{max} were predicted to increase 2.54- and 1.64- fold, respectively, following co-administration of a single 5- or 20-mg dose of palovarotene with 500 mg erythromycin QID (4 times a day).
L2588: ## *Effects of Strong CYP2C8 or CYP2C19 Inhibitors*
L2589: The predicted effects of strong CYP2C8 or CYP2C19 inhibitors are considered inadequate due to the uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 in the metabolism of palovarotene. As mentioned above, the f_{m,CYP3A} value in the palovarotene PBPK model was optimized to be 0.7 based on the ketoconazole DDI study. The Applicant assigned (b) (4) to CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 (b) (4).
L2590: . However, there is no reason to believe that this assignment appropriately reflects the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 in palovarotene elimination since the f_{m,CYP3A} value estimated from the same recombinant CYP enzyme study could not reproduce the effect of ketoconazole. Furthermore, approximately 30% of the administered dose recovered in the human ADME study were metabolites whose chemical structure had not been identified; thus, there is uncertainty about the enzymes involved in their catalysis. Therefore, due to the uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19, the predicted effects of gemfibrozil (strong CYP2C8 inhibitor), fluoxetine (strong CYP2C19 inhibitor) and fluconazole (moderate CYP3A inhibitor and strong CYP2C19 inhibitor) are considered inadequate.
L2591: ## *Effect of the Moderate CYP3A Inducer Efavirenz*
L2592: The predicted effect of efavirenz on palovarotene PK is considered inadequate for the following reasons: 1) Although the palovarotene PBPK model could recover the effect of ketoconazole, the model underpredicted the effect of rifampin on AUC and C_{max} of palovarotene (b) (4) when the default model of rifampin was used. The reason for the underprediction is unclear; thus, the ability of the palovarotene model to predict the effect of other inducers is in question. 2) A clinical DDI study showed that efavirenz reduced the AUC of CYP2C19 sensitive substrate omeprazole by 46%. Currently, there are no validated induction parameters of
L2593: CYP2C19 in the efavirenz PBPK model. 3) As mentioned above, there is uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C19 in the disposition of palovarotene.
L2594: ## Can PBPK Analyses Predict the effects of Organ Impairment on the PK of Palovarotene?
L2595: No. Besides uncertainty about the contribution of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19 in the disposition of palovarotene, approximately 30% of the administered dose recovered in the human ADME study were metabolites whose chemical structure and enzyme involved in their formation had not been identified. Due to the uncertainty about elimination pathways of palovarotene, it is inadequate to predict the effects of hepatic or renal impairment using the PBPK approach. Furthermore, the verification of the population models submitted by the Applicant is insufficient to support the use of the organ impairment models to predict the effects of renal impairment on palovarotene and inform dose recommendation.
L2596: ## Conclusions
L2597: - The PBPK analyses are adequate to evaluate the effects of the moderate CYP3A inhibitor erythromycin on the PK of palovarotene. Drug interactions of palovarotene with erythromycin was approximately 2.5-fold increase in AUC, which is similar to the observed effect of ketoconazole.
- Because the metabolic pathways of palovarotene have not been well characterized, the PBPK analyses are inadequateto evaluate the effects of strong CYP2C19 inhibitors, strong CYP2C8 inhibitors and moderate CYP3A inducer efavirenz
- to evaluate the effects of organ impairment

L2624: ## 15. Trial Design: Additional Information and Assessment
L2625: ## 15.1. Study PVO-1A-301: Protocol Synopsis
L2626: Following is the latest version, Amendment 5, dated October 30, 2020, for this pivotal phase 3 study of palovarotene in patients with FOP.
L2627: ## Title
L2628: MOVE Trial: A Phase 3, Efficacy and Safety Study of Oral Palovarotene for the Treatment of Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva (FOP)
L2629: ## Sponsor
L2630: Clementia Pharmaceuticals Inc.
L2631: ## Objectives
L2632: ## Primary Objectives
L2633: - To evaluate the efficacy of palovarotene in decreasing HO in adult and pediatric subjects with FOP as assessed by low-dose, whole-body computed tomography (WBCT), excluding head, as compared to untreated subjects from Clementia's FOP natural history study over 24 months.
- To evaluate the safety of palovarotene in adult and pediatric subjects with FOP.
L2634: ## Secondary Objectives
L2635: - To evaluate the effect of palovarotene on flare-up rate and proportion of subjects reporting at least one flare-up.
- To evaluate the effect of palovarotene on range of motion (ROM) as assessed by the Cumulative Analogue Joint Involvement Scale (CAJIS) for FOP.
- To evaluate the effect of palovarotene on physical function using age-appropriate forms of the FOP-Physical Function Questionnaire (FOP-PFQ).
- To evaluate the effect of palovarotene on physical and mental health using age-appropriate forms of the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health Scale.
- To evaluate the pharmacokinetics of palovarotene. Secondary Objective (Part B)
- To continue to provide palovarotene to adult and pediatric subjects with FOP and to monitor longer-term safety.
L2636: ## **Secondary Objective (Part C)**
L2637: - To implement safety measures based on data monitoring committee (DMC) recommendations in order to ensure that assessments of safety continue for up to 2 years post last dose of study treatment for skeletally immature subjects.
L2638: ## **Study Design**
L2639: A phase 3, multicenter, open-label study in adult and pediatric subjects with FOP will be conducted in three parts: Part A, the main part of the study; Part B, the 24-month extension; and Part C, the up-to-2-year post last dose of study treatment follow-up for skeletally immature subjects. Sources of subjects eligible for enrollment in Part A of the MOVE Trial will include: (1) subjects from Study PVO-1A-001 (the natural history study [NHS]); (2) additional subjects clinically diagnosed with FOP with the R206H ACVR1 mutation or other FOP variants reported to be associated with progressive HO (who have not previously participated in any Clementia-sponsored study); and (3) phase 2 Study PVO-1A-202 or Study PVO-1A-204 subjects who cannot receive the chronic/flare-up regimen due to country of residence or those traveling long distances to participate in the phase 2 trial. Up to a maximum of 110 subjects will be enrolled into the MOVE Trial (up to 99 with the R206H mutation and no previous exposure to palovarotene, and up to 11 with other mutations or previous participation in the phase 2 trials), and receive chronic dosing for up to 24 months and undergo flare-up-based treatment should they experience an eligible flare-up or traumatic event as confirmed by the Investigator.
L2640: As of December 4, 2019, all subjects &lt;14 years of age were required to interrupt study drug due to a partial clinical hold placed on the palovarotene clinical development program by the US FDA. Treatment will subsequently not be restarted in children &lt;14 years of age.
L2641: The efficacy of palovarotene treatment in the MOVE Trial Part A, as measured by the change in new HO volume, will be compared to that observed in untreated subjects who participated in the NHS.
L2642: In Part B, the study will be extended for an additional 24 months in order to provide the chronic/flare-up palovarotene dosing regimen to all subjects until commercial availability and to obtain longer-term safety data. No new subjects will be enrolled into Part B.
L2643: ## **Chronic Treatment: Part A**
L2644: Subjects will receive orally administered 5 mg palovarotene once daily (weight-adjusted for skeletally immature subjects [i.e., subjects under the age of 18 years with less than 90% skeletal maturity on hand-wrist radiography at screening]) as chronic dosing for up to 48 months. Note: all weight-based dosing, both chronic and flare-up, will cease when subjects achieve ≥90% skeletal maturity based on hand-wrist radiography, but radiographic assessment of the growth plate (performed at Study Months 6, 12, 18, and 24) will continue until these subjects achieve 100% closure of the growth plate at both locations.
L2645: Additional radiographic assessments will be performed at Study Months 3, 9, 15, or 21 in those subjects who (1) received the flare-up dosing regimen in the period of time since their last radiographic assessment; and (2) had not achieved 100% skeletally maturity on their last radiographic assessment. All subjects will undergo the procedures and assessments specified in
L2646: the Schedule of Assessments Table 1 (see Table 132), including low-dose, WBCT (excluding head) at Screening and at site visits at Months 6, 12, 18, and 24.
L2647: In order to ensure consistent interpretation of the acquired images, a central imaging laboratory will perform blinded reads of all images obtained in this study as well as those obtained from the natural history study (control group) using standardized procedures as documented in the Image Acquisition Guidelines and Independent Review Charter. Remote visits (e.g., at home, at a local medical facility, or via video-conference or telephone contact from clinical site personnel) will occur at Week 6 and at Study Months 3, 9, 15, and 21 unless the Investigator deems that a site visit is necessary; urine pregnancy tests will be performed each month for females of childbearing potential (FOCBP).
L2648: ## **Chronic Treatment: Part B**
L2649: The assessments conducted in Part A will continue into Part B except that WBCT imaging will be performed annually thereafter at Months 36 and 48.
L2650: ## **Flare-up-Based Treatment: Parts A and B**
L2651: Subjects will report potential flare-up symptoms to site personnel; such symptoms include, but are not limited to pain, swelling, redness, decreased range of motion, stiffness, and warmth. Only one symptom is required to define a flare-up. If these symptoms are consistent with previous flare-ups, include a subject-reported onset date, and are confirmed by the Investigator as associated with a flare-up, subjects will immediately begin flare-up-based treatment. Flare-up-based dosing should also be initiated if the Investigator confirms the presence of a substantial high-risk traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up.
L2652: Palovarotene 20 mg for 4 weeks (28 days) once daily. The first dose will be taken upon flare-up or traumatic event confirmation by the Investigator (Flare-up Day 1).
L2653: To be followed by palovarotene 10 mg for 8 weeks (56 days) once daily. For a total flare-up treatment duration of 12 weeks (84 days).
L2654: If the investigator deems it necessary, the subject can be evaluated at the clinical site to confirm the presence of a flare-up. Based on clinical signs and symptoms as determined by the Investigator, treatment may be extended in 4-week intervals while on-treatment with 10 mg palovarotene and continue until the flare-up resolves and the 4-week extension treatment has been completed.
L2655: Subjects will be provided with the appropriate dose of study drug to be used to initiate treatment with palovarotene when a flare-up or traumatic event is confirmed by the investigator.
L2656: Flare-up dosing will be weight-adjusted in subjects under the age of 18 years with less than 90% skeletal maturity on hand-wrist radiography at Screening.
L2657: Should a subject experience an intercurrent flare-up (defined as a new flare-up location or marked worsening of original flare-up), or substantial traumatic event likely to lead to a flare-up, at any time during flare-up-based treatment, the 12-week dosing regimen will restart upon new intercurrent flare-up or traumatic event confirmation by the Investigator (i.e., 4 weeks of 20 mg palovarotene followed by 8 weeks of 10 mg palovarotene [or weight-based equivalents]). A Flare-up Cycle will include the first flare-up or traumatic event and any subsequent intercurrent flare-ups or traumatic events during the same dosing period. Flare-up Cycle Safety Day 1 is
L2658: NDA 215559
Sohonos, palovarotene capsules
L2659: defined as the first day that study drug is administered for the first flare-up or traumatic event during that cycle. Safety assessments will be performed at Flare-up Cycle Safety Day 1 and then every 12 weeks thereafter until treatment of the last flare-up or traumatic event in the cycle is completed. If any flare-up in a cycle has not resolved after 12 weeks, treatment and safety assessments will be extended, and 10 mg palovarotene (or the weight-based equivalent) will be administered in 4-week intervals until all flare-ups resolve and flare-up-based treatment has been completed. It is possible that subjects may experience more than one Flare-up Cycle during the study.
L2660: Subjects receiving flare-up-based treatment will undergo the procedures and assessments specified in the Schedule of Assessments Table 2 (see Table 133). All assessments will occur remotely unless the Investigator deems it necessary to evaluate subjects at the clinical site.
L2661: Once all flare-ups in a cycle have resolved and flare-up-based treatment has been completed, subjects will resume chronic treatment with 5 mg palovarotene once daily (weight-adjusted doses for skeletally immature subjects).
L2662: Subjects currently receiving flare-up-based treatment in Study PVO-1A-202 or Study PVO-1A-204 will not enroll into Study PVO-1A-301 until flare-up treatment is complete and at least 4 weeks have elapsed since the last flare-up symptom.
L2663: ## Off-treatment Part C
L2664: No study drug will be administered in Part C. For skeletally immature subjects in Part C, added Year 1 (Y1) and Year 2 (Y2) post last dose of study treatment assessments that include linear height, knee height, weight, physical exam, vital signs, radiographic assessments of the knee and hand-wrist, low-dose WBCT imaging, adverse events, and concomitant medications.
L2665: Once subjects reach skeletal maturity their participation in Part C will end. The total duration of participation, on and off treatment, is a maximum of 4 years (\pm 1 month).
L2666: ## Number of Subjects
L2667: Up to a maximum of 110 subjects will be enrolled; up to 99 of the enrolled subjects will have the R206H mutation and will not have been previously treated with palovarotene.
L2668: ## Total Number of Sites
L2669: Approximately 20 international investigational sites.
L2670: ## Study Population
L2671: ## Inclusion Criteria
L2672: Subjects must meet all of the following criteria to be eligible for enrollment:
L2673: - Written, signed, and dated informed subject/parent consent; and for subjects who are minors, age-appropriate assent (performed according to local regulations).
- Male or female at least 4 years of age.
- Previous participation in the NHS; or clinically diagnosed with FOP, with the R206H ACVR1 mutation or other FOP variants reported to be associated with progressive HO (who have not previously participated in any Clementia-sponsored study); or participants
L2674: in Study PVO-1A-202 or Study PVO-1A-204 who cannot currently receive the chronic/flare-up regimen due to country of residence or those traveling long distances to participate in the phase 2 trial.
L2675: - No flare-up symptoms within the past 4 weeks, including at the time of enrollment.
- Females of child-bearing potential must have a negative blood or urine pregnancy test (with sensitivity of at least 50 mIU/mL) prior to administration of palovarotene. Male and FOCBP subjects must agree to remain abstinent from heterosexual sex during treatment and for 1 month after treatment or, if sexually active, to use two effective methods of birth control during and for 1 month after treatment. Additionally, sexually active FOCBP subjects must already be using two effective methods of birth control 1 month before treatment is to start. Specific risk of the use of retinoids during pregnancy, and the agreement to remain abstinent or use two effective methods of birth control will be clearly defined in the informed consent and the subject or legally authorized representatives (e.g., parents, caregivers, or legal guardians) must specifically sign this section.
- Must be accessible for treatment and follow-up, and be able to undergo all study procedures. Subjects living at distant locations from the investigational site must be able and willing to travel to a site for the initial and all on-site follow-up visits. Subjects must be able to undergo low-dose, WBCT (excluding head) without sedation.
L2676: ## Exclusion Criteria
L2677: Subjects meeting any of the following criteria are not eligible for enrollment:
L2678: - Weight &lt;10 kg.
- If currently using vitamin A or beta carotene, multivitamins containing vitamin A or beta carotene, or herbal preparations, fish oil, and unable or unwilling to discontinue use of these products during palovarotene treatment
- Exposure to synthetic oral retinoids other than palovarotene within 4 weeks prior to screening
- Concurrent treatment with tetracycline or any tetracycline derivatives due to the potential increased risk of pseudotumor cerebri
- History of allergy or hypersensitivity to retinoids, gelatin, or lactose (note that lactose intolerance is not exclusionary)
- Concomitant medications that are strong inhibitors or inducers of cytochrome P450 (CYP450) 3A4 activity; or kinase inhibitors such as imatinib (see Section 5.2.1).
- Amylase or lipase &gt;2x above the upper limit of normal (ULN) or with a history of chronic pancreatitis.
- Elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) or alanine aminotransferase (ALT) &gt;2.5x ULN.
- Fasting triglycerides &gt;400 mg/dL with or without therapy.
- Female subjects who are breastfeeding.
- Subjects with uncontrolled cardiovascular, hepatic, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocrine, metabolic, ophthalmologic, immunologic, psychiatric, or other significant disease.
- Subjects experiencing suicidal ideation (type 4 or 5) or any suicidal behavior within the past month as defined by the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS).
L2679: - Simultaneous participation in another interventional clinical research study (other than palovarotene studies) within 4 weeks prior to Screening; or within five half-lives of the investigational agent, whichever is longer.
- Any reason that, in the opinion of the Investigator, would lead to the inability of the subject and/or family to comply with the protocol.
L2680: ## Investigational Product
L2681: Palovarotene supplied as powder-filled hard gelatin capsules. The capsules may be swallowed whole or opened and the contents added onto specific foods as specified in the dosing instructions.
L2682: ## Dose/Route/Regimen for Chronic Dosing
L2683: Palovarotene: 5 mg daily or weight-based equivalents for those subjects who are skeletally immature (&lt;90%) at entry into the study / taken orally with food / at approximately the same time each day. For 5 mg palovarotene, weight equivalent doses for &lt;20 kg, 20 to &lt;40 kg, 40 to &lt;60 kg, and ≥60 kg will be 2.5 mg, 3 mg, 4 mg, and 5 mg, respectively.
L2684: ## Dose/Route/Regimen for Flare-up Dosing
L2685: Palovarotene initiated at the start of an eligible flare-up: 20 mg for 4 weeks (28 days), 10 mg for 8 weeks (56 days) for a total of 12 weeks (84 days) (may be extended in 4-week intervals if flare-up is ongoing and continue until flare-up resolves) / weight-adjusted for skeletally immature subjects (&lt;90%) / taken orally with food / at approximately the same time each day.
